en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Path of Purification (First Part).
The Discourse on the Causes and so forth:
A wise person, established in virtue, developing the mind and wisdom—
a bhikkhu ardent and discerning— he shall disentangle this tangle.

Thus this was said. But why was it said? It is said that while the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, a certain son of the gods approached him during the night and, for the sake of dispelling his own doubt, asked:
"The inner tangle, the outer tangle—the people are entangled by a tangle.
Gotama, I ask you this: who can unravel this tangle?"
He asked this question. Its meaning in brief is as follows: *Jaṭā* is a designation for the net of craving (*taṇhā*).

For it is called *jaṭā* because, by way of weaving together, it is like the entanglement of branches in a bamboo thicket or similar growth, arising again and again in relation to objects such as forms, alternating between lower and higher levels. Furthermore, regarding one’s own requisites and the requisites of others...
Because it arises within one's own personal existence and that of others, as well as within internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*), it is called "the inner tangle" and "the outer tangle.
By means of this tangle arising in such a way, all beings (*pajā*) are entangled.

Just as bamboos and other plants are entangled by bamboo thickets and the like, so too is this entire class of beings known as the "multitude of creatures" entangled and ensnared by this tangle of craving (*taṇhājaṭā*).
The meaning is "interwoven. And because it is thus entangled, he says, "I ask you that, O Gotama," and therefore he asks him.

He addresses the Blessed One by his clan name as "Gotama. "Who would disentangle this tangle?"—he asks who could disentangle this tangle that stands thus entangling the three realms, and who is capable of disentangling it.
Thus questioned, the Blessed One— the god of gods, the supreme Sakka among Sakkas, the supreme Brahmā among Brahmās, whose range of knowledge is unimpeded regarding all phenomena;
who is confident in the four grounds of self-confidence, who possesses the ten powers, whose knowledge is unobstructed,
and who is the universal eye— expounded that matter as follows:
"Established in virtue, a wise man, developing his mind and wisdom—
a bhikkhu who is ardent and discerning— he shall disentangle this tangle.
Thus he spoke this verse.
Now, as this verse was spoken by the Great Seer,
I shall explain its meaning— divided into virtue and the other factors— exactly as it is.
Having obtained the going forth in the Conqueror’s dispensation, which is so very difficult to find;
Those here who desire purity, yet do not know as it truly is the secure and straight path of purification comprised of virtue and the rest—
even those striving practitioners do not attain purity.
I shall speak the Path of Purification, which brings joy to those who dwell in the Great Monastery,
which is based on the method of teaching of the Mahāvihāra residents,
and which contains perfectly purified analysis. Listen attentively as I speak it.
"All you who desire purity, listen well, O virtuous ones. 3.
In this context, "purity" (visuddhi) should be understood as Nibbāna, which is devoid of all defilements and is absolutely pure.
The "Path of Purity" (Visuddhimagga) is the path to that purity. "Path" (magga) refers to the means for attainment. The meaning is: "I shall speak that Path of Purity."
Furthermore, this Path of Purification is taught in some places by means of insight alone, as it is said:
"When one perceives with wisdom that 'all conditioned phenomena are impermanent,' then one becomes disenchanted with suffering; this is the path to purification."
In some instances, it is by way of jhāna and wisdom; as it is said:
"He in whom there is both jhāna and wisdom is indeed close to Nibbāna.
In some instances, it is by way of kamma and so forth; as it is said:
“Action, knowledge, and the Dhamma, virtue as the supreme way of life—by these mortals are purified, not by lineage or wealth.
In some instances, it is by way of virtue and so forth. As it has been said:
“Always endowed with virtue, wise and well-concentrated, Ardent and resolute,
he crosses the flood so difficult to cross. In some instances,
this is by way of the foundations of mindfulness and so forth, as it has been said:
“Bhikkhus, this is the one-way path for the purification of beings... for the realization of Nibbāna; that is to say, the four foundations of mindfulness.
This same method applies to the right efforts and so forth as well. However, in this exposition of the question, it is taught by way of virtue and the other factors.
Herein, this is the brief commentary: “Established in virtue” means standing in virtue, fulfilling virtue itself.
And herein, one is said to be "established in virtue. Therefore, the meaning here is: "having become firmly established in virtue by means of fulfilling virtue.
"A person" (*nara*) refers to a sentient being (*satta*). "Possessing wisdom" (*sapañño*) means being wise through the wisdom of rebirth-linking that is born of kamma and the root-conditions.
"They develop the mind and wisdom" means they develop both concentration and insight; for here, concentration is indicated by the heading "mind" (*citta*).
And "insight" is by way of the name "wisdom. "Ardent" means possessing energy; for energy is called "ardor" (*ātāpa*) in the sense of burning away and tormenting the defilements.
One who has that is "ardent. "Circumspect" (*nipaka*): "circumspection" (*nepakka*) is said to be wisdom;
the meaning is that he is endowed with it. By this term, he shows the wisdom of retention. For in this answering of the question, [the word "circumspect"] occurs three times.
Wisdom has arrived. Therein, the first is the wisdom of birth, the second is the wisdom of insight (vipassanā), and the third is the sustaining wisdom that guides all duties.
One is called a *bhikkhu* because he beholds the terror in *saṃsāra*.
"He should disentangle this tangle"—by means of this virtue, this concentration indicated by the heading of "mind," and this threefold wisdom, he [should disentangle it].
And by "ardor" is meant a bhikkhu endowed with six qualities. Just as if a man, standing on the ground,
were to lift a well-sharpened sword and disentangle a great thicket of bamboo, even so, standing on the ground of virtue,
with the hand of supporting wisdom grasped by the strength of energy, he wields the well-sharpened sword of insight-wisdom upon the rock of concentration.
Having uprooted it, one should disentangle, sever, and shatter that entire tangle of craving which has fallen into one’s own continuum.

At the moment of the Path, one is said to be disentangling that tangle; at the moment of the Fruit, having disentangled the tangle, one becomes the foremost recipient of offerings in the world including the devas. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Firmly established in virtue, a wise man developing his mind and wisdom—the ardent and discerning bhikkhu shall unravel this tangle.
Regarding that wisdom by which he is called “wise,” there is nothing further for him to do in that regard; it comes about solely through the power of his previous kamma.
That [path] of his is accomplished. By means of the energy described here as "ardent" (*ātāpī*) and "careful" (*nipaka*), he acts with persistence and acts with clear comprehension (*sampajañña*).
Having established himself in virtue (*sīla*), he should develop serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*)—which are described here by way of mind and wisdom (*paññā*).
In this context, the Blessed One shows the Path of Purification (*visuddhimagga*) by way of virtue, concentration, and wisdom.
To this extent, the three trainings, the teaching that is good in three ways, the necessary support for the state of possessing the threefold knowledge and so forth,

the avoidance of the two extremes and the practice of the middle way, the means for transcending the states of misery and so forth, the abandoning of the defilements in three ways, the antidote to transgressions and the like, the purification from the three types of corruption,
and the cause for the status of a stream-enterer and so forth, have been elucidated.

How so? For herein, by means of virtue (sīla), the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) is revealed; by means of concentration (samādhi), the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā); and by means of wisdom (paññā), the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā).
Furthermore, by means of virtue, the excellence at the beginning of the Dispensation (sāsana) is revealed. This is because of the statement, "And what is the beginning of wholesome states?
Virtue that is perfectly purified," and because of the statement beginning with, "The non-doing of all evil. Thus, virtue is [the beginning] of the Dispensation.
The beginning is good because it brings about qualities such as freedom from remorse. Through concentration (*samādhi*), the goodness of the middle is revealed;

for, according to the statement beginning with "the undertaking of what is wholesome," concentration is the middle of the Teaching, and it is good because it brings about qualities such as the various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*).
Through wisdom (*paññā*), the goodness of the end of the Teaching is revealed by the words: "The purification of one's own mind."
For according to the statement, "This is the teaching of the Buddhas," and because wisdom is supreme, wisdom is the culmination of the teaching;
and that [wisdom] is beautiful, as it brings about a state of equanimity toward the desirable and the undesirable.
"Just as a solid mass of rock is not shaken by the wind..."
"Thus, in the face of blame and praise, the wise do not waver.
So it was said.

Likewise, by means of virtue, the necessary condition for the state of possessing the threefold knowledge (*tevijjatā*) is revealed. For, depending upon the perfection of virtue, the three [knowledges]...
One attains true knowledge (*vijjā*), but not beyond that. By means of concentration (*samādhi*), the necessary support for the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*) is demonstrated.
For, depending on the perfection of concentration, one attains the six direct knowledges, and not beyond that.

By means of wisdom (*paññā*), the necessary support for the various analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*) is demonstrated. For, depending on the excellence of wisdom, one attains the four analytical insights, and not by any other cause.

By means of virtue, the avoidance of the extreme characterized as devotion to sensual pleasure is revealed; by means of concentration, the avoidance of the extreme characterized as devotion to self-mortification is revealed;

and by means of wisdom, the cultivation of the middle way is revealed. Likewise, by means of virtue, the method for transcending the states of deprivation is revealed; by means of concentration, the method for transcending the sense-sphere realm is revealed; and by means of wisdom, the method for transcending all states of existence is revealed.

By virtue of morality (*sīla*), the abandoning of defilements (*kilesa*) is shown by way of abandoning through its constituent parts; by concentration (*samādhi*), by way of abandoning through suppression; and by wisdom (*paññā*), by way of abandoning through complete eradication.

Likewise, by virtue of morality, the antidote to the transgression of defilements is shown; by concentration, the antidote to their active manifestation (*pariyuṭṭhāna*); and by wisdom, the antidote to their underlying tendencies (*anusaya*).

Furthermore, by virtue of morality, the purification from the corruption of misconduct is shown; by concentration, the purification from the corruption of craving (*taṇhā*); and by wisdom, the purification from the corruption of views (*diṭṭhi*).

Thus, by means of virtue (sīla), the cause for the state of a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) and a once-returner (sakadāgāmī) is revealed; by concentration (samādhi), the cause for the state of a non-returner (anāgāmī);
and by wisdom (paññā), the cause for arhatship (arahatta). For it is said that the stream-enterer is "one who fulfills his duties in regard to virtue," as is the once-returner.
The non-returner, however, is "one who fulfills his duties in regard to concentration. The arhat, moreover, is "one who fulfills his duties in regard to wisdom."
Thus, up to this point, nine things have been explained: the three trainings; the Dispensation that is good in three ways; the proximate cause for the state of the threefold knowledge and so forth;

the avoidance of the two extremes and the practice of the middle way; the means for transcending the states of deprivation and so forth; the abandonment of defilements in three ways; the antidote to transgressions and the like;
the purification from the three types of corruption; and the cause for the status of a stream-enterer and so forth. Other such triads of qualities have also been elucidated.
1. The Description of Virtue:
A Discussion on the Nature of Virtue, etc. 6.
Furthermore, although this Path of Purification has been taught by way of virtue, concentration, and wisdom—which comprise manifold qualities—...
It is taught in extreme brief; therefore, it is not sufficient for the benefit of all.
To show its detailed exposition, there is this line of inquiry concerning virtue (*sīla*):

What is virtue? In what sense is it virtue? What are its characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause? What is the benefit of virtue? How many kinds of virtue are there? What is its defilement, and what is its purification?

Herein, this is the answer: What is virtue? It consists of the states beginning with volition in one who abstains from killing living beings and so forth, or in one who fulfills the performance of duties. For this is said in the *Paṭisambhidā*:
"What is virtue? Volition is virtue; mental concomitants are virtue; restraint is virtue; non-transgression is virtue. Therein, what is called "volition as virtue" is...
The volition (*cetanā*) of one who abstains from killing living beings and so forth, or of one who fulfills the performance of duties; this is called mental virtue (*cetasika-sīla*).

Abstinence (*virati*) from killing living beings and so forth for one who refrains from them is also called mental virtue. Furthermore, the volitional virtue (*cetanā-sīla*) consists of the seven courses of action (*kamma-patha*) of one who abandons killing living beings and so forth.
Mental virtue consists of [the thought]: "Having abandoned covetousness, with a mind free from covetousness..."
The phenomena of non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view are stated by way of such methods as “he dwells,” and so forth.
Regarding the phrase “restraint is virtue” (*saṃvaro sīlaṃ*), restraint here should be understood as fivefold:

restraint of the Pātimokkha, restraint of mindfulness, restraint of knowledge, restraint of patience, and restraint of energy. In this context, he is “endowed with” and “fully endowed with” this restraint of the Pātimokkha.
This is restraint by the Pātimokkha. One guards the faculty of the eye and attains restraint over the faculty of the eye—this is restraint by mindfulness.
"Whatever streams there are in the world, O Ajita," said the Blessed One, "mindfulness is their dam."
“I call it the restraint of the streams; by means of wisdom they are closed off.
This is the restraint of knowledge (*ñāṇasaṃvara*). The practice of using requisites (*paccayapaṭisevana*) is also included right here.

Furthermore, that which is described in the manner beginning with “he is patient with cold and heat,” etc., is called the restraint of patience (*khantisaṃvara*). And as for this [restraint] that has arisen...
"Does not tolerate thoughts of sensual desire," and so forth—this is what is called "restraint through energy" (*vīriyasaṃvara*).

Purity of livelihood (*ājīvapārisuddhi*) is also included right here. Thus, this fivefold restraint, as well as the abstinence from the bases of success for clansmen who fear evil—all of this should be understood as "restraint virtue" (*saṃvarasīla*). Non-transgression (*avītikkama*).
"Virtue" (*sīla*) is the non-transgression of bodily and verbal conduct by one who has undertaken virtue. This, first of all, is the answer to the question "What is virtue?
(7). Regarding the remaining [questions], in what sense is it virtue? It is virtue in the sense of "steadying" (*sīlana*). What is this so-called steadying?
It means either composure, in the sense of the non-distraction of bodily action and so forth through the state of good conduct; or it means upholding, of wholesome states.
The meaning is that its state as a support consists in being the foundation for phenomena (*dhammā*). It is precisely these two meanings here that those learned in the characteristics of words admit.
Others, however, explain the meaning here by such methods as "the sense of the head is the sense of virtue (*sīla*)," or "the sense of coolness is the sense of virtue," and so forth. 8.
Now, regarding the question, "What are its characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause?"—here:

The characteristic of that [mindfulness] is its visibility, even when it is divided in many ways, just as visibility is the characteristic of the sense-base of form (rūpāyatana) even when it is divided in many ways.

For just as visibility is the characteristic of the sense-base of form, even though it is divided in many ways through distinctions such as blue, yellow, and so forth, [so too is the characteristic of mindfulness].

Even though it is divided by distinctions such as blue and so forth, it does not transcend the state of being visible. Likewise, even though virtue (sīla) is divided in many ways by distinctions such as volition (cetanā) and so forth, that which is called "virtuous conduct" (sīlana)—described in terms of the stabilization of bodily actions and the like, and the foundation for wholesome states (kusala-dhamma)—is its very characteristic;
for even though it is divided by distinctions such as volition, it does not transcend the state of being a stabilization and a foundation.
Regarding its characteristic, however, it is said:
The destruction of immorality, as well as the quality of blamelessness,
In the sense of the fulfillment of the task, is called its "flavor."

Therefore, this so-called virtue (sīla) should be understood as having the function of destroying immorality by way of its essential property (rasa), and as having the nature of blamelessness by way of its perfection. For among the characteristics and so forth, it is precisely the function or the perfection that is called the "essential property.
Its manifestation is purity; and this, when analyzed by the wise, is described as having moral shame (hirī) and moral dread (ottappa) as its proximate cause.
That virtue has as its manifestation the aforementioned forms of purity—purity of body, purity of speech, and purity of mind;
it manifests as purity and thus becomes an object of apprehension.

Furthermore, moral shame (*hiri*) and moral dread (*ottappa*) are described as its proximate cause (*padatthāna*), meaning they are the immediate conditions. For when moral shame and moral dread are present, virtue arises.
And it persists. When absent, it neither arises nor persists. Thus should the characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause of virtue be understood.

9. Discussion on the Benefits of Virtue: What is the benefit of virtue? Its benefit is the acquisition of numerous qualities such as freedom from remorse. For this has been said: “Ānanda, wholesome virtues have freedom from remorse as their purpose and freedom from remorse as their benefit.”
Furthermore, it is said: “Householders, there are these five benefits for one who is virtuous through the perfection of virtue. What are the five?
Here, householders, one who is virtuous and perfected in virtue acquires, through heedfulness, a great mass of wealth;
this is the first benefit for one who is virtuous through the perfection of virtue. Furthermore, householders, for one who is virtuous and perfected in virtue...”
A good reputation spreads abroad; this is the second benefit for one who is virtuous and perfected in virtue.

Furthermore, householders, whatever assembly a virtuous person perfected in virtue approaches—whether an assembly of kṣatriyas, an assembly of brahmins, an assembly of householders, or an assembly of ascetics—they approach it with confidence.
Being free from confusion—this is the third benefit for one who is virtuous through the perfection of virtue.
Furthermore, householders, one who is virtuous and endowed with virtue dies unconfused; this is the fourth benefit for one who is virtuous through the perfection of virtue.
Furthermore, householders, one who is virtuous and endowed with virtue, upon the breakup of the body after death, [reappears] in a good destination, a heavenly world...
“He is reborn in a happy world; this is the fifth benefit for one who is virtuous through the perfection of virtue.

Furthermore, according to the method beginning with, “Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu should desire: ‘May I be dear and agreeable to my fellow practitioners of the holy life, respected and esteemed,’ he should fulfill his conduct in the precepts alone,” [the text describes] being dear and agreeable, and so forth.
Many benefits of virtue have been stated, culminating in the destruction of the taints (*āsava*). Thus, virtue possesses manifold qualities and benefits, such as freedom from remorse. Furthermore:
"In the Dispensation, there is no foundation for sons of noble family without it;
who could describe the limit of its benefits?"
Neither the Ganges nor the Yamunā, nor the Sarabhū or the Sarasvatī;
neither the Āciravatī river nor the Mahī, that great river—
none of these are able to cleanse the defilement of living beings here.
That water of virtue which purifies the defilement of beings—
neither rain-bearing winds, nor yellow sandalwood,
nor pearl necklaces, nor jewels, nor even the rays of the moon can do so.
It pacifies here the fever of beings that is so difficult to guard;
this noble virtue is utterly cool.
Where indeed could there be a fragrance equal to the fragrance of virtue?
That which blows equally with the wind, against the wind, and in between— that stairway for ascending to heaven,
or rather the gate for entering the city of Nibbāna— where else can anything equal to virtue be found?
Kings adorned with pearls and gems do not shine as much as ascetics adorned with the ornament of virtue;
for virtue utterly destroys the fear of self-reproach and the like.
It generates fame and laughter, and virtue is always the birthright of those who possess virtue.
Thus, this introduction to the discourse on benefits should be understood as pertaining to virtue, which is the root of all qualities and the destroyer of the strength of faults.
The Exposition of the Analysis of Virtue (Sīlappabhedakathā) 10.

Now, regarding what was asked—“In how many ways is this virtue?”—this is the answer: First of all, this entire virtue is of one kind by virtue of its own characteristic of “virtuous conduct” (sīlana).

It is of two kinds by way of positive engagement (cāritta) and negative restraint (vāritta); likewise, it is of two kinds by way of the higher life of right conduct (ābhisamācārika-ādibrahmacariyaka) and by way of abstinence (virati) and non-abstinence (avirati).

It is fourfold by way of being dependent or independent, by way of having a temporal limit or lasting until the end of life, by way of being limited or unlimited, and by way of being mundane or supramundane.
It is threefold by way of being inferior, mediocre, or superior. Likewise, it is threefold by way of being dominated by self, dominated by the world, or dominated by the Dhamma.

[It is analyzed] by way of being grasped, not grasped, and subsided; by way of being pure, impure, and doubtful; and by way of being that of one in training, that of one beyond training, and that of one who is neither.

It is fourfold by way of leading to decline, leading to stagnation, leading to distinction, and leading to penetration. Likewise, it is analyzed by way of the virtue of monks, nuns, those not fully ordained, and householders;

by way of natural virtue, customary virtue, virtue arising from the nature of things, and virtue with a prior cause; and by way of the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha, restraint of the sense faculties, purity of livelihood, and virtue dependent on the requisites.
It is fivefold by way of virtue of limited purity and so forth. This is also stated in the *Paṭisambhidā*: "There are five kinds of virtue:
virtue of limited purity, virtue of unlimited purity, virtue of complete purity, virtue of non-attachment purity, and virtue of tranquility purity.
Likewise, it is fivefold by way of abandoning, abstaining, volition, restraint, and non-transgression.
11. In that regard, the meaning of the singlefold division should be understood in the manner already stated.
In the twofold division, "conduct" (*cāritta*) is the fulfillment of those training rules (*sikkhāpada*) prescribed by the Blessed One as "this should be done.

"Abstention" (*vāritta*) is the non-performance of that which has been prohibited as "this should not be done. Herein, this is the etymological derivation: they conduct themselves (*caranti*) within those virtues (*sīla*).

It is called *cāritta* because it proceeds by way of fulfilling [the training]. It is called *vāritta* because one protects (*tāyati*) or guards (*rakkhati*) what has been prohibited (*vāritaṃ*) by means of it.
In this context, *cāritta* is accomplished through faith and energy, while *vāritta* is accomplished through faith alone. Thus, it is twofold by way of *cāritta* and *vāritta*.
In the second dyad, *abhisamācāra* means the highest conduct. That which consists of such conduct is *ābhisamācārika*. [The term] *abhisamācāraṃ*...

That which is prescribed with reference to [the training] concerning higher conduct (*abhisamācārika*) is a designation for the remaining moral virtue beyond the eightfold livelihood (*ājīvaṭṭhamaka*).

It is called "pertaining to the beginning of the holy life" (*ādibrahmacariyaka*) because it constitutes the initial state of the holy life of the Path; this is a designation for the moral virtue of the eightfold livelihood.
For that [virtue] constitutes the initial state of the Path, since it must be purified precisely in the preliminary stage. Therefore, he said:
“Furthermore, his bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood were previously quite purified.

Those training rules which are called “minor and lesser” constitute the morality of higher conduct (*ābhisamācārika-sīla*). The remainder constitutes that which pertains to the fundamental spiritual life (*ādibrahmacariyaka*).
Alternatively, that which is included in the two Vibhaṅgas pertains to the fundamental spiritual life; that which is included in the Khandhakas and the Vattas pertains to higher conduct.
Through its fulfillment, that which pertains to the beginning of the holy life (ādibrahmacariyaka) is accomplished. Thus it was said:
“Bhikkhus, it is impossible that a bhikkhu, without fulfilling the dhamma pertaining to right conduct (ābhisamācārika), should fulfill the dhamma pertaining to the beginning of the holy life.
In this way, it is twofold by way of the dhamma pertaining to right conduct and the dhamma pertaining to the beginning of the holy life.

In the third dyad, the virtue of abstinence (*virati-sīla*) consists merely of the refraining from killing living beings and so forth. The remainder—volition and the rest—is the virtue of non-abstinence (*avirati-sīla*). Thus, it is twofold by way of abstinence and non-abstinence.
In the fourth dyad, "support" refers to two supports: the support of craving (*taṇhā-nissaya*) and the support of views (*diṭṭhi-nissaya*).
Among these, that which is undertaken by one desiring the excellence of existence, thinking, "By this virtue I shall become a god or some other kind of deity," [is the support of craving].
That which is dependent on craving is "dependent on craving. That which proceeds from the view of purification, such as "purification comes through virtue," is "dependent on views.
However, that which is supramundane, and that which is mundane but serves as its equipment (sambhāra), is "independent.

Thus, it is twofold by way of being dependent or independent. In the fifth dyad, virtue undertaken after setting a time limit is "limited by time. That which is undertaken for as long as life lasts and practiced accordingly until the end of one's natural term of life is "until the end of life. Thus, it is twofold by way of being limited by time or lasting until the end of life.
In the sixth dyad, that which has a limit is called "with limit" (sapariyanta) by way of gain, fame, relatives, limbs, and life;
the opposite is "without limit" (apariyanta). And this is also stated in the *Paṭisambhidā*:
"What is that virtue with a limit? There is virtue limited by gain, there is virtue limited by fame, there is virtue limited by relatives..."
“Virtue has gain as its limit; there is virtue that has life as its limit. What is that virtue which has gain as its limit?
Here, someone, for the sake of gain, on account of gain, because of gain, transgresses a training rule as it was undertaken.
This is that virtue which has gain as its limit. In this same manner, the others should also be elaborated. In the exposition of the unlimited [virtue] as well:

It is said: "What is that virtue which does not have gain as its limit? Here, someone, for the sake of gain, with gain as cause, and with gain as motive, does not even give rise to a thought of transgressing a training rule as it has been undertaken; how much less would he actually transgress it?
This is that virtue which does not have gain as its limit. By this same method, the others should also be elaborated. Thus...
It is twofold by way of being limited and unlimited.
In the seventh dyad, all virtue that is accompanied by taints (*sāsava*) is mundane (*lokiya*); that which is without taints (*anāsava*) is supramundane (*lokuttara*).

Among these, the mundane brings about a distinction in existence and serves as a requisite for the escape from existence. As it has been said: "The discipline (*vinaya*) is for the sake of restraint; restraint is for the sake of non-remorse..."
Non-remorse is for the sake of gladness; gladness is for the sake of rapture; rapture is for the sake of tranquility;

tranquility is for the sake of happiness; happiness is for the sake of concentration; concentration is for the sake of knowledge and vision of things as they really are; knowledge and vision of things as they really are is for the sake of disenchantment;
disenchantment is for the sake of dispassion; dispassion is for the sake of liberation; liberation is for the sake of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
"The knowledge and vision of liberation is for the sake of final Nibbāna through non-clinging;

this is the purpose of the discourse, this the purpose of the consultation, this the purpose of the underlying support, and this the purpose of lending an ear: namely, the liberation of the mind through non-clinging.
Thus it is twofold, by way of the mundane and the supramundane: the supramundane brings about escape from existence and is the ground for the knowledge of reviewing.
12. Regarding the first triad: that which is set in motion by inferior desire, thought, energy, or investigation is inferior;
that set in motion by middling desire and so forth is middling; that set in motion by sublime [desire and so forth] is sublime.

Alternatively, that undertaken out of a desire for fame is inferior; that undertaken out of a desire for the fruit of merit is middling; and that undertaken with the thought, "This must indeed be done," is of the nature of the Noble Ones.

That which is undertaken by depending [on a teacher or precept] is "exquisite. That which is defiled by self-exaltation, disparagement of others, and so forth—thinking, "I am endowed with virtue, but these other bhikkhus are immoral and of evil character"—is "inferior. Mundane virtue that is undefiled is "middling.
Supramundane virtue is "exquisite. Alternatively, that which is practiced for the sake of existence and sensual enjoyment under the influence of craving is "inferior."
The middle [type of virtue] is that which is practiced for the sake of one’s own liberation.

The superior virtue is the perfection-ethics (pāramitāsīla) practiced for the sake of the liberation of all beings. Thus, it is threefold according to the categories of inferior, middle, and superior.
In the second triad, that which is practiced out of self-regard and self-respect by one who desires to abandon what is unbecoming to oneself—

That which is practiced out of self-respect by one who desires to master oneself is "self-sovereignty" (*attādhipateyya*). That which is practiced out of respect for the world and reverence for the world by one who desires to avoid worldly reproach is "world-sovereignty" (*lokādhipateyya*).
And that which is practiced out of respect for the Dhamma and reverence for the Dhamma by one who desires to honor the greatness of the Dhamma is "Dhamma-sovereignty" (*dhammādhipateyya*).
Thus, it is threefold by way of self-sovereignty and so forth.
In the third triad, that which was described in the dyads as "supported" (nissita) is "clung-to" (parāmaṭṭha) because it is adhered to by craving and views.
That which serves as the equipment for the path for the virtuous worldling and is associated with the path for those in training (sekha) is "not clung-to" (aparāmaṭṭha).
That which is associated with the fruit for those in training and those beyond training (asekha) is "allayed" (paṭippassaddha). Thus, it is threefold by way of being clung-to and so forth.
In the fourth triad, that which has been fulfilled by one who has not committed an offense, or which has been restored after committing one, is "pure.
That which has not been restored by one who has committed an offense is "impure.

When there is doubt regarding the basis (*vatthu*), the offense (*āpatti*), or the transgression (*ajjhācāra*), the virtue is called "doubtful virtue" (*vematika-sīla*). In this regard, the practitioner should [avoid] impure virtue.
It is to be purified; in cases of doubt, one should dispel the uncertainty without committing an offense regarding the matter, thinking, "In this way, he will find ease.
Thus it is threefold by way of being pure and so forth.

In the fifth tetrad, virtue associated with the four noble paths and the first three fruits of recluseship is that of the trainee (*sekha*). That associated with the fruit of arahantship is that of the non-trainee (*asekha*). The remainder is neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee. Thus it is threefold by way of being trainee and so forth.

In the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, however, because in the world the natural disposition of various beings is also called "virtue" (sīla)—referring to which people say, "This one is of a pleasant disposition, this one is of a painful disposition, this one is of a quarrelsome disposition, this one is of an ornamental disposition"—therefore, by that figurative method, it is said:
"There are three kinds of virtue: wholesome virtue, unwholesome virtue, and indeterminate virtue. Thus...

It is said that [virtue] is threefold by way of the wholesome and so forth. In this context, the unwholesome does not accord with even a single one of the characteristics and other attributes of the virtue intended here;
therefore, it is not included here. Consequently, its threefold nature should be understood according to the method already stated.
13. Regarding the first tetrad among the tetrads:
He who associates with the immoral and does not associate with the virtuous,
being ignorant, does not see the fault in transgressing against the foundations [of morality].
Abounding in wrong intentions, he does not guard his sense faculties.
Indeed, for one such as this, virtue becomes partaking of decline.
But he who is dissatisfied here with his attainment of virtue does not apply his mind to the practice of the meditation subject.
For that bhikkhu who is content with mere virtue alone and does not strive for what is higher,
that virtue becomes "conducive to stability. But he who,
being perfected in virtue, strives for the sake of concentration—
This bhikkhu possesses virtue that partakes of distinction.
Not being satisfied with mere virtue, he devotes himself to disenchantment;
thus his virtue becomes that which partakes of penetration.
Thus, it is fourfold by way of the categories beginning with that which partakes of decline.

In the second tetrad, the training rules prescribed concerning monks, and those which must be observed [by them] because they were prescribed for the nuns—this is the virtue of monks. The training rules prescribed concerning nuns...
And those [precepts] which must be guarded by monks as they have been laid down constitute the *bhikkhunī-sīla*.
The ten precepts of male and female novices (*sāmaṇera* and *sāmaṇerī*) constitute the virtue of those not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*).

For lay followers (*upāsaka* and *upāsikā*), there are five training rules (*sikkhāpada*) by way of constant virtue, or ten when there is the effort [to observe more], and eight by way of the factors of the Uposatha; this is the virtue of the householder. Thus, it is fourfold according to the virtue of monks and so forth.
In the third tetrad, the non-transgression [of natural laws] by the humans of Uttarakuru is natural virtue (*pakatisīla*).
The respective customary conduct within the boundaries of one's own family, country, and sect is conduct virtue (*ācārasīla*).

As it is said: “It is the natural law (*dhammatā*), Ānanda, that when the Bodhisatta has descended into his mother’s womb, no thought connected with the strands of sensual pleasure arises in the Bodhisatta’s mother toward men.”
Thus has been described the virtue of the Bodhisatta’s mother as natural virtue (*dhammatāsīla*).

However, the virtue of pure beings such as Mahākassapa and the virtue of the Bodhisatta in his various successive births is "virtue rooted in past causes" (*pubbahetukasīla*). Thus, virtue is fourfold according to these categories, beginning with natural virtue.
Regarding the fourth tetrad, that which was stated by the Blessed One: "Here, a bhikkhu dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort..."
The virtue described as "seeing danger in even the slightest faults, one trains by undertaking the rules of training" is what is called the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha.
Furthermore, that which is stated: "Having seen a form with the eye, he does not grasp at its signs or its secondary characteristics;
because, if he were to dwell with the faculty of the eye unrestrained, covetousness and dejection might arise... [and so forth].
If evil, unwholesome states should flow in upon him, he practices for their restraint; he guards the eye-faculty and attains mastery over the eye-faculty.
Having heard a sound with the ear... [and so on]... having smelled an odor with the nose... [and so on]...
having tasted a flavor with the tongue... [and so on]... having touched a tangible object with the body... [and so on]... having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind.
“It does not seize upon signs… [and so on] …it attains restraint over the mind-faculty”— this is the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasaṃvara-sīla*).
Furthermore, that which occurs by way of the transgression of the six training rules prescribed for the sake of livelihood,
and by way of evil qualities such as "hypocrisy, flattery, hinting, belittling, and the pursuit of gain through gain," is [the opposite].
Abstinence from wrong livelihood is the virtue of purification of livelihood (*ājīvapārisuddhisīla*). The use of the four requisites purified by reflection,
as stated in the method beginning with, “Reflecting wisely, he uses the robe only for protection against cold,” etc.,
is called the virtue dependent on requisites (*paccayasannissitasīla*).
The Virtue of Restraint by the Pātimokkha.
14. Herein, this is the exposition of the analysis together with a word-by-word commentary starting from the beginning.
"Here" means in this Dispensation. "Bhikkhu" [is so called] either because he beholds (ikkhati) the fear in *saṃsāra*, or because he wears torn robes (*bhinnapaṭa*), and so forth.
Thus is the designation for a clansman who has gone forth out of faith. Regarding the phrase "restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha":

here, *pātimokkha* refers to the virtue of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*). For that which protects (*pāti*) one who guards it and liberates (*mokkheti*) one from the sufferings of the states of woe and so forth—therefore it is called *pātimokkha*.
*Saṃvara* means restraint; this refers to non-transgression in bodily and verbal actions.

The name [is as follows]. The *pātimokkha* itself is the restraint; thus it is "restraint of the *pātimokkha*" (*pātimokkhasaṃvara*). One who is restrained by that restraint of the *pātimokkha* is "restrained by the restraint of the *pātimokkha*" (*pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuta*);

the meaning is that he has approached it and is endowed with it. "Dwells" (*viharatī*) means he conducts himself. The meaning of "endowed with proper conduct and resort" (*ācāragocarasampanno*) and so forth should be understood according to the method already set forth in the *Pāḷi*. For this has been said:
“Endowed with proper conduct and resort” means there is proper conduct and there is improper conduct.
In this regard, what is improper conduct? Transgression by way of body, transgression by way of speech, and transgression by way of both body and speech—this is called improper conduct.
All immorality is also improper conduct. Here, someone [engages in] the giving of bamboo, or the giving of alms-bowls...
Or if one makes a living by giving flowers, fruits, bathing powders, or tooth-sticks; or by flattery, or by bean-soupery, or by servility,
or by running errands on foot, or by any other kind of wrong livelihood censured by the Buddha—
this is called improper conduct.
In this context, what is conduct (*ācāra*)? Non-transgression by way of body, non-transgression by way of speech, and non-transgression by way of both body and speech—this is called conduct.
Furthermore, the entire restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*) is conduct.
Here, someone does not [practice] by the giving of bamboo, nor by the giving of leaves, flowers, fruits, or bathing materials, nor by the giving of tooth-sticks, nor by flattery, nor by bean-soupery.

Nor does one maintain one's livelihood through buffoonery, nor by running errands on foot, nor by any other kind of wrong livelihood censured by the Buddha—this is called *ācāra* (proper conduct). As for *gocara* (range of activity):
there is that which is a proper range and there is that which is not a proper range.
In this regard, what is an improper resort (*agocara*)? Here, a certain person has prostitutes as his resort, or widows, unmarried girls, eunuchs, or bhikkhunīs;
or he has taverns as his resort. He dwells in association with kings, royal ministers, members of other sects, and followers of other sects, through an inappropriate association.
Or else, he frequents those families that are faithless and lacking in confidence.
Those families that have become like a precipice— those who revile and abuse, who desire no welfare, no benefit, no comfort,
and no security from bondage for the bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās— to frequent, associate with,
and attend upon such families is called "an improper resort" (agocara).
In this regard, what is the proper resort (*gocara*)? Here, a certain person does not frequent the quarters of prostitutes...
nor does he frequent taverns; he dwells unassociated with kings... nor with the disciples of other sects, avoiding improper association.
Rather, he frequents those families that are faithful and confident, which serve as a well for the Sangha, where the yellow robes shine like lamps, and which are cooled by the breezes from the sages.
He frequents, associates with, and attends upon families that desire the welfare of the bhikkhus... [and so on] ...desiring their security from bondage;
such families as these he frequents, associates with, and attends upon—this is called his resort (*gocara*).
Thus, being endowed with this conduct and this resort, fully endowed, approached, fully approached, attained, perfected, and possessed thereof, for that reason he is so called.
“Endowed with proper conduct and resort.
Furthermore, in this context, conduct and resort should be understood according to the following method. For improper conduct is twofold: bodily and verbal.
In that regard, what is bodily improper conduct? Here, someone, even when in the midst of the Saṅgha, acts without respect toward the elder bhikkhus...
He stands while bumping [others], he sits while bumping [others]; he stands in front [of others], he sits in front [of others];
he sits on a high seat; he sits having covered himself with his upper robe; he speaks while standing; he speaks while waving his arms;
he walks back and forth wearing sandals while elder bhikkhus are walking back and forth without sandals; [he sits] on a low [seat].
While others were walking on a walking-path, he walks on a high walking-path; while others are walking on the ground, he walks on a walking-path;
he stands encroaching upon senior monks, he sits encroaching upon them; he even preempts new monks from their seats;
and in the sauna, without asking permission, he throws wood into the fire and closes the door.
Even at a water-ford, he enters while jostling senior bhikkhus, or he enters ahead of them;
he bathes while jostling them, or he bathes ahead of them; he emerges while jostling them, or he emerges ahead of them;
even when entering an inhabited house, he walks while jostling senior bhikkhus, or he walks ahead of them, and he passes by them.
He walks right in front of the elder bhikkhus; he even enters impulsively into those private and secluded inner rooms of families where women of the family and young girls sit,
and he even touches the head of a young boy— this is called bodily misconduct.

In this regard, what is improper conduct by way of speech? Here, someone, even when present in the Saṅgha, speaks the Dhamma without showing respect, without having asked the elder bhikkhus for permission;
he answers questions, recites the Pātimokkha, speaks while standing, speaks while waving his arms about, or, having entered among the houses, says such things to a woman or a girl.
“O [so-and-so] of such-and-such a clan, what is there? Is there rice-gruel? Is there a meal? Is there solid food?
What shall we drink? What shall we eat? What shall we consume? Or what will you give me?”—to prattle in this manner is called verbal misconduct (*vācasiko anācāro*).
Its opposite, however, should be understood as proper conduct (*ācāra*).
Furthermore, a bhikkhu who is respectful and deferential, endowed with shame and fear of wrongdoing, well-clad and properly robed,
possessing a serene demeanor in his advancing and retreating, his looking ahead and looking aside, his bending and stretching, with downcast eyes and perfected deportment,
guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderate in eating, devoted to wakefulness, and possessed of mindfulness and clear comprehension—

One who is thus endowed—having few desires, being contented, energetic, performing duties with thorough care regarding the rules of proper conduct, and dwelling with great reverence and respect—is said to possess "conduct" (*ācāra*).
In this way, first, conduct is to be understood.

Furthermore, the "range" (*gocara*) is threefold: the range as support (*upanissaya-gocara*), the range as protection (*ārakkha-gocara*), and the range as binding (*upanibandha-gocara*). Among these, what is...

What is the objective sphere of the decisive support? It is a virtuous friend endowed with the ten qualities of the "Ten Grounds of Discourse," relying upon whom one hears what has not been heard, clarifies what has been heard, overcomes doubt, straightens one's view, and gains confidence in the mind;
or, by training in accordance with him, one increases in faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom.
This is called the resort of dependence (*upanissaya-gocara*).

What is the resort of protection (*ārakkha-gocara*)? Here, a bhikkhu who has entered among the houses and set out upon a street walks with downcast eyes, looking only a yoke’s length ahead, well-restrained;
he does not look at an elephant, nor a horse, nor a chariot... [and so forth].
One who walks without looking at a woman, nor a man; without looking upward, nor looking downward;
and without glancing about in the various directions—this is called the range of protection (*ārakkhagocara*).
What is the range of anchoring (*upanibandhagocara*)? It is the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) where the mind is anchored. For this has been said:
The Blessed One said: “And what, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu’s own resort, his ancestral domain? It is these four foundations of mindfulness.
This is called the resort of close attachment. Thus, being endowed with this conduct and this resort...
[as above] ...being possessed of them, he is for that reason called one who is accomplished in conduct and resort.

“Seeing danger in even the slightest faults” means one whose nature is to see danger in faults of even minute measure—such as those consisting of unintentional transgressions of the training rules (*sekhiya*) or the arising of unwholesome states of mind.

“Having undertaken them, he trains in the precepts of training” means that whatever is to be trained in among the precepts of training, he trains in all of it having correctly undertaken it. And here, [the phrase] “restrained by the restraint of the *Pātimokkha*”...
To this extent, the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha has been shown through the teaching based on the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*).

However, it should be understood that the entire passage beginning with "endowed with proper conduct and resort" (*ācāra-gocara-sampanno*) was spoken in order to show that practice by which, for one who practices accordingly, that virtue is perfected.
[Next is] the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃvara-sīla*).
15. Now, as for that virtue of restraint of the sense faculties which was shown immediately following that in the manner beginning with “Having seen a form with the eye,” therein:
“he” refers to the bhikkhu established in the virtue of restraint by the Pātimokkha. “Having seen a form with the eye” means:
having seen a form with the eye-consciousness—which is capable of seeing forms and is conventionally designated as the “eye” by way of its instrumentality. The Ancients [say]:
However, they say: "The eye does not see form because it is devoid of consciousness; the mind does not see because it is devoid of the eye.
Rather, when there is a collision between the door and the object, one sees by means of the mind based upon the eye-sensitivity.
But this is a figurative expression (sasambhārakathā), like saying 'one pierces with a bow'; therefore, the meaning here is simply that one sees form by means of eye-consciousness."
"Not seizing upon signs" means that he does not grasp at the sign of a woman or a man, nor at signs such as beauty which serve as the basis for defilements;

he remains established in the mere sight [of the object]. "Not seizing upon secondary characteristics" refers to the various modes such as the hands, feet, smiles, laughter, speech, and glances, which are called "secondary characteristics" (*anubyañjana*) because they manifest the underlying defilements and make them evident.
It does not grasp at the appearance; it grasps only that which is real therein, like the Elder Mahātissa who dwelt at Cetiyapabbata.

It is said that as the Elder was coming from Cetiyapabbata to Anurādhapura for alms, a certain daughter-in-law of a noble family, having quarreled with her husband, had adorned and decorated herself like a celestial maiden and was already at Anurādhapura early in the morning.
Having gone forth, while on her way to her relatives’ home, she saw him and, her mind being perverted, she laughed a great laugh.
The Elder, looking up and wondering, "What is this?", attained Arahantship upon gaining the perception of foulness regarding her jawbone. Therefore it was said:
"Seeing her jawbone, he recalled his former perception."
Standing right there, that elder attained arahantship.
Meanwhile, her husband, following along the path, saw the elder and asked, "Venerable sir, do you see a woman? The elder said to him:
"I do not know whether a woman or a man has gone this way."
"Furthermore, this collection of bones goes along the great highway.

Regarding the passage beginning with *yatvādhikaraṇamenaṃ*, the word *yaṃ* (that which) refers to the cause; by reason of that lack of restraint of the eye-faculty (*cakkhundriyāsaṃvara*), for that reason, these states of covetousness and so forth [arise] in this person who dwells with the eye-faculty unrestrained, having failed to close the door of the eye with the bolt of mindfulness (*satikavāṭa*).

“Dhammas might flow in and pursue him. He “practices for its restraint” means he practices for the purpose of closing the door of mindfulness over that eye-faculty. It is precisely by practicing in this way that one guards the eye-faculty;
thus one is said to “attain restraint over the eye-faculty. In this regard, although there is either restraint over the eye-faculty...
Or rather, there is no non-restraint (asaṃvara). For mindfulness or forgetfulness does not arise dependent upon the eye-sensitivity (cakkhupasāda).

Furthermore, when a visible-object (rūpa) comes into the range of the eye, then, after the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) has arisen and ceased twice, the functional mind-element (kiriyamanodhātu) arises and ceases, performing the function of adverting (āvajjana). Thereafter, eye-consciousness (cakkhuviññāṇa) [arises].

The function of seeing. Thereafter, the resultant mind-element performs the function of receiving. Thereafter, the resultant rootless mind-consciousness-element performs the function of investigating.
Thereafter, the functional rootless mind-consciousness-element arises and ceases while accomplishing the function of determining;
immediately after that, the impulsion (javana) occurs.
Even there, restraint or non-restraint does not exist during the moment of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), nor during any of the moments such as adverting (āvajjana).
However, in the moment of impulsion (javana), if misconduct, forgetfulness, ignorance, impatience, or indolence arises, there is non-restraint.
When this occurs, it is called "non-restraint with respect to the eye-faculty" (cakkhundriye asaṃvaro).
It is so called. Why? Because when that [door] exists, the door itself remains unguarded, as do the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and the process-consciousnesses such as adverting (āvajjana).

How is this so? Just as when the four gates of a city are left unsecured, even though the inner house doors, gate-towers, chambers, and so forth may be well-secured, nevertheless all the goods within the city remain unprotected and unguarded. By means of the city gate...
Just as thieves, having entered [a house], would do whatever they desire, even so, when unwholesome states such as immorality arise in the "swift" [consciousness],
and there is that lack of restraint, the door is unprotected, as are the life-continuum and the process-consciousnesses beginning with adverting.
But when wholesome states such as virtue arise, the door is protected, as are the life-continuum and the process-consciousnesses beginning with adverting.

How is this so? Just as when the city gates are closed, although the houses and other buildings within may be unsecured, nevertheless all the goods inside the city remain well-protected and well-guarded;

for when the city gates are shut, there is no entry for thieves—exactly so, when the "swift" virtues such as morality (sīla) have arisen, the gateway is guarded and the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) as well.
The process-minds, beginning with adverting, are also included. Therefore, even though it arises at the moment of impulsion (*javana*), it is called "restraint of the eye-faculty.

The same method applies to the passages beginning with "having heard a sound with the ear. Thus, this virtue of restraint of the faculties should be understood, in brief, as having the characteristic of avoiding the grasping of signs and so forth that lead to the persistence of defilements regarding visible forms and other objects.
[Next is] the virtue of purity of livelihood (*ājīvapārisuddhisīla*).
16. Now, regarding the virtue of purity of livelihood mentioned immediately after the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties:

concerning the six training rules prescribed on account of livelihood—those which state: "If, for the sake of livelihood, for the cause of livelihood, one who is of evil desire and overcome by longing proclaims a non-existent, unreal superhuman state, it is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika). For the sake of livelihood, for the cause of livelihood..."
If he engages in matchmaking, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).

For the sake of livelihood, for the purpose of livelihood, if he says, “The monk who dwells in that monastery is an arahant,” there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya) for one who understands [the meaning].
For the sake of livelihood, for the purpose of livelihood, if a monk who is not ill, having requested fine foods for his own sake, eats them, there is an offense.

Regarding the *pācittiya*: if a nun, for the sake of her livelihood and for the purpose of livelihood, being not ill, requests and eats fine foods for her own benefit, there is an offense entailing confession (*pāṭidesanīya*).

If, for the sake of her livelihood and for the purpose of livelihood, being not ill, she requests and eats either soup or boiled rice for her own benefit, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); thus they were laid down.
Six training rules: of these six training rules.
Regarding "guile" (*kuhana*) and so forth, this is the canonical text: "In that regard, what is guile?

For one who is dependent on gain, honor, and fame, who has evil desires, and who is driven by desire—that which, by means of what is termed the use of requisites or by indirect speech, [is directed toward] deportment..."

Or, the assuming, the placing, the fixing, the frowning, the state of frowning, the scheming, the act of scheming, and the state of having schemed—this is called scheming (*kuhanā*). In this context, what is flattery (*lapanā*)?
It is the speech of one who is dependent on gain, honor, and fame; who has evil desires; and who is driven by longing.

Whatever addressing of others, talking, conversing, chatting, chattering, inciting, instigating, urging, persuading, speaking what is agreeable, flattery, bean-soupery, and servility—this is called "flattery" (*lapana*).
In that regard, what is "hinting" (*nemittikatā*)? It is [the behavior] of one who is dependent on gain, honor, and fame, who has evil desires, and who is driven by craving.
Whatever sign-giving for others, hinting, illumination, hinting by illumination, indirect talk, or roundabout speech—this is called "hinting" (*nemittikatā*).
In that regard, what is "belittling" (*nippesikatā*)? It is the behavior of one who is dependent on gain, honor, and fame, who has evil desires, and who is driven by longing.

That which consists of reviling, disparaging, censuring, upbraiding, upbraiding severely, mocking, mocking thoroughly, detesting, detesting thoroughly, slandering, and backbiting directed toward others—this is called *nippesikatā* (depreciation).
In this context, what is "seeking gain through gain"? It is being dependent on gain, honor, and fame, and possessing evil desires.
Driven by desire, one takes the material gain obtained here and carries it there, or takes the material gain obtained there and brings it here.
Whatever such seeking, searching, questing, longing, seeking out,
and pursuit for material gain by means of material gain is called "the hankering after gain with gain."
17. Furthermore, the meaning of this passage should be understood as follows. First, regarding the exposition of "deceit" (*kuhana*):
"of one dependent upon gain, honor, and fame" means of one who relies upon material profit, hospitality, and reputation; the sense is "one who yearns for them.

"Of one with evil desires" (*pāpiccha*) means of one who wishes to display non-existent virtues. "Of one overcome by desire" (*icchāpakata*) means of one who is subdued by desire; the sense is "of one who is afflicted by it."
From here on, since three bases for hypocrisy (*kuhanavatthu*) have been presented in the *Mahāniddesa* by way of the solicitation of requisites,
hinting, and dependence on deportment, this threefold [classification] is set forth beginning with the words "or by the so-called solicitation of requisites," etc.,
in order to demonstrate them. Therein, when one who is actually in need of robes and so forth is invited with robes and such, yet acts out of evil desire...

By means of refusing [the gifts] out of dependence [on the donors], and having recognized that those householders were firmly established in faith toward him, he [acted] solely out of a desire to favor them when they, employing various means, brought forward excellent robes and other requisites, thinking: "Oh, this noble one is so modest that he does not wish to accept anything at all; it would be a great gain for us if he would accept even a small thing."

By means of both revealing [one's spiritual attainments] and accepting [offerings], from that time forward, even the act of inducing [donors] through the presentation of loads on carts—which serves as the cause for such inducement—is to be understood as a basis for hypocrisy known as the "acceptance of requisites. For this has been said in the *Mahāniddesa*:
"What is the basis for hypocrisy known as the acceptance of requisites? Here, householders invite a bhikkhu..."
[He provides] robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. Yet, being of evil desire and driven by craving, seeking robes...
[and so on] ...medicinal requisites for the sick, he renounces robes out of a desire for more.
He renounces almsfood... [and so on] ...lodgings. He renounces medicinal requisites for the sick. He says this: "What [use have] robes for a recluse?"

What is the use of an expensive robe for a recluse? It is fitting that a recluse should gather rags from a charnel ground, a rubbish heap, or a shop, and having made them into a patched cloak, wear it. What is the use of expensive almsfood for a recluse?
It is fitting that a recluse should maintain his life by the practice of gleaning, through the morsels of food obtained as alms. What is the use for a recluse...?
‘It is fitting for a recluse to be a tree-root dweller or an open-air dweller rather than one with costly lodgings.
What need has a recluse for costly medicinal requisites for the sick?
It is fitting for a recluse to prepare medicine from fermented urine or pieces of gallnuts. Taking that as his standard, he wears coarse robes.
He maintains [these practices]: he consumes coarse almsfood, resorts to a coarse lodging, and uses coarse medicinal requisites for the sick.
Householders perceive him thus: “This ascetic is of few desires, contented, secluded, unattached, energetic, and a proponent of the ascetic virtues (dhuta).
Consequently, they increasingly invite him with robes... [and so on] ...with medicinal requisites.
Thus he spoke: “Through the coming together of three things, a faithful clansman produces much merit.

Through the coming together of faith, a faithful clansman produces much merit. Through the presence of the object to be given... [and so on] ...through the coming together of those worthy of offerings, a faithful clansman produces much merit. Now, you yourselves possess this faith.”

‘The gift exists, and I am the recipient; if I do not accept it, you will be excluded from merit, whereas for me there is no need for this. Nevertheless, out of compassion for you alone, I shall accept it.
Taking that as a basis, he accepts much robe-cloth... much almsfood... [and so on].”
“He accepts medicinal requisites. Such frowning, frownishness, scheming, scheming behavior, and state of being a schemer—this is the basis for scheming known as the utilization of requisites.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the act of deceiving others by speaking in various ways to indicate the attainment of superhuman states while one still possesses evil desires is the basis for scheming known as “hinting. As it has been said:

“What is the ground for hypocrisy known as hinting (*sāmantajappana*)? Here, a certain person of evil desires, driven by desire and intent on gaining esteem, thinking ‘In this way people will hold me in high esteem,’ utters speech connected with the noble Dhamma, saying:
‘He who wears such a robe is a monk of great influence; he who uses such a bowl or a metal dish [is a monk of great influence].’”
“He uses a water-strainer, a strainer with a frame, a key, a waist-band, and sandals; he is a monk of great influence,” he says.

For whomsoever such a person is preceptor, teacher, co-resident under the same preceptor, co-student under the same teacher, friend, confidant, or companion—whosoever dwells in such a dwelling, whether in a small hut, a large mansion, a palace, a gabled house, or a cave.
"He dwells in a hut, a gabled house, a watchtower, a multi-storied building, a high platform, an assembly hall, a pavilion, or at the foot of a tree;
therefore, this ascetic is one of great influence," he says. Or else: "He is excessively frowning, full of contortions, deceitful, talkative, and flattering;
this ascetic [is merely a pretender to] these kinds of peaceful dwellings and meditative attainments."
"‘A gainer’— he speaks such talk that is profound, hidden, subtle, concealed, supramundane, and connected with emptiness.
Such frowning, frownishness, scheming, scheming behavior, and state of being a schemer—
this is the basis for scheming known as hinting."

Furthermore, the deception practiced by one who possesses evil desires through a mode of conduct performed with the intention of gaining esteem should be understood as the basis for hypocrisy (*kuhana*) dependent on deportment (*iriyāpatha*). As it is said: "What is the basis for hypocrisy consisting of deportment?
Here, someone with evil desires, driven by desire and intent on gaining esteem, thinking 'In this way people will esteem me,' composes his gait."
He composes his standing, composes his sitting, and composes his lying down; he walks with intention, stands with intention, sits with intention, and lies down with intention;
he walks as if concentrated, stands as if concentrated, sits as if concentrated, and lies down as if concentrated;
he is one who meditates within range [of the senses]; such is the [composure] of the postures.
“Assuming, maintaining, adjusting, frowning, frowningness, scheming, schemingness, and schemedness—
this is called the ground for scheming consisting of deportment.
In that context, “by what is reckoned as the utilization of requisites” means by the utilization of requisites reckoned in this way.
Or by what is reckoned as such. "By conversing nearby" means by speaking in close proximity. "Of the posture" means of the four postures.
"Setting down," and so forth, refers to placing; or it is placing with care. "Setting down" (ṭhapanā) is the manner of placing. "Arranging" (saṇṭhapanā) is the act of composing;
it is said to be the making of a pleasing appearance. "Frowning" (bhākuṭikā) is [so called] because of showing the state of being fixed in a prominent, forward position.
*Ābhākuṭikaṃ* means the contraction of the face; this is what is meant. One whose habit is the contraction of the face is *ābhākuṭika*. The state of being *ābhākuṭika* is *ābhākuṭiyaṃ*.
*Kuhanā* is deception. The act of deceiving (*kuha*) is *kuhāyanā*. The state of one who has deceived is *kuhitattaṃ*.
In the exposition of *lapanā*, *ālapanā* refers to seeing people who have come to the monastery and [asking], "For what purpose, sirs, have you come? What..."
“Come, monks, to invite [me]; if you go thus, I will follow behind taking the bowl”—this is flattery from the very beginning.
Or else, presenting oneself: “I am Tissa; the king has confidence in me;
such-and-such and such-and-such royal ministers have confidence in me”—this is flattery consisting of self-presentation. This is called *lapanā* (flattery).
*Puṭṭhasallapana* is the speaking in the manner already described when one is being questioned.

*Sallapana* is the repeated speaking well, having given opportunity after opportunity, by one who is afraid of causing dissatisfaction among householders. *Ullapana* is speaking by exalting [oneself], saying such things as "I am a great householder," "I am a great ship-owner," or "I am a great lord of alms-giving.
*Samullapana* is speaking by exalting oneself from every side.
“Unnahanā” means binding upwards; it is said to mean wrapping. It refers to [the pressure] from saying, “Lay followers, you gave new gifts at such times in the past; why do you not give now?
until they reply, “We shall give, venerable sir, we have not found the opportunity,” and so forth.
Alternatively, seeing someone with sugarcane in their hand, he asks, “From where was this brought, lay follower?”
“From a sugar-cane field, venerable sir. “Is the sugar-cane there sweet? “It must be known by eating it, venerable sir.
“It is permissible, lay follower, to say: ‘Give sugar-cane to the bhikkhu. Such talk that entangles even one who is trying to disentangle is *unnahanā* (entangling).
Entangling again and again from every side is *samunnahanā* (thorough entangling).
*Ukkācanā* means "praising" (*kācanā*). It is *ukkācanā* because one praises by exalting [the family], thinking: "This family knows me alone; if any gift arises here, they will give it to me alone.
This is what is meant by "hinting. The story of Telakaṇḍarika should be cited here as an example.
Furthermore, praising repeatedly from every side is *samukkācanā*.
"Flattery" (*anuppiyabhāṇitā*) means merely speaking what is pleasing again and again without regard for the truth or the Dharma.
"Fawning" (*cāṭukamyatā*) means behaving in a lowly manner, conducting oneself by placing oneself lower and lower.
"The bean-soup simile" (*muggasūpyatā*) refers to being like bean soup. For just as when beans are being cooked, some may not cook while the rest do, [so it is with those who fawn].
Thus, that person whose speech contains some truth while the rest is false is called a "muggasūpya" (bean-soup person).
The state of being such is *muggasūpyatā*. *Pāribhaṭyatā* is the state of being a *pāribhaṭya*.
For one who carries a noble youth like a nurse—either on the hip or on the shoulder—the meaning is that he supports him. Of that carrier (*paribhaṭa*)...
“Kamma” means acting as a servant. The state of being a servant is “pāribhaṭyatā.
In the description of “hinting” (*nimittikatā*), “a sign” (*nimitta*) refers to any bodily or verbal action that produces in others the perception that one is giving requisites.
“Acting on a sign” (*nimittakamma*) refers to seeing someone walking along carrying food and asking, “Did you get any food? and so forth.
"Making a sign" means by way of inference. "Light" refers to talk connected with conditions.
"Acting as a light" is like seeing cowherds and asking, "Are these calves milk-calves or buttermilk-calves?
When they reply, "They are milk-calves, venerable sir," one says, "They are not milk-calves; if they were milk-calves, the monks would also receive milk."
Having informed the parents of those children in this manner, one makes a request for the provision of milk and so forth;
this is "making an intimation" (*obhāsakaraṇa*). "Whispering in the vicinity" (*sāmantajappā*) means whispering after having drawn near.

Here, the story of the monk who frequented families (*kulūpaka-bhikkhu*) should be told: it is said that a monk who frequented families, desiring to eat, entered a house and sat down. Seeing him, the mistress of the house, being unwilling to give, [acted].
Saying, "There is no rice," she went to a neighbor's house as if wishing to fetch some rice.
The monk, having entered the inner room and looked about, saw sugarcane in the corner of the door, sugar in a vessel, salted fish-scales in a basket, rice in a jar, and ghee in a pot;
having seen these, he came out and sat down. The mistress of the house thought, "I did not get any rice."
She arrived. The bhikkhu said, "Lay devotee, I saw a sign beforehand that today almsfood would not be obtained.
"What was it, venerable sir? "I saw a snake like a stalk of sugarcane placed in the corner of the door-panel;
looking at it with the thought, 'I will strike it,' I saw a stone like a lump of sugar placed in the bowl; and [I saw] what was done by the snake when struck by the clod."
His hood was like a salt-fish scale placed in a basket; his teeth were like rice grains in a pot as he intended to bite that clod of earth;
and from the mouth of the enraged one issued saliva mixed with poison, like clarified butter poured into a jar.
Thinking, "It is not possible to deceive this shaveling," she gave him sugarcane and cooked some rice.
"She gave everything together with the pot, the molasses, and the fish"—thus, instigating by bringing things close at hand should be understood as *sāmantajappā* (indirect instigation).
*Parikathā* (indirect talk) is speaking by way of circumlocution so that one obtains what is desired.

In the exposition of *nippesikatā* (depreciation), *akkosanā* (reviling) is reviling by means of the ten grounds for reviling; *vambhanā* (contempt) is [speaking] after having treated [the person] with contempt.
“Speaking” (*kathana*) means this. “Reproaching” (*garahaṇā*) means the attribution of faults in such a manner as: “He is faithless, he has no conviction,” and so forth.

“Excluding” (*ukkhepanā*) means the verbal act of setting someone aside by saying, “Do not speak of this here. “Complete exclusion” (*samukkhepanā*) is the act of excluding while making it all-encompassing, providing both a basis and a reason.
Alternatively, seeing someone who is not giving and yet exclaiming, “Oh, what a generous patron!”—such an act of setting them aside is “exclusion.”
"Mahādānapati" (Great Master of Giving) refers to thorough disparagement (*samukkhepanā*). "Throwing out" (*khipanā*) is mocking by saying, "What is this man’s life worth? He eats only seeds.
"Throwing together" (*saṃkhipanā*) is even more thorough mockery, saying, "Why do you call him a non-giver, when he constantly says, 'I have nothing' for everyone?
"Causing to fall" (*pāpanā*) refers to [causing] the state of being a non-giver or [the spreading of] disrepute.

Slandering (*pāpana*). Slandering in every respect is thorough slandering (*sampāpanā*). "Carrying off disrepute" (*avaṇṇahārikā*) means carrying off disrepute from house to house, village to village, and district to district, thinking, "He will give [me] disrepute even out of fear of [my own] disrepute.

"Backbiting" (*parapiṭṭhimaṃsikatā*) means speaking dispraise behind someone's back after having spoken sweetly to their face; for this is done toward one who is unable to look directly at [the speaker].
It is like eating the back-flesh of those who have their backs turned; therefore it is called "backbiting" (*parapiṭṭhimaṃsika*).
This is called "denigration" (*nippesikatā*): because, just as one might scrape off oil with a bamboo scraper, one scrapes away or wipes off another's virtue;
or because, just as one searches for fragrance by grinding fragrant substances, one grinds away at another's virtues.
Having crushed [the truth], this is the way of seeking gain; therefore, it is called "hinting" (*nippesikatā*).
In the exposition on "seeking gain through gain," "seeking" (*nijigīsanatā*) means searching for.
"Obtained from here" means obtained from this house. "There" means in that house. "Seeking" (*eṭṭhī*) means desiring. "Searching" (*gaveṭṭhī*) means looking for. "Pursuing" (*pariyeṭṭhī*) means...

"Seeking again and again": this refers to the story of the monk who, from the very beginning, gave whatever alms he received here and there to the children of various families, and only at the end received milk-rice; that story should be told here.
"Esanā" and so forth are synonyms for "eṭṭhi" and so forth; therefore, *eṭṭhi* means seeking (*esanā*). *Gaveṭṭhi* means searching (*gavesanā*), and *pariyeṭṭhi* means...
“Seeking. Thus should the construction here be understood. This is the meaning of *kuhana* (hypocrisy) and the others.
Now, regarding the phrase “and such evil qualities,” the word “and so forth” (*ādi*) includes:
“Or how some worthy recluses and brahmins, having eaten meals given out of faith, maintain their livelihood by such low arts and wrong living...”

One should understand that this refers to the inclusion of many evil practices mentioned in the *Brahmajāla Sutta* by way of such passages as: "They practice [astrology], namely: the limbs [of the body], signs, portents, dreams, bodily marks, mouse-bites, fire-sacrifices, and grass-sacrifices.
Thus, this refers to those six training rules prescribed for the sake of one's livelihood.

Wrong livelihood is that which proceeds by way of transgression and by way of these evil states such as "deceit, talkativeness, hinting, belittling, and pursuing gain with gain. The abstention from all such forms of wrong livelihood is the virtue of purification of livelihood (*ājīvapārisuddhisīla*).
Herein, this is the etymology: they live depending on this, thus it is "livelihood" (*ājīva*).
What is this? It is the effort of seeking requisites. *Pārisuddhi* means purity. The purity of livelihood is "livelihood-purity" (*ājīvapārisuddhi*).
Regarding the morality dependent on requisites mentioned immediately after that: therein, "wise reflection" (*yoniso paṭisaṅkhā*)— [is as follows].

"By means of the method, having reflected and known"—the meaning is "having reviewed. And here, it should be understood that "wise reflection" (*yoniso paṭisaṅkhā*) refers precisely to the reviewing stated in the manner beginning with "for the warding off of cold.
In this context, "robe" (*cīvara*) refers to any one among the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*) and so forth.
"He uses" (*paṭisevati*) means he makes use of it, or he wears it as an undergarment or puts it on as an upper garment. "Only to the extent that" (*yāvadeva*)—
The statement regarding the determination of the purpose and limit is as follows: for this alone is the purpose for a yogin in the use of robes, namely, "for the warding off of cold," and so forth;

there is nothing beyond this. "Of cold" means of any cold whatsoever that has arisen, either through the disturbance of the internal elements or through the transformation of external seasonal conditions. "For the warding off" means...
