For the purpose of warding off [cold]. For the purpose of dispelling it so that it does not produce affliction in the body.
For when the body is struck by cold, one whose mind is distracted is unable to apply oneself with wise attention;
therefore, the Blessed One permitted the use of a robe for the sake of warding off cold. This same method applies everywhere. Only here, "of heat" refers to the heat of fire.
Its occurrence should be understood in relation to forest fires and the like. Regarding the phrase "the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things":
here, *daṃsa* refers to the gadfly (*daṃsanamakkhikā*), which is also called the "blind fly" (*andhamakkhikā*). *Makasa* refers simply to mosquitoes.
*Vāta* refers to winds distinguished as those with dust, without dust, and so forth. *Ātapa* refers to the heat of the sun. *Sarīsapā* refers to whatever creatures move by crawling.
There are snakes such as the *dīghajātika* and others; their contact is twofold: the contact of being bitten and the contact of being touched.
That [contact] does not afflict one who is sitting after having put on the robe; therefore, he makes use of it in such places for the purpose of warding off those [creatures].
The phrase "only so far" (*yāvadeva*) is stated again for the purpose of showing the limit of the fixed purpose.
For the purpose of concealing the *hirikopīna* is constant, whereas the others are occasional. In this context, *hirikopīna* refers to each respective private part.
For when any particular limb is uncovered, modesty (*hirī*) is disturbed—that is, destroyed—and because it disturbs modesty, that part is called *hirikopīna*.
And the purpose [of the robe] is for the concealment of that *hirikopīna*.
For the purpose of covering the private parts (*hirikopīna*). There is also a reading: "for the purpose of covering what is shameful" (*hirikopīna-paṭicchādanatthaṃ*).
"Alms-food" (*piṇḍapāta*) refers to any kind of food. For whatever food falls into a monk’s bowl by way of alms-gathering (*piṇḍolya*), it is called "alms-food.
Alternatively, "alms-food" (*piṇḍapāta*) is the "falling of alms" (*piṇḍānaṃ pāto*); that is, the alms obtained here and there.
"Concourse" (*sannipāta*) means a gathering (*samūha*). "Neither for amusement" (*neva davāya*) means not for the sake of play, as with village children and the like;

it is said to mean "for the purpose of sport. "Neither for intoxication" (*na madāya*) means not for the sake of pride, as with boxers and the like; it is said to mean "for the purpose of pride in physical strength and pride in personal prowess.
"Neither for adornment" (*na maṇḍanāya*) means not for the purpose of decoration, as with women of the harem, courtesans, and the like; [it refers to] the limbs and members of the body...
"What has the purpose of making [the body] plump" is what is meant. "Not for the sake of adornment" means not for the sake of decoration like actors, dancers, and so forth;
"what has the purpose of making the complexion of the skin clear" is what is meant. And herein, "not for sport" is said for the purpose of abandoning the underlying tendency to delusion (*moha*);

"not for intoxication" is said for the purpose of abandoning the underlying tendency to hatred (*dosa*). "Not for beautification, not for adornment"—[this is for the purpose of abandoning the underlying tendency to lust].
This is for the purpose of abandoning the underlying tendency toward lust. "Neither for sport nor for intoxication"—this is for the purpose of preventing the arising of fetters within oneself.
"Neither for adornment nor for beautification"—this is for the purpose of preventing the arising of fetters in another as well.
It should be understood that by all four of these, the abandonment of unwise practice and the pursuit of sensual pleasure is stated.
"Only so far" (*yāvadeva*) refers to the meaning already stated. "Of this body" (*imassa kāyassa*) means of this material body composed of the four great elements.

"For its stability" (*ṭhitiyā*) means for the sake of continuous persistence. "For its maintenance" (*yāpanāya*) means for the sake of the non-interruption of its occurrence, or for the sake of its endurance over a long period.
For [the nutriment] is like the house-pillar used by the owner of an old house, or like the axle-oil used by a cartwright, for the sake of the body.
He consumes this almsfood for the purpose of stability and for the purpose of maintenance, not for the purpose of sport, intoxication, adornment, or beautification.
Furthermore, "stability" (ṭhiti) is a designation for the life-faculty (jīvitindriya);

therefore, it should be understood that by the phrase "for the stability and maintenance of this body," what is meant is "for the purpose of maintaining the activity of the life-faculty of this body."
“With the cessation of affliction”: affliction (*vihiṃsā*) means hunger in the sense of being a source of distress.
He partakes of this almsfood for the purpose of its cessation, just as one applies an ointment to a wound or uses remedies against heat, cold, and so forth.

“For the support of the holy life” (*brahmacariyānuggahāya*): it is for the sake of supporting both the holy life of the entire Dispensation and the holy life of the Path. For this [almsfood] is a condition for the partaking of almsfood...
Relying on physical strength, one who practices for the purpose of crossing the wilderness of existence by means of devotion to the three trainings consumes it for the support of the holy life,
just as those seeking to cross a wilderness consume the flesh of their own son, as those seeking to cross a river use a raft, and as those seeking to cross the ocean use a ship.
"Thus, by means of this consumption of alms-food, I shall ward off old feelings of hunger and not give rise to new feelings"— this is how one thinks:
"I shall ward off the old feeling of hunger and not produce a new feeling caused by excessive eating,
like those brahmins who, as some of them do, eat until they are full, stuffing themselves with their hands, or using a cloth, or a tray, or a bowl, or a crow's beak."
One does not indulge [in unwholesome conduct] even with the thought "I shall produce [suffering]," just as a sick person takes medicine.
Alternatively, that which is called "old feeling" arises by way of the condition of past kamma, depending upon present unsuitable and immoderate eating;
by destroying its condition through suitable and moderate eating, one counteracts that old feeling. And as for this [new feeling] produced now...
It is called "new feeling" because it arises in the future depending on the accumulation of kamma from improper enjoyment.
By means of proper enjoyment, one does not produce its root; thus, the meaning here should be understood as: "I shall not give rise to that new feeling.
To this extent, there is the inclusion of proper enjoyment, the abandoning of devotion to self-mortification, and the non-relinquishing of righteous happiness.
And it should be understood that [this] is also illuminated.

"And there will be sustenance for me" means: because of moderate consumption, there will be sustenance for me—consisting in a long life—due to the absence of any danger that would cut off the life-faculty or destroy the postures, for one whose existence depends upon these requisites.
He also makes use of it for the sake of his body, like one who is free from illness, on account of that [medicine]. "Faultlessness and comfortable living":
by avoiding improper seeking, receiving, and using, there is faultlessness; by using in moderation, there is comfortable living.
Discontent, lethargy, and restlessness arise due to the causes of unwholesome and immoderate use. Because of the absence of faults such as being censured by the wise...

Or there is blamelessness: through the arising of bodily strength due to the condition of eating what is suitable and in moderation, there is a comfortable dwelling. Or he partakes [of food] with the thought:
"By avoiding eating until the stomach is full and overflowing, there will be blamelessness through the abandoning of the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of drowsiness;
and by eating four or five mouthfuls less than required, there will be a comfortable dwelling through the restoration of fitness for the four postures. For this has been said:
“Having eaten four or five mouthfuls, one should drink water;
this is sufficient for a bhikkhu of resolute mind to dwell in comfort.
It should be understood that up to this point, the discernment of the purpose and the middle way of practice have been illustrated.
“Resting place” (*senāsana*) means both a bed (*sena*) and a seat (*āsana*). For wherever one lies—whether in a monastery (*vihāra*) or in a gabled hall (*aḍḍhayoga*) and so forth—that is a bed.
Wherever one sits or reclines, that is a seat. Taking these together, it is called a “resting place.

Regarding the phrase “for the purpose of warding off the perils of the climate and for delighting in seclusion”: in the sense of being something to be endured, the climate itself is the “peril of the climate” (*utuparissaya*).

For the purpose of dispelling dangers from the climate and for the purpose of delighting in seclusion. This means: for the purpose of dispelling whatever unsuitable climate causes bodily affliction or mental distraction—which must be dispelled by resorting to a suitable lodging—and for the sake of the bliss of solitude.
Granted, the dispelling of dangers from the climate has already been mentioned by way of warding off cold and so forth; however, [it is stated here] as follows:
It is said that in the use of robes, the purpose of covering the private parts with a sense of shame (*hirī*) is a constant necessity, whereas the other purposes occur only occasionally;
likewise, here too, it should be understood that this statement was made with reference to the constant warding off of the dangers of the climate (*utu-parissaya*).
Alternatively, the "climate" mentioned here is of the kind already described. However, "dangers" (*parissaya*) are of two kinds: manifest dangers and...
And there is the concealed danger. Therein, the manifest dangers are lions, tigers, and so forth; the concealed dangers are lust, hatred, and so forth.

Having understood and reflected upon that lodging which does not cause affliction through lack of protection or through seeing unsuitable forms and the like, the bhikkhu who makes use of it with wise consideration is one who uses the lodging with wise reflection (*paṭisaṅkhā yoniso senāsanaṃ*).
It should be understood that he makes use of it for the purpose of warding off the perils of the climate.
Regarding "requisites of medicine as support for the sick": here, "support" (paccaya) is in the sense of counteracting a disease; the meaning is "in the sense of going against [the illness].
This is a designation for whatever is suitable [as medicine]. It is called "the physician's work" because it has been permitted by him.
Medicine (*bhesajja*). Medicine as a requisite for the sick is "medicine-as-a-requisite-for-the-sick" (*gilānapaccaya-bhesajja*);

this refers to whatever is suitable for the sick, such as the physician’s treatment, oil, honey, molasses, and so forth. As for the term "requisite" (*parikkhāra*), in passages such as "well-equipped with the seven requisites of a city," it is said to mean a retinue or equipment.
However, in the verse: "The chariot has virtue as its equipment, meditation as its axle, and energy as its wheels," [it means something else].
In such contexts as these, it is an "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*). In passages such as, "And those requisites for life which must be procured by one who has gone forth," it is an "equipment" (*sambhāra*).

But here, both "equipment" and "retinue" (*parivāra*) are appropriate. For that medicinal support for the sick is indeed a retinue for life, and it is also equipment because it protects by not allowing an interval for the arising of diseases that destroy life.
Because it functions for a long time as its cause, it is therefore called a "requisite" (*parikkhāra*).
Thus, since it is both a requisite for the support of the sick and a medicine, it is "the requisite of medicine as a support for the sick. That is the requisite of medicine as a support for the sick.
Whatever is suitable for the sick, permitted by physicians—such as oil, honey, molasses, and so forth—is the "requisite for life."
This has been said. "Of those that have arisen" means of those that are born, become, and produced. Regarding the term "afflictive" (*veyyābādhika*):

here, "affliction" (*byābādha*) refers to the disturbance of the elements (*dhātu-kkhobha*) and the skin diseases, swellings, pustules, and so forth, which originate from it. They are called "afflictive" because they arise from affliction.

"Of feelings" (*vedanānaṃ*) refers to painful feelings, which are the results of unwholesome kamma. [The phrase is] "of those afflictive feelings. "For the sake of supreme non-affliction" (*abyābajjhaparamatāya*).
"By the state of ultimate freedom from suffering. The meaning is: "As long as that suffering has not all been abandoned.
Thus, in brief, this virtue dependent on requisites should be understood as having the characteristic of the wise reflection on the use of requisites.
As for the etymology here: because one uses robes and so forth by depending upon and relying on them...

Living beings go forth and proceed by means of them; therefore, they are called "conditions" (*paccaya*). That which is dependent upon those conditions is "dependent on conditions" (*paccayasannissita*). 19.
Thus, in this fourfold morality, the restraint of the *Pātimokkha* is to be accomplished through faith. Faith is the means of accomplishment.
For he is beyond the domain of disciples because of the laying down of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*). And here, the refusal to request the laying down of training rules is the illustration.
Therefore, having undertaken the training rule exactly as it was laid down in its entirety with faith, one should accomplish it thoroughly, without regard even for life. For this has been said:
“Just as a hen guards her eggs, as a yak guards its tail,
as a mother guards her beloved son, or as one guards a single eye—
so too should they guard their virtue.”
“Be exceedingly zealous and always respectful.

Furthermore, it has been said: “In this very way, Pāhārāda, whatever training rule I have laid down for my disciples, my disciples do not transgress it even for the sake of their lives. And regarding this matter, by robbers in the forest...
The stories of the bound elders (baddhathera) should be understood.
It is said that in the Mahāvattani forest, robbers bound an elder with black creepers and made him lie down.
While remaining exactly as he lay, the elder cultivated insight for seven days, attained the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), and passing away right there, was reborn in the Brahma-world.
Furthermore, they bound another elder in the island of Tambapaṇṇi with a rotting creeper and made him lie down. When a forest fire approached, he did not cut the creeper;
instead, having established insight (*vipassanā*), he attained final nibbāna as one who has reached the goal simultaneously with his body.
The Elder Abhaya, a reciter of the *Dīgha Nikāya*, seeing this while traveling with five hundred monks, cremated the elder’s body and erected a shrine.
Therefore, another faithful son of good family,
purifying the Pātimokkha, would rather give up his life than break the restraint of virtue prescribed by the Lord of the World.
And just as restraint by the Pātimokkha is accomplished through faith, so too restraint of the sense faculties is to be accomplished through mindfulness.
For that [restraint] has mindfulness as its instrument, because the sense faculties, when established in mindfulness, cannot be overrun by covetousness and other such defilements. Therefore:
"It would be better, bhikkhus, for the eye-faculty to be touched by a red-hot iron pin, burning, blazing, and glowing..."

By recollecting the "Discourse on the Burning" (*Ādittapariyāya*) according to the method beginning with, "It is thoroughly polished, but one does not grasp at the signs or secondary characteristics among forms cognizable by the eye," he—

by means of unclouded mindfulness— restrains the grasping at signs and so forth that would otherwise be followed by covetousness and other defilements in the consciousness proceeding through the eye-door and other doors toward objects such as forms.

It must be properly accomplished. For if this is not accomplished, even the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha becomes non-enduring and short-lived, like a crop that lacks the protection of surrounding branches.

Moreover, one is plundered by the thieves of the defilements, just as a village with its gates wide open is seized by robbers. And passion pierces through one's mind, just as rain penetrates a poorly-thatched house.
It is like rain. For it has been said:
“Guard the sense-faculty with regard to forms, sounds, tastes, scents, and tangibles;”
For these doors are left open and unguarded,
striking down those who plunder another’s wealth, just as a village is destroyed by raiders.
Just as rain penetrates a poorly-thatched house, so does craving pierce through the mind.
“In this way, lust pierces through the uncultivated mind.
But when that [virtue] has been accomplished, even the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha becomes enduring and long-lasting, like a crop well-surrounded by branches.
And it is not destroyed by the thieves of the defilements, just as a village with well-guarded gates is not plundered by others. It does not...
His mind is pierced by lust, just as rain penetrates a poorly roofed house. And this has been said:
“Guard the sense-faculty regarding forms, sounds, and likewise tastes, Smells, and tangibles.”
For these doors are closed and well-guarded;
they do not seize the property of another as plunderers do in a village.
Just as rain does not penetrate a well-roofed house, so too [does no evil enter one whose senses are guarded].
“In this way, when the mind is well-developed, lust does not penetrate it.
This, however, is an extremely exalted teaching.

For the mind is indeed quick to change; therefore, having dispelled arisen lust by means of attention to the foul (*asubha*), one must achieve restraint of the sense faculties, just as was done by the Elder Vaṅgīsa shortly after his going forth.
It is said that as this elder, who had recently gone forth, was walking for alms, lust arose upon seeing a certain woman. Thereupon, he said to the Elder Ānanda:
"I am burning with sensual lust; my mind is consumed by fire.
Pray, out of compassion, O Gotama, tell me how to extinguish it."
The Elder said:
"Because of the perversion of perception, your mind is burning;
avoid the sign associated with lust that appears beautiful."
“Develop the mind through the meditation on foulness, one-pointed and well-concentrated.
See conditioned phenomena as alien, as suffering, and not as self;
extinguish great passion, lest you burn again and again.”

The Elder, having dispelled lust, went for alms. Furthermore, a monk who fulfills the restraint of the sense faculties should be like the Elder Cittagutta, who dwelt in the Kuraṇḍaka Mahāleṇa Cave, or like the Elder Mahāmitta, who dwelt in the Coraka Mahāvihāra.
It is said that in the Kuraṇḍaka Mahāleṇa, there was a delightful mural painting of the Great Renunciation of the seven Buddhas.
A number of bhikkhus, while wandering about looking for lodgings, saw a piece of painted work and said, "Venerable sir, this painted work is beautiful.
The elder said, "Friends, for more than sixty years I have lived in this cave, yet I did not even know that there was such a thing as painted work;
it is only today, by relying on those with vision, that it has been known. [Thus spoke] the elder.
It is said that during his stay for such a long period, he had never before looked up at the cave even with his eyes open.
At the entrance of the cave there was a great *nāga* tree, which the Elder also had never looked up at.
He would know when it was in bloom simply by seeing the falling of its pollen on the ground every year.
Having heard of the Elder’s perfection of virtue, the king, desiring to pay him homage, sent for him three times;

but when the Elder did not come, he had the breasts of women with young children in that village bound up and caused them to be bribed, saying, “Let the children receive no milk until the Elder arrives. Out of compassion for the children, the Elder went to Mahāgāma.
Having heard this, the king said, “Go, my good man, and have the Elder enter; I shall receive the precepts.
He had the Elder brought to the inner palace, paid homage to him, and fed him. Then, saying, “Venerable sir, there is no opportunity today;

I shall receive the precepts tomorrow,” he took the Elder’s bowl, followed him a short distance, and having paid homage together with the queen, he turned back. Whether it was the king or the queen who paid homage, the Elder [accepted].
Or he would say, “May you be well, Great King. In this way, seven days passed.
The monks asked, “Venerable sir, why do you say, ‘May you be well, Great King,’ even when the king is bowing and the queen is bowing?
The Elder replied, “Friends, I do not make a distinction between ‘king’ or ‘queen. After the seven days had elapsed—
Thinking, "It is difficult for the Elder to dwell here," the King dismissed him. The Elder went to the Kuraṇḍaka Great Cave and, during the night, ascended the walking path.
A deity dwelling in a *nāga* tree stood there holding a staff-lamp.
Then, his meditation subject became exceedingly pure and manifest to him. The Elder thought, "Why is it that today my meditation subject has become so very..."
“...he makes it clear,” he said, joyful and having attained Arahantship immediately after the middle watch of the night, making the entire mountain resound. Therefore,
another clansman who desires his own welfare—
like a monkey in the wilderness, like a wild deer wandering in the forest— should likewise act.
Like a child, one should not be terrified, nor should one have restless eyes.
One should cast one's gaze downward and look only as far as the distance of a yoke;
one should not fall under the sway of a mind as fickle as a forest monkey.
A disease of poisonous swellings arose in the mother of the Elder Mahāmitta; her daughter had gone forth among the bhikkhunīs.
She said to her, "Go, noble lady, go to my brother, report my state of ill health, and bring back medicine.
She went and reported it. The Elder said, "I do not collect root medicines and such things..."
"I know how to prepare medicine; moreover, I shall prescribe medicine for you:
'From the moment I went forth, I have never before broken my sense-faculties and looked upon a form of a different sex with a mind accompanied by greed.
By this word of truth, may my mother be at ease. Go and say this to the laywoman."
“...and rub your body. She went and, having reported this matter, did exactly so.
At that very moment, the abscess on the laywoman melted away like a lump of foam and vanished.
Rising up, she thought, “If the Perfectly Enlightened One were still living, why would he not stroke with his webbed hand the head of a monk who resembles my own son?”
He uttered words of joy. Therefore:
"O sons of good family, may others too, having gone forth in this teaching, abide like the Elder Mitta in the excellent restraint of the faculties."
Just as restraint of the sense faculties is accomplished through mindfulness, so too is purity of livelihood to be accomplished through energy.
For that purity is achieved by means of energy, since the abandonment of wrong livelihood is possible for one who has applied energy correctly.

Therefore, having abandoned improper modes of seeking, this purity should be accomplished through right seeking—such as the practice of alms-gathering—by means of energy, ensuring that only what is obtained from a pure source is accepted.
One who makes use of requisites should avoid those of impure origin as one would a venomous snake.

In this regard, for one who has not undertaken the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), requisites obtained from the Saṅgha, from a group, or from lay followers who have gained confidence through his virtues such as teaching the Dhamma, are said to be of pure origin.
However, those obtained through the practice of alms-gathering (*piṇḍapāta-cariyā*) and so forth are of an exceedingly pure origin. This is the case for one who has undertaken the ascetic practices.

The ascetic practices (dhutaguṇa) such as the practice of alms-gathering (piṇḍapātacariyā), when undertaken by those who have faith in him according to the rules of the ascetic vows (dhutaṅga-niyama) and arising from a pure source,
are said to be "purely arisen. Furthermore, when putrid myrobalan and the four sweet substances (catumadhura) arose for him to allay a single ailment,
he thought, "Other fellow-celibates (sabrahmacārī) will also consume the four sweets," and [offered] only a piece of myrobalan.
For one who makes use [of requisites], the undertaking of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) is appropriate.

Indeed, such a person is called a "bhikkhu who follows the supreme noble lineage. Regarding those requisites, such as robes and so forth, for any bhikkhu who purifies his livelihood, it is not permissible to engage in making signs, hints, indirect talk, or direct requests concerning robes and almsfood. However, regarding lodgings...
For one who has not formally undertaken the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), it is permissible to engage in talk regarding signs and manifestations.

In this context, a "sign" (*nimitta*) refers to the reply "No one," given by a monk when laypeople ask him while he is preparing the ground or performing other such tasks for the sake of a dwelling, "Venerable sir, what are you doing?
Who is having this done? Or it refers to any other similar act of signaling. A "manifestation" (*obhāsa*) refers to [the following]: "Lay followers..."
“Where do you live? “In a palace, Bhante. Now, the statement, “But for monks, O lay followers, a palace is not permitted,” or whatever other such indirect hinting (*obhāsakamma*) there may be;

as well as what is called “indirect talk” (*parikathā*), namely the statement, “The lodging for the Saṅgha of monks is crowded,” or whatever other such figurative speech there may be; and regarding medicine, everything [is permitted].
It is permissible. However, as for medicine obtained in such a manner, once the illness has been cured, is it permissible to consume it or not?

Regarding this, the Vinayadharas say, "The Blessed One has provided the opening; therefore, it is permissible. The Suttantikas, however, say, "Even though there is no offense, it corrupts one's livelihood; therefore, it is not permissible.
But as for one who, even though permitted by the Blessed One, refrains from making gestures, hints, indirect talk, or explicit requests, and instead possesses qualities such as fewness of desires—
Relying [on this], even when the end of life has arrived, he makes use of arisen requisites other than light and so forth;
such a person is called "one whose way of life is supremely austere," just like the Elder Sāriputta.
It is said that on one occasion, while cultivating solitude together with the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, that venerable one—
He was dwelling in a certain forest, when one day a stomach-wind ailment arose and caused him extreme suffering.
In the evening, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna went to attend upon that venerable one;
seeing the elder lying down, he inquired about his condition and asked, "Friend, what used to relieve you in the past? The elder replied:
“In my time as a householder, friends, my mother would prepare milk-rice with unbroken grains, mixing it with ghee, honey, sugar, and so forth, and give it to me;
by that, I was comfortable. That venerable one replied, “Let it be so, friend. If there is merit for either me or you, perhaps we shall obtain it tomorrow.”
Now, a deity dwelling in a tree at the end of the walkway heard this conversation between them and thought, "Tomorrow I shall provide milk-rice for the noble one.
She went immediately to the family that supported the Elder, entered the body of the eldest son, and caused him great suffering.
When the kinsmen had gathered for his medical treatment, she said to them:
“If you prepare such rice porridge for the Elder tomorrow, I shall release him. They replied,
“Even without being told by you, we regularly give alms-food to the Elders,” and on the following day,
they prepared such rice porridge.
The Elder Mahāmoggallāna arrived early in the morning and said, "Friend, remain right here until I have returned from my almsround," and then he entered the village.
Those people came out to meet him, took the elder’s bowl, filled it with the aforementioned milk-rice, and gave it to him. The elder made a gesture as if to depart. They said, "Eat."
“Venerable sir, we shall give you yet another,” they said; and having fed the Elder, they gave him another bowlful.
The Elder went and offered it, saying, “Come, friend Sāriputta, eat this. When the Elder saw it, he thought, “This rice porridge is most pleasing;
how indeed was it obtained? Seeing the source of its origin, he said, “Friend Moggallāna,…”

“...the alms-food is not fit for consumption. Without even giving rise to the thought, “Alms-food brought by one such as I is not being consumed,” that venerable one took the bowl by its rim with a single word and turned it upside down to one side.
As soon as the milk-rice touched the ground, the Elder’s affliction vanished; from that time forth, [he lived for] forty-five years.
For years it did not arise again. Then he said to Mahāmoggallāna:
"Friend, even though the rice gruel produced by means of verbal intimation has come out through the anus and is moving upon the ground, it is still unfit to be consumed.
And he uttered this inspired utterance:
“If I were to eat this honeyed milk-rice produced by the manifestation of vocal intimation, my livelihood would be censured.
Even if my intestines were to come out and trail outside;”
“I would not break my livelihood even at the cost of giving up my life.
I shall satisfy my own mind and avoid wrong search;
I will never engage in a wrong search that is censured by the Buddha.”
The story of the Elder Mahātissa, who lived at Ciragumba and ate mangoes, should also be told here. Thus, in every respect:
“A wise ascetic who has gone forth out of faith should purify his livelihood, without even giving rise to a thought of improper search.”
Just as purity of livelihood is achieved through energy, so too should virtue dependent on the requisites be accomplished through wisdom.
For that virtue is established by wisdom, since one possessed of wisdom is capable of seeing both the danger and the benefit in the requisites.
Therefore, having abandoned greed for requisites, one should—when requisites have arisen through lawful and righteous means—apply wisdom according to the method already described.
One who uses [the requisites] after reflecting must achieve this.
In this regard, reflection is twofold: at the time of receiving the requisites and at the time of using them.
For even at the time of receiving, having reflected upon robes and so forth—either by way of their elements or by way of their repulsiveness—one should set them aside; beyond that...
For one who enjoys [the gift], the enjoyment is indeed blameless even at the time of enjoyment. In this regard, there is this definitive analysis:
there are four kinds of enjoyment—enjoyment by theft, enjoyment as a debt, enjoyment as an inheritance, and enjoyment as an owner.
Among these, the enjoyment of one who is immoral, even while sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha, is enjoyment by theft.
...so it is called. For one who is virtuous, using [requisites] without reflection is called "using them in debt.

Therefore, a robe should be reflected upon with each use; almsfood, with every morsel. One unable to do so should reflect during the morning meal, the afternoon meal, the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch of the night.
If dawn should rise while he is still not reflecting, he stands in the position of one who uses [requisites] in debt. This applies to the lodging as well.
One must reflect upon it each time it is used. Regarding medicinal requisites, mindfulness as a requisite condition is required both at the time of receiving them and at the time of using them.
Nevertheless, while this is so, there is an offense for one who exercises mindfulness at the time of receiving but not at the time of using;
however, there is no offense for one who fails to exercise mindfulness at the time of receiving but does so at the time of using.
Purification is indeed fourfold: purification by confession, purification by restraint, purification by search, and purification by reflection.
Therein, "purification by confession" refers to the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha; for it is called "purification by confession" because it is purified through confession.
"Purification by restraint" refers to the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties; for [it is so called] because of the thought, "I shall not do so again."
It is called "purity of restraint" because it is purified by the very restraint of the resolve of the mind.

"Purity of search" refers to the virtue of livelihood-purification; for that is called purity of search because it is purified by the search of one who, having abandoned wrong means of livelihood, procures requisites in accordance with the Dhamma and in a righteous manner. "Purity of reflection" refers to the virtue dependent on requisites.
For it is called "purity through reflection" because it is purified by the aforementioned kind of reflection. Therefore it was said:
"But there is no offense for one who applies mindfulness to the enjoyment [of requisites] rather than to the receiving.
The enjoyment of requisites by the seven types of trainees (sekkhas) is called "enjoyment as an inheritance," for they are indeed the sons of the Blessed One.
Therefore, being heirs to the requisites belonging to their father, they enjoy those requisites.
But do these [monks] enjoy the requisites of the Blessed One, or do they enjoy the requisites of householders?
Even though they are given by householders, because they have been authorized by the Blessed One, they belong to the Blessed One; therefore, they enjoy the requisites of the Blessed One.
[This] should be understood. Here, the *Dhammadāyāda Sutta* (The Discourse on the Heirs of the Dhamma) is the supporting proof.

The enjoyment by those whose taints are destroyed is called "enjoyment as owners. For they enjoy [the requisites] having become owners because they have transcended the servitude of craving (*taṇhā*).
Among these types of enjoyment, both "enjoyment as owners" and "enjoyment as heirs" are appropriate for all; however, "enjoyment as debtors" [is not].
It is not permissible. There is no discussion at all regarding enjoyment through theft.

However, this enjoyment by one who is virtuous and reflective is either an enjoyment free from debt—since it is the opposite of enjoyment under a debt—or it falls within the category of enjoyment as an inheritance.
For even a virtuous person, by virtue of being endowed with this training, is reckoned simply as a "learner" (sekha).

It goes. Now, among these types of enjoyment, since the enjoyment of ownership is the foremost, a bhikkhu who desires it should fulfill the virtue dependent on requisites by enjoying them after reflecting in the manner already described.
For one who acts in this way is a doer of what ought to be done. And this has been said:
“Alms-food, the monastery, and the lodgings,
as well as water and the removal of dust from the outer robe—
having heard the Dhamma taught by the Sugata,”
Having reflected, the disciple of supreme wisdom should practice accordingly:
"Therefore, regarding alms-food, bedding, and seats,
as well as the removal of dust and dirt from one's outer robe;"
Unstained by these things,
the bhikkhu is like a drop of water on a lotus leaf;
having received timely assistance from others.
Regarding hard foods, soft foods, and refreshments,
he should always know the proper measure, remaining constantly mindful,
just as one does with the application of ointment and the healing of a wound.
“Just as one eats the flesh of one’s own son in the wilderness, or as one uses oil as lubrication for an axle, so should one take food for the sake of maintenance, without being intoxicated by it.

And regarding the fulfillment of this virtue dependent on requisites, the story of the novice Saṅgharakkhita, his nephew, should be told. For he consumed [food] after having reflected properly. As it is said:
“My preceptor, while I was eating well-cooked rice, said:
‘O novice, do not, being unrestrained, burn your tongue!
Having heard my preceptor’s words, I then experienced a sense of spiritual urgency.”
Sitting upon a single seat, I attained arahantship:
“I, with my purpose fulfilled like the moon on the fifteenth day, have completely exhausted all taints;
now there is no further becoming.”
“Therefore, another who desires the complete destruction of suffering,
having reflected thoroughly, should make use of the requisites.
Thus, it is fourfold by way of the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha and so forth.
The First Pentad of Virtue (Paṭhamasīlapañcaka) 20.
The meaning of the first pentad among the fivefold divisions should be understood by way of the virtue of those not fully ordained, and so forth. For this is said in the *Paṭisambhidā*:
"What is virtue of limited purification? It is the virtue of the limited training rules for those not fully ordained. This...
The virtue of limited purity. What is the virtue of unlimited purity? The training rules of those who are fully ordained (upasampadā) are unlimited;
this is the virtue of unlimited purity. What is the virtue of fulfilled purity?
That of virtuous worldlings (puthujjanakalyāṇaka) who are devoted to wholesome states, who fulfill [the training] up to the limit of the trainee (sekha), and who are indifferent to body and life.
For those who have renounced their lives—this is the virtue of complete and pure purification (*paripuṇṇapārisuddhisīla*). What is the virtue of unattached purification (*aparāmaṭṭhapārisuddhisīla*)?
That of the seven types of trainees (*sekkha*)—this is the virtue of unattached purification. What is the virtue of tranquilized purification (*paṭippassaddhipārisuddhisīla*)?
That of the disciples of the Tathāgata who have destroyed the taints, of the paccekabuddhas, and of the Tathāgatas, the Arahants, the perfectly enlightened Buddhas.
“This is the virtue of purification by tranquility.

In this context, the virtue of those who are not fully ordained should be understood as “virtue of limited purification,” because it is limited by way of enumeration. For those who are fully ordained:
“Nine thousand million, and eight hundred million;”
“Fifty-one hundred thousand and another thirty-six:
these restraints of the Vinaya were proclaimed by the Fully Awakened One;
they are indicated by way of summary as the training in the restraint of the Vinaya.”

Thus, although it has a limit in terms of enumeration, it is called "virtue of boundless purification" (*apariyantapārisuddhisīla*) with reference both to its state of being undertaken in its entirety and to its having no perceived limit in terms of gain, fame, relatives, limbs, and life—just like the virtue of the Elder Mahātissa the Mango-eater who lived for a long time in a thicket.

For that venerable one was as follows: [The rest of the passage describes the Elder Mahātissa’s extreme asceticism and his refusal to eat even a single mango from a tree despite the entreaties of the king.]
“One may give up wealth for the sake of a limb, one may give up a limb while protecting one’s life;
a man who recollects the Dhamma may give up limb, wealth, and even his entire life.

Not forsaking this recollection of the True Person (sappurisānussati), he did not transgress the training rule even when his life was in danger. Relying on that very same morality of boundless purity, he attained Arahantship right there on the back of the lay follower. As it is said:
“Neither your father nor your mother, neither your kinsmen nor your relatives would perform such a deed for the sake of one who is virtuous.
Having aroused a sense of spiritual urgency and having reflected thoroughly, [you have done this].”
"While staying on his back, he attained Arahantship.
The virtue of the "virtuous ordinary persons" (puthujjanakalyāṇaka), from the moment of their full admission (upasampadā) onwards, is as utterly pure as a well-washed gem or well-refined gold;
because it is so exceedingly pure, it is free from even the slightest stain of a thought-moment and serves as the very foundation for Arahantship.
Because it exists, it is called "complete purity," as in the case of the Elder Saṅgharakkhita, the nephew of the Great Saṅgharakkhita.

It is said that when the Elder Saṅgharakkhita, who was over sixty years of age, lay upon his deathbed, the community of monks asked him about his attainment of the supramundane states. The Elder replied, "I have no supramundane dhamma. Then his attendant...
The young bhikkhu said, "Venerable sir, people from all around twelve yojanas have gathered together because you have attained final Nibbāna;
with the passing away of an ordinary person (puthujjana) such as yourself, the great multitude will fall into remorse.
"Friend, I did not apply myself to insight meditation with the thought, 'I shall see the Blessed One Metteyya. Therefore, please have me sit down."
"Please grant me the opportunity. He had the Elder sit down and went outside. As soon as he had gone out, the Elder attained *arahantship* and signaled for him with a fan.
The Sangha assembled and said, "Venerable sir, it was a difficult feat you performed to produce supramundane dhamma at such a time of death. "Friends, this was not difficult," [he replied].
Furthermore, I shall tell you what is difficult to do: "Friends, from the time of my going forth, I have never seen an action committed through lack of mindfulness or ignorance.
His nephew also attained Arahantship at the age of fifty in exactly the same way.
"Even if one has little learning, if one is not established in virtue..."
People censure him for both his conduct and his learning.
But if one has heard little yet is well-composed in virtue,
they praise him for his virtue, and his learning will come to fruition.
“Even if one is very learned, if one is not concentrated in virtue,
people censure them for their lack of virtue, and their learning does not bear fruit.
But even if one is very learned, if one is well-concentrated in virtue...”
They praise him for both his virtue and his learning:
"The disciple of the Buddha, who is learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, and possessed of wisdom—he is like a gem from the Jambū River; who would be fit to censure him?"
"The gods praise it, and even by Brahmā it is praised.

Furthermore, the virtue of those in training (sekkha) should be understood as "purity through non-attachment" because it is not adhered to by way of views; or else, the virtue of worldlings (puthujjana) that is not adhered to by way of lust should be understood as "purity through non-attachment," as in the case of the Elder Tissa, the son of a householder.
It was like his virtue. For that venerable one, desiring to establish himself in arahantship by relying on such virtue, said to his adversaries:
"Having broken both your feet, I shall make you understand:
I am repelled and ashamed; I loathe death with its lust."
“Having thus reflected and having investigated thoroughly with proper wisdom,
when the dawn had arrived, I attained Arahatship.
Another great elder, being severely ill and unable even to consume food with his own hand, was [surrounded] by his own urine and excrement.
Sinking down, he rolled about. Seeing him, a certain young man said, "Alas, the formations of life are suffering!
The great elder said to him: "Friend, if I were to die right now, I would attain the excellence of heaven;
of this I have no doubt. But as for the attainment gained by breaking this virtue—that is like abandoning the training after having attained it."
Having said, "It is like the state of a householder I have already attained," and thinking, "I shall die together with my virtue alone," he lay down right there.
While contemplating that very illness, he reached Arahantship and explained it to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with these verses:
"Stricken by a certain disease, ... [text continues]"
For one who is severely afflicted and tormented by disease,
this body quickly withers away,
like a flower placed in the dust under the sun.
“The ignoble is reckoned as noble, the impure is considered pure,
for one who does not see the true nature of the body, which is filled with various kinds of filth.
Woe to me, this afflicted, putrid body— foul-smelling, impure, and subject to disease!”
“Wherein people, being negligent and infatuated, let slip the path to rebirth in the world of the Sugata.

However, the virtue of the Arahants and others should be understood as “purity by subsiding” (*paṭippassaddhipārisuddhi*), because it is purified through the complete subsiding of all distress. Thus, it is fivefold by way of purity of limits (*pariyantapārisuddhi*) and so forth.
This is the second pentad of virtue.
In the second pentad, the meaning should be understood by way of the abandoning of killing living beings and so forth. For this is said in the *Paṭisambhidā*:
"The five precepts are: the virtue of abandoning killing living beings, the virtue of abstention, the virtue of volition, the virtue of restraint, and the virtue of non-transgression.
[These apply] to taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and malicious speech..."
of harsh speech, of idle chatter, of covetousness, of ill will, and of wrong view;
by renunciation, of sensual desire; by non-ill will, of ill will; by the perception of light, of sloth and torpor;
by non-distraction, of restlessness; by the discernment of phenomena, of doubt; by knowledge, of ignorance; and by gladness, of discontent.
By the first jhāna, the hindrances; by the second jhāna, applied and sustained thought;
by the third jhāna, rapture; by the fourth jhāna, pleasure and pain;

by the attainment of the base of infinite space, the perception of form, the perception of sensory reaction, and the perception of diversity; and by the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness, the perception of the base of infinite space.

of the perception of the base of infinite consciousness in relation to the attainment of the base of nothingness; of the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in relation to the attainment of the base of nothingness;
of the perception of permanence in relation to the contemplation of impermanence; of the perception of pleasure in relation to the contemplation of suffering;
of the perception of self in relation to the contemplation of non-self; of delight in relation to the contemplation of disenchantment; and of lust in relation to the contemplation of dispassion.
Through the contemplation of cessation, [one abandons] arising; through the contemplation of relinquishment, grasping;
through the contemplation of destruction, the perception of compactness; through the contemplation of vanishing, accumulation; through the contemplation of change, the perception of permanence;

through the contemplation of the signless, the sign; through the contemplation of the desireless, longing; through the contemplation of emptiness, misapprehension; and through the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena...

Through the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are, there is the relinquishing of adherence to grasping at the core; through the contemplation of danger, there is the relinquishing of adherence to delusion;
through the contemplation of reflection, there is the relinquishing of non-reflection; through the contemplation of turning away, there is the relinquishing of adherence to bondage;

and by means of the path of stream-entry, there is the relinquishing of those defilements associated with views; and by means of the path of once-returning, there is the relinquishing of gross defilements.
The abandoning of the underlying tendencies of the defilements by means of the path of non-returning, and the abandoning of all defilements by means of the path of arahantship, is virtue;
it is abstinence, volition, restraint, and non-transgression—this is virtue.
Such virtues lead to non-remorse of the mind, they lead to gladness, they lead to rapture, and they lead to tranquility.
They lead to gladness; they lead to cultivation; they lead to development;
they lead to frequent practice; they lead to adornment; they lead to equipment; they lead to retinue;
they lead to fulfillment; they lead to utter disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, and enlightenment.
“...they lead to Nibbāna.
And here, there is no such thing as “abandoning” apart from the mere non-arising of the aforementioned acts such as killing living beings.
For that specific abandoning is, in the sense of being the foundation for each respective wholesome state, [Nibbāna].
There is the act of bearing [in mind], and the undertaking by way of making it free from wavering.
Therefore, it is called "virtue" (*sīla*) in the sense of "habitual conduct" (*sīlana*), which consists of the aforementioned bearing and composure.

The other four factors [of virtue] are so designated by way of abstaining from this or that, by way of the restraint (*saṃvara*) of this or that, by way of the volition (*cetanā*) associated with both of those, and by way of the non-transgression of this or that for one who does not transgress.
And this was said with reference to the actual occurrence of the mind. However, their meaning as virtue has already been explained previously.
Thus, virtue is fivefold by way of the virtue of abandoning and so forth.

Up to this point, the answers to these questions have been completed: What is virtue? In what sense is it virtue? What are its characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause? What is the benefit of virtue? And how many kinds of virtue are there?

21. Regarding what was asked—"What is its defilement? What is its purification?"—we reply: The state of being broken and so forth is the defilement of virtue (*sīla*); the state of being unbroken and so forth is its purification. Furthermore, that state of being broken and so forth is caused by gain, fame, and the like.
And it is comprised by way of its divisions and by way of the sevenfold union of sexual intercourse.
For instance, if a person has broken a training rule at either the beginning or the end among the seven classes of offenses, their virtue is called "broken," like a garment torn at the edge.
But for one whose [virtue] is broken in the middle, [it is called "mottled"].
In the center of that [body], there is what is called a "hole," like a hole in a garment with a rent.

That whose [flesh] is split in two or three places in succession is called "spotted" (*sabala*), like a cow whose body color—black, red, or some other—is variegated by a dissimilar color arising on its back or belly.
That whose [flesh] is split here and there is variegated by drops of dissimilar color appearing here and there.
It is called "karmāsa" (corrupted) like a cow. Thus, first of all, through division caused by gain and so forth, there comes to be the state of being broken and so on.
Likewise, by way of the sevenfold union of sexual intercourse. For it was said by the Blessed One:
"Here, Brahmin, a certain ascetic or brahmin, claiming to be one who lives the holy life rightly, does not indeed..."
He engages in sexual intercourse with a woman; moreover, he consents to a woman’s anointing, massaging, bathing, and rubbing down, and he relishes that, desires it, and finds satisfaction in it.
This too, brahmin, is a breach, a flaw, and a blemish of the holy life.
“...and even sexual intercourse. This, brahmin, is called practicing an impure holy life;
one is fettered by the bond of sexual union and is not liberated from birth, nor from aging and death... [as before] ...I say that one is not liberated from suffering.
“Furthermore, brahmin, here a certain ascetic or... [as before] ...claiming to be such, does not indeed [engage] with a woman...”
Together with a woman, he enters into the attainment of the couple. He does not consent to the anointing of a woman...
[and so on] ... nor to her embrace. Rather, he laughs, plays, and dallies with a woman; he relishes that... [and so on] ...
I say that he is not liberated from suffering.
“Furthermore, brahmin, here a certain ascetic or [brahmin]... does not indeed engage in sexual intercourse with a woman.
Nor does he consent to being rubbed by a woman...
Nor does he laugh, play, or joke with a woman. However, he [looks] from eye to eye with a woman.”
“He contemplates and gazes upon it; he relishes it... [as before] ...I say that he is not liberated from suffering.
“Furthermore, brahmin, here a certain ascetic or... [as before] ...neither with a woman, nor by means of a woman, nor for the sake of a woman...
[as before] ...he gazes upon her. Moreover, he hears the sound of a woman.”
"Whether behind a wall or behind a fence, while laughing, speaking, singing, or weeping—if one relishes that...
[as before] ...I say it is suffering.
"Furthermore, brahmin, here a certain ascetic or... [as before] ...neither with a woman, nor for a woman..."

Nor does he [suffer] because of a woman... nor because of a woman’s... [and so on]... nor even when she is weeping. Rather, he recollects those things that were previously shared with a woman—laughing, talking, and playing—and he relishes them... [and so on]... I say this is suffering.
"Furthermore, brahmin, here a certain ascetic or... [and so on]... indeed not because of a woman... [and so on]... nor even..."
...of a woman... nor does he recall those former instances of laughing, conversing, and playing with her.
Rather, he sees a householder or a householder’s son endowed with and possessed of the five cords of sensual pleasure, diverting themselves; he relishes that... I say this is suffering.
“Furthermore, brahmin, here a certain ascetic or [brahmin]... does not consort with women...
nor does he see a householder or a householder’s son... enjoying himself. Rather, he leads the holy life aspiring for one or another order of gods, thinking:
‘By this virtue, or vow, or austerity, or holy life, may I—’”
‘I shall become a god, or some other kind of deity. He relishes that, he desires that, and he finds satisfaction in that.
This too, Brahmin, is a breach, a flaw, a blemish, and a mottling of the holy life.

Thus, it should be understood that the state of being breached and so forth is comprised both by the sevenfold breach caused by gain and other motives, and by the sevenfold union of sexual intercourse.

Furthermore, the state of being "unbroken" and so forth regarding the training precepts consists in: (1) the non-violation of the precepts in every respect; (2) the performance of the necessary remedies for those that have been violated, provided they are remediable;

(3) the absence of the sevenfold union of sexual misconduct; and (4) the absence of other evil qualities such as anger, enmity, hypocrisy, spite, envy, avarice, deceit, guile, obstinacy, aggression, conceit, arrogance, vanity, and negligence.
It is comprised for the sake of non-arising and for the arising of qualities such as fewness of wishes, contentment, and effacement.
For those precepts which are unbroken even for the sake of gain and so forth; or which, though broken through the fault of negligence, have been restored;
or which are not impaired by sexual intercourse, anger, resentment, or other evil states—all these are entirely unbroken.
They are said to be "without cracks, without flaws, and without blemishes. Precisely because they bring about the state of being free, they are "free";
because they are praised by the wise, they are "praised by the wise"; because they are not adhered to by craving or views, they are "unadhered to";
and because they lead to access concentration or absorption concentration, they are "conducive to concentration."
Therefore, this state of theirs—being "unbroken" and so forth—should be understood as "cleansing.
Furthermore, this cleansing comes about in two ways: by seeing the danger in the failure of virtue, and by seeing the benefit in the perfection of virtue.
In this regard, it is said: "Bhikkhus, there are these five dangers for one who is immoral due to the failure of virtue..."
In this manner, according to the method of the Suttas, the danger of failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*) is to be seen.
Furthermore, a person who is immoral, on account of that immorality, becomes disagreeable to gods and humans; he is not to be instructed by his fellow celibates (*sabrahmacārī*);
he suffers under the censures for immorality; and he feels remorse when hearing the praise of those possessing virtue. And because of that state of immorality—
He is as ugly as a hempen garment. For those who follow his example, he is a painful touch, since it brings them suffering in the states of deprivation for a long time.
To those from whom he accepts gifts, he is of little value, since he renders their offering fruitless.
He is as difficult to cleanse as a cesspool of excrement that has collected over many years. Like a firebrand from a charnel ground, he is excluded on both sides.
Even while claiming the status of a bhikkhu, he is no bhikkhu at all—like a donkey following a herd of cattle;

like a man who is constantly terrified by his enemies; like a corpse unworthy of communal association; even if endowed with qualities such as learning, he is unworthy of honor from his fellow celibates, like the cremation fire to brahmins;
and he is incapable of attaining distinction, like a blind man regarding the sight of forms.
He is hopeless regarding the true Dhamma, like a low-caste boy regarding a kingdom.
Even while thinking "I am happy," he is actually suffering because he shares in the suffering described in the *Agniskandha-pariyāya* (The Simile of the Mass of Fire).

For the minds of the immoral—those whose hearts are attached to the gratification found in the enjoyment of the five strands of sensual pleasure, in homage, and in honor—are [bound] by that very cause.

Even by the mere recollection [of this], the Blessed One— who has made the ripening of kamma manifest in every way— showed an exceedingly bitter suffering capable of producing heart-burning and causing the vomiting of hot blood,
and said: "Bhikkhus, do you see that great mass of fire, burning and blazing?"
"Is it aflame?"—"Yes, venerable sir. "What do you think, monks? Which would be better:
to embrace that great mass of fire, burning, blazing, and aflame, and sit down near it or lie down upon it;
or [to embrace] a Kṣatriya maiden, or a Brāhmaṇa maiden, or a householder’s daughter, with their soft and delicate hands and feet?"
"Having embraced her, one might sit down near her or lie down near her. "Venerable sir, it would be better indeed that one should embrace a noble maiden...
or lie down near her. For it is painful, venerable sir, that one should [sit down near or] lie down near that great mass of fire...
It is this, bhikkhus, that I announce to you; it is this, bhikkhus, that I declare to you: namely, this very thing."
It would be better for that immoral person— of evil nature, impure and suspicious conduct,
one whose actions are concealed, a non-recluse claiming to be a recluse, an unchaste person claiming to be chaste,
internally rotten, lustful, and like a putrid drain— to lie down upon that great mass of fire... Why is that?
"For on that account, monks, he might meet death or experience suffering equal to death;
yet for that reason alone, with the breakup of the body after death, he would not reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, downfall, or hell.

Having thus shown, by means of the simile of the mass of fire, the suffering conditioned by the enjoyment of the five cords of sensual pleasure dependent on women, [the Blessed One] said this by the same method—
“What do you think, monks? Which is better:

that a strong man should wrap a stout, hairy rope around both your shins and rub it, thereby cutting through the outer skin, having cut through the outer skin, cutting through the hide, having cut through the hide, cutting through the flesh, having cut through the flesh, cutting through the sinew, and having cut through the sinew, [cutting through] the bone?”

“He would cut through the bone, and having cut through the bone, he would stand striking right into the marrow,” or “he would accept the salutation of wealthy kṣatriyas, wealthy brahmins, or wealthy householders.
“What do you think, monks? Which is better: that a strong man should [strike one] with a sharp spear...”
“Or he might strike one on the chest with it while it is still dripping wet; or he might accept the salutation with joined palms from wealthy khattiyas, wealthy brahmins, or wealthy householders.
“What do you think, monks? Which would be better: that a strong man should [strike one] with a red-hot iron plate...?”
“...or one might wrap one’s body in a blazing, flaming, and glowing iron sheet;
or one might use a robe given out of faith by wealthy kṣatriyas, wealthy brahmins, or wealthy householders.
“What do you think, monks? Which of these two would be better: that a strong man [should wrap one’s body] with a red-hot iron spike...”

Suppose one were to open one's mouth with it burning, blazing, and glowing, and then throw into the mouth a red-hot iron ball, burning, blazing, and glowing; it would burn the lips, burn the mouth, the tongue, the throat, and the stomach,
and having taken hold of the intestines and the mesentery, it would pass out through the lower part— just as [it would happen to] a noble...
“...or would he enjoy almsfood given in faith by brahmins or wealthy householders?

And: “What do you think, monks? Which is better: that a strong man should seize one by the head or by the shoulder and place one upon a red-hot iron bed or an iron chair—blazing, flaming, and glowing—or [the other]?”
“Or he might have one sit down or lie down upon it, or he might use a bed or chair given in faith by kṣatriyas, brahmins, or wealthy householders. [The Buddha said:
“What do you think, monks? Which is better: that a strong man should [hold one] with his feet upwards…”
Having seized him by the feet and head, one might throw him into a glowing iron cauldron— blazing, fiercely burning, and aflame—
and while being cooked there amidst a mass of froth, he would go up at one moment, down at another, and across at another;
yet whatever [gift] was given out of faith by Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, or wealthy householders...
“...or enjoy a monastery.

By means of these similes—the wild rope, the sharp spear, the heated iron plate, the iron ball, the iron bed, the iron chair, and the iron cauldron—he demonstrated the suffering involved in the conditions of salutation, the performance of añjali, and the use of robes, almsfood, beds, chairs, and monasteries. Therefore:
“The bitter fruit is a suffering more intense than the pain of embracing a mass of fire;”
For one who has not abandoned sensual pleasure, how can there be happiness for one whose virtue is broken?

What kind of happiness is there for one whose virtue has failed, who partakes in suffering exceeding even the pain of being struck by a strong rope of hair? What indeed is the pleasure for one who accepts salutations?
What pleasure is there for the immoral man in accepting the salutations of those with faith,
which is the cause of excessive suffering such as the pain of being struck by a sword?
What indeed is the pleasure of using robes for one who is unrestrained?
For one who must long experience the touch of blazing iron spikes in hell,
even a sweet alms-meal is like deadly poison for the immoral person;
by him, glowing iron balls must be swallowed for a long time.
Even that which is considered pleasant is suffering for one lacking virtue:
the use of beds and chairs, when they will long torment him with glowing iron beds and chairs.
What delight can there be in dwelling in a monastery given by the faithful for one who is immoral?
One must dwell among those who are like iron cauldrons,
by whom [the wicked] are placed therein. The World-Honored One,
censuring the one who is of suspicious conduct, born of dregs, impure, evil, and rotten within, spoke thus.
Futile is the life of one who is unrestrained, who merely wears the garb of a recluse;
for that non-recluse, his life is ruined as he carries about a self that is utterly wasted.
Like excrement or a corpse, those desiring adornment avoid him here in this world.
What indeed is the life of one who possesses virtue yet is not virtuous?
He is not freed from all fears, but is deprived of all the happiness of attainment;
he has bolted the gates to heaven and has ascended the path to the lower realms.
Who else indeed is the object of compassion for compassionate people, other than the immoral person?
"The immoral one is like a creeper"—thus there are manifold faults.
By such reflection, one should understand the vision of the danger in the failure of virtue, and conversely, the vision of the benefits in the perfection of virtue. Furthermore—
His manner of wearing the bowl and robes is inspiring;
fruitful is the renunciation of one whose virtue is perfectly stainless.
For a bhikkhu of pure virtue, there is no fear of self-reproach or the like.
Like the sun [dispelling] darkness, it does not penetrate his heart.
A bhikkhu, shining with the perfection of virtue in the forest of asceticism,
shines like the moon in the sky with its attainment of radiance.
The fragrance of the body of a virtuous bhikkhu brings joy even to the gods;
what need is there to speak of the fragrance of his virtue?
It surpasses the excellence of all other kinds of perfumes.
Unimpeded in all directions, the fragrance of virtue wafts abroad.
Even small services rendered to those possessed of virtue yield great fruit;
thus one becomes virtuous, a recipient of honor and respect.
The taints pertaining to this present life do not afflict the virtuous one.
The virtuous one digs out the root of sufferings in future lives.
Whatever prosperity there is among humans, and whatever excellence there is among the gods—
For one who is accomplished in virtue, this is not difficult to obtain if they so desire.
But that which is ultimate peace, this attainment of Nibbāna—
toward that alone does the mind of one accomplished in virtue run.
"The wise person should thus contemplate the manifold benefits of virtue, which is the root of all success.
For one who contemplates in this way, the mind becomes inclined toward the perfection of virtue, having become fearful of its failure. Therefore:
Having seen this disadvantage of the failure of virtue and this benefit of the perfection of virtue as they have been described, one should purify one’s virtue with all diligence.

Up to this point, virtue has been explained within the Path of Purification (*Visuddhimagga*), which was taught under the headings of virtue, concentration, and wisdom by means of the verse: "A wise man, established in virtue... (Dhp 1–2).
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of Virtue," in the *Visuddhimagga* composed for the delight of the virtuous. 2.
The Description of the Ascetic Practices (*Dhutaṅga*).

22. Now, in order to fulfill those qualities such as fewness of wishes and contentment by which there is the purification of the aforementioned kind of virtue, a practitioner who has undertaken virtue must undertake the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*).

For in this way, his defilements are washed away by the water of qualities such as fewness of wishes, contentment, effacement, seclusion, reduction [of greed], the arousal of energy, and being easy to support.

His virtue will become perfectly pure and his observances will be successfully fulfilled. Thus, with all his conduct purified by the quality of blameless virtue and observances, and having established himself in the first three ancient noble lineages, he will become worthy of attaining the fourth noble lineage, which is known as delighting in meditation.
Therefore, we shall begin the discourse on the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*).

For the Blessed One has prescribed the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas) for those sons of good family who have renounced worldly gain, who are indifferent to both body and life, and who desire to accomplish the practice that is in accordance with the Dhamma. They are as follows:

the practice of wearing rag-robes, the practice of wearing the three robes, the practice of eating only by alms, the practice of wandering for alms from house to house, the practice of eating at a single sitting, and the practice of eating from a single bowl.

The practice of eating only one meal a day, the forest-dweller’s practice, the tree-root-dweller’s practice, the open-air-dweller’s practice, the charnel-ground-dweller’s practice, the any-bed-user’s practice, and the sitter’s practice. Regarding these:
In terms of their meaning, characteristics, and so forth, And in terms of their undertaking and method of performance;
The detailed exposition should be understood by way of its divisions and classifications, by way of the specific benefits of each,
by way of the triad of the wholesome, by way of the analysis of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) and so forth, and also by way of both summary and detail.

23. Regarding that, first, as for the term *paṃsukūla*: it is called *paṃsukūla* in the sense of being "protruding" because it stands upon the dust of any place such as a street, a charnel ground, or a heap of refuse;
or else, it is called *paṃsukūla* because it "goes to (*ulati*)" a state of loathsomeness (*kucchita-bhāva*) like dust—that is to say, it becomes something loathsome. Thus...
The wearing of rag-robes (*paṃsukūla*) that have been obtained is *paṃsukūla*; one whose habit (*sīla*) is that is a rag-robe wearer (*paṃsukūlika*).
A limb of the rag-robe wearer is a "rag-robe-wearer limb" (*paṃsukūlikaṅga*). "Limb" (*aṅga*) is said to mean a cause.
Therefore, it should be understood as a designation for that undertaking by which one becomes a rag-robe wearer.

In this same manner, one who has the three robes—consisting of the *saṅghāṭi*, *uttarāsaṅga*, and *antaravāsaka*—as his virtue is called a *tecīvarika*. The factor of one who possesses the three robes is the *tecīvarika-aṅga*.
Furthermore, *piṇḍapāta* is the falling (*pāta*) of morsels of food (*piṇḍa*) reckoned as alms;
what is meant is that the morsels given by others fall into the bowl. One who "gathers" (*uñchati*) that *piṇḍapāta* by approaching various families [is a *piṇḍapātika*].

He is called a *piṇḍapātīka* because he seeks alms (*piṇḍa*). Alternatively, his practice (*vata*) is to fall upon (*patituṃ*) for alms; thus he is a *piṇḍapātī*. "To fall" means to wander for them; one who is a *piṇḍapātī* is therefore a *piṇḍapātīka*.
The factor of the alms-seeker is the "alms-seeker's factor" (*piṇḍapātikaṅga*).
"Gift" (*dāna*) is said to mean cutting off (*avakhaṇḍana*); that which is free from gift is "without-cutting-off" (*apadāna*), meaning non-interruption. Together with...
"By means of *apadāna*, [they] go from house to house (*sapadāna*); what is meant is that they move without skipping any houses.
One whose virtue is to wander in this manner is a *sapadānacārī*; one who is a *sapadānacārī* is a *sapadānacāriko*. A constituent part of that is the *sapadānacārika-aṅga*.
Eating at a single sitting is *ekāsana*; one whose virtue is that is an *ekāsaniko*. A constituent part of that is the *ekāsanika-aṅga*."
Because the use of a second vessel has been rejected, the alms-food taken in only a single bowl is called *pattapiṇḍa*.
Now, having formed the perception of "bowl-alms" (*pattapiṇḍa*) regarding the taking of alms in the bowl, one who has this as his virtue (*sīla*) is a *pattapiṇḍika*.
The factor of such a person is the *pattapiṇḍika-aṅga* (the practice of eating only from the bowl).
*Khalu* is a particle used in the sense of prohibition. *Pacchābhatta* means food obtained after one has already been invited (*pavārita*).

The eating of that *pacchābhatta* is *pacchābhattabhojana*. Having formed the perception of "after-meal" (*pacchābhatta*) with respect to that *pacchābhattabhojana*, one for whom the precept (*sīla*) is "not after-meal" is a *pacchābhattika*; [the opposite] is a non-*pacchābhattika*.
"One who eats only what is left over" (*khalupacchābhattiko*). This is the name for one who has renounced eating food that has been left over by formal undertaking.
However, it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "The word *khalu* refers to a certain bird. Having taken a fruit in its beak, once that has fallen, it does not eat another again.
One who is like that is a *khalupacchābhattiko*. The practice of such a person is the 'practice of eating only what is left over' (*khalupacchābhattika-aṅga*)."
One whose habit is dwelling in the forest is a forest-dweller (*āraññika*). The factor of that [dwelling] is the forest-dweller’s factor (*āraññikaṅga*).

Dwelling at the foot of a tree is “at the foot of a tree” (*rukkhamūla*); one whose habit is that is a tree-root dweller (*rukkhamūlika*). The factor of a tree-root dweller is the tree-root dweller’s factor (*rukkhamūlikaṅga*). The same method applies to the factors of an open-air dweller (*abbhokāsika*) and a charnel-ground dweller (*sosānika*).
“Whatever bedding there is, however it has been spread—that reaches you”; this refers to the lodging that was first assigned in such a manner.

It is a designation. One who has the habit of dwelling in whatever seat is provided is a *yathāsañthatika*. The practice of such a person is the *yathāsañthatika-aṅga* (the practice of using whatever seat is provided).
One who has the habit of dwelling in a sitting posture, having rejected lying down, is a *nesajjika*. The practice of such a person is the *nesajjika-aṅga* (the practice of the sitting posture).
All these, however, are factors (*aṅga*) of a bhikkhu who has shaken off the defilements (*dhuta-kilesa*) through their respective undertakings;
or else, they are called "ascetic practices" (*dhutaṅga*) because knowledge—which is conventionally termed "shaken off" (*dhuta*) due to its shaking off of defilements—is a factor for them.
Alternatively, they are called "ascetic practices" because they are both "shaken off" (*dhuta*) by the shaking off of opposing qualities and "factors" (*aṅga*) of the practice. Thus...
The analysis of these [ascetic practices] should be understood here according to their meaning.
Furthermore, all of these have the characteristic of volition consisting in undertaking. And this has been said: "He who undertakes is the person;
those by which he undertakes are the states of consciousness and mental factors; that volition which consists in the undertaking is the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga); and that..."

...he rejects it; that is the basis. And all of them have the function of destroying greediness, they are manifested as the state of being free from greediness, and their proximate cause is the noble qualities such as fewness of wishes.
Thus should the exposition here be understood by way of their characteristics and so forth.
Regarding the five [points] beginning with "as to the method of undertaking," all the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) were indeed undertaken by the Blessed One himself while he was still living.
They should be undertaken in the presence of [the Teacher]. In the absence of the Teacher, they should be undertaken in the presence of a Great Disciple who has attained *parinibbāna*.

If he is not available, one may undertake them in the presence of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), a Non-returner (*anāgāmī*), a Once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*), a Stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), one versed in the Three Piṭakas, one versed in the Two Piṭakas, one versed in the One Piṭaka, one versed in a single recitation (*ekasaṅgītika*), or a teacher of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathācariya*).
If he is not available, one may do so in the presence of one who maintains the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅgadharo*); if even he is not available...
Having swept the precincts of the shrine (*cetiyaṅgaṇa*) and sitting in the *ukkuṭika* posture, these [vows] should be undertaken as if speaking in the presence of the Fully Enlightened One;
moreover, it is indeed appropriate to undertake them oneself as well.

In this context, the story of the elder brother of the two Bhātika Theras at Cetiyapabbata should be told, illustrating his desire for the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*). This, then, is the general discourse.
1. The Discourse on the Refuse-Rag-Wearer’s Practice (Paṃsukūlikaṅgakathā) 24. Now we shall explain the undertaking, the method, the classification, the breach, and the benefits of each practice.

First, regarding the refuse-rag-wearer’s practice (*paṃsukūlikaṅga*), there are these two [formulations]: “I reject robes given by householders; I undertake the refuse-rag-wearer’s practice. Regarding these two:
Among the various statements, one has undertaken [the practice] by means of one or another. This, first of all, is the undertaking here.

Now, for him who has thus undertaken the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga), there is clothing from a charnel ground, clothing from a shop, cloth from a highway, cloth from a rubbish heap, cloth from a weaver’s loom, cloth from a bathing place, cloth from a ford, cloth discarded after being used, cloth burnt by fire, cloth gnawed by cattle, or cloth gnawed by termites.
Having taken any one of these robes— a mouse-gnawed one, one cut at the edge, one with frayed borders, one brought as a banner, a stupa-cloth,
a robe belonging to a recluse, one used for consecration, one produced by supernormal power, a traveler’s robe, one brought by the wind,
one given by a deity, or one from the ocean— having torn it apart, having discarded the weak parts, and having washed the strong parts, he should make a robe.
One should discard an old householder’s robe and then use it.
In this context, "cemetery cloth" (*sosānika*) refers to what has fallen in a cemetery. "Shop cloth" (*pāpaṇika*) refers to what has fallen at the door of a shop.
"Street cloth" (*rathiyacoḷa*) refers to a discarded rag thrown onto a street through a window by those seeking merit. "Refuse cloth" (*saṅkāracoḷa*) refers to [cloth found] in a place of refuse.
"Discarded cloth" (*chaḍḍitacoḷakaṃ*): "Sotthiya" refers to a garment discarded after wiping away the impurities of childbirth.

It is said that the mother of the minister Tissa had the birth impurities wiped with a cloth worth a hundred [pieces] and discarded it on the Tālaveḷi Road, thinking, "The refuse-rag wearers (*paṃsukūlika*) will take it.
The monks take it only for the purpose of patching worn areas. "Bathing cloth" (*nhānacoḷaṃ*): that which is used by those who treat spirits...
