Barbers go away after discarding their lead [used for hair-dyeing], thinking it is "the rags of ill-fortune" (*kāḷakaṇṇicoḷa*).
"Bathing-rags" (*titthacoḷa*) refers to pieces of cloth discarded at bathing-places.

"Rags from those who have gone and returned" (*gatapaccāgata*) refers to what people discard after going to the cemetery, returning, and bathing. "Burnt by fire" (*aggiḍaḍḍha*) refers to a place burnt by fire; for people...
They discard them. Items such as those gnawed by cattle and the like are well known; people indeed discard even such things. Regarding "brought on a banner":
those boarding a boat fasten a banner and ascend; it is permissible to take that after they have passed out of sight.
Also, a banner fastened and set up on a battlefield may be taken once both armies have departed.
*Thūpacīvara* (stupa-cloth) refers to that which was offered as a ritual oblation after surrounding an anthill. *Samaṇacīvara* (ascetic-cloth) refers to what belongs to a bhikkhu.

*Ābhisekika* (consecration-cloth) refers to cloth discarded at the site of a king’s consecration. *Iddhimaya* (supernormal-cloth) refers to the robe of one who comes as a bhikkhu by means of psychic power (*ehibhikkhu*).
*Panthika* (road-cloth) refers to what has been dropped along the way. Furthermore, that which has been dropped through the forgetfulness of its owners—
One should take it after guarding it for a short time. "Brought by the wind" means that which has been struck by the wind and cast far away;
it is permissible to take that when the owner is not seen. "Given by deities" refers to what was given by deities, as in the case of the Elder Anuruddha.
"From the sea" refers to what has been washed ashore by the waves of the ocean.
However, that which is given with the words "We give this to the Saṅgha," or that which is obtained by those wandering for scraps of cloth, is not *paṃsukūla*.
Also, regarding gifts from monks (*bhikkhudattiya*), that which is given after having been assigned by the annual distribution (*vassagga*), or which is bedding or robe-cloth, is not *paṃsukūla*.
Only that which is given without having been assigned is *paṃsukūla*. Even in that case, that which [is placed] at the feet of a monk by the donors...
It was set aside; however, because it was given by that monk after placing it in the hand of a paṃsukūlika (rag-robe wearer), it is called "pure on one side.
That which was given by placing it in the hand of a monk, but then placed at his feet, is also "pure on one side.
That which was placed at the feet of the monk and given back in exactly the same manner is "pure on both sides. That which...
What is obtained by placing it in one’s hand and placed right there in the hand is called “unexcellent rag-robe.
Thus, having understood this classification of rag-robes, a wearer of rag-robes should use the robe; this is the rule in this matter.
Now, as for the sub-classification: there are three types of rag-robe wearers—the strict, the moderate, and the mild. Among these, [the strict] uses only that from a charnel ground...
One who takes it up himself is "strict. One who takes what has been set aside with the thought, "Those who have gone forth will take it," is "middling.
One who takes what is given after being placed at his feet is "gentle.
Among these, for anyone of them, the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) is broken at the very moment he consents to a gift from a householder according to his own preference. This is the distinction here.
Furthermore, this is the benefit: because of the statement, "The going-forth is dependent upon rag-robe clothing," there is the presence of practice in accordance with that dependence;
establishment in the first noble lineage (ariyavaṃsa); absence of the suffering of guarding [possessions]; independence in livelihood; fearlessness from the danger of thieves;
absence of craving for enjoyment; being a requisite suitable for a recluse; and [the fact that] they are few and easily obtained.
And those [requisites] are blameless— this is the Blessed One’s praise of the nature of the requisites, their inspiring quality,
the accomplishment of the fruits of fewness of wishes and so forth, the cultivation of right practice, and the induction of following one’s example in future generations.
For the destruction of Māra’s army, the ascetic wears rag-robes.
Clad in armor for battle, he shines like a noble warrior (khattiya).
Having cast aside fine garments such as those from Kāsi,
who would not wear this rag-robe (paṃsukūla) worn by the Honored One of the World?
"Therefore, indeed, a bhikkhu, recollecting his own promise,

should delight in rag-robes which are suitable for one practicing yoga. This concludes, first of all, the commentary on the undertaking, the methods, the classifications, the distinctions, and the benefits regarding the practice of wearing rag-robes (*paṃsukūlikaṅga*).
2. Discussion on the Practice of Wearing Only Three Robes (Tecīvarikaṅga) 25.

Immediately following that, however, the practice of wearing only three robes (*tecīvarikaṅga*) is undertaken by means of one of these two statements: “I reject a fourth robe; I undertake the practice of wearing only three robes.
Now, when that wearer of three robes obtains cloth for a robe, he must not use it until he is unable to make it due to physical discomfort.
It should be set aside as long as he does not obtain someone to look after it, or as long as some necessity such as a needle does not arise for him;
there is no fault in setting it aside for those reasons. However, from the time it has been dyed onwards, it is not permitted to set it aside;
one who does so is called a "thief of the ascetic practice" (*dhutaṅga*). This is its procedure.

As for its classification, this too is threefold. In that regard, according to the strictest rule (*ukkaṭṭha*), at the time of dyeing, one should first dye either the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*) or the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*).
Having dyed that, one should wear it and then dye the other. Having dyed that, one should dye the outer cloak (*saṅghāṭi*).
However, it is not permitted to wear the *saṅghāṭi* as an undergarment. This is the proper conduct (*vatta*) for him when staying in a monastery within a village boundary.
In the forest, however, it is permissible for two to wash together and then dye [the robes].
One should sit in a place close enough so that, upon seeing someone, one is able to pull the saffron robe over oneself and cover it.

For the middle-ranking bhikkhu, there is what is called a "dyeing-saffron-robe" in the dye-hall; it is permissible to perform the dyeing work while wearing that either as an undergarment or as an upper robe.
It is permissible for one who is gentle to perform dyeing work after having put on or wrapped himself in the robes of bhikkhus who are like-minded.
In that case, it is also permissible for him to use a rug belonging to those bhikkhus while staying there. However, it is not permissible to carry it about.
It is also permissible to use the robes of like-minded bhikkhus from time to time. This applies to one who observes the ascetic practice of using only three robes (*tecīvarika*).
However, only a shoulder-cloth (*aṃsakāsāva*) currently in use is permissible; moreover, it must be exactly one span wide and three cubits long.
At the very moment these three robes are accepted, the fourth ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*) is broken. This is the distinction here.
This, however, is the benefit: the monk who uses only three robes is content with a robe that merely serves to cover the body.
Consequently, his movement is like that of a bird—taking up only what he needs; there is little exertion for him; he avoids the accumulation of clothing;
his way of life is light; he abandons greed for extra robes; through moderation regarding what is permissible, his life is austere; and [he fosters] fewness of wishes and so forth.
"The accomplishment of the fruit" refers to the fact that such qualities as these come to be.
Having abandoned craving for extra robes and avoiding hoarding, the wise yogi,
relishing the flavor of the happiness of contentment, becomes one who wears the three robes.

Therefore, like a bird with its wings, the excellent yogi who has taken up the practice of wearing only three robes should take delight in the restriction of robes if he wishes to wander in happiness. This concludes the commentary on the undertaking, the method, the classification, the analysis, and the benefits of the factor of the three robes.
3. The Discussion on the Practice of Begging for Alms (Piṇḍapātikaṅga) 26.
The practice of begging for alms is undertaken by means of one of these formulas: “I reject extra acquisitions; I undertake the practice of begging for alms.
Now, that alms-collector [should avoid] communal meals, meals designated for a specific person, invitations to meals, meals provided by tickets, ...

The fourteen kinds of meals that should not be accepted are: the fortnightly meal, the Uposatha meal, the first-of-the-month meal, the meal for newcomers, the meal for those departing, the meal for the sick, the meal for those attending the sick, the monastery meal, the meal for those on duty, and the meal by rotation.
However, if it is not said in such a manner as "Take the meal for the Saṅgha," etc., [then it may be accepted].
"If the Saṅgha would accept alms in our house, you too may accept alms," having said this, they are given;
it is permissible to accept those. It is also permissible to accept non-material voting sticks (*salākā*) from the Saṅgha, as well as cooked rice prepared in the monastery; such is its regulation.
As for its classification, however, this too is threefold. Among these, the strict (*ukkaṭṭha*) [type] accepts alms brought from both the front and the back.
He accepts alms; he also gives to those standing at the door of his bowl as they take their bowls.

He accepts the food given after returning from his alms-round, but on that particular day he does not accept alms while sitting down. The one of medium capacity accepts alms even while sitting down on that day, but he does not consent to an invitation for the following day.
The gentle one consents to alms for the following day and even for the day after.
Neither of those two obtains the happiness of dwelling as a servant; only the superior one (ukkaṭṭha) obtains it. It is said that in a certain village there was a noble lineage (ariyavaṃsa).
The superior one said to the others, "Come, friends, for the sake of hearing the Dhamma.
Among them, one said, "Venerable sir, I have been made to sit by a certain person. Another said, "Venerable sir, I have accepted an alms-offering from one person for tomorrow's meal."
Thus both of them have fallen away. The other, however, having gone out for alms early in the morning and returned, experienced the flavor of the Dhamma.
For all three of these, the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) is broken at the very moment they consent to an extra gain, such as a meal provided by the Saṅgha. This is the distinction here.
Furthermore, this is the benefit: because of the statement, "The going forth is dependent upon eating alms-food," there is the presence of a practice in accordance with that dependence.

Establishment in the second noble lineage; independence in livelihood; being a requisite praised by the Blessed One as "both few, easy to obtain, and blameless"; the crushing of indolence; purity of livelihood;
fulfillment of the training rules; not being supported by others; acting for the benefit of others; the abandoning of pride; and the warding off of craving for flavors.
There is non-offensiveness regarding the training rules on eating in groups and eating in succession; there is living in conformity with fewness of wishes and other virtues;
there is the cultivation of right practice; and there is compassion for future generations.
One who is content with alms-food scraps lives a life independent of others.
Having abandoned greed for food, the wanderer becomes impartial in all directions.
He dispels slothfulness, and his livelihood becomes purified.
Therefore, a wise person should not despise the practice of wandering for alms.
For such a one as this—
“The alms-gathering bhikkhu,
who supports himself and does not support others;”
“Even the gods envy such a one,
provided he is not dependent on gain and fame.
This concludes the commentary on the undertaking, the method, the classification, the divisions, and the benefits of the practice of eating only almsfood.
4. Discussion on the Factor of Begging for Alms from House to House (Sapadānacārikaṅga) 27.

The factor of begging for alms from house to house is undertaken by means of one of these statements: “I reject wandering for the sake of greed; I undertake the factor of begging for alms from house to house.
That person who begs for alms from house to house, however, must stand at the village gate and observe whether there is any danger. For whomsoever...
If there is danger on the street or in the village, it is permissible to abandon that place and wander elsewhere.
If one receives nothing at a certain house-door, on the street, or in the village, one should go after designating that area as "not a village.
However, it is not permissible to leave a place where one does receive something. Furthermore, this bhikkhu should enter [the village] earlier than others.
For in this way, he will be able to leave the place where he is unwell and go elsewhere.
However, if people who are giving alms at his monastery or those coming along the road take his bowl and give him alms-food, that is permissible.
And while traveling on this path, even when it is time for the alms-round, he must certainly wander through any village he reaches without passing it by.
In this regard, the rule for it is that one should wander through the village in sequence, whether obtaining nothing at all or obtaining only a little.

As for its classification, however, this too is threefold. Among these, the strict (ukkaṭṭha) does not accept alms brought from the front, nor alms brought from behind, nor even what is given after he has returned; rather, at the bowl-door (pattadvāra), he holds out his bowl—
He relinquishes [the bowl]. Indeed, in this ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*), there is no one equal to the Elder Mahākassapa.
Even for him, only the place where he relinquished his bowl is known. The Middle One accepts alms brought either from the front or from behind, even those brought while he is returning;
he also relinquishes the bowl at the door, but he does not sit waiting for alms. Thus he is a superior *piṇḍapātika*.
It conforms [to the rule]. On that day, one who is weak-minded sits down and waits.
However, for these three types of people, the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) is broken the very moment a desire for gain arises.

This is the point of failure here. Furthermore, the benefits are as follows: being like a constant guest among families, being like the moon, abandoning stinginess regarding families, and receiving equal compassion.

The absence of the disadvantages associated with being a benefactor to families, not delighting in invitations, having no desire for offerings, and living in accordance with fewness of wishes and other such qualities.
Like the moon, he is ever-new among families;
free from stinginess, he is compassionate toward all equally.
Free from the dangers of seeking alms within one's own circle,
the bhikkhu here wanders for alms in regular succession;
therefore, having abandoned the practice of greed, he proceeds.
With downcast eyes, looking only a yoke’s length ahead,
the wise man, desiring to move with the gait of a serpent upon the earth, should practice the alms-round from house to house.

This concludes the commentary on the undertaking, the method, the classification, the breach, and the benefits regarding the practice of going for alms from house to house in uninterrupted succession. 5.

Discussion of the Practice of Eating at a Single Sitting (Ekāsanika-aṅga) The practice of eating at a single sitting is undertaken by means of one of these two formulas: “I refuse food from various seats; I undertake the practice of eating at a single sitting.”
Furthermore, when that one who eats at a single sitting (ekāsanika) sits in the dining hall, he should not sit in the seat of the elders;
rather, he should observe a suitable seat, thinking, "This will come to me," and then sit down.
If his teacher (ācariya) or preceptor (upajjhāya) arrives while his meal is unfinished, it is proper for him to rise and perform the duties of hospitality. Thus said the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷābhaya.
He further said: "One should guard either the seat or the food; this one has left his meal unfinished, therefore let him perform the duty, but let him not eat. This is the rule for him.
As for its classification, it is also threefold. In that regard, whether it be little or much, for whomsoever—
When one inserts the hand into the food, one may not take anything else from there.
Even if people bring ghee and other items, thinking, "The elder has eaten nothing," these are permitted only for the purpose of medicine and not for the purpose of food.
The middle [type of restraint] allows one to take more as long as the food in the bowl has not been exhausted. This is the *bhojanapariyantika* (the restraint regarding the limit of eating).
It is called "muduka" (gentle). One who is gentle is permitted to eat as long as he does not rise from his seat.
For he is either "limited by water," meaning he eats until he takes the water for washing the bowl, or "limited by the seat," meaning he eats until he rises.
However, for all three of these, the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) is broken at the moment the meal is eaten while sitting in various places. This is the distinction here.

The benefits, moreover, are: freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness, strength, a comfortable dwelling, no offense due to the condition of not having leftovers, the dispelling of craving for flavors, and living in conformity with fewness of wishes and other such qualities.
One who delights in eating at a single sitting—
No ailment arises from the condition of food for one who is not greedy for flavors;
such a person endures [sickness] and does not neglect his own duty.
Thus, with a mind purified, one should generate [joy] toward that which causes dwelling in comfort,
which is practiced by those who delight in pure effacement.
"He restrains himself regarding food at a single sitting.
This concludes the commentary on the undertaking, the method, the classification, the divisions, and the benefits of the practice of eating at a single sitting (*ekāsanika*).
6. Discussion of the Practice of Eating from the Alms Bowl (*pattapiṇḍika*).

29. The practice of eating from one’s alms bowl (*pattapiṇḍikaṅga*) is undertaken by means of either of these two statements: “I reject a second vessel; I undertake the practice of eating from one’s alms bowl.

However, when that person who eats from their alms bowl is at the time of drinking rice-gruel (*yāgu*), having placed it in the bowl, if a curry is obtained, he should either eat the curry first or drink the rice-gruel. But if he puts [the curry] into the rice-gruel, [it is as if he were putting it] into rotten fish, etc.
When a condiment is added, the gruel becomes repulsive; therefore, it is permissible to consume it only after making it non-repulsive.
It was with reference to such a condiment that this was said. However, that which is non-repulsive, such as honey, sugar, and so forth, may be added.
And when taking it, one should take only a moderate amount. Raw vegetables [may be taken] with the hand.

It is permissible to take it and eat it; however, one should not do so, but rather place it directly into the bowl. Since the use of a second vessel is prohibited, even another leaf from a tree is not permitted; such is the rule for this.
Furthermore, in its classification, this too is threefold. Among these, for one who is strict (ukkaṭṭha), even refuse is [not permitted] except at the time of eating sugarcane.
It is not permissible to discard [the food]. It is not permissible to eat by breaking apart even a lump of boiled rice, fish, meat, or cakes.
For one of medium capacity, it is permissible to break it with one hand and eat; such a person is called a "hand-yogi.
However, one who is weak is called a "bowl-yogi"; for him, whatever can be placed in the bowl, all of that is taken with the hand.
Or it is permissible to break it with one's teeth and eat it.
However, for all three of these [types of bowls], the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*) is broken at the very moment one consents to a second vessel.

This is the point of distinction here. As for the benefits: there is the dispelling of craving for various flavors; the abandoning of discontent; seeing only the purpose of food; the absence of weariness from carrying bowls and such; eating without distraction; and living in conformity with fewness of wishes and other virtues.
Having abandoned the distraction of various vessels,
with eyes cast downward like one digging for the roots of craving for flavors, the one of noble vows,
with a joyful mind, bore contentment as if it were his own form.
"Who else but the bowl-almsman would eat his food?
This concludes the commentary on the undertaking, the method, the classification, the breach, and the benefits regarding the factor of the bowl-almsman.
7. Discussion of the Factor of Not Eating After the Proper Time.

30. The practice of eating only one meal a day (*khalupacchābhattika-aṅga*) is undertaken by means of one of these two formulas: “I reject eating leftover food; I undertake the practice of eating only one meal a day.

However, that practitioner who observes the practice of eating only one meal a day must not, after having invited others to eat (*pavāretvā*), again have food made permissible (*kappiyaṃ kāretvā*) and then eat it.

This is its rule. As for its classification, this too is threefold. Among these, the strict practitioner (*ukkaṭṭha*) is so called because the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) occurs with the very first morsel.
There is no offense in that case; however, when he is swallowing [the food], it constitutes an offense for him if he rejects other [food].
Therefore, having been thus invited, after swallowing the first morsel, he does not eat a second morsel. One of medium temperament eats only that specific food with which he was invited.
One of mild temperament, however, continues eating as long as he does not rise from his seat.

However, for all three of these types of those who have invited [others to eat], the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) is broken at the moment of eating after having had something made allowable (kappiyaṃ).

This is the point of its failure here. Its benefit, moreover, is this: it keeps one far from the offense of eating what is not left over; it prevents gluttony; it ensures there is no storage of worldly things; there is no need for further searching; and it is a way of living in conformity with fewness of wishes and other virtues.
The wise man does not succumb to the fatigue of searching, nor does he make a store.
The yogi who eats only one meal a day abandons gluttony.
Therefore, a yogi who wishes to shake off faults should cultivate this ascetic practice (dhutaṅga), which is praised by the Sugata and generates qualities such as contentment and progress.

This concludes the commentary on the undertaking, the method, the classification, the breach, and the benefits regarding the practice of eating only after the meal. 8. Discussion of the Forest-Dweller’s Practice (Āraññikaṅga). 31.
The forest-dweller’s practice is undertaken by means of either of these two statements: “I reject a dwelling within a village; I undertake the practice of being a forest-dweller.”

However, that forest-dweller must abandon his lodging in a village and cause the dawn to rise in the forest. In this context, "a village lodging" refers to the village itself together with its precincts.
A "village" means any place whatsoever—whether consisting of a single hut or many huts, enclosed or unenclosed, inhabited by humans or non-humans—even a caravan encamped for more than four months.
The "precincts of a village" refer to the area surrounding an enclosed village; if it has two boundary markers (*indakhīla*), as in the case of Anurādhapura...
The range of a stone-throw is the distance from which a man of medium strength standing at the inner *indakhīla* (city gate pillar) can throw a clod of earth.
Regarding its definition, the Vinaya experts state that it is the area within which a clod thrown by young men who, displaying their strength, extend their arms and fling it would fall;
however, the Suttantikas [define it] according to the rule for warding off crows.

They say "thrown" means this: in an unenclosed village, the area within which a woman standing at the door of the most remote house throws water from a vessel is the vicinity of the house (*gharūpacāra*).
Beyond that, according to the method already stated, one stone’s throw is the village, and a second stone’s throw is the vicinity of the village.
Regarding the forest (*arañña*), first, according to the method of the Vinaya, it is stated: "With the exception of the village and its precincts, all this is forest.
According to the method of the Abhidhamma, it is stated: "Having gone out beyond the threshold pillar, all this is forest.
However, according to the method of the Suttanta, it is stated: "A forest dwelling (*āraññaka*) is a resting place that is at least five hundred bow-lengths distant [from a village]."

This is the characteristic. It should be determined by measuring from the boundary post (*indakhīla*) of a village that is enclosed by a fence using a teacher’s bow that has been strung, or from the first throw of a clod of earth in the case of an unenclosed village, up to the enclosure of the monastery (*vihāra*).
However, if the monastery is unenclosed, it should be measured starting from whichever is the very first dwelling or dining hall.
It is stated in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā* that even if a permanent assembly hall, a Bodhi tree, or a shrine is far from the dwelling, one should measure the area by defining its boundaries.

However, in the *Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that one should measure between the two stone-throw distances after extending the precincts of both the monastery and the village. This is the standard in this matter.
Even if a village is nearby, and the sound of humans is heard by those staying in the monastery, it may not be possible to go directly because of obstructions such as mountains or rivers.

Whatever its usual path may be—even if one must travel by boat—one should take a distance of five hundred dhanus along that route. However, for the purpose of fulfilling the requirements regarding a nearby village...
If one blocks the path here and there, this person is a thief of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga).

However, if the preceptor or teacher of a forest-dwelling bhikkhu falls ill, and he cannot obtain suitable care in the forest, he should bring him to a lodging within a village and attend to him. But having departed from there at the proper time...
The dawn must be made to rise while one is still in the place where the [ascetic] factors are practiced. If their illness increases at the time of sunrise, they should perform their duties;
one should not be obsessed with the purity of the ascetic factor (*dhutaṅga*). This is its regulation. As for its classification, it is also threefold.

Among these, the strict practitioner (*ukkaṭṭha*) must always make the dawn rise in the forest. The intermediate practitioner (*majjhima*) is permitted to dwell in a village during the four months of the rains. The mild practitioner (*muduka*) may do so even during the winter.

Furthermore, for any of these three [types of persons], when they have come from the forest to a village lodging to hear the Dhamma during the prescribed time, the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) is not broken even if dawn has already risen.
For those who, having heard it, are departing, it is not broken even if dawn rises while they are on the way.
However, if—even though the preacher has risen—they think, "We will lie down for a moment and then go," [the practice is broken].

The breach of this ascetic practice occurs when dawn breaks while one is still sleeping, or when one allows dawn to break while staying in a village dwelling by one's own choice; this is the point of failure here.
Furthermore, this is the benefit: a forest-dwelling bhikkhu who attends to the perception of the forest is capable of obtaining what he has not yet obtained.
Whether to attain concentration or to protect what has been attained, the Teacher is pleased with him. As it is said:
"Therefore, Nāgita, I am pleased with that bhikkhu’s dwelling in the forest.
For one who dwells in remote lodgings, unwholesome forms and other sense objects do not distract the mind; he becomes free from anxiety and abandons attachment to life.
He relishes the flavor of the bliss of seclusion, and even his state as a wearer of rag-robes becomes fitting for him.
Secluded and unassociated, delighting in remote lodgings,
he gratifies the heart of the Protector through dwelling in the forest.
The happiness that an ascetic finds dwelling alone in the forest—
neither the gods, nor even those led by Indra, can find its flavor.
Wearing the rag-robe like a suit of armor, he indeed possesses it.
Having gone to the forest-battle, with the remaining ascetic practices as his weapons,
he is capable before long of conquering Māra and his host;
therefore, a wise person should find delight in dwelling in the forest.
This is the commentary on the undertaking, the methods, the classifications, the divisions, and the benefits of the forest-dweller’s practice (*āraññikaṅga*). 9.

Discourse on the Tree-root Dweller’s Practice (*rukkhamūlikaṅga*) 32. The tree-root dweller’s practice is undertaken by means of either of these two formulas: “I reject a roofed dwelling; I undertake the tree-root dweller’s practice,” or “I undertake the tree-root dweller’s practice.”
However, for that one who dwells at the foot of a tree, the rule is as follows:

having avoided these types of trees—a boundary-tree, a shrine-tree, a resinous-tree, a fruit-tree, a bat-tree, a hollow-tree, and a tree standing in the middle of a monastery—one should take a tree standing on the outskirts of the monastery. This is the procedure for him.
Furthermore, this is also threefold by way of classification. Among these, the superior [type] may not have a tree selected according to his own preference tended;
he must dwell there after removing the fallen leaves with his foot. The intermediate [type] may have it tended by those who happen to arrive at that place.
The inferior [type], having summoned monastery attendants (*ārāmika*) or novice monks (*samaṇuddesa*), may have it cleaned.
Having had it leveled, having had sand sprinkled over it, having had a perimeter wall constructed, and having had a gate installed, one should dwell there.
On the Uposatha day, however, the tree-root dweller should not sit there, but should sit elsewhere in a concealed place.

The moment any of these three take up residence under a roof, the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) is broken. According to the reciters of the Aṅguttara Nikāya, it is broken the very instant dawn breaks while they know they are under a roof. This is the point of its breach.
Furthermore, this is the benefit: because of the statement, “Going forth is dependent upon the root of a tree as a lodging,” there is the presence of a practice corresponding to that dependence;
because of the Blessed One’s praise of the requisites as being “few, easy to obtain, and blameless”;
because of the arousal of the perception of impermanence by frequently observing the changes in young leaves; and [the abandonment] of stinginess regarding lodgings and delighting in work...
Absence of company, dwelling together with deities, and living in accordance with fewness of desires—
this is praised by the Supreme Buddha and called a "reliance.
Where else is there a dwelling for one who seeks seclusion like that at the foot of a tree?
Free from stinginess regarding dwellings, protected by the deities,
living in seclusion at the foot of a tree, he is truly virtuous.
The leaves are green and delightful, while some have turned pale and fallen.
Passing by the leaves of trees, one dispels the perception of permanence.
Therefore, the wise person should not despise a secluded foot of a tree— the inheritance of the Buddhas and the abode for those who delight in meditation.
This concludes the commentary on the undertaking, the method, the classification, the analysis, and the benefits of the tree-root-dweller’s practice (*rukkhamūlika-aṅga*). 10.

Discussion of the Open-Air-Dweller’s Practice (*abbhokāsika-aṅga*): The open-air-dweller’s practice is undertaken by means of one of these declarations: “I reject both the covered [dwellings] and the root of trees; I undertake the open-air-dweller’s practice.”
However, it is permissible for that open-air dweller to enter the Uposatha hall for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma or for the Uposatha ceremony.
If it rains while he has entered, he should not leave while the rain is falling; rather, he should depart once the rain has ceased.
Or, having entered the dining hall or the fire-hall, he may perform his duties; [in the case] of the dining hall, [he should attend] upon the elder bhikkhus...
It is permissible to enter a sheltered place after having asked permission from the resident monk, or while reciting or causing others to recite;
it is also permissible to bring beds, chairs, and so forth that were left outside into the interior.
If one traveling on a road has taken up the requisites of senior monks, it is permissible to enter a hall standing by the middle of the road if it is raining. If nothing [has been taken],...
Once it has been taken up, it is not permissible to go with haste thinking, "I will stay in the hall.
However, having gone at one's natural pace, once one has entered, one may stay until the end of the rains; this is the rule for him. The same method applies to the tree-root dweller as well.
As for the classification, he too is of three kinds. Among them, for the one who is strict (ukkaṭṭha), [the dwelling] is either a tree, a mountain, or a house.
It is not permissible to dwell depending upon [these]. One should dwell having constructed a robe-tent (cīvarakuṭi) in an open space itself.
For one of medium capacity, it is permissible to dwell depending upon trees, mountains, or houses, provided one does not enter inside them.

For one of mild capacity, even a mountain slope that is not enclosed by a boundary, a bower of branches, a bench or mat, or a hut standing on its own site abandoned by field-watchers and the like, is permissible.

However, for any of these three, the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) is broken at the very moment one enters a dwelling or the foot of a tree for the purpose of staying there. According to the reciters of the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, it is broken as soon as dawn has risen after one has become aware of being there.
This is the point of failure here. As for the benefits: it severs the impediment of a fixed residence; it dispels sloth and torpor;

it accords with the praise, "Like deer, the bhikkhus wander unattached and dwell without a home"; it brings about freedom from attachment; it provides the state of belonging to all four quarters; and it ensures a lifestyle in conformity with fewness of wishes and other such virtues.
In an open space, suitable and not difficult to find for the state of homelessness—
a canopy of stars and gems, illuminated by the light of the moon-lamp—
the bhikkhu dwelt with a mind like that of a deer.
Having dispelled sloth and torpor, and being devoted to delighting in meditation,
one soon finds the flavor of the taste of seclusion;
therefore, indeed, the wise person should be one who delights in the open air.
This concludes the commentary on the undertaking, the method, the classification, the breach, and the benefits of the practice of living in the open air (*abbhokāsikaṅga*). 11.

The Discussion on the Practice of Dwelling in Cemeteries (*sosānikaṅga*) 34. The practice of dwelling in cemeteries is undertaken by means of one of these formulas: "I do not reject the cemetery; I undertake the practice of dwelling in cemeteries."
Furthermore, that forest-dweller should not live in a place where people, when settling a village, designate as "this is a charnel ground.
For it is not called a charnel ground while a corpse is still burning;
rather, from the time it has been cremated onwards, even if it has remained abandoned for twelve years, it is indeed a charnel ground.

Furthermore, one who dwells there should not do so by having walkways, pavilions, and so forth constructed, nor by arranging beds and chairs, nor by setting out drinking water and water for washing, nor by teaching the Dhamma.
For this ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) is a heavy one;

therefore, in order to ward off any dangers that may arise, one should dwell with diligence after informing either the senior monk of the Saṅgha or an official of the king. While walking, one should keep one's gaze directed only a short distance ahead.
One should walk back and forth while looking toward the cremation ground.
When going to the charnel ground, one should avoid the main road and travel by a by-path.
One should define the object of meditation during the day itself; for in this way, it will not be terrifying for him at night, as non-human beings [do not appear] at night.
Even while wandering about after crying out [in distress], one must not be struck by anyone. It is not permitted to go to the charnel ground for even a single day.
The reciters of the Aṅguttara Nikāya say that it is permissible to spend the middle watch at the charnel ground and return during the last watch.
Non-human beings do not like offerings of sesame flour, bean cakes, fish, meat, milk, oil, sugar, or other kinds of hard and soft food.
It should be frequented. "One should not enter a family home"—this is its rule.
As for its classification, it is also threefold. Therein, for one who is strict (ukkaṭṭha), he must dwell only where there is constant burning, constant corpses, and constant wailing.
For one who is moderate (majjhima), it is permissible provided any one of these three is present. For one who is mild (muduka), according to the method already stated...
It is sufficient merely to reach the cemetery.

However, for these three [ascetics], the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*) is not broken by making their dwelling in the cemetery. "On the day they have not yet gone to the cemetery," say the reciters of the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*. This is the distinction here.
Furthermore, the benefit is this: the attainment of mindfulness of death, dwelling in heedfulness, the realization of the sign of the foul, and the dispelling of sensual lust.
Frequent observation of the nature of the body, abundance of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), the abandoning of pride in health and so forth,
endurance of fear and terror, being held in high esteem by non-human beings, and living in conformity with fewness of desires and other such qualities—
this is indeed the state of one who dwells in a charnel ground, owing to the power of the meditation on death.
Even when he has fallen asleep, the faults of negligence do not touch him;
and as he beholds many corpses,
his mind does not come under the sway of the power of sensual desires.
He experiences vast spiritual urgency and does not fall into intoxication;
seeking nibbāna, he strives correctly.
Because it brings manifold virtues, he undertakes the practice of dwelling in charnel grounds.
"It should be practiced with a heart inclined toward Nibbāna.
This concludes the commentary on the undertaking, the methods, the classifications, the distinctions, and the benefits of the charnel-ground-dweller’s practice (sosānika-aṅga).
12. Discussion of the Practice of Sleeping Wherever One Is (yathāsanthatika-aṅga).

35. The practice of accepting whatever seat is offered (*yathāsanthatika-aṅga*) is undertaken by means of one of these two formulas: “I reject greed for lodgings; I undertake the practice of accepting whatever seat is offered.

Now, that practitioner who accepts whatever seat is offered should be content with whatever lodging has been assigned to him, thinking, “This is yours,” and he should not cause another to be brought up.
This is its procedure. As for its classification, this too is threefold. Among these, the one who is strict (*ukkaṭṭha*) [considers] his own obtained lodging to be far away...
One is not permitted to ask whether it is too near, or whether it is harassed by non-human beings such as *dīghajātika* spirits, or whether it is hot or cold.
One who is of middle character is permitted to ask. However, even he is not permitted to go and inspect it.
But one who is mild-natured may go and inspect it; if it does not please him, he is permitted to take another.
However, the breach of this ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) occurs as soon as greed for any of these three types of lodgings arises;

this is the point of its failure here. Its benefits, moreover, are: acting upon the instruction that says, "One should be content with what one has received"; wishing for the welfare of one's fellow celibates;
abandoning the discrimination between the inferior and the superior; the relinquishing of attachment and aversion; and the closing of the door against excessive desire.
The practice in accordance with fewness of wishes and so forth:
Content with whatever he receives, the ascetic who lives wherever he is assigned to stay sleeps happily and without conceptual elaboration, even on a bed of straw.
He does not crave for what is superior, nor does he become angry when receiving what is inferior;
he shows compassion and benefits his junior fellow-celibates.
Therefore, one should practice that which is observed by the noble ones and praised by the Bull among Sages.
"A wise person should apply himself to it, as much as he finds comfortable.
This concludes the commentary on the undertaking, the methods, the classifications, the analysis, and the benefits of the practice of "as-it-is-spread" (yathāsanthatika).
13. Discussion of the Practice of Sitting (nesajjika).
36. The practice of always sitting (*nesajjikaṅga*) is undertaken by means of either of these two formulas: “I reject lying down; I undertake the practice of always sitting.

However, that one who always sits must rise during one of the three watches of the night and engage in walking meditation (*caṅkama*). For among the postures, lying down is simply not permitted for him.
This is its rule. As for its classification, this too is threefold. Among these, for the most rigorous practitioner, there is neither a backrest nor a cloth folded into a cushion.
An āyogapaṭṭa (a cloth band) is not permitted. For one of medium [strength], any one of these three is permitted.
For one of weak [strength], even a back-rest, a pillow made of cloth, an āyogapaṭṭa, a bolster, a five-limbed [pillow], or a seven-limbed [pillow] is permitted.
The five-limbed one is made together with a back-rest. The so-called seven-limbed one has, in addition to the back-rest, [two] on both sides...
It is done together with [using] supports. It is said that they made this for the Elder Miḷābhaya; the elder, having become a non-returner (anāgāmī), attained final nibbāna.
However, for these three as well, the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) is broken the very moment one has arranged a bed. This is the point of distinction here. As for the benefit:
it is contrary to what was said [in the Sutta], "He dwells devoted to the pleasure of beds, the pleasure of couches, and the pleasure of drowsiness."
It is the severing of mental fetters, suitability for application to all meditation subjects, inspiring deportment,
conformity with the arousal of energy, and the strengthening of right practice.
Having folded his legs crosswise and set his body erect;
As he sits, the Wanderer causes the heart of Māra to tremble.
Having abandoned the pleasure of lying down and the pleasure of sloth,
the bhikkhu who has aroused energy and delights in sitting makes the forest of asceticism shine.
"Since one attains spiritual joy and happiness,
therefore the wise should devote themselves to the practice of perpetual sitting.
This is the commentary on the undertaking, the methods, the classifications, the divisions, and the benefits of the perpetual-sitting factor.
The Miscellaneous Discussion on the Ascetic Practices (Dhutaṅga-pakiṇṇaka-kathā) 37.
Now, [this will be explained] from the perspective of the wholesome triad (kusalattika) and by way of the classification of the ascetic practices (dhuta) and so forth.
"And the exposition should be understood both by way of summary and analysis"—this is the commentary according to this verse.

Therein, "by way of the triad of the wholesome" means that all the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) may be wholesome, or they may be indeterminate, depending on whether they belong to those in training (*sekkha*), worldlings (*puthujjana*), or those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*); there is no ascetic practice that is unwholesome.

But as for one who might say, "The ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) is even unwholesome because of such statements as 'one who has evil desires and is overcome by longing is a forest-dweller,'" he should be told:
We do not say that one dwells in the forest with an unwholesome mind.
For whoever has his dwelling in the forest is a forest-dweller; and he may either have evil desires or few desires. However, these [ascetic practices]—by this or that...
They are called *dhutaṅgas* because they are the limbs (*aṅga*) of a bhikkhu who has shaken off the defilements (*kilesa*) through undertaking [the practice];
or alternatively, they are called *dhutaṅgas* because knowledge—which has acquired the designation "shaken off" (*dhuta*) due to its shaking off of defilements—is their limb.

Or again, they are called *dhutaṅgas* because they are both "shaken off" (*dhuta*)—in the sense of having shaken off their opposites—and "limbs" (*aṅga*) of the practice. Furthermore, no one becomes "shaken off" (*dhuta*) by means of what is unwholesome.

If these factors were present, yet one did not shake off any unwholesome state such that they could be called "ascetic practices" (*dhutaṅga*) by virtue of being its components, nor did they shake off unwholesome states such as greed for robes while serving as a factor of the practice, then it would be incorrect;
therefore, this is well said: "There is no unwholesome ascetic practice."

“Furthermore, for those [teachers] who hold that there are ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) not included within the triad of the wholesome (kusalattika), there is in fact no such thing as an ‘ascetic practice’ in terms of its actual meaning.

Since it does not exist, what could it be that is ‘shaken off’ (dhunana) to be called an ‘ascetic practice’? Moreover, this would contradict the statement: ‘One conducts oneself having undertaken the qualities of asceticism (dhutaguṇa).
Therefore, that view should not be accepted. This, first of all, is the commentary from the perspective of the triad of the wholesome.

Regarding the classification of the ascetic practices (*dhuta*) and so forth: the ascetic practitioner (*dhuta*) is to be understood; the proponent of asceticism (*dhutavāda*) is to be understood; the ascetic qualities (*dhutadhamma*) are to be understood; the ascetic factors (*dhutaṅga*) are to be understood; and it is to be understood for whom the cultivation of the ascetic factors is suitable.
In this context, "ascetic" (*dhuta*) refers either to a person whose defilements have been shaken off (*dhutakilesa*), or to the teaching that shakes off defilements (*kilesadhunana*).

Regarding the term "proponent of asceticism" (*dhutavāda*): there is one who is ascetic but not a proponent of asceticism; there is one who is not ascetic but a proponent of asceticism; there is one who is neither ascetic nor a proponent of asceticism; and there is one who is both ascetic and a proponent of asceticism.

In this regard, one who has shaken off his own defilements by means of an ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*), yet does not exhort or instruct others in an ascetic practice—such as the Elder Bākula—is "ascetic" (*dhuta*) but not "one who speaks of asceticism" (*dhutavāda*).
As it is said: "Thus, the venerable Bākula was ascetic but not one who spoke of asceticism.
On the other hand, one who has not shaken off his own defilements by means of an ascetic practice, but [merely] [exhorts others] in an ascetic practice...
One who counsels and instructs like the Elder Upananda is "not a dhuta practitioner, though he speaks of the dhutas. As it is said:

"Thus, the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son is not a dhuta practitioner, though he speaks of the dhutas. One who has failed in both [the practice and the teaching] like Lāḷudāyī is "neither a dhuta practitioner nor one who speaks of the dhutas.
As it is said: "Thus, the Venerable Lāḷudāyī is neither a dhuta practitioner nor one who speaks of the dhutas."
But he who is endowed with both, like the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta), is both a dhuta practitioner and one who speaks of the dhutas. As it was said:
"Thus, this venerable Sāriputta is both a dhuta practitioner and one who speaks of the dhutas.
The dhuta qualities should be understood as: fewness of wishes, contentment, effacement, seclusion, and earnestness in purpose.

These five qualities that accompany the volition for the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) are called "ascetic qualities" (dhutadhamma) because of such statements as, "relying on contentment alone," and so forth.
Among them, fewness of wishes (appicchatā) and contentment (santuṭṭhitā) are non-greed (alobha).
Asceticism (sallekhatā) and seclusion (pavivekatā) fall under two qualities: non-greed and non-delusion (amoha). Being established in this [state] is simply knowledge (ñāṇa). And therein...
By means of non-greed, one shakes off greed for the things that are prohibited; by means of non-delusion, one shakes off delusion, which conceals the danger inherent in those very same things.
Furthermore, by means of non-greed, one shakes off devotion to sensual pleasure, which occurs through the practice of what is permitted;

and by means of non-delusion, one shakes off devotion to self-mortification, which occurs through excessive austerity in the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga). Therefore, these states should be understood as "ascetic qualities" (dhutadhamma).

"The ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas) should be understood" means that the thirteen ascetic practices should be understood, namely: the practice of wearing rag-robes... [and so on] ...up to the practice of sitting. These have already been explained in terms of their meaning and their characteristics, etc.
For whom is the cultivation of the ascetic practices suitable? It is for one of a lustful temperament and for one of a deluded temperament. Why?
Because the cultivation of the ascetic practices is both a difficult way of practice and a state of effacement. And it is by relying upon a difficult way of practice that lust is stilled.
By relying on effacement, delusion is abandoned by one who is diligent.

Furthermore, the practice of the forest-dweller’s factor and the tree-root-dweller’s factor is suitable even for one of a hateful temperament; for when he dwells there without being disturbed, his hatred is also pacified.
This is the explanation of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) and so forth according to their classification.
Regarding "in brief and in detail": these ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), however, consist of eight in total—namely, three principal factors and five non-confused factors.

Among them, the practice of wandering for alms from house to house (*sapadānacārika*), the practice of eating at a single sitting (*ekāsanika*), and the practice of living in the open air (*abbhokāsika*) are the three principal factors.

For one who guards the practice of wandering for alms from house to house will also guard the practice of eating only alms-food (*piṇḍapātika*). And [the same applies to] the practice of eating at a single sitting.
For one who guards [these], the factors of eating only from the alms-bowl and of not accepting food after the meal will also be well-guarded.
For one guarding the factor of dwelling in the open air, what indeed remains to be guarded regarding the factors of dwelling at the foot of a tree and of using whatever seat is available?
Thus, these three head-factors—the forest-dweller’s factor, the refuse-rag-wearer’s factor, the triple-robe-wearer’s factor, and the sitter’s factor—[are to be observed].
The "charnel-ground dweller's factor" (*sosānika-aṅga*) and these five unmixed factors (*asambhinna-aṅga*) thus make eight.
Furthermore, there are two connected with robes, five connected with almsfood, five connected with lodgings, and one connected with energy;
thus, they amount to four [sets]. Among those, the "sitter's factor" (*nesajjika-aṅga*) is connected with energy. The others are self-evident.
Furthermore, by way of dependence, there are two types: twelve dependent on conditions and one dependent on energy.

Also, by way of what should be practiced and what should not be practiced, there are likewise two types. For one whose meditation subject increases while practicing a dhutaṅga, those should be practiced;
for one whose meditation subject declines while practicing them, they should not be practiced. But for one...
Even for that which increases whether cultivated or not cultivated, and does not diminish, one should cultivate it out of compassion for future generations.
Even for that which does not increase whether cultivated or not cultivated, one should nevertheless cultivate it for the sake of future mental impression (*vāsanā*).
Thus, although all these are twofold according to what should and should not be cultivated, they are all of one kind by way of volition (*cetanā*).
Indeed, there is only one ascetic practice (dhutaṅga), which is the volition of undertaking it. This is also stated in the Commentary: "They call that volition an ascetic practice.

In detail, however, there are thirteen for bhikkhus, eight for bhikkhunīs, twelve for male novices (sāmaṇeras), seven for female trainees (sikkhamānās) and female novices (sāmaṇerīs), and two for male and female lay followers (upāsakas and upāsikās);
thus, there are forty-two in total. Furthermore, if one is endowed with the forest-dweller’s practice (āraññikaṅga) while staying in the open air...
It is a cemetery; yet even a single bhikkhu is able to practice all the dhutaṅgas simultaneously.

However, for bhikkhunīs, two of these—namely, the forest-dweller’s practice (*āraññikaṅga*) and the later-food-eater’s practice (*khalupacchābhattikaṅga*)—are prohibited by two training rules (*sikkhāpada*).

These three—the open-air-dweller’s practice (*abbhokāsikaṅga*), the tree-root-dweller’s practice (*rukkhamūlikaṅga*), and the cemetery-dweller’s practice (*sosānikaṅga*)—are difficult to maintain. For a bhikkhunī, [the practice of living] with a companion...
It is not permissible to live without [a companion]. In such circumstances, it is difficult to find a companion who shares the same inclinations.

Even if one were to find her, one would not be freed from living in close association. This being the case, the very purpose for which she would practice the ascetic virtue (dhutaṅga) would not be fulfilled.
Because it is impossible to enjoy [the practice] in this way, having abandoned five [of the rules], [it was established] for the nuns...

It should be understood that there are exactly eight [dhutaṅgas]. Among those already mentioned, however, with the exception of the triple-robe practice (*tecīvarika-aṅga*), the remaining twelve are to be understood as applicable to male novices (*sāmaṇera*), while seven are applicable to female trainees (*sikkhamānā*) and female novices (*sāmaṇerī*).

For male and female lay followers (*upāsaka* and *upāsikā*), however, there are two dhutaṅgas—the single-session practice (*ekāsanika-aṅga*) and the alms-bowl practice (*pattapiṇḍika-aṅga*)—which are both appropriate for them and capable of being utilized.
Thus, taken in detail, there are forty-two; this is the commentary according to both summary and detail.

And up to this point, regarding the Path of Purification (Visuddhimagga) taught under the headings of virtue, concentration, and wisdom through the verse beginning, "A wise man, established in virtue," [it has been shown] by which qualities such as fewness of wishes and contentment the aforementioned kind of virtue [is fulfilled].
This is the purification; the discourse on the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) that should be undertaken for the purpose of accomplishing them has thus been spoken.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Ascetic Practices," in the *Visuddhimagga* composed for the delight of virtuous people.
3. The Description of Taking Up a Meditation Subject (Kammaṭṭhānaggahaṇaniddesa) 38.

Now, since one who is established in this virtue—which has been purified by qualities such as fewness of wishes accomplished through the observance of the ascetic practices—should, according to the words:
“A wise man, being established in virtue, develops consciousness and wisdom,” [proceed as follows].
Concentration is indicated by way of its heading as "mind" (*citta*) in the verbal expression; it must be developed.

However, because it was taught in such extreme brevity, it is not even easy to understand, let alone develop. Therefore, this series of questions is intended to show its detailed exposition and the method of its development.
What is concentration? In what sense is it concentration? What are its characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause?
How many kinds of concentration are there? What is its defilement? What is its purification? How is it developed? What is the benefit of the development of concentration?
Herein, this is the answer. "What is concentration? Concentration is of many kinds and of various types. To explain them all:

If an answer were given that did not accomplish the intended meaning and would instead lead to further distraction, we shall therefore speak here with reference only to what is intended: concentration is one-pointedness of wholesome consciousness.
In what sense is it "concentration"? It is concentration in the sense of concentrating. What is this so-called concentrating? It is [the state] upon a single object.
It is the equal and correct placing (*samādhāna*) of the mind and mental factors; what is meant is their "establishment.

Therefore, it should be understood that *samādhāna* is that state of a phenomenon by whose power the mind and mental factors abide equally and correctly upon a single object, being neither distracted nor dispersed.
Regarding the characteristics, functions, manifestations, and proximate causes of concentration (*samādhi*): here, concentration has non-distraction as its characteristic;

its function is the destruction of distraction; it is manifested as imperturbability; and, according to the statement “the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated,” happiness is its proximate cause.
39. How many kinds of concentration are there? First, it is of one kind by way of the characteristic of non-distraction. It is of two kinds by way of access (*upacāra*) and absorption (*appanā*);

likewise, by way of the mundane (*lokiya*) and the supramundane (*lokuttara*), by way of being with rapture (*sappītika*) and without rapture (*nippītika*), and by way of being accompanied by pleasure (*sukhasahagata*) and accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhāsahagata*).

It is of three kinds by way of the inferior (*hīna*), the intermediate (*majjhima*), and the superior (*paṇīta*); likewise, by way of being with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitakkasavicāra*), etc., and by way of being accompanied by rapture (*pītisahagata*), etc.
And by way of limited, sublime, and measureless [states]. It is fourfold by way of the difficult path with sluggish direct knowledge and so forth;

likewise, it is fourfold by way of limited and limited-object states and so forth, by way of the factors of the four jhānas, by way of the categories beginning with "partaking of diminution," by way of the sense-sphere realm and so forth, and by way of predominance.
It is fivefold according to the system of the fivefold jhāna by way of the five jhāna factors.
Commentary on the Singlefold Section of Concentration:
Therein, the singlefold section is clear in meaning. In the twofold section, there are these:

the six subjects of recollection (*anussati-ṭṭhāna*), mindfulness of death (*maraṇassati*), mindfulness of peace (*upasamānussati*), the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment (*āhāre paṭikūlasaññā*), and the analysis of the four elements (*catudhātuvavatthāna*). Of these—

The one-pointedness of mind obtained by way of [access], as well as the one-pointedness that occurs in the preliminary stage prior to the absorptions (appanā-samādhi), is access concentration (upacāra-samādhi).

However, based on such statements as, "The preparation for the first jhāna is a condition for the first jhāna by way of proximity-condition (anantara-paccaya)," the one-pointedness that occurs immediately after the preparation is absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi). Thus, it is twofold by way of access and absorption.

In the second dyad, one-pointedness of consciousness in the three planes that is wholesome is mundane concentration (*lokiya-samādhi*). One-pointedness associated with the Noble Path is supramundane concentration (*lokuttara-samādhi*). Thus, it is twofold by way of being mundane and supramundane.
In the third dyad, one-pointedness in two of the jhānas according to the fourfold system, or in three according to the fivefold system, is concentration accompanied by rapture (*sappītiko samādhi*).

One-pointedness in the remaining two jhānas is concentration devoid of rapture (*nippītiko samādhi*). Furthermore, access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*) may be either accompanied by rapture or devoid of rapture.
It may be "without rapture" (*nippītiko*); thus, it is twofold according to the categories of "with rapture" and "without rapture.
In the fourth dyad, within the three jhānas of the fourfold method and the four jhānas of the fivefold method, concentration accompanied by happiness (*sukhasahagato samādhi*) is present;

in the remainder, it is concentration accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhāsahagato samādhi*). However, access concentration (*upacārasamādhi*) may be either accompanied by happiness or [accompanied by equanimity].
"Accompanied by equanimity" (*upekkhāsahagata*): thus it is twofold, according to being accompanied by pleasure (*sukha*) or accompanied by equanimity.
Regarding the commentary on the triads (*tīka*):

in the first triad, it is threefold according to inferior, medium, and superior—where "inferior" means merely attained, "medium" means not well-cultivated, and "superior" means well-cultivated and reached to mastery (*vasippatta*).
In the second triad, the concentration of the first jhāna, together with access concentration, is accompanied by both applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
In the fivefold system, the concentration of the second jhāna is without applied thought and consists of sustained thought alone (*avitakkavicāramatta*).

For one who, seeing danger in applied thought alone but not in sustained thought, desires only the abandoning of applied thought and thus transcends the first jhāna, that [concentration] is without applied thought and consists of sustained thought alone.

He attains concentration. It is with reference to this that it was said. However, in the fourfold system, in the second and subsequent jhānas, and in the three jhānas beginning from the third in the fivefold system, the unification of mind is "concentration without applied thought and sustained thought. Thus, it is threefold according to the categories of "with applied thought and sustained thought" and so forth.
In the third triad, in the first two jhānas of the fourfold system and in the [first] three jhānas of the fivefold system, the unification of mind is accompanied by rapture (*pītisahagata*).
Concentration (*samādhi*). Within those same third and fourth jhānas, concentration is one-pointedness accompanied by pleasure;
at the conclusion, it is accompanied by equanimity. Access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*), however, is either accompanied by rapture and pleasure or accompanied by equanimity.
Thus, it is threefold according to its accompaniment by rapture and so forth.

In the fourth triad, one-pointedness on the level of access concentration is limited concentration (*paritta-samādhi*). One-pointedness associated with wholesome states of the fine-material and immaterial spheres is exalted concentration (*mahaggata-samādhi*).
One-pointedness associated with the Noble Path is immeasurable concentration (*appamāṇa-samādhi*);
thus, it is threefold by way of being limited, exalted, and immeasurable.

Commentary on the Tetrad of Concentrations: In the first tetrad among the tetrads, there is concentration that is painful in its progress and slow in direct knowledge; there is that which is painful in its progress and quick in direct knowledge; there is that which is pleasant in its progress and slow in direct knowledge; and there is that which is pleasant in its progress and quick in direct knowledge.
Therein, from the initial application of attention until the access stage of each respective jhāna arises—
The development of concentration proceeding up to that point is called "the way" (*paṭipadā*).

However, the wisdom proceeding from the stage of access (*upacāra*) up to absorption (*appanā*) is called "direct knowledge" (*abhiññā*). Now, for some, this way is painful; it is difficult because of the persistence of opposing states such as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), meaning it is practiced with discomfort.
For others, due to the absence of those [obstacles], it is pleasant. Direct knowledge, too, is slow for some.
For some it is dull and not quick in its occurrence; for others it is swift, not dull, and quick in its occurrence.

In this regard, concerning those things we shall later describe—the suitable and unsuitable conditions, the preliminary duties such as the severing of impediments, and the skill in absorption—for one who pursues what is unsuitable, the practice is painful and higher knowledge is slow.

There is. For one who cultivates what is suitable, the practice is pleasant and direct knowledge is swift. However, for one who, having cultivated what is unsuitable in the earlier stage, later becomes a cultivator of the suitable;
or who, having cultivated what is suitable in the earlier stage, later becomes a cultivator of the unsuitable—for such a person, a mixed state should be understood.
Likewise, [this applies] to one who has not performed the preliminary duties, such as the severing of impediments.
For one devoted to the development [of concentration], the practice is painful; by the reverse, it is pleasant.
However, for one who does not achieve skill in absorption, direct knowledge is sluggish; for one who achieves it, it is swift.
Furthermore, their distinction should be understood by way of craving and ignorance, and also by way of the respective predominance of serenity and insight.
For one overcome by craving, the practice is painful; for one not overcome by it, it is pleasant.

For one overcome by ignorance, direct knowledge is sluggish; for one not overcome by it, it is swift. Furthermore, for one who has not performed the preliminary work regarding serenity, the practice is painful;
for one who has performed that work, it is pleasant. As for one who has not performed the preliminary work regarding insight—
For one who has performed the preliminary work, direct knowledge is swift; for others, it is sluggish.

Furthermore, their distinction should be understood by way of the defilements and the faculties. For one with sharp defilements and dull faculties, the practice is painful and direct knowledge is sluggish;
however, for one with sharp faculties, direct knowledge is swift. And for one with mild defilements and dull faculties, it is pleasant...
The way is sluggish and direct-knowledge is slow; however, for one with keen faculties, direct-knowledge is swift.

Thus, among these ways and types of direct-knowledge, the concentration that a person attains by means of a painful way and slow direct-knowledge is called "concentration with a painful way and slow direct-knowledge. This same method applies [to the other cases].
"Regarding the three knowledges (*ñāṇa*): thus, [concentration] is fourfold by way of the painful practice with sluggish direct knowledge (*dandhābhiññā*), and so forth.
In the second tetrad: there is concentration that is limited (*paritta*) with a limited object; there is that which is limited with an immeasurable object;
there is that which is immeasurable with a limited object; and there is that which is immeasurable with an immeasurable object. Therein, as for the concentration..."
That which is unskilled and unable to serve as a condition for higher jhāna is limited (*paritta*).

That which occurs with an undevolved object is limited-object (*parittārammaṇa*). That which is skilled and well-developed, and is able to serve as a condition for higher jhāna, is immeasurable (*appamāṇa*). And that which occurs with a developed object is immeasurable-object (*appamāṇārammaṇa*).
The mixed method, however, should be understood through the mixing of the characteristics already stated. Thus, it is fourfold by way of being limited with a limited object, and so forth.

In the third tetrad, there is the first jhāna with five factors—consisting of applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), rapture (*pīti*), happiness (*sukha*), and concentration (*samādhi*)—for those who have suppressed the hindrances;
then the second, which has three factors as applied and sustained thought have subsided; and then that from which rapture has faded away.
The third [jhāna] has two factors; then, by way of concentration accompanied by the feeling of equanimity from which pleasure has been abandoned, the fourth has two factors.
Thus, there are four types of concentration that constitute the factors of these four jhānas. In this way, it is fourfold by way of the factors of the four jhānas.
In the fourth tetrad, there is concentration partaking of decline, there is concentration partaking of stability, and there is concentration partaking of distinction.

There is that which partakes of penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*). In this context, it should be understood that there is the state of partaking of decline (*hānabhāgiyatā*) by way of the manifestation of opposing states;

the state of partaking of stability (*ṭhitibhāgiyatā*) by way of establishing mindfulness in accordance with those [states]; the state of partaking of distinction (*visesabhāgiyatā*) by way of the attainment of higher distinctions; and the state of partaking of penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiyatā*) by way of the manifestation of perception and attention accompanied by disenchantment (*nibbidā*).
As it is said: "For one who has attained the first *jhāna*, [perceptions] accompanied by sensual desire..."

When perceptions and acts of attention associated with decline prevail, wisdom partakes of decline. When mindfulness established in accordance with those [perceptions] remains steady, wisdom partakes of stability.
When perceptions and acts of attention accompanied by non-thinking prevail, wisdom partakes of distinction.
When perceptions and acts of attention accompanied by disenchantment and connected with dispassion prevail, wisdom partakes of penetration.
“Wisdom. Furthermore, the concentrations associated with that wisdom are also fourfold. Thus, there are four kinds according to the classification of those conducive to decline and so forth.

In the fifth tetrad, there are four types of concentration: sense-sphere concentration, fine-material-sphere concentration, immaterial-sphere concentration, and the unconcentrated (unincluded) concentration.
Among these, all one-pointedness of mind belonging to access concentration is sense-sphere concentration.

Likewise, the one-pointedness of wholesome consciousness belonging to the fine-material sphere and so forth, together with the other three [factors], constitutes the fourfold [classification] according to the sense-sphere and so on.
In the sixth tetrad: "If, monks, a bhikkhu gains concentration by making desire the dominant influence, he gains one-pointedness of mind;

this is called concentration through desire... If, monks, a bhikkhu... makes energy the dominant influence... If, monks, a bhikkhu... makes consciousness the dominant influence... If, monks, a bhikkhu... makes investigation the dominant influence..."
“Making that [investigation] predominant, this bhikkhu attains concentration, attains one-pointedness of mind; this is called ‘concentration through investigation.
Thus, it is fourfold by way of predominance.
Regarding the fivefold division, the second jhāna mentioned in the fourfold classification is the second by means of transcending mere applied thought (vitakka).
By transcending applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), it is the third; thus, having divided them in this twofold way, the five jhānas are to be understood.
And the five concentrations that constitute their factors—thus, by way of the five jhāna-factors, their fivefold nature is to be understood.
40. As for "What is its defilement? What is its purification?", the answer here has already been stated in the *Vibhaṅga*. For it was said:

In this context, "defilement" refers to a state conducive to decline (*hānabhāgiya-dhamma*), and "purification" refers to a state conducive to distinction (*visesabhāgiya-dhamma*). Therein, the state conducive to decline should be understood according to this method:
"When one has attained the first *jhāna*, perceptions and mental orientations associated with sensual desire (*kāma*) arise;
this is wisdom conducive to decline. [Likewise,] "perceptions and mental orientations unaccompanied by applied thought (*avitakka*)"...
By this method, the state conducive to distinction (*visesabhāgiyadhamma*) is to be understood through the passage: "They practice so that wisdom partakes of distinction.
41. Regarding the question "How is it to be developed?":
here, first of all, concerning the statement "this [development] is twofold, by way of the mundane and the supramundane," and so forth—
The concentration associated with the Noble Path has been described; its method of development is included within the very method for developing wisdom.
For when wisdom is developed, that [concentration] is developed as well. Therefore, with reference to that, we say nothing further regarding how it should be developed separately.
As for this mundane [concentration], it is practiced by one who, having purified the moral virtues in the manner already stated, is firmly established in perfectly pure virtue.
Having severed whatever obstacle exists among the ten obstacles, he should approach a virtuous friend who bestows a meditation subject; then,
having taken one of the forty meditation subjects suitable to his own temperament,
and having abandoned a monastery unsuitable for the development of concentration, he should dwell in a suitable monastery, performing the severance of minor obstacles.
Having performed all the procedures for development, it should be cultivated without omitting anything—this is the summary here.
This, however, is the detailed explanation: regarding what was stated, "having severed whatever obstacle exists among the ten obstacles," therein:
The dwelling, the family, gain, the group, and the task as the fifth;
“Travel, relatives, illness, books, and psychic powers—these are the ten.
These are called the ten impediments (*palibodha*). In this context, “dwelling” itself is the dwelling-impediment; the same method applies to the family and the others.
Therein, “dwelling” refers to even a single room, a single courtyard, or the entire monastic complex (*saṅghārāma*). This [term]...

It is not an obstacle for everyone. However, it is an obstacle only for one who here applies himself to new building projects and the like, or who has a large accumulation of goods, or whose mind is attached through some reason due to longing; it is not an obstacle for another.
In this regard, there is this story: two sons of good family, it is said, departed from Anurādhapura and eventually arrived at the Thūpārāma monastery.
They went forth. Among them, one who had mastered two *mātikās* and reached five years of seniority, having performed the *pavāraṇā*, went to the place called Pācinakhaṇḍarāji.
Another remained right there. Having lived for a long time at Pācinakhaṇḍarāji and having become an elder (*thera*), he thought:
"This place is suitable for seclusion; well now, let me inform my friend of this as well. Then—
Having departed, he entered the Thūpārāma monastery by stages.
As soon as he saw him entering, the Elder Samānavassika went out to meet him, received his bowl and robes, and performed the customary duties of hospitality.
The visiting elder entered his lodging and thought, "Now my friend will surely send me some ghee, or molasses, or a medicinal drink; for he is well-known in this place."
"He has been a long-time resident of this city. Not receiving anything during the night, he thought at dawn, "Now they will send rice-gruel and solid food brought by their attendants.
Not seeing even that, he thought, "There is no one to send it; they will likely give it to me once I have entered.
Thus, at dawn, he entered the village together with him. Having walked through one street, those two obtained a bowlful of rice-gruel.
Having sat down in the assembly hall, they drank [the gruel]. Then the newcomer thought, "I suppose there is no regular supply of gruel;
at mealtime, people will now give us fine food. Thus, even at mealtime, he went for alms and ate only what he had obtained.
The other asked, "Venerable sir, do you always subsist in this way? "Yes, friend," he replied.
“Venerable sir, Pācīnakhaṇḍarājī is comfortable; let us go there. As the elder was departing from the city by the southern gate, he set out on the road to Kumbhakāragāma.
The other asked, “But why, venerable sir, have you set out on this road?
“Friend, did you not praise Pācīnakhaṇḍarājī? “What then, venerable sir?”
"In the place where you have stayed for all this time, do you have no extra requisites? "Yes, friend, the bed and chair belong to the Saṅgha;
they have already been put away, and there is nothing else. "But as for me, Bhante, my staff, oil-flask, and sandals-bag are still right there.
"Friend, having stayed for only a single day, have you left behind so much?"
“Yes, venerable sir. With a confident heart, he paid homage to the Elder and said, “Venerable sir, for those such as you, dwelling in the forest is indeed everywhere.
However, at the Thūpārāma there is the enshrining of the relics of the four Buddhas;
