one can hear the Dhamma conducive to well-being in the Lohapāsāda, behold the Mahācetiya, and meet with the Elders. Here, it is as if the time of the Buddhas has returned. Right here, you—”
“Stay,” he said; and on the second day, taking his bowl and robes, he went there himself. For one such as this, a dwelling place does not become an impediment.
As for a family: it may be a family of relatives or a family of supporters.

For some, even a family of supporters becomes an impediment when they dwell in close association with them, according to the principle of “being happy among those who are happy,” and so forth; [such a person] cannot do without the people of that family.
He would not even go to a neighboring monastery to hear the Dhamma.
For some, even their parents do not become obstacles, as in the case of the young bhikkhu who was the nephew of the elder living at Koraṇḍaka Vihāra.
It is said that he went to Rohaṇa for the purpose of receiving instruction. The elder’s sister, a laywoman, constantly [inquired] about the elder’s welfare regarding him.
He asked. One day, the Elder set out toward Rohaṇa, thinking, "I shall bring the young man back. The young man also thought, "I have lived here for a long time;
now I shall go see my preceptor and learn of the laywoman's welfare," and he departed from Rohaṇa.
Both of them met on the bank of the Gaṅgā. At the foot of a certain tree, he—
Having performed his duties for the elder, when he was asked, "Where are you going?", he reported the matter to him. The elder said, "You have done well;
the laywoman asks about this constantly, and I too have come for this very purpose.
You may go, but I shall remain right here and observe the rains retreat. On the very day of the entry into the rains retreat, he [the layman] went to that monastery.
He had obtained it; indeed, his father himself had built that very dwelling for him.
Then, on the following day, his father came and asked, "Venerable sir, to whom has our dwelling been assigned?
Hearing the reply, "To a young newcomer," he approached him, paid homage, and said: "Venerable sir, our..."
“There is a duty for one who has entered the rains residence in a monastery. “What is it, lay follower? “For three months, you must receive almsfood from our house alone;
then, after the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), you must ask for leave when the time comes to depart. He consented by remaining silent.
The lay follower also went home and said, “A certain visiting venerable has arrived at our residence; he should be served with due care.”
He said, "Very well," and the female lay follower, having accepted, prepared excellent hard food and soft food.
Even though he was young, he went to his relatives' home at mealtime; no one recognized him.
Having consumed almsfood there for three months, and having completed the rains retreat, he asked for leave, saying, "I am going."
Then his kinsmen said, "Go tomorrow, venerable sir," and on the following day, having fed him right there in their house, they filled an oil tube,
gave him a lump of sugar and a nine-cubit cloth, and said, "Go now, venerable sir.
Having offered words of thanksgiving, he set out toward Rohaṇa.
His preceptor, having performed the *pavāraṇā* ceremony, was returning along the same path and saw him at the very place where he had seen him before.
At the foot of a certain tree, the novice performed the duties for the elder. Then the elder asked him, "My dear boy, did you see the female lay devotee?
He replied, "Yes, venerable sir," and having reported the entire incident, [he offered] that oil to the elder.
Having smeared his feet with molasses and made a drink from it, he gave that garment as well to the Elder;

then, after paying homage to the Elder, he departed, saying, "Venerable sir, Rohaṇa alone is suitable for me. The Elder also returned to the monastery and on the following day entered the village of Koraṇḍaka.
The female lay devotee also stood constantly watching the road, thinking, "My brother is now coming back with my son.
Seeing him approaching all alone, she thought, "I suppose my son is dead;
this elder is coming by himself," and falling at the elder’s feet, she wept and lamented. The elder said, "Surely the youth, out of fewness of desires..."
“Without letting me know, he has gone. Having comforted her thus and reported everything that had occurred, he took that cloth out from his bowl-bag and showed it to her.
The female lay devotee, gaining confidence, lay down on her chest facing the direction her son had gone and, paying homage, said: “To me—”

Indeed, I consider that the Blessed One, treating this bhikkhu as if he were his own son, taught him the practice of the *Rathavinīta*, the *Nālaka*, and the *Tuvaṭṭaka* suttas, as well as the practice of the Great Noble Lineage (*mahāariyavaṃsa*) which illuminates contentment with the four requisites and delight in meditation.
Even while eating for three months in the house of one who had just given birth to him, he would not say, "I am your son; you are my mother."
“Oh, what a wonderful person! Even one’s own mother and father do not become an obstacle for such a person, let alone any other family of supporters.
“Gain” refers to the four requisites. How do they become an obstacle? When a meritorious bhikkhu goes from place to place, people provide him with requisites accompanied by a large retinue.
As he expresses his thanks to them and teaches the Dhamma, he [neglects] the duty of a recluse...
He finds no opportunity to do so. From the time of dawn until the first watch of the night, his contact with people does not cease.

Then, at the very time of the powerful dawn, those who live in abundance and those who wander for alms arrive and say, "Venerable sir, such-and-such a lay follower, a lay follower, a minister, or a minister’s daughter wishes to see you. He says, "Take it, friends."
"Thinking, 'My bowl and robes,' he remains ready to go; thus he is constantly preoccupied. Those very requisites become an impediment for him.
Therefore, having abandoned the group, he should wander alone in a place where they do not know him. In this way, that impediment is severed.
"Group" means a group of Sutta specialists or a group of Abhidhamma specialists—those from whom he receives recitation or questioning.
If he does not find an opportunity for the practice of the ascetic’s duty (*samaṇadhamma*), that very group becomes an impediment; therefore, it should be severed in this way.
If those monks have taken much and only a little remains, he should enter the forest after they have finished that [little].
If they have taken little and much remains, he should not go more than a league away.
Within a distance of one *yojana*, he should approach another group-leader and say, "Venerable sir, please include these people in the recitation and other duties.
If he does not obtain this, he should leave the group, saying, "Friends, I have a task;
you may go to whatever place is convenient for you," and then perform his own work.

"Building work" (*kamma*) means new construction. For one who performs it, there must be knowledge of what has been obtained or not obtained by carpenters and others, and one must exert oneself regarding what has been done and what remains to be done;
thus, it is always an impediment. That too should be terminated in this way: if little remains, it should be finished.
If much remains, and if the building work belongs to the Saṅgha, [it should be handed over] to the Saṅgha or to those monks who bear the burden of the Saṅgha.
Or it should be handed over. If it belongs to oneself, it should be handed over to those who carry one's own burden.
If such persons are not available, one should go after having relinquished it to the Saṅgha.
"On a journey" means traveling on a road. For one who has a desire for ordination somewhere, or who requires requisites—

There is something that must be obtained. If, not obtaining it, one is unable to endure [the situation], then even for one who has entered the forest and is practicing the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*), the so-called "mind intent on going" (*gamikacitta*) is difficult to dispel;
therefore, having gone and completed that task, one should exert oneself in the duty of a recluse.

"Relatives" refers to those in a monastery—such as preceptors, teachers, co-residents, pupils, and those who share the same preceptor or teacher—as well as those in a household, such as mother, father, and brothers.
When they are ill, they become an impediment for him;
therefore, that impediment must be severed by attending to them and restoring them to their normal state.
In that regard, first, if the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) falls ill and does not recover quickly, he must be attended to even for the rest of his life.

The same applies to the teacher of going-forth (*pabbajjācariya*), the teacher of full ordination (*upasampadācariya*), the co-resident student (*saddhivihārika*), the pupil ordained or gone-forth by him (*antevāsika*), and those who share the same preceptor.

However, as long as [the relationship lasts], this also applies to the teacher of dependence (*nissayācariya*), the teacher of instruction (*uddesācariya*), the pupil dependent on him (*nissayantevāsika*), the pupil receiving instruction from him (*uddesantevāsika*), and those who share the same teacher.

As long as the dependence and the formal assignment (*uddesa*) have not been terminated, they must be looked after. Even when one has sufficient means, one must continue to look after them beyond that point.
One should behave toward one's mother and father just as toward one's preceptor (*upajjhāya*).
For even if they are established in sovereignty and expect service from their son, it must certainly be performed. If they lack medicine, [one should provide] what belongs to oneself.

It must be given. Even if there is no food obtained through alms-round, it must certainly be given after searching for it. However, in the case of brothers and sisters, it should be given only by providing what belongs to them.
If one has nothing of one's own, one may give it on loan and later take it back when it is received.
If it is not received, one should not press them for it. [This applies even to] medicine for an unrelated sister’s husband.
It is not permissible to perform [the rite] or to give [the requisites]. However, having said, "Give them to your husband," they should be given to the sister-in-law.
The same rule applies to the brother-in-law as well. But since their children are indeed his own relatives, it is permissible to perform [the rite] for them.
"Illness" refers to any kind of disease. When it afflicts one, it becomes an impediment; therefore, it should be severed by means of administering medicine.
But if, even after taking medicine for a few days, it does not subside, one should reproach one's own person, thinking: "I am neither your slave nor your hireling;
indeed, by supporting you, I have encountered suffering throughout the beginningless cycle of existence," and then the duty of a recluse (samaṇadhamma) should be performed.
"Books" means the carrying of the scriptures. This is an impediment for one who is constantly occupied with recitation and the like, but not for another. Here are some examples:
It is said that the Elder Devasa, a reciter of the Majjhima Nikāya, went to the Elder Devasa of the Malaya region and requested a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
The elder asked, "Friend, what is your level of mastery in the scriptures? He replied, "Venerable sir, the Majjhima Nikāya is familiar to me."
“Friend, this *Majjhima Nikāya* is difficult to master: while one is reciting the first fifty suttas, the middle fifty come;
and while reciting those, the final fifty arrive. Where will you find time for your meditation subject?
“Venerable sir, having received my meditation subject from you, I shall not look at it again. Having thus taken his meditation subject, he departed.
Having failed to perform recitation for nineteen years, he attained Arahatship in the twentieth year.
When monks came to him for the purpose of recitation, he said, "Friends, it has been twenty years since I last looked at the scriptures;
nevertheless, I am well-practiced in this, so please begin. From the beginning until the very end, he did not have even a single doubt regarding even a single syllable.
The Elder Nāga, a resident of Karuḷiyagiri, also set aside the scriptures for eighteen years and recited the *Dhātukathā* to the monks.
As they compared it with the versions held by the village-dwelling elders, not even a single question appeared out of sequence.
Furthermore, in the Mahāvihāra, the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷābhaya, without having studied the commentaries, [recited] in the assembly of the five Nikāyas...
Thinking, "I shall cause the three Piṭakas to be recited," he had a golden drum beaten.
The Saṅgha of bhikkhus said, "Let each person state the learning of his own teachers; otherwise, we will not allow [the recitation] to proceed.
When his preceptor saw him come to attend upon him, he asked, "Friend, did you have the drum beaten? "Yes, venerable sir."
“What is the reason? “Venerable sir, it is because I intend to recite the scriptures. “Friend Abhaya, how do the teachers explain this passage?

“They explain it thus, venerable sir. The Elder said, “Hunt! He replied, “They explain it thus, venerable sir,” three times in various ways. The Elder rebuffed him each time with “Hunt! and finally said, “Friend, [you have not learned it correctly].”

“The path of the teachers was indeed first explained by her; however, because it was not personally received from the mouth of a teacher, she was unable to establish it with the words, ‘Thus do the teachers say.
Go and hear it in the presence of your own teachers.
“Where shall I go, venerable sir? “Beyond the Gaṅgā, in the Rohaṇa country, at the Tulādhārapabbata Monastery, there is one who has mastered the entire scriptural tradition.”
“There dwells a monk named the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita; go into his presence.
“Very well, venerable sir,” he replied, and having paid homage to the elder, he went into the presence of that elder together with five hundred monks. After paying homage, he sat down.
The elder asked, “Friend, for what purpose have you come? “To hear the Dhamma, venerable sir. “Friend Abhaya, in the *Dīgha Nikāya* and the *Majjhima Nikāya*...”
"They question me from time to time, but for the remaining thirty years or so, this has never been looked into by me.
Furthermore, you should recite it in my presence at night; I shall explain it to you during the day.
"Very well, venerable sir," he replied, and did accordingly. Having had a great pavilion constructed at the gate of the monastery courtyard, the village dwellers [assembled] day after day.
They came for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma. The Elder recited it at night; then, explaining it during the day, he gradually brought his teaching to a conclusion.
Sitting on a mat in the presence of the Elder Abhaya, he said, "Friend, explain a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) to me.
"Venerable sir, what are you saying? Have I not heard it from you yourself? What should I..."
“Shall I tell you what you do not yet know? Then the Elder said to him, “Friend, this is another path for one who has already gone.

It is said that at that time the Elder Abhaya was a stream-enterer (sotāpanna). After giving him a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), he returned and, while reciting the Dhamma in the Lohapāsāda, heard that the Elder had attained final Nibbāna (parinibbuto). Having heard this, he said, “Bring it, friend!”
“Robe,” he said, putting on his robe: “Friend, the path to arahantship is suitable for our teacher.

Our teacher, friend, is upright and well-bred. He sat on a mat in the presence of his own Dhamma-pupil and said, ‘Tell me your meditation subject. Friend, the path to arahantship is suitable for that elder.”
For such as these, study is not an impediment.
"Supernormal power" (iddhi) here refers to the mundane supernormal power. For that is difficult to maintain, like a child lying on its back or like young grain;
it breaks with even the slightest [negligence]. Moreover, that is an impediment to insight (vipassanā), but not to concentration (samādhi).

Because it is to be attained after reaching concentration. Therefore, one who seeks insight must sever the impediments to success (*iddhipalibodha*), while the others must be severed by the other [the practitioner of concentration].
This, then, is the detailed explanation regarding the impediments. The Commentary on the One Who Bestows the Meditation Subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
42. Regarding the phrase "having approached a spiritual friend who bestows a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*)," there are two kinds of meditation subjects:
the universal meditation subject (*sabbatthaka-kammaṭṭhāna*) and the practical meditation subject (*pārihāriya-kammaṭṭhāna*).

Among these, the universal meditation subject consists of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and mindfulness of death (*maraṇassati*) directed toward the community of monks and so forth; some also include the perception of foulness (*asubhasaññā*).
For a bhikkhu who takes a meditation subject as his practice, he should first delimit the field and develop loving-kindness toward the Sangha of bhikkhus within that boundary, thinking:
"May they be happy; may they be free from affliction. After that, toward the deities dwelling within that boundary. Then, toward the ruling authorities in the village where he goes for alms.
Then, starting with the human beings there, he should extend it to all sentient beings. For by means of loving-kindness toward the Sangha of bhikkhus...
He generates a gentle state of mind toward those living with him; consequently, they become pleasant to live with.
Through loving-kindness toward the deities dwelling within his boundary, he becomes well-protected by those deities whose hearts have been softened, through their righteous protection.

In the village where he goes for alms, through loving-kindness toward the local lords, he has his requisites well-guarded by those lords whose mental continuums have been softened, through their righteous protection.
There, among human beings, he wanders unscorned by those whose minds have been gladdened through loving-kindness (*mettā*).
Through loving-kindness toward all beings, his conduct is everywhere unimpeded.

By means of the mindfulness of death (*maraṇassati*), thinking "I must certainly die," he abandons wrong livelihood, becomes one whose sense of urgency increases ever further, and conducts himself without attachment. For one whose mind is cultivated with the perception of foulness (*asubhasaññā*)...
Even divine objects do not overwhelm his mind through greed.

Because it is so very helpful, it is called a "universal meditation subject" (*sabbatthaka-kammaṭṭhāna*) because it is intended as that which should be maintained and desired in all circumstances, and because it is the basis for the work of devotion to yoga.
Furthermore, among the forty meditation subjects, whichever one is suitable to a person's temperament should be constantly carried about by them.
Because it serves as the proximate cause (*padatthāna*) for each successive stage of the work of meditation, it is called a "meditation subject for mastery" (*pārihāriyakammaṭṭhāna*).
Thus, he who gives these two kinds of meditation subjects is called a "giver of a meditation subject. To that giver of a meditation subject—one who is a "good friend" (*kalyāṇamitta*)—[he should go].
"One who is dear, venerable, and inspiring; one who speaks and is patient with what is said;

one who delivers profound discourse and does not urge one toward what is improper"—such is the virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitta) endowed with these and other qualities, who is exclusively well-wishing and stands on the side of progress.

“For it is by coming to me as their good friend, Ānanda, that beings subject to birth are liberated from birth,” because of such words as these, the Perfectly Enlightened One alone is the good friend endowed with every excellence.
Therefore, while he is present, the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) received in the presence of that very Blessed One is well-received. But when he has attained final Nibbāna, [among] the eighty...
It is appropriate to receive it from one among the great disciples who maintains it. In his absence,

one should receive it from a *khīṇāsava* (one whose taints are destroyed) who has reached the destruction of the taints by first developing the fourfold and fivefold jhānas based on whichever meditation subject he wishes to take up, and then increasing insight that has the jhāna as its proximate cause.
But does one who has destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava) proclaim himself, saying, "I am one whose taints are destroyed"? What can be said to this?

He proclaims it because he knows his own state as an agent. Did not the Elder Assagutta, knowing that a certain bhikkhu had begun his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), spread out a piece of leather in the air and, sitting cross-legged upon it, teach him the meditation subject, thinking, "This man is a practitioner of the meditation subject"?

Therefore, if one obtains [a teacher] whose taints are destroyed, that is good; if not, then from among those who have attained the fruit of non-returning, once-returning, stream-entry, or who are worldlings possessing jhāna, or who are bearers of the Three Piṭakas, the Two Piṭakas, or the One Piṭaka—one should receive it from each preceding one.

Even if there is no bearer of the One Piṭaka, it should be received from one who has mastered even a single recitation (saṅgīti) together with its commentary, provided that he is modest. For such a person is a bearer of the lineage (tantidhara).
The teacher who guards the lineage and protects the tradition possesses only the teacher’s wisdom; he does not rely on his own wisdom.
For this very reason, the ancient elders said three times: "One who is conscientious will protect it; one who is conscientious will protect it.
Furthermore, those previously mentioned, such as those whose taints are destroyed, explain only the path they have themselves realized. But the one of great learning—
Having approached various teachers and purified his learning through study and questioning, he will—
having discerned the suttas and their underlying reasons from here and there, and having applied what is suitable and what is unsuitable—
expound the meditation subject like a great elephant showing the main highway as he proceeds along a difficult terrain. Therefore, [seek] such a giver of a meditation subject.
Having approached a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitta) and performed the duties of service toward him, one should receive the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).
If this can be obtained in the very same monastery, that is well; if it cannot be obtained there, one must go to where he dwells.
When going, one should not wear washed and polished sandals nor carry an umbrella with feet that have been washed and anointed.
Having taken oil-tubes, honey, molasses, and so forth, and having had them carried by his pupils, he should go surrounded by his students. However,
having fulfilled the duties of one going on a journey, taking his own bowl and robes himself, he should travel along the way entering whatever monastery he comes upon,
performing the proper conduct in all places, with light requisites and living in the highest state of austerity.
One entering that monastery must first have a tooth-stick prepared as allowable by someone on the very path, take it with him, and then enter;
he must not enter another cell thinking, "I will rest for a moment and then go to the teacher after washing my feet, anointing them, and so forth.
Why? Because if there were monks there who were unsuitable companions for the teacher...
If they were to ask the reason for his coming and, having expressed disapproval of the teacher,
cause him remorse by saying, "You are ruined if you have come into his presence," he might turn back right there; therefore,
one should ask for the teacher's dwelling place and go straight to that very spot.
If the teacher is younger, one should not consent to receiving his bowl and robes, and so forth.
If he is older, one should go, pay homage to the teacher, and stand [aside]. When told, "Friend, put away your bowl and robes," they should be put away.
When told, "Drink some water," if one wishes, one may drink. When told, "Wash your feet..."
One who has been told this should not wash his feet immediately. For if it were water brought by the teacher, it would be improper.

However, when told, "Wash them, friend; it was not brought by me, but by others," he should sit down in a concealed place where the teacher cannot see him, or in the open air, or at one side of the monastery, and there wash his feet.
If the teacher brings the oil tube, one should stand up and receive it respectfully with both hands.
For if one were not to receive it, the teacher might become suspicious, thinking, "This bhikkhu is spoiling our relationship from this very moment.
Having received it, however, one should not smear one's feet with it right away; for if that oil used for anointing the teacher’s limbs [were so used]...
If it were otherwise, it would not be appropriate. Therefore, after anointing the head, one should anoint the shoulders and other parts.

However, if someone says, "Friend, this is all-purpose oil; anoint your feet as well," one should apply a small amount to the head, anoint the feet, and say, "Venerable sir, I am setting aside this oil-tube," and give it back when the teacher takes it.
One should not say, "Venerable sir, please teach me the meditation subject starting from the day I arrive.
However, starting from the second day, if the teacher has a regular attendant, one should request him and perform the duties.
If he does not grant permission even when requested, one should perform them only when an opportunity arises. While performing them, [one should attend to] the small, medium, and great [duties].
Three tooth-sticks should be offered. Two kinds of water for rinsing the mouth and bathing—cold and warm—should be prepared.
Thereafter, whatever the teacher consumes for three days, exactly that same kind should be offered regularly.
Alternatively, for one who consumes whatever is available without restriction, whatever is obtained should be offered. What need is there to say more?
As it was said: "Monks, a pupil should behave properly toward his teacher. In this regard, this is proper behavior:
having risen early, removing his sandals, and arranging his upper robe over one shoulder, he should offer a tooth-stick and water for rinsing the mouth, and prepare a seat. If there is rice-gruel..."
"Having washed the vessel, rice gruel should be offered," and so forth— whatever right conduct (*sammāvatta*) has been prescribed in the Khandhaka,
all of that must be performed. Thus,
by pleasing the teacher through the perfection of one's duties, one should depart after paying respects in the evening when dismissed with the words, "Go."
When he asks, "For what purpose have you come?", then the reason for coming should be told.

If he does not ask, but nevertheless consents to the formal conduct (*vatta*), then even if one has not gone [to him] on a day released after ten days or a fortnight has passed, one should request an opportunity and announce the reason for coming.
Or, having gone at an improper time, when asked, "For what purpose have you come?"—
It must be announced. If he says he will come early in the morning, one should go early in the morning.

However, if at that time his stomach burns due to a bile disorder, or his food does not digest because of weak digestion, or some other illness afflicts him, he should disclose that as it truly is and [inform him of] his own suitable time.

Having announced this, one should approach [the teacher] at that very time. For even if the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is explained at an unsuitable time, it is not possible to direct the mind to it.
This is the detailed explanation for the phrase "having approached the spiritual friend who bestows the meditation subject.
The Description of Conduct (Cariyāvaṇṇanā).
43. Now, regarding the phrase "conducive to one’s own temperament" (*attano cariyānukūla*):

here, "temperament" (*cariyā*) refers to the six temperaments—namely, the temperament of lust (*rāga*), the temperament of hatred (*dosa*), the temperament of delusion (*moha*), the temperament of faith (*saddhā*), the temperament of intelligence (*buddhi*), and the temperament of discursive thought (*vitakka*). Some, however, maintain that there are fourteen [temperaments] by adding four more based on the combination and conjunction of lust and the others, as well as faith and the others;
thus, together with these eight, they assert fourteen. In this way...
However, when the classification is stated in detail, there are many temperaments (cariyā) formed by combining passion and the other [defilements] with faith and the other [faculties].
Therefore, in brief, only six temperaments should be understood. Temperament (cariyā), nature (pakati), and predominance (ussannatā) are identical in meaning.

According to these, there are only six types of persons: one of lustful temperament (rāgacarita), one of hateful temperament (dosacarita), one of deluded temperament (mohacarita), one of faithful temperament (saddhācarita), one of intellectual temperament (buddhicarita), and one of discursive temperament (vitakkacarita).
In this context, because faith is powerful at the time of the arising of the wholesome for one of lustful temperament—since it possesses qualities proximate to lust—it is as follows:
just as on the unwholesome side lust is smooth and not too harsh, so too is faith on the wholesome side.

Just as lust seeks out sensual objects as its basis, so does faith seek out qualities such as virtue. And just as lust does not relinquish what is harmful, [so too faith does not relinquish what is beneficial].
Thus, faith does not abandon what is beneficial; therefore, one whose temperament is characterized by faith is similar to one whose temperament is characterized by lust.

However, because wisdom is powerful at the time of the arising of the wholesome for one whose temperament is characterized by hatred—since wisdom is a quality proximate to hatred—just as, on the side of the unwholesome, hatred is devoid of moisture and does not cling to its object, so too is wisdom on the side of the wholesome.
Just as hatred seeks out even a non-existent fault, so does wisdom seek out only the actual fault.

Just as hatred functions by way of avoiding living beings, so does wisdom function by way of avoiding conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*); therefore, the temperament of wisdom is similar to the temperament of hatred.

Furthermore, because for one striving for the arising of unarisen wholesome states, thoughts that generally act as obstacles arise for one of deluded temperament—since thought has a characteristic proximate to delusion.
For just as delusion is unstable due to its extreme confusion, so too is thought due to its tendency toward various kinds of thinking. And just as delusion...

It is restless because it does not encompass [its object]. Likewise, applied thought (*vitakka*) is so because of its quick conceptualization; therefore, for one whose temperament is delusion (*moha*), a temperament of applied thought is of a similar nature.
Others speak of three further temperaments by way of craving (*taṇhā*), conceit (*māna*), and views (*diṭṭhi*). Among these, craving is simply lust (*rāga*).

And since conceit is associated with that [greed], both of these do not transcend the temperament of greed. Furthermore, because wrong view has delusion as its source, the temperament of view follows after the temperament of delusion itself.

44. Now, what is the source of these temperaments? And how is it to be known: "This person is of greedy temperament; this person is of one of the other temperaments, such as hatred"? What is suitable for a person of which temperament?
Regarding that, some say that the first three temperaments (carita) have their origins in past habitual practice and in the humors and defects of the physical elements (dhātu-dosa).

It is said that one who was previously abundant in the application of desirable things and in wholesome deeds becomes one of lustful temperament (rāga-carita), or one who has fallen from the heavenly realms and been reborn here.
One who was previously abundant in acts of cutting, killing, binding, and enmity becomes one of hateful temperament (dosa-carita), or one who has fallen from the hells or the womb of nāgas.

"Reborn here": they say that the "causal basis of former habits" refers to one who was previously habituated to drinking intoxicants and devoid of learning and inquiry, and thus possessed of a deluded temperament; or one who, having passed away from the animal realm, has been reborn here.
Furthermore, a person becomes of a deluded temperament due to the predominance of two elements: the earth element and the water element. Due to the predominance of the other two [elements],...

One is of "hate-temperament" (*dosacarita*). But one who possesses all [humors] in equal measure is of "lust-temperament" (*rāgacarita*). Furthermore, among the humors, one with an excess of phlegm (*semha*) is of lust-temperament;

one with an excess of wind (*vāta*) is of delusion-temperament (*mohacarita*); or one with an excess of phlegm is of delusion-temperament, while one with an excess of wind is of lust-temperament. Thus they say these are the causes based on the humors and the faults.
In this regard, because even those who previously performed many desirable applications and beautiful deeds, having fallen from heaven, have been reborn here...

Not all are exclusively of lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*), nor are the others exclusively of hateful or deluded temperament (*dosamohacarita*). Likewise, there is no fixed rule regarding the predominance (*ussada*) of the elements according to the method already stated.
Furthermore, in the determination of the [predominant] faults, only the pair of lust and delusion is mentioned, and that too is internally contradictory.
Moreover, not even a single cause for the temperaments such as faith-practice (*saddhācarita*) and the rest has been stated. Therefore, all of this—
This is an indeterminate statement.
However, here is the analysis according to the opinion of the commentators (Aṭṭhakathācariyas); for this was said in the *Ussadakittana*:

“These beings, by the necessity of their past causes, are those with a predominance of greed (*lobhussada*), those with a predominance of hatred (*dosussada*), those with a predominance of delusion (*mohussada*), those with a predominance of non-greed (*alobhussada*), and those with a predominance of non-hatred (*adosussada*).”
And there is an abundance of non-delusion.

For when, at the moment of accumulating karma, greed is strong and non-greed weak, while non-hatred and non-delusion are strong and hatred and delusion are weak, that weak non-greed is unable to overcome the greed; however, the non-hatred and non-delusion, being strong, [are able to do so].

He is able to overcome hatred and delusion. Therefore, having been reborn through the power of that karma which provided his rebirth-linking, he is fierce, virtuous in conduct, free from anger, wise, and possesses wisdom like a thunderbolt.
However, for one at the moment of accumulating karma whose greed and hatred are strong while non-greed and non-hatred are weak, and whose non-delusion is strong—
Delusion is dull; by the same principle as before, such a person is both greedy and corrupt. However, one who possesses wisdom has knowledge like a thunderbolt, like the Elder Dattābhaya.

When, at the moment of accumulating kamma, greed, non-hatred, and delusion are strong while the others are dull, that person is both greedy and dull by the same principle as before, yet they are virtuous and free from anger, like the Elder Bākula.

Likewise, at the moment of accumulating karma, for one in whom greed, hatred, and delusion are powerful while non-greed and the others are weak, that person—by the same method as before—is greedy, hateful, and deluded.

However, for one in whom non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are powerful while the others are weak, that person—by the same method as before—is not greedy and has few defilements; even upon seeing a divine object, he remains unshaken. Yet, he may be hateful and slow-witted.

Furthermore, for one at the moment of accumulating karma whose non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are strong while the others are weak, he is—by the same method as before—both non-greedy and non-hating and possesses virtue, yet he is slow-witted.

Likewise, for one at the moment of accumulating karma whose non-greed, hatred, and non-delusion are strong while the others are weak, he is—by the same method as before—both non-greedy and wise, yet he is hating and prone to anger.

"But he for whom, at the moment of accumulating kamma, all three—non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion—are powerful while greed and the others are weak, is neither greedy nor hateful and is wise, just like the Elder Mahā-Saṅgharakkhita according to the method previously stated.

And herein, he who is called "greedy" is one of lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*). Those who are "hateful" or "dull-witted" are of hateful or deluded temperaments respectively. The "wise" one is of intellectual temperament (*buddhicarita*).

Those who are "neither greedy nor hateful" are of faithful temperament (*saddhācarita*) due to their naturally clear disposition. Or, as with [the case of] non-delusion being surrounded by [other factors]...

One who is born through karma characterized by wisdom is one whose temperament is intellectual (*buddhicarita*). Likewise, one who is born through karma accompanied by powerful faith is one whose temperament is faithful (*saddhācarita*).
One who is born through karma accompanied by sensual thoughts and the like is one whose temperament is discursive (*vitakkacarita*).

One who is born through karma accompanied by a mixture of greed and other factors is one whose temperament is mixed (*vomis-sacarita*). Thus, it is the karma accompanied by any one of these—greed and so forth—that produces rebirth-linking.
It should be understood that action (*kamma*) is the source of temperament (*carita*).
Furthermore, regarding what was stated—"How is it to be known that this person is of lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*)? and so forth—the method for this is as follows:
From posture, from activity, from food, from seeing, and so forth;
"And by means of the manifestation of the temperament through the occurrence of states":
herein, regarding the postures, one of lustful temperament walks with a graceful gait when walking in his ordinary manner;
he places his foot slowly, places it evenly, and lifts it evenly, and his step is high.
The one of a hateful temperament walks as if digging with the tips of his feet;
he places his foot down abruptly and lifts it up abruptly, and his footprint is dragged along. The one of a deluded temperament walks with a completely confused gait;
he places his foot down as if trembling and lifts it up as if trembling, and his footprint is pressed down abruptly.
It is so. And this has also been said in the introduction to the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta:
"For one who is lustful, the footfall is hopping;
for one who is hateful, the footfall is dragging."
"For one who is deluded, there is a sudden oppression;
for one whose veil has been lifted, such is this state.

Furthermore, the posture of one whose temperament is dominated by lust is pleasing and sweet in appearance; that of one whose temperament is dominated by hatred is rigid in appearance; and that of one whose temperament is dominated by delusion—

It has a disordered appearance. The same method applies to sitting as well. One of lustful temperament, not being in a hurry, prepares his bed evenly, lies down slowly, and having drawn together his limbs, sleeps in a pleasing manner;
and when being awakened, he does not rise quickly, but gives a reply slowly as if apprehensive. One of hateful temperament, being in a hurry, [acts] as follows...
Alternatively, having prepared his bed in such a way, he lies down with his body tossed about and his face contorted;
and when being awakened, he rises quickly and gives a reply as if he were angry.

One of deluded temperament prepares a poorly arranged bed and mostly lies down with his body sprawled and his face turned downward; and when being awakened, he responds slowly while making a grunt of protest.

He emerges. Since those of faithful temperament (*saddhācarita*) and the others are similar to those of lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*) and so forth, their deportment (*iriyāpatha*) is likewise the same;
thus, one should first discern the temperaments by way of deportment.
By way of function (*kicca*): in such tasks as sweeping, one of lustful temperament takes up the broom with great care and without haste.
One of pure temperament sweeps cleanly and evenly, scattering the sand without disturbing it, as if creating a carpet of sinduvāra flowers.
One of hating temperament grasps the broom tightly and sweeps with haste, tossing the sand to both sides with a harsh noise, sweeping uncleanly and unevenly.
One of deluded temperament grasps the broom loosely and sweeps by turning it around.
One who sweeps unevenly and impurely while being restless is of greedy temperament (*rāgacarita*).
Just as with sweeping, so too in all tasks such as washing and dyeing robes, one who acts skillfully, sweetly, evenly, and conscientiously is of greedy temperament.

One who acts harshly, rigidly, unevenly, and improperly is of hateful temperament (*dosacarita*). One who acts unskillfully, in a confused manner, unevenly, and without discernment is of deluded temperament (*mohacarita*).
One of deluded temperament (mohacarita). For one of lustful temperament, the wearing of the robes is neither too tight nor too loose;
it is pleasing and well-rounded. For one of hateful temperament, it is too tight and not well-rounded. For one of deluded temperament, it is loose and disheveled.

Those of faithful temperament and so forth should be understood by following the same principle as these, because they share similar characteristics. Thus one should discern the temperaments according to their functions.
Regarding food: one of lustful temperament is fond of smooth and sweet food;
when eating, he makes a moderately large, round mouthful and eats while experiencing the flavor, without haste, and upon obtaining even a little something tasty, he falls into a state of joy.
One of hating temperament is fond of coarse and sour food; when eating...
And filling his mouth with a mouthful, he eats hurriedly without experiencing the flavor;
and having received something that is not savory, he falls into dejection. One whose temperament is dominated by delusion has no fixed preference;
while eating, he makes irregular and small mouthfuls, dropping them into the bowl, smearing his face, and thinking various thoughts with a distracted mind.

He eats. Those characterized by faith (*saddhācarita*) and the others should also be understood according to their respective counterparts, as they share similar qualities. Thus one should discern the temperaments (*cariyā*) from the manner of eating. From "seeing and so forth":
one of lustful temperament, upon seeing even a slightly beautiful form, gazes for a long time as if struck with wonder;
he clings to even a minor virtue and does not notice a fault even when it is present; and even when departing, he acts as if unwilling to let go.
One of a hating temperament (dosacarita), upon seeing even a slightly unpleasing form, looks at it for no long time as if weary;
he is repelled by even a slight fault, does not acknowledge even an existing virtue, and when departing, he leaves without regard, as if wishing to be rid of it.
One of a deluded temperament (mohacarita), having seen any kind of form whatsoever, acts under the influence of others...
When one hears another being criticized, one criticizes; when one hears another being praised, one praises;
but oneself, through equanimity based on ignorance, one remains merely indifferent. This same method applies to hearing sounds and so forth as well.

Those whose temperament is dominated by faith and the rest should be understood according to those very [faculties], because they share that same nature. Thus should one discern the temperaments starting from seeing and so forth.

"And because of the occurrence of states": for one of greedy temperament (*rāgacarita*), such states as deceit (*māyā*), craftiness (*sāṭheyya*), conceit (*māna*), evil desire (*pāpicchatā*), great desire (*mahicchatā*), lack of contentment (*asantuṭṭhitā*), stubbornness (*siṅga*), and restlessness (*cāpalya*) frequently occur.

For one of hating temperament (*dosacarita*), such states as anger (*kodha*), enmity (*upanāha*), disparagement (*makkha*), spite (*paḷāsa*), envy (*issā*), and avarice (*macchariya*) [frequently occur]. For one of deluded temperament (*mohacarita*), sloth (*thina*)...
Drowsiness, restlessness, remorse, doubt, stubbornness, and difficulty in relinquishing—these and others like them.

For one of faithful temperament (saddhācarita), there are freedom from stinginess, a desire to see the Noble Ones, a desire to hear the true Dhamma, abundance of gladness, lack of deceit, lack of guile, and confidence in things that inspire confidence—these and others like them.
For one of Buddha-temperament (buddhicarita), there is readiness to speak.

These include: having virtuous friends, knowing the proper measure in eating, mindfulness and clear comprehension, devotion to wakefulness, a sense of spiritual urgency regarding things that inspire urgency, and systematic striving when one feels such urgency—and so forth.

For one whose temperament is dominated by discursive thought (vitakkacarita), there is excessive talkativeness, delighting in social groups, a lack of interest in applying oneself to what is wholesome, instability in one's duties, smoldering at night, and blazing by day.
"Running here and there"—such states as these occur frequently. Thus one should discern the temperaments by way of the occurrence of mental states (*dhamma*).

However, since this method for discerning temperaments has not been handed down in its entirety either in the Canon (*pāḷi*) or in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), but is stated solely according to the opinion of the teachers (*ācariya*), it should not be accepted as the ultimate truth. [Regarding] the temperament of lust (*rāgacarita*):
For indeed, even those of a temperament characterized by hatred and so forth are able to perform the postures and other such acts when they dwell in heedfulness.
Furthermore, for a person whose temperament is mixed, it is impossible for postures and the like to possess mutually contradictory characteristics.
As for this method for discerning temperaments described in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), that alone should be accepted as the essential point. For this has been said:
“The teacher who has attained the knowledge of others’ minds will know the temperament and explain the meditation subject;

otherwise, the pupil must ask him. Therefore, one should find out by means of the knowledge of others’ minds, or by questioning that person, whether this individual is of a lustful temperament or of one of the other temperaments, such as hatred and so forth.
46. Regarding the question, "What is suitable for a person of what temperament?"—first, as for the lodging:

for one of lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*), it is suitable to stay in a dwelling that has unwashed railings, stands on the ground, lacks a constructed overhang, consists of a grass hut or a leaf-hut, or any other such place;
one that is covered in dust, filled with bats, dilapidated and crumbling, too high or too low, arid, or dangerous.
A place suitable for this is one on an impure and uneven path, where even the beds and chairs are infested with bugs, unsightly, and discolored—
such that loathing arises in one merely by looking at them. As for the lower and upper robes, those that are torn at the edges,
strewn with dangling and hanging threads like a net of honey-cakes, coarse to the touch like sackcloth, soiled, heavy, and difficult to maintain, are suitable.
Even an alms-bowl is permissible if it is discolored, or a clay bowl, or an iron bowl with a handle and a knob; however, one that is heavy, ill-shaped, or as loathsome as a lead skull is not.
The path for the alms-round is also unsuitable if it is unpleasant, lacks a nearby village, or is uneven.

Even the village for the alms-round is unsuitable if people move about there as if they do not see anyone, or where one must leave after failing to obtain even a single portion of alms from a single household.

“Come, venerable sir,” they say, and having led him into the dining hall and given him rice gruel and food, they depart like cattle being driven into a pen, going away without looking back; such a person is suitable.

As for the people who serve the meal—whether they be slaves or laborers—if they are ugly, unsightly, dressed in dirty clothes, foul-smelling, and loathsome, and they serve the rice gruel without showing respect...
They serve as if they were throwing it away; such things are suitable.

Even if the gruel, rice, and snacks are coarse, unsightly, and made of millet, kudrūsaka, broken rice, and so forth—even if it is putrid curd, sour gruel, or stale vegetables and soups—anything at all that merely fills the belly is sufficient.
As for his posture, either standing or walking is appropriate. As for the object of meditation...
Among the color-kasinas, such as blue and so forth, any that is not of a pure color is suitable for one of lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*).
For one of hateful temperament (*dosacarita*), the lodging should be neither too high nor too low, well-provided with shade and water, with walls, pillars, and steps well-proportioned,
and with a ground surface that is bright, even, smooth, and soft, adorned with well-finished floral designs, creeper-work, and various kinds of painting.
Suitable is a lodging that is like a Brahma-palace, adorned with a canopy of cloth variegated with flower garlands, provided with well-laid-out, pure, and delightful rugs, couches, and seats;
fragrant here and there with the scents of flowers and perfumes placed for the sake of scenting;
which, by its mere sight, generates rapture and joy—such is what is suitable. Furthermore, the path leading to that lodging is free from all dangers.
A clean, level floor that has been properly prepared is required.

As for the furniture and requisites for the dwelling, they should not be too numerous, as this would provide a basis for insects, bugs, long-legged spiders, and mice; only a single bed and stool are permitted.
As for his lower and upper robes, whatever is most refined—such as Chinese silk, *somāra* cloth, silk from Kosala, fine cotton, or fine linen—is appropriate.
A single-layered or double-layered cloth, light, suitable for a recluse, well-dyed a beautiful red, and of pure color, is appropriate.
An alms-bowl made of iron, well-shaped like a water-lily bud, polished like a gem, stainless, and of perfectly pure color suitable for a recluse, is appropriate.
The path for wandering for alms should be free from dangers, level, pleasant, and with a village neither too far nor too near.

It is permissible. Even a village for alms-round where people, thinking, "Now the noble one will arrive," prepare a seat on a spot that has been sprinkled and swept, go out to meet him, take his bowl, lead him into the house, have him sit on the prepared seat, and respectfully serve him with their own hands—such a place is permissible. However, as for those who serve him...
They should be handsome, pleasing, well-bathed, well-anointed, fragrant with the scent of incense and flowers, adorned with various beautiful, charming garments and ornaments, and diligent;

such persons are suitable. As for the gruel, rice, and snacks, they should be endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and flavor, nourishing, delightful, exquisite in every respect, and sufficient to satisfy one's needs.
His posture—whether lying down or sitting—is also [to be considered].

Alternatively, it is suitable [for him]; as for the object, any one among the color-kasinas such as blue that is perfectly pure in color—this is appropriate for one of a hating temperament (dosacarita).
For one of a deluded temperament (mohacarita), a dwelling facing a direction and free from confinement is suitable, where the directions appear open to one sitting there;
and among the postures, walking meditation (caṅkama) is suitable. As for his object, however, it should be small, the size of a palm-leaf fan or a shallow bowl.
Or rather, a small one is not suitable. For in a cramped space, the mind falls into even greater confusion;

therefore, a broad, large kasiṇa is suitable. The rest is exactly as described for the person of hating temperament (*dosacarita*); this is what is suitable for the person of deluded temperament (*mohacarita*).

For the person of faithful temperament (*saddhācarita*), every procedure described for the hating temperament is suitable. And among objects of focus, the subjects of recollection (*anussati-ṭṭhāna*) are also suitable for him.
For one of a Buddha-nature temperament (*buddhicarita*), there is nothing unsuitable regarding lodgings and such.

However, for one of a discursive-thought temperament (*vitakkacarita*), a lodging that is open and facing the cardinal directions—where, while sitting, one perceives the delightful beauty of monasteries, groves, and lotus ponds, as well as the successive rows of villages, market towns, and provinces, and mountains with their blue luster—is not appropriate; for that...

It is a condition for the very running about of applied thought; therefore, one should dwell in a lodging such as a deep mountain cleft, hidden by forest, resembling the Elephant’s Belly, the Pabbhāra Cave, or the Mahinda Cave.
Even a vast object is not suitable for him, for such an object becomes a condition for the mind to run away through the influence of applied thought.
However, a limited object is suitable.
"The rest is exactly as stated for one of lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*); this [subject] is suitable for one of discursive-thought temperament (*vitakkacarita*).
This is the detailed explanation of the classification, source, and suitability regarding the types of temperament mentioned here under the heading 'conducive to one’s own temperament.
However, the meditation subject conducive to that temperament has not yet been revealed in its entirety; for that belongs to the next section of the matrix (*mātikā*)."
This will be made clear in detail later on.
Regarding the commentary on the forty meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna), concerning the statement: "Therefore, having taken one of the forty meditation subjects," here—

The determination of the meditation subject should first be understood by way of these ten aspects: from the description of its factors, from its bringing about access and absorption, from the classification of jhāna, from surmounting, from increase and non-increase, from the object, from the plane, from apprehension, from conditions, and from suitability to temperament.
Regarding that, "by way of the exposition of the formulated" refers to what was stated as "among the forty meditation subjects. Herein, these forty meditation subjects are:
ten kasiṇas, ten foulness subjects, ten recollections, four divine abidings, four immaterial states, one perception, and one defining.

In this context, the ten *kasiṇas* are: the earth-*kasiṇa*, water-*kasiṇa*, fire-*kasiṇa*, air-*kasiṇa*, blue-*kasiṇa*, yellow-*kasiṇa*, red-*kasiṇa*, white-*kasiṇa*, light-*kasiṇa*, and the limited-space-*kasiṇa*.
The ten *asubhas* (foulnesses) are: the bloated, the livid, the festering, the cut up, the gnawed, the scattered, the hacked and scattered, the blood-stained, the worm-infested, and the skeleton.

The ten recollections (*anussati*) are: recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of virtue, recollection of generosity, recollection of the deities, recollection of death, mindfulness directed to the body, mindfulness of breathing, and recollection of peace.
The four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) are: loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. The four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) are:
the base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
These are the four formless states. The perception of repulsiveness in nutriment is one perception. The analysis of the four elements is one analysis.
Thus the exposition should be understood by way of this description of the enumerations.
As for "bringing access and absorption": with the exception of mindfulness occupied with the body and mindfulness of breathing, the remaining eight recollections—
The perception of repulsiveness in nutriment and the analysis of the four elements—these ten meditation subjects here bring about access concentration (*upacāra*).
The remaining ones bring about absorption (*appanā*). Thus, it is according to whether they bring about access or absorption.
Regarding the classification by jhāna: among those that bring about absorption, ten kasiṇas together with mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*) consist of four jhānas.

They are as follows: the ten foulness meditations (*asubha*), together with mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*), possess the first jhāna. The first three divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*) possess three jhānas.
The fourth divine abiding and the four formless attainments (*āruppa*) possess the fourth jhāna. Such is the classification according to the jhānas. Regarding "surpassing" (*samatikkama*):
there are two kinds of surpassing, namely, the surpassing of factors (*aṅga-samatikkama*) and the surpassing of objects (*ārammaṇa-samatikkama*). Therein:

In all meditation subjects consisting of the threefold and fourfold jhānas, there is a "surpassing of factors," because after surpassing the jhāna-factors such as applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), one must attain the second jhāna and so forth upon those very same objects. The same applies to the fourth divine abode (*brahmavihāra*);
for that too must be attained by surpassing mental joy (*somanassa*) while remaining upon the very objects of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the others. However, in the four...
In the formless attainments, there is a transcending of the object. For, having transcended one or another of the first nine kasinas, the base of infinite space is to be reached;
and having transcended space and so forth, the base of infinite consciousness and the others are reached.
Since there is no such transcending in the remaining [kasinas], it is called "by way of transcending."
Regarding "expansion and non-expansion": among these forty meditation subjects, only the ten kasiṇas are to be expanded.

For to whatever extent one pervades a space with a kasiṇa, within that range one becomes capable of hearing sounds with the divine ear-element, seeing forms with the divine eye, and knowing the minds of other beings with one's own mind.
Furthermore, mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati) and the foulness meditations (asubha) should not be expanded.
Why? Because they are limited by their specific location and because they lack further benefit. That limitation by location will become clear in the method of cultivation.
If these were expanded, only a heap of corpses would increase; there would be no benefit whatsoever. This has also been stated in the *Sopāka-pañhā-byākaraṇa*:
“Lord, the perception of form has been mastered, while the perception of the skeleton has not yet been mastered.

For in that case, the perception of form is said to be “mastered” by way of increasing the sign (*nimitta*), whereas the perception of the skeleton is said to be “unmastered” by way of not increasing it.
As for what was said, “With the perception of the skeleton alone, he pervaded this earth,” that refers to one who possesses [the attainment].
This was stated by way of the mode of appearance. For just as in the time of King Dhammāsoka, the karavīka bird,
seeing its own reflection on mirrors on all sides, perceived it as other karavīka birds in every direction and uttered its sweet song,
so too the Elder, because he had attained the perception of bones, saw the sign appearing in all directions and [perceived] even the entire...
"He thought, 'The earth is filled with bones.
If this is so, does it not contradict what was said regarding the fact that the subjects of foulness meditations (*asubha-jhāna*) are immeasurable? It does not contradict it.
For one person grasps the sign (*nimitta*) in a bloated corpse or in large bones, while another grasps it in small ones. By this...
In one sense, for some, the jhāna has a limited object; for others, it has an immeasurable object.
Or rather, it is said to have an "immeasurable object" with reference to one who increases it while failing to see the danger in such expansion.
However, because there is no benefit [in doing so], they should not be increased.

And as with these, so too the remaining [meditations] should not be expanded. Why? Because, first, for one who expands the sign of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānanimitta*), it is merely a mass of air that is being expanded, and it is limited by space.
Thus, because it is accompanied by disadvantages and because it is limited by space, it should not be expanded.
The divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) have sentient beings as their object; for one who expands their sign—
It would merely increase by a factor of seven, yet there is no purpose served by that; therefore, it should not be increased.
As for what was said, "having pervaded one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness," and so forth—that was stated by way of inclusion (*pariggaha*).
For, by including the beings of one direction in succession—starting with those living in a single dwelling, then two dwellings, and so on—one cultivates [the meditation].
"Having pervaded one direction" is what is said; it does not mean increasing the sign (*nimitta*). Furthermore, there is no counterpart sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*) here that he could increase.
Here, the state of having limited or immeasurable objects should be understood solely by way of the delimitation (*pariggaha*).
Even among the formless objects, space is merely the removal of the kasiṇa; for that must be brought to mind precisely by way of the disappearance of the kasiṇa. Beyond that—

Even when increasing it, nothing happens; for consciousness is a phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-dhamma*). Indeed, it is impossible to increase a phenomenon that possesses intrinsic nature.

The departure from consciousness is merely the absence of consciousness. Because the object of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception possesses intrinsic nature, it likewise cannot be increased.
The remaining [objects] cannot be increased because they are signless (*animitta*); for it is the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*) that can be increased.
It would not be so named. Furthermore, for the recollections of the Buddha and so forth, there is no counterpart sign as their object; therefore, that [object] should not be expanded.
Thus, it is "by way of expansion and non-expansion. Regarding "by way of object":
among these forty meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*), there are the ten kasinas, the ten foulness subjects (*asubha*), and mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*).
"Mindfulness directed to the body" refers to these twenty-two objects that are counter-images (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*). The remaining ones do not have counter-images as their objects.

Likewise, among the ten recollections (*anussati*), with the exception of mindfulness of breathing and mindfulness directed to the body, the remaining eight recollections, the perception of repulsiveness in food, the analysis of the four elements, the base of infinite consciousness, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception [do not have counter-images as their objects].

These twelve are objects consisting of the intrinsic nature of things (*sabhāva-dhamma*). The ten kasiṇas, the ten foulness subjects (*asubha*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*), and mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*)—these twenty-two are sign-objects (*nimitta-ārammaṇa*). The remaining six are objects that cannot be so described.
Likewise, the bloated, the bloody, the worm-infested, mindfulness of breathing, the water kasiṇa, the fire kasiṇa, the air kasiṇa, and that which [is included] in the light kasiṇa...
"The orb of light of the sun and so forth" refers to these eight moving objects; however, these are such only in the preliminary stage, whereas in the counterpart sign they become perfectly still.
The remaining ones are not moving objects. This is the analysis by way of object. As for "by way of plane":
here, the twelve consisting of the ten kinds of foulness, mindfulness occupied with the body, and the perception of repulsiveness in food—these are [the subjects].
They do not occur among the gods. These twelve, together with mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*), these thirteen do not occur in the Brahma-world.

However, in the formless existence (*arūpabhava*), with the exception of the four formless [attainments], none of the others occur. Among humans, all of them occur. Thus it is according to plane (*bhūmi*).
As for "according to apprehension" (*gahaṇato*), the analysis here should be understood by way of apprehending what is seen, touched, and heard. Therein, setting aside...
The air-kasiṇa and the remaining nine kasiṇas—these ten foul objects (asubha)—these nineteen are to be grasped by what is seen (*diṭṭha*).

The meaning is that in the preliminary stage, the sign (*nimitta*) for these must be grasped after looking with the eye. In the case of mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*), the fivefold skin-group is grasped by what is seen, while the remainder is grasped by what is heard;
thus, its object is to be grasped by both what is seen and what is heard. Mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*)...
By "contact": the air-kasiṇa is taken by what is seen and touched; the remaining eighteen are to be grasped by hearing.

Furthermore, the sublime abiding of equanimity and the four formless attainments are not to be grasped by a beginner here; the remaining thirty-five are to be grasped—thus it is according to the method of grasping. According to conditionality:
among these meditation subjects, with the exception of the space-kasiṇa, the remaining nine kasiṇas are conditions for the formless attainments.
They are conditions as follows: the ten kasiṇas are conditions for the direct knowledges; the first three divine abidings are conditions for the fourth divine abiding;
each lower formless attainment is a condition for each higher one; the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is a condition for the attainment of cessation;
and all of them are conditions for pleasant abiding, insight, and the success of existence. Thus they are [conditions] by way of conditionality.
"According to suitability for temperament": here the exposition should be understood according to what is suitable for the various temperaments. To wit:

first, for one of lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*), eleven meditation subjects are suitable here—namely, the ten kinds of foulness (*asubha*) and mindfulness occupied with the body (*kāyagatāsati*).

For one of hateful temperament (*dosacarita*), eight are suitable—the four divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*) and the four colored kasinas (*vaṇṇakasiṇa*). For one of deluded temperament (*mohacarita*) and for one of discursive temperament (*vitakkacarita*)...
And there is one meditation subject, namely mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*). For those of faithful temperament (*saddhācarita*), there are the first six recollections (*anussati*).

For those of intellectual temperament (*buddhicarita*), there are four: mindfulness of death (*maraṇassati*), the recollection of peace (*upasamānussati*), the analysis of the four elements (*catudhātuvavatthāna*), and the perception of repulsiveness in food (*āhāre paṭikūlasaññā*).
The remaining *kasiṇas* and the four formless attainments (*āruppa*) are suitable for all temperaments. Among the *kasiṇas*, any limited (*paritta*) one may be used.
"For one of speculative temperament, [the meditation subject] is immeasurable; for one of deluded temperament, it is immeasurable.
Thus, in this context, the analysis should be understood according to what is suitable to the temperament.

All of this has been stated by way of direct opposition and by way of extreme suitability. However, [these subjects] do not suppress lust and the other defilements, nor do they assist faith and the other faculties.
There is no such thing as the cultivation of the wholesome. And this has been said in the Meghiya Sutta: "Four things are to be further cultivated:
the meditation on the foul is to be cultivated for the abandoning of lust; loving-kindness is to be cultivated for the abandoning of ill will;
mindfulness of breathing is to be cultivated for the cutting off of discursive thought; the perception of impermanence is to be cultivated..."
“For the uprooting of the conceit ‘I am’.
In the Rāhula Sutta as well, seven meditation subjects are taught for a single person in the manner beginning with, “Rāhula, develop the meditation on loving-kindness,” and so forth.
Therefore, without adhering to the mere literal expression, the underlying intention must be sought in every instance.
"Having taken this meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*)"—herein lies the detailed exposition of the meditation subject.

Regarding the word "having taken," this is the explanation of its meaning: having approached a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitta*) who bestows a meditation subject, in the very manner described in the passage beginning with "that yogi, having approached the spiritual friend who bestows the meditation subject."

Having surrendered oneself to the Buddha, the Blessed One, or to a teacher, and having become possessed of a resolute intention and a resolute inclination, one should request a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
In that regard, one should say to the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Blessed One, I relinquish this self-existence (*attabhāva*) to you. Thus [one speaks] to the Buddha, the Blessed One.

One must surrender oneself. For if one dwells in remote lodgings without having surrendered oneself in this way, and being unable to remain steadfast when a terrifying object comes into range, one might descend to the vicinity of a village, become associated with householders, fall into wrong livelihood, and meet with ruin and disaster.
But for one who has surrendered their person, even when a terrifying object comes into range...
Fear does not arise. However, for one who reflects, "O wise one, did you not previously offer yourself to the Buddhas?", only joy arises.
For example, if a man possessed a most excellent Kāsī cloth and it were eaten by a mouse or insects, distress would arise in him; but if...

But if one were to give that [robe] to a monk who has no robe, then even upon seeing it being torn to pieces by that monk, only joy would arise in him. It should be understood that this case is exactly like that.
Even when handing oneself over to a teacher, one should say: "Venerable sir, I relinquish this self-body to you."
Thus, one who has not surrendered his own person is either unrefusable, or he is difficult to speak with and does not accept advice;

or he goes wherever he pleases, wandering about without asking permission from his teacher. Consequently, the teacher does not sustain him with either material gifts or the Dhamma, nor does he teach him the hidden texts.
Failing to receive these two kinds of support, he—
He finds no firm footing in the Dispensation and, before long, falls into either immorality or the state of a householder.
However, one who has surrendered his very being is neither to be reproached nor free to go wherever he pleases; rather, he is easy to speak with and lives entirely dependent on his teacher.
Receiving a twofold support from his teacher, he attains growth, increase, and maturity in the Dispensation, like the pupils of the Elder Cūḷapiṇḍapātika Tissa.
It is said that three monks came into the presence of the Elder.
One of them said, "Venerable sir, when it is said, 'I am for your sake,' I would venture to leap from a precipice a hundred fathoms high.
The second said, "Venerable sir, when it is said, 'I am for your sake,' I would rub this body from the feet upward against a stone surface until it is completely worn away."

"He would be able to strive" means he said this. The third one, when told "Venerable sir, for your sake," said "I would be able to strive to bring about my death by arresting the inhalation and exhalation.
The Elder, thinking "These bhikkhus are capable," taught them a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).
Standing by his instruction, all three of them attained Arahantship. This is the benefit in dedicating oneself [to another]. By that—
It is said: "Having surrendered oneself to the Buddha, the Blessed One, or to a teacher.
Regarding the phrase "having become one whose underlying tendency (*ajjhāsaya*) is perfected and whose resolution (*adhimutti*) is perfected":

here, that yogi must possess an underlying tendency that is perfected in six ways by means of non-greed and the other [wholesome roots]. For it is when one's underlying tendency is thus perfected that the three...
One attains one of the various forms of enlightenment. As it has been said: "Six inclinations lead to the maturation of enlightenment for Bodhisattvas:
Bodhisattvas with an inclination toward non-greed perceive greed as a fault; Bodhisattvas with an inclination toward non-hatred perceive hatred as a fault;
Bodhisattvas with an inclination toward non-delusion perceive delusion as a fault; and Bodhisattvas with an inclination toward renunciation..."
And Bodhisattvas see the fault in the household life; Bodhisattvas, having a disposition for seclusion, see the fault in social company;
and Bodhisattvas, having a disposition for renunciation, see the fault in all states of existence.
For whoever there may be—past, future, or present—whether stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, those whose taints are destroyed, paccekabuddhas, or perfectly enlightened Buddhas...
All of them have attained the specific excellence to be reached by each individually through these very six modes. Therefore, one should possess an inclination toward these six modes.
Furthermore, by being intent upon them, one should possess resolute conviction (*adhimutti*).
One should be intent on concentration, respectful toward concentration, leaning toward concentration; intent on Nibbāna, respectful toward Nibbāna.
The meaning is that one must become inclined toward Nibbāna. 50.

Now, when he who has thus attained such an inclination and resolve requests a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), his teacher—who possesses the knowledge of penetration of others' minds—should observe the movement of his mind and discern his temperament.
By another [means], [the student] should be asked: "What is your temperament? Or which mental states [do you possess]?"
They frequently practice [which one]? Or what brings them ease when they attend to it?

Toward which meditation subject does their mind incline? Having asked in such ways as these, it must be understood. Once this is known, a meditation subject suitable to their temperament should be taught.
And when teaching, it should be taught in three ways: for one who has already mastered a meditation subject by nature, one or two sessions...
Having performed the recitation (*sajjhāya*), it should be given. To one living nearby, it should be explained at every moment he arrives.
To one who has mastered it and wishes to go elsewhere, it should be explained neither too concisely nor too diffusely.

In that regard, first, when explaining the earth-kasiṇa (*pathavīkasiṇa*), one should explain the four defects of the kasiṇa, the preparation of the kasiṇa, and [the procedure] for what has been prepared...

The method of development consists of nine aspects that must be explained: the two kinds of signs, the two kinds of concentration, the sevenfold suitability and unsuitability, the ten skills in absorption, the balancing of energy, and the procedure for absorption.

In the case of the remaining meditation subjects as well, what is appropriate for each should be explained; all of this will be made clear in the section on the methods of development for those subjects.
While this meditation subject is being explained, that yogi should grasp the sign and listen.
"Grasping the sign" means: "This is the preceding word, this is the subsequent word;
this is its meaning, this is its intention, this is the simile"—thus, it means binding each respective aspect in mind. Having thus grasped the sign, he should listen with careful attention.
For the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is well grasped; then, by depending on that, the attainment of distinction succeeds for him, but not for the other.
This is the explanation of the meaning of the phrase "having taken.
Up to this point, the phrases "having approached a good friend" and "having taken one of the forty meditation subjects suitable to one's own temperament" have been explained in their entirety.

Thus ends the section entitled "The Description of Taking Up a Meditation Subject" in the Chapter on the Development of Concentration within the *Visuddhimagga*, composed for the delight of virtuous people.
The Third Chapter.
4. The Description of the Earth-Kasina. 51.
Now, as for what was said: "By abandoning an abode unsuitable for the development of concentration and dwelling in a suitable abode..."
In this regard, if one who lives in the same monastery as the teacher finds comfort there, he should remain right there while purifying his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
If he does not find comfort there, he should live in another suitable monastery within a *gāvuta*, half a *yojana*, or even a full *yojana* away. For when this is so, the meditation subject—
If, at some point, doubt or forgetfulness should arise regarding mindfulness, one should perform the monastery duties early in the morning, wander for alms along the way,
and upon the conclusion of the meal, go to the teacher’s dwelling.
Having clarified the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) in the presence of the teacher that very day, one should pay homage to the teacher on the following day, depart, and [continue] along the way.
Having wandered for alms, he will be able to return to his own dwelling place without even becoming weary. However,
one who does not find a comfortable location even within the distance of a league (*yojana*) should cut through every knot of doubt regarding the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*),
