make the meditation subject thoroughly pure and connected with clear mental advertence (*āvajjanā*), and then go even a great distance to develop concentration (*samādhi*).
Having abandoned an unsuitable dwelling, one should dwell in a suitable dwelling.
Regarding the unsuitable dwelling:
herein, "unsuitable" means being possessed of any one of eighteen faults. These eighteen are as follows:
The disadvantages are: its greatness, its newness, its decayed state, its dependence on the road, the presence of a tavern,
leaves, flowers, fruits, desirability, dependence on a city, dependence on timber, dependence on fields, the presence of dissimilar persons,
dependence on a port, dependence on a border region, and dependence on a royal boundary.
One who is possessed of any one of these eighteen faults—such as unsuitability or the failure to obtain virtuous friends—is said to be "unsuitable. One should not dwell there. Why?
Because in a large monastery, many people with diverse inclinations gather; due to their mutual antagonism, [conflict arises].
They do not perform the duties; the bodhi-tree precincts and other areas remain unswept; the drinking water and washing water have not been set out.

In this regard, if one who has taken up bowl and robe and set out with the thought, "I will go for alms in the village for almsfood," sees that the duties have not been performed or that the water-jar is empty, then he must perform those duties himself.
Water should be set out. One who fails to do so incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the breach of duty. If he does provide it, time passes;
having entered [the village] too late, he receives nothing when the alms-round is finished.

Even when he has gone into seclusion, he is distracted by the loud noise of novices and junior monks and by the formal acts of the Saṅgha. However, in a place where all the duties have indeed been performed...
Furthermore, there is no crowding in the remaining [monasteries]. One may dwell even in such a great monastery (*mahāvihāra*).

In a new monastery, however, there is much building work (*navakamma*); people complain of one who does not do it. But where monks say, "Venerable sir, please practice the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*) as you please; we shall do the building work," in such a place one may dwell.

In an old monastery, however, there is much maintenance to be done; people complain of one who does not maintain even his own lodging (*senāsana*), yet for one who does maintain it, his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) suffers decline.
In a great earth-dwelling monastery situated along a main road, visitors gather day and night.
Those who arrive at an improper time must, after giving up their own lodging, dwell at the foot of a tree or on a stone slab;
and since this happens likewise on the following day, there is no opportunity for the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). One should therefore reside where such crowding by visitors does not occur.
There was a stone lotus-pool named Soṇḍī; there a great multitude of people gathered for the sake of drinking water.
Disciples of the elder monks who were dependents of the royal family from the city also came there for the purpose of dyeing cloth.
As they asked for vessels, wooden troughs, and so forth, he had to point out to them, "They are at such-and-such a place and such-and-such a place. Thus, he was constantly occupied at all times.
Where there are various kinds of vegetables and leaves, even if one has taken up the meditation subject and is sitting for the day’s rest nearby,
vegetable-gatherers singing and picking leaves create an obstacle to the meditation subject through the impact of discordant sounds.
Likewise, where there are various flowering shrubs in full bloom, there too such a calamity occurs.
Where there are various kinds of fruits such as mangoes, rose-apples, and jackfruits, those seeking fruit come there and beg;
they become angry with one who does not give, or they take it by force.

Seeing them walking in the middle of the monastery at evening time, when he asks, "Why, lay followers, do you act in this way?", they revile him as they please and even strive to drive him away from his residence.

Furthermore, people who hear that he is dwelling in a monastery—such as Dakkhiṇagiri, Hatthikucchi, Cetiyagiri, or Cittalapabbata—which is considered a secure refuge and is worthy of veneration, will gather from all sides, desiring to pay him homage.
Because of this, he finds no comfort; however, for one to whom such conditions are favorable, he should go elsewhere during the day and return to stay there at night.

When a monastery is situated near a city, discordant objects enter the field of vision: even slave-girls carrying water-jars pass by, and having descended [from their vehicles], they do not yield the path;
even men of high status sit in the middle of the monastery, having surrounded themselves with a screen of cloth.
But when it is situated near a forest, where there are trees for firewood and timber for building materials, wood-gatherers [pass by].
Like those previously mentioned who carry away vegetables and flowers, they cause discomfort;
people come and cut down trees that exist in the monastery, thinking, "We will build houses by cutting these down.

If, having emerged from the meditation hall in the evening and walking in the middle of the monastery, one sees them and says, "Why, lay followers, are you doing this?", they revile him as they please.
They even exert themselves against his lack of dwellings.
However, in the case of one who is dependent on fields and surrounded on all sides by fields, people there build a threshing floor right in the middle of the monastery and thresh grain;
they sleep in the courtyards and cause much other inconvenience as well.
Even where there is great property belonging to the Saṅgha, if monastery attendants block people's cattle, prevent access to water,
or if people take up ears of rice and show them to the Saṅgha, saying,

"Look at the work of your monastery attendants," one must go to the doors of kings and royal ministers for various such reasons; this too is included under the category of "that which is dependent on fields."
"Because there exist persons who are dissimilar": where monks who are mutually dissimilar and hostile dwell,
and while quarreling, even when being restrained with the words, "Venerable sirs, do not do this," they say,
"Ever since this refuse-rag wearer arrived, we have been ruined."

Furthermore, those who depend on a port by water or a port by land cause inconvenience by constantly crowding them, saying, "Give us space for people arriving by ship or caravan; give us drinking water; give us salt.
However, people living near a border are generally lacking in faith toward the Buddha and the rest of the Triple Gem.
Those living near a frontier between kingdoms face the danger of kings; for one king will think of that territory, "It does not submit to my authority."
"He strikes; the other, too, does not remain under my control. In this regard, this bhikkhu sometimes wanders within the realm of this king and sometimes within that of the other.
Then, suspecting him to be a spy, they bring about his ruin and disaster.
"Unsuitability" means unsuitability due to the convergence of discordant objects such as visible forms, or because the place is possessed by non-human beings.
This is the story: It is said that a certain elder lived in the forest. Then a certain *yakkhinī*, standing at the door of his leaf-hut, began to sing.
He came out and stood at the door; she went and sang at the head of the walking-path (*caṅkama*). The elder went to the head of the walking-path.
She stood on the edge of a precipice a hundred fathoms deep and sang. The elder turned back. Then she came toward him with great speed—
Having taken them, he said, “Venerable sir, it is not just one or two like you that have been eaten by me.

Regarding the non-attainment of good friends: this refers to a place where it is impossible to find a good friend who is either a teacher (ācariya) or equal to a teacher, or a preceptor (upajjhāya) or equal to a preceptor.
In such a case, that non-attainment of good friends is indeed a great fault.
One who possesses any one of these eighteen faults should be understood as being unsuitable.
And this has also been said in the commentaries:
"A large dwelling, a new dwelling, an old dwelling, and a dwelling on a road;"
A tavern, a leaf-hut, flowers, fruit, and even one’s own desire;
a city made of wood, a field, a port with dissimilar inhabitants,
a border region, a frontier boundary, and a place where no friend is found.
"A wise person, understanding these eighteen states,
should avoid them from afar, just as one would a path beset with danger. This is the dwelling in accordance [with the Dhamma].
53. However, that which possesses five factors—such as being neither too far from nor too near the village where one seeks alms—is called "suitable.
For this was said by the Blessed One: "And how, monks, does a lodging possess five factors?
Here, monks, a lodging is not too far away, not too near, and is well-served for coming and going..."
It is not crowded by day, quiet at night, and free from noise; it is free from the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and creeping things.
Furthermore, while dwelling in such a lodging, the requisites of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal supplies for the sick arise with little difficulty.
Moreover, in that lodging dwell elder monks who are learned, masters of the tradition, and bearers of the Dhamma.
Those who are holders of the Vinaya and holders of the Mātikā approach them from time to time, inquire, and question them, saying:

"Venerable sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this? Those venerable ones reveal what has not been revealed to him, clarify what has not been made clear, and dispel his doubt regarding various matters that are grounds for uncertainty.
“Thus, monks, a lodging is endowed with five factors.
This is the detailed explanation for the passage: “By one who, having abandoned a dwelling unsuitable for the development of concentration, dwells in a suitable dwelling.
[Now follow] the minor impediments.
54. "Having removed minor impediments": while dwelling in such a suitable monastery, whatever minor impediments one may have, those too must be removed.
For example: long hair, nails, and body hair should be cut.
Repairs or darning should be done for worn-out robes, or [stains] that have become soiled...
[The bowls] must be washed. If there is dirt in the bowl, the bowl must be boiled. The beds, chairs, and so forth must be cleaned.
This is the detailed explanation for the phrase, "Having thus severed the minor impediments. [Now follows] the method for the development [of meditation].

55. Now, as for the statement "it should be developed by one who does not omit any part of the method of development," here follows a detailed exposition of all meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna), beginning with the earth-kasiṇa.

For a bhikkhu whose minor impediments have been severed, having returned from his alms round after the meal and dispelled the drowsiness caused by eating, sitting comfortably in a secluded place—whether or not he has already performed the preliminary work—[should proceed as follows].
The sign should be grasped from the earth. For this has been said:
"One who is learning the earth-kasiṇa grasps the sign in earth that is prepared or unprepared, limited, not unlimited;
with a boundary, not without a boundary; with a circumference, not without a circumference; finite, not infinite."
Whether it be the size of a spoonful or the size of a saucer, he grasps that sign well, retains it well when retained,
and defines it well when defined. Having grasped that sign well, having retained it well when retained, and having defined it well when defined,
he perceives its benefits, regards it as a treasure, and establishes a sense of reverence for it.
“Delighting in it, he binds his mind to that object, thinking: ‘Surely by this practice I shall be liberated from aging and death.
Thus, secluded from sensual pleasures... [he] enters and dwells in the first jhāna.

In this context, one who—having gone forth in a past life, or having gone forth in the Dispensation (sāsana) or into the ascetic life (isipabbajjā)—[has developed] the fourfold and fivefold jhānas upon the earth-kasiṇa...

For one such as this—possessing merit and endowed with the necessary support (*upanissaya*)—a sign arises even on unplowed ground, whether in a plowed field or in a threshing floor, as was the case with the Elder Mallaka.
It is said that as the Venerable One was looking at a plowed field, a sign arose exactly the size of that area. Having enlarged it, he attained the five jhānas.
Having produced [the kasiṇa] and established insight (vipassanā) with the jhāna as its proximate cause, he attained Arahantship.

However, one who has not yet performed this work should prepare the kasiṇa in the presence of a teacher, without violating the method for the meditation subject learned from him, and while avoiding the four faults of the kasiṇa. This is done by way of the distinctions of blue, yellow, red, and white.

For these are the four defects of the earth-kasiṇa. Therefore, without taking clay of blue or other colors, one should prepare the kasiṇa from clay of the color of dawn, similar to the clay found in the bed of the Ganges.
Furthermore, it should not be made in the middle of the monastery in a place where novices and others frequent;
rather, it should be made in a secluded spot on the outskirts of the monastery, such as a mountain cave or a leaf-hut, and it may be portable.
Alternatively, a fixed one (*tatraṭṭhaka*) may be made. Among these, the portable one (*saṃhārima*) is to be made by binding rags, leather, or a matting of reeds to four sticks;

then, having smeared a circle of the prescribed dimensions there with well-kneaded clay that has had grass, roots, gravel, and potsherds removed, it should be constructed. At the time of preparation, it should be spread upon the ground.
It should be observed as follows. The "eightfold" [structure] should be made by driving stakes into the ground in the shape of lotus pericarp centers and binding them together with creepers.

If that clay is insufficient, one should add more below and fashion a circle on the well-cleansed upper surface with clay the color of dawn, measuring one span and four finger-breadths in width. For this indeed is the proper measure.
With this in mind, it is said: "the measure of a cup or the measure of a bowl. However, the phrase "limited, not unlimited," and so forth, is stated for the purpose of defining its boundaries.
Therefore, having established the limit of the measure thus described, the tree-hand gesture produces a color that is dissimilar [to the original].
Therefore, without taking that [wood], one should rub it with a stone-hand and make it even like the surface of a drum;

then, having swept that spot, bathed, and returned, one should sit on a well-spread seat provided with legs a span and four fingers high, situated at a distance of two and a half cubits from the *kasiṇa* disk. For one sitting further away than that, [the object would not be clear].
For if one sits too far away, the meditation object (kasiṇa) does not appear clearly, and the defects of the kasiṇa become apparent when one is closer.
If one sits too high, one must look down by bending the neck; if one sits too low, the knees ache.

Therefore, sitting in the manner already described, one should reflect on the danger in sensual pleasures (*kāma*) by way of such passages as "Sensual pleasures are of little gratification," and so forth, and [turn] toward the escape from sensual pleasures, which is the means for transcending all suffering.
Having generated rapture and gladness by recollecting the virtues of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha through the desire born for renunciation,
and having developed reverence for the practice with the thought, "This is now that very path of renunciation practiced by all Buddhas,
Paccekabuddhas, and noble disciples," he thinks: "Surely, by means of this practice, I shall partake in the flavor of the bliss of seclusion."
Having generated enthusiasm, one should develop [the meditation] by opening the eyes in an even manner and grasping the sign.
For if one opens them too wide, the eyes become fatigued and the disk becomes overly distinct; consequently, the sign does not arise for him.
If one opens them too little, the disk is indistinct and the mind becomes sluggish; likewise, the sign does not arise.
It does not arise. Therefore, it should be developed by opening the eyes evenly, as one who sees the reflection of a face on the surface of a mirror, grasping the sign;
one should not review the color, nor attend to the characteristics.
Furthermore, without abandoning the color, having made it the same color as its support, one should establish the mind upon the concept (paṇṇatti-dhamma) by way of its prominence.

It should be kept in mind. Among the names for earth—such as *pathavī*, *mahī*, *medinī*, *bhūmi*, *vasudhā*, *vasundharā*, etc.—whichever one is desired, whichever is suitable for one’s own perception, that should be used. Furthermore, the name "earth" (*pathavī*) alone is well-known;
therefore, it should be developed precisely according to its common usage as "earth, earth. At times one should open the eyes, and at times...

Having closed the eyes, one should direct the mind. As long as the learning sign (uggahanimitta) does not arise, one should develop it by this same method for a hundred times, a thousand times, or even more than that. 57.
When, for one developing it in this way, [the sign] comes into range upon closing the eyes just as it did when the eyes were open, [then it has arisen].
Then it is said that the learning sign (*uggahanimitta*) has arisen. From the moment it arises, one should no longer sit in that place;
rather, having entered one’s own dwelling, one should develop [the meditation] while seated there.
For the purpose of avoiding the inconvenience of washing one's feet, however, a single-slipper sandal and a walking stick are required. Then, if his concentration is still tender...
If it is lost due to some unsuitable circumstance, one should put on sandals, take a walking stick, go to that place, take note of the signs, and return;

then, sitting comfortably, one should develop it, repeatedly attending to it, striking it with applied thought (*takkā*) and sustained thought (*vitakkā*). As he does this, the hindrances (*nīvaraṇāni*) are gradually suppressed.
The defilements subside, the mind becomes concentrated through access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*), and the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*) arises.
In this regard, the distinction between the previous learning sign (*uggaha-nimitta*) and this [counterpart sign] is as follows: in the learning sign, the defects of the kasiṇa are apparent;
the counterpart sign is like a mirror-disk taken out from its case, or like a well-washed conch-shell bowl.
Like the orb of the moon emerging from behind a cloud, like a crane appearing at the mouth of a cloud, the learning sign appears as if it has burst forth;
having emerged from that, it becomes a hundredfold or a thousandfold more perfectly pure.
Yet it possesses neither color nor shape. For if it were such [as those], it would be cognizable by the eye.
It might be coarse, reaching the stage of comprehension and struck by the three characteristics; however, this is not like that.
For it is merely a mode of appearance to one who has attained concentration, consisting simply of perception.
Furthermore, from the very moment it arises, the hindrances are suppressed, the defilements are stilled, and the mind is concentrated by access concentration.
Concentration is indeed twofold: access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*) and absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*). The mind becomes concentrated in two ways:
either on the plane of access or on the plane of attainment. Therein, on the plane of access, the mind is concentrated through the abandoning of the hindrances;
on the plane of attainment, it is concentrated through the manifestation of the factors [of jhāna].
Now, this is the distinction between the two types of concentration: in access concentration, the factors are not yet firmly established.

Because the factors are not firmly established, just as a young child, when lifted up and set down, falls back to the ground again and again, even so, when access concentration has arisen, the mind at times takes the sign as its object, and at times it sinks back into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
In absorption, however, the factors become firm; because of their firmness,
just as a strong man might stand for even a whole day after rising from his seat, so too when absorption concentration has arisen, the mind—
having once cut off the flow of the life-continuum— remains for an entire night or an entire day, proceeding solely by way of a succession of wholesome impulsion moments.
In this regard, the production of that counterpart sign which has arisen together with access concentration is exceedingly difficult.
Therefore, if he is able to reach absorption by expanding that sign while remaining in that very same cross-legged posture, it is excellent.
If he is not able, then he must, with diligence, [expand] that sign as one who possesses the potential for a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*).
It must be guarded like that. For thus it is said:
"For one who guards the sign, there is no loss of what has been gained;
when guarding is absent, whatever is gained is lost."
The Seven Things Conducive to Health (59). Herein, this is the method of protection:
Dwelling, pasture, speech, person, food, and climate;
Regarding the modes of conduct, one should avoid the seven things that are unsuitable and cultivate the seven that are suitable.
For one who practices in this way, absorption will arise before long.
In this regard, that dwelling where, while one is staying, a sign that has not yet arisen does not arise, or one that has arisen perishes;
where unestablished mindfulness does not become established, and an unconcentrated mind does not become concentrated—this is unsuitable.
But where a sign arises and remains stable, mindfulness becomes established, and the mind becomes concentrated—that is suitable.
This is suitable, as was the case for the Elder Padhāniya Tissa who dwelt at Nāgapabbata.
Therefore, in a monastery where there are many dwellings, one should stay for three days in each one; then, wherever the mind becomes one-pointed, there one should remain.
For it was by virtue of the suitability of the dwelling that those living in the Cūḷanāgaleṇa on the island of Tambapaṇṇi [attained their goal].
Taking up that very same meditation subject right there, five hundred bhikkhus attained arahantship.

As for those who had become stream-enterers and so forth elsewhere, and those who attained arahantship there after having reached the plane of the noble ones (ariyabhūmi) elsewhere, their number is beyond counting.
It was the same in other monasteries as well, such as the Cittalapabbata Vihāra.

As for the village as a resort (*gocaragāma*): that which lies neither too far from the lodging—within one and a half *krośas* to the north or south—and where alms-food is easily obtained, is suitable;

the opposite is unsuitable. As for talk (*bhassa*): that which is included among the thirty-two types of low conversation is unsuitable, for it leads to the disappearance of the signs [of concentration]. That which is based on the ten topics of discourse is suitable, but even that should be spoken in moderation. As for the person (*puggala*):
one who avoids low conversation and is endowed with virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*) is suitable, depending upon whom the unconcentrated mind [becomes concentrated].
That which is suitable is such that one becomes concentrated, or the concentrated mind becomes more stable.
However, one who is full of bodily rigidity and given to frivolous talk is unsuitable; for he makes the mind turbid, just as mud makes clear water dirty.
By resorting to such a person, even the attainment of a young monk living at Koṭapabbata was lost, let alone the sign.
Furthermore, for some, sweet food is suitable, while for others, sour food is suitable. Likewise, for some, a cool temperature is suitable, while for others, a warm one is suitable.

Therefore, whatever food or temperature brings ease to one who partakes of it, or causes an unconcentrated mind to become concentrated, or makes a concentrated mind more stable—that food and that temperature are suitable.
Other food and other climate may be unsuitable.
Among the postures as well, walking may be suitable for one person, while for another, any one of lying down, standing, or sitting may be suitable.
Therefore, after examining that dwelling for three days—just as one would examine the lodging—one should determine which posture is unsuitable for concentration.
The mind becomes concentrated, or if already concentrated, it becomes more stable; that is suitable. The other should be understood as unsuitable.

Thus, having avoided these seven kinds of the unsuitable, one should cultivate the suitable. For one who practices in this way and frequently cultivates the sign, absorption (appanā) will arise before long for some.
This is the tenfold skill in absorption.
60. But for one who does not succeed even while practicing in this way, tenfold skill in absorption (appanā-kosalla) must be perfected.

Herein is the method: skill in absorption should be sought through ten modes—by making the basis pure, by bringing the faculties to evenness, by skill in the sign, and by uplifting the mind at the time when the mind should be uplifted;

[and likewise by restraining it when it should be restrained, by looking on with equanimity when it should be looked upon with equanimity, by knowing the right time for concentration, by knowing the right time for energy, and by knowing the right time for equanimity]. When the mind should be uplifted, he uplifts the mind at that time.
At whatever time the mind should be restrained, at that time he restrains the mind;
at whatever time the mind should be gladdened, at that time he gladdens the mind;

at whatever time the mind should be looked upon with equanimity, at that time he looks upon it with equanimity—by avoiding persons who are unconcentrated, by associating with persons who are concentrated, and by being intent upon that [concentration].
61. Herein, "making the basis clean" means making the internal and external bases clean.
For when one's hair of the head, nails, and body hair are long, or when the body is covered with sweat and grime, then the internal basis is unclean and impure.
But when one's robe is worn out, soiled, and foul-smelling, [the external basis is likewise].
Or when the lodging is dirty, then the external object is unclear and impure.

When both the internal and external objects are unclear, the knowledge regarding the consciousness and mental factors that have arisen is also impure, like the radiance of a lamp-flame produced by depending on an impure oil-soaked wick and vessel. By means of such impure knowledge...

When one comprehends formations, even the formations themselves do not become clear; for one who is devoted to the meditation subject, the meditation subject does not reach growth, increase, or expansion.

But when the internal and external bases are clear, the knowledge regarding the consciousness and mental factors that have arisen becomes clear and purified, just as the wick, the bowl, and the oil of a lamp are purified.
It is like the radiance produced by the flame of a lamp. When one comprehends formations with purified knowledge, the formations themselves become clarified;
and for one who devotes himself to the meditation subject, that meditation subject attains growth, increase, and abundance. 62.
"Balancing the faculties" means making the faculties, such as faith and the rest, equal in strength. If...
If his faculty of faith is strong while the others are weak, then the faculty of energy cannot perform its function of exertion,
the faculty of mindfulness its function of establishing, the faculty of concentration its function of non-distraction, and the faculty of wisdom its function of seeing; therefore,
by means of reflecting on the specific nature of phenomena, or by attending to them in whatever way [is appropriate], [he should bring them into balance].
When [an faculty] has become strong, it must likewise be diminished by means of non-attention. The story of the Elder Vakkali is an illustration of this here.

However, if the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*) becomes too strong, then the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) is unable to perform its function of resolution, nor can the others perform their respective functions;
therefore, that [excess of energy] must be diminished through the cultivation of tranquility (*passaddhi*) and the other [faculties].

In this regard, the story of the Elder Soṇa should be cited. Thus, when one of these factors is predominant, it should be understood that the others are incapable of performing their respective functions.
In particular, here they praise the balance between faith and wisdom, and between concentration and energy.
For one who has strong faith but weak wisdom becomes blindly devoted; he places his trust in what is not a proper basis.
One with strong wisdom but weak faith sides with the faction of the crafty; like a disease arising from medicine, he becomes incurable.
Through the balancing of both, one gains confidence in the object itself.

However, when there is strong concentration but weak energy, laziness overcomes concentration because laziness is the opposite side of concentration. When there is strong energy but weak concentration, energy [overcomes it].
Because it belongs to the side of agitation, agitation overcomes concentration. However, when concentration is joined with energy, it cannot fall into indolence;
and when energy is joined with concentration, it cannot fall into agitation.
Therefore, these two must be made equal. For through the equality of both, absorption (*appanā*) occurs. Furthermore, for one whose task is concentration...
Strong faith is also required. One who has such faith and conviction will reach absorption (*appanā*). However, regarding concentration and wisdom:

for one whose task is concentration, strong one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*) is required; for it is thus that he reaches absorption. For one whose task is insight (*vipassanā*), strong wisdom is required;
for it is thus that he reaches penetration of the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa-paṭivedha*). But when both are in equilibrium, [it is likewise effective].
Absorption certainly occurs; however, mindfulness must be strong in all instances.

For mindfulness protects the mind from falling into agitation through the influence of faith, energy, and wisdom—which belong to the side of agitation—and from falling into indolence through concentration, which belongs to the side of indolence.
Therefore, it is like salt seasoning in all curries, and like a minister with general jurisdiction over all affairs.
Mindfulness is desirable in all matters of royal business and everywhere. Therefore he said: "And mindfulness has been called 'all-beneficial' by the Blessed One.
For what reason? Because the mind has mindfulness as its refuge, and mindfulness is manifested as protection; for without mindfulness, there is neither the exertion nor the restraint of the mind."
63. Skill in the sign (nimittakosalla) means skill in producing the sign for one-pointedness of mind—such as the earth-kasiṇa and so forth—which has not yet been produced;
skill in developing it once it has been produced; and skill in protecting that which has been obtained through development. This is what is intended here. 64.
And how does one exert the mind at the time when the mind should be exerted?

When his mind becomes sluggish due to excessive laxity of energy and other such factors, he does not develop the three factors beginning with tranquility (passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga), but develops those beginning with the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor (dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga). For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, suppose a man wished to kindle a small fire, and he were to place wet... [wood] there..."

"Suppose, monks, one were to throw grass into it, throw fresh cow dung into it, throw fresh wood into it, provide it with water and air, and sprinkle it with dust—would that man, monks, be able to kindle even a small fire?
"Certainly not, Bhante. "In the same way, monks, at whatever time..."

The mind is sluggish; at that time it is the wrong occasion for the development of the tranquility factor of enlightenment, the wrong occasion for the development of the concentration factor of enlightenment... [and so on] ...the wrong occasion for the development of the equanimity factor of enlightenment. Why is that?
Because, monks, a sluggish mind is difficult to rouse by means of these states. And when, monks, the mind is sluggish...

The mind becomes sluggish; at that time it is the right occasion for the development of the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment, the right occasion for the development of the energy factor of enlightenment, and the right occasion for the development of the rapture factor of enlightenment. Why is that?
Because, monks, a sluggish mind is easily stirred up by these states. Just as if, monks, a man were to [take] a small...

“Suppose, monks, a man wished to kindle a fire; he would throw dry grass into it, he would throw dry cow dung into it, he would throw dry wood into it, he would blow upon it with his mouth, and he would not sprinkle it with dust.
Would that man, monks, be able to kindle even a small fire?”—“Yes, venerable sir.”
And here, the development of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor and the others should be understood according to their respective nutriment. For this has been said:
"Bhikkhus, there are wholesome and unwholesome states, blameworthy and blameless states, inferior and superior states, dark and bright states with their counterparts.
In this regard, frequent application of wise attention is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor..."
“...it leads to the arising of the dhamma-investigation enlightenment factor that has not yet arisen, or to the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of that which has already arisen.
Likewise: “There is, monks, the element of initiative, the element of exertion, the element of perseverance. In this regard, wise...”

“Frequent attention is the nutriment that leads to the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of energy, or to the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of energy.
Likewise: “There are, monks, states conducive to the enlightenment factor of rapture. Frequent attention directed toward them therein...”

“This nutriment leads to the arising of the unarisen factor of enlightenment that is rapture, or to the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen factor of enlightenment that is rapture.
In this context, attention proceeding by way of penetration of the specific and general characteristics regarding the wholesome and so forth is *yoniso* (wise).

"Attention" (manasikāra) means: attention that occurs by way of generating the element of initiative (ārambhadhātu) and so forth is called "wise attention" (yoniso manasikāra) toward the element of initiative and the rest. In this context, the "element of initiative" refers to initial energy (paṭhamavīriya).

The "element of exertion" (nikkamadhātu) is stronger than that, because it has emerged from indolence. The "element of perseverance" (parakkamadhātu) is so called because it advances to ever-higher stages.
Even stronger than that is the phrase "states conducive to the enlightenment factor of rapture"; this is simply a name for rapture itself.
Furthermore, the appropriate attention that gives rise to it is indeed what is called "wise attention" (yoniso manasikāra).
Moreover, seven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena: being inquisitive, [seeking instruction, etc.]... [text fragment] ...being inquisitive.
Purifying the basis, balancing the faculties, avoiding persons of poor wisdom, associating with persons possessed of wisdom,
reflecting on the practice of profound knowledge, and devotion thereto—
these eleven qualities lead to the arising of the energy enlightenment factor. Reflecting on the fear of states of deprivation and so forth [is also included].
Seeing the benefits of attaining the distinctions of both mundane and supramundane states which depend upon energy;
reflecting on the path of progress by thinking, "The path traveled by Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and great disciples must be traveled by me, and that cannot be traveled by one who is indolent";
honoring the alms-food by making it of great fruit for the donors; and being a speaker in praise of the exertion of energy.
"The Teacher is such, his teaching is not to be transgressed, and he has been of great benefit to us;
thus, when the practice is honored, the Teacher is truly honored, and not otherwise"—this is the reflection on the greatness of the Teacher.
"The great inheritance known as the True Dhamma must be taken up by me, and that cannot be taken up by one who is indolent"—this is the reflection on the greatness of the inheritance.
The dispelling of sloth and torpor by means of the perception of light, attention, changing postures, and resorting to open spaces;
avoiding persons who are indolent; associating with persons who have aroused energy; reviewing the right efforts;
and being intent upon that—these eleven things lead to the arising of the joy enlightenment factor. [Likewise] recollection of the Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha... [and so forth].

Recollection of virtue, recollection of generosity, recollection of deities, recollection of peace, avoidance of persons who are harsh, association with persons who are kindly, reflection on discourses that inspire confidence, and devotion thereto.
Thus, by arousing these states through these aspects, one is said to develop the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor and the others. This is the time when the mind should be exerted.
At that time, he exerts the mind.
65. How does he restrain the mind at the time when it should be restrained?

When his mind has become agitated due to over-exertion of energy and so forth, then he [cultivates] the three factors beginning with the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor (dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga).
Having abandoned [the hindrances], he develops the enlightenment factor of tranquility and the others. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Suppose, monks, a man wished to extinguish a great mass of fire;
he would throw dry grass into it... and would not scatter dust over it. Would he be capable [of extinguishing it]?"
“Monks, could a man extinguish a great mass of fire? “No indeed, venerable sir.
“In the same way, monks, at whatever time the mind is agitated, that is not the time for the development of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor;
it is not the time for the development of the energy enlightenment factor... nor for the development of the rapture enlightenment factor. Why is that?”
“Monks, an excited mind is difficult to pacify by means of these states.
But, monks, at whatever time the mind is excited, that is the time for the development of the tranquility factor of enlightenment;
that is the time for the development of the concentration factor of enlightenment; that is the time for the development of the equanimity factor of enlightenment.”
For what reason? Because, monks, an agitated mind is easily pacified by these qualities.
Just as if, monks, a man wishing to extinguish a great mass of fire were to throw wet grass onto it...
[and so on] ...and were to sprinkle it with dust—would he, monks, be capable [of extinguishing it]?
“...a man to extinguish a great mass of fire?”—“Yes, venerable sir.
Here too, the development of the factors of enlightenment, such as tranquility of body and mind, should be understood according to their respective nutriment. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“There is, bhikkhus, tranquility of body and tranquility of mind. Therein, the frequent application of wise attention...”

“This nutriment leads to the arising of the unarisen factor of enlightenment that is tranquility, and to the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen factor of enlightenment that is tranquility.
Likewise: “There is, bhikkhus, the sign of serenity, the sign of non-distraction. Therein, the frequent application of wise attention...”

“This nutriment leads to the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of concentration, or to the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of concentration.
Likewise: “There are, monks, states conducive to the enlightenment factor of equanimity. Therein, the frequent application of wise attention—”
“This nutriment leads to the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of equanimity, or to the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of equanimity.
In this context, having observed the manner in which serenity and the other factors previously arose, one should [apply it] by way of producing them.
Appropriate attention (*yoniso manasikāra*) is precisely the attention that occurs in these three instances. "The sign of serenity" (*samathanimitta*) is a designation for serenity itself;
and in the sense of non-distraction, it is the "sign of non-confusion" for that very same [serenity].
Furthermore, seven things lead to the arising of the tranquility enlightenment factor (*passaddhisambojjhaṅga*): the practice of consuming refined food, ...
Devotion to pleasant food, devotion to pleasant postures, maintaining a state of equanimity, avoiding persons with agitated bodies,
associating with persons of tranquil bodies, and being intent upon that—
these eleven things lead to the arising of the concentration enlightenment factor. Purity of the basis and skillfulness regarding the sign [of concentration]...
The balancing of the faculties; the restraining of the mind at the proper time; the exerting of the mind at the proper time;
the encouraging of the flavorless mind by means of faith and a sense of spiritual urgency; the maintaining of equanimity toward the mind that is proceeding rightly;
the avoidance of persons who are not concentrated; the cultivation of persons who are concentrated; the reviewing of the jhānas and liberations; and being intent upon those.
Five things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of equanimity:

neutrality toward sentient beings, neutrality toward formations, avoidance of persons who are partial toward sentient beings and formations, association with persons who are neutral toward sentient beings and formations, and being intent upon that [equanimity].
Thus, by these modes, one who arouses these states [arouses] the enlightenment factors beginning with tranquility.
This is what is called "developing. Thus, at whatever time the mind is to be restrained, at that time he restrains the mind.
66. How, at whatever time the mind is to be gladdened, at that time does he gladden the mind?
When his mind becomes dispirited due to a deficiency in the application of wisdom, or due to the non-attainment of the bliss of tranquility, [he gladdens it].
Then he arouses a sense of spiritual urgency in him by reflecting upon the eight bases for spiritual urgency.
The eight bases for spiritual urgency are: birth, aging, sickness, and death—these four; the suffering of the woeful states as the fifth; the suffering rooted in the round of existence in the past;

the suffering rooted in the round of existence in the future; and the suffering rooted in the search for nutriment in the present. [He does so] by recollecting the virtues of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.
He generates confidence in it. Thus, at whatever time the mind should be gladdened, at that time he gladdens the mind.
How, at whatever time the mind should be looked upon with equanimity, does he look upon the mind with equanimity?
When, by practicing in this way, his mind is neither sluggish nor agitated, is not dissatisfied, proceeds evenly toward the object, and has entered the path of serenity (samatha).
When the mind is thus, it does not engage in the functions of exertion, restraint, or encouragement,
just as a charioteer [remains neutral] when the horses are proceeding evenly. Thus, at whatever time the mind is to be looked upon with equanimity,
at that time he looks upon the mind with equanimity.

Avoidance of persons who are not concentrated means the complete shunning from afar of those individuals who have never ascended the path of renunciation, who are preoccupied with manifold affairs, and whose hearts are distracted.
Cultivation of persons who are concentrated means approaching from time to time those individuals who have entered the path of renunciation and have attained concentration.
Devotion to that means devotion to concentration; the meaning is being respectful toward concentration, leaning toward concentration, inclining toward concentration, and tending toward concentration.
In this way, these ten kinds of skill in absorption should be mastered.
For one who masters this skill in absorption,
once the sign has been acquired, absorption proceeds effectively.
For one who practices in this way, even if that [result] does not arise, the wise man should nevertheless not abandon his application; he should simply strive on.
For by abandoning right effort, a youth will surely not attain distinction.
It is impossible for one to attain even the slightest [result] if this is not so.
Therefore, the wise person, observing the mode of the mind's activity,
should repeatedly apply himself to the balancing of energy.
If the mind falls even slightly into laxity, one should uplift it;
having restrained excessive exertion, one should cause it to proceed with equanimity.
[One should observe] dust, a lotus petal, a thread, a boat, and a balance-beam.
Just as the activity of bees and others has been correctly described,
so too should one direct the mind toward the sign, having completely freed it from all states of dullness and agitation.
68. Directing [the mind] toward the sign.

Here is the explanation of the meaning: Just as a clever bee, knowing that a flower has blossomed on a certain tree, flies toward it with swift speed, and having passed it by, returns and reaches it once the pollen has been exhausted.
Another, being unskilled, leaps with slow speed and reaches only the withered [flowers]. But one who is skilled, leaping with even speed,
easily reaches the heap of flowers, takes as much pollen as he desires, prepares honey, and experiences its sweet flavor.

Just as when students of a surgeon are practicing surgery on lotus leaves placed in a water basin, one who is unskilled, striking with the knife too hastily, either cuts the lotus leaf in two or lets it sink into the water;
while another who is unskilled, out of fear of cutting or letting it sink, does not even dare to touch it with the knife; but the skilled one—
Having demonstrated the application of the sword there with even skill, and having become one whose craft is purified,
he gains profit by performing his work in such places.
And just as he who brings a spider’s thread measuring four fathoms receives four thousand [pieces of money].
When the king had spoken, one unskilled man pulled at the spider’s thread with haste, cutting it here and there.
Another unskilled man, out of fear of cutting it, did not even dare to touch it with his hand.
But the skilled man, starting from the end, drew out the stalks by applying even pressure and brought them forth, thereby obtaining his reward.
Just as an unskilled pilot, while filling the hold with cargo in a strong wind, causes the ship to founder in a foreign land;
whereas another unskilled pilot, while emptying the hold in a light wind, leaves the ship stranded right there;
but a skilled pilot, having filled the hold in a light wind and then emptied it by half in a strong wind, reaches the desired destination in safety.
And just as when a teacher tells his pupils that whoever fills a tube without spilling any oil will receive a reward, one who is unskilled and greedy for gain fills it hastily and spills the oil;
another, being unskilled, does not even dare to pour it in for fear of spilling it;
but the skilled one, filling it with a balanced application, receives the reward.
In the same way, one bhikkhu, when the sign has arisen, exerts intense energy, thinking, "I shall quickly reach absorption.
Because his mind is characterized by over-exerted energy, it falls into agitation, and he is unable to reach absorption.
Another, seeing the fault in over-exerted energy, thinks, "What is the use of absorption now? and slackens his energy; for him—
The mind falls into indolence because of excessive laxity in energy, and it too is unable to reach absorption (*appanā*).

However, he who releases even slightly the sluggish mind from its state of sluggishness and the over-excited mind from agitation, and directs it toward the sign with balanced application, reaches absorption;
one must become such as this. It is with reference to this meaning that this was said:
Just as the activity of bees and others upon pollen, a lotus petal, thread, a boat,
or a tube has been correctly described, so too,
having completely liberated [the mind] from states of dullness and agitation—
"Thus, direct the mind toward the sign.
Regarding the first jhāna:
as he thus directs the mind toward the sign, it will now succeed in reaching absorption (appanā).

Having interrupted the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), mind-door adverting consciousness arises, taking as its object that very earth-kasiṇa which has appeared through the application of the practice "earth, earth.
Thereafter, four or five impulsion (javana) consciousnesses impel upon that same object.

Among these, the last one belongs to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), while the remaining ones belong to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). Compared with the natural (pakati) states of consciousness...

The stronger stages of applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), zest (*pīti*), happiness (*sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*citt’ekaggatā*) are called "preliminary exercises" (*parikamma*) because they serve as the preparation for absorption (*appanā*).

Just as the area near a village or city is called the "vicinity of the village" (*gāmūpacāra*) or "vicinity of the city" (*nagarūpacāra*), so too these are called "access concentrations" (*upacāra*) because they are close to absorption or because they are in its immediate vicinity.
These precede the preliminary exercises and follow them in conformity with the subsequent absorption.

They are also called "conformities" (*anuloma*). Furthermore, that which is the very last among these is called "change-of-lineage" (*gotrabhū*) because it overcomes the lineage of the limited (*paritta*) and develops the lineage of the sublime (*mahaggata*).

By taking what has not been previously mentioned, here the first is the preliminary work (*parikamma*), the second is access (*upacāra*), the third is conformity (*anuloma*), and the fourth is change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*). Alternatively, the first is access, the second is conformity, and the third...

The *gotrabhū* (change-of-lineage) consciousness is the fourth or fifth absorption-consciousness (*appanā-citta*). For it enters absorption either at the fourth or the fifth moment, depending on whether one possesses quick or sluggish direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
After that, the impulsion (*javana*) occurs. Then there is the occasion for the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
However, the Venerable Godatta Thera, an expert in the Abhidhamma, [said]: "The preceding wholesome states [serve as the condition] for the succeeding ones..."

Having stated this Sutta—"A wholesome state is a condition for wholesome states by way of the condition of repetition" (*āsevanapaccaya*)—he said that by way of the condition of repetition, each subsequent state becomes stronger;
therefore, absorption (*appanā*) occurs even in the sixth and seventh moments.
This was rejected in the Commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), stating, "This is merely the Elder’s own opinion. [In fact, it occurs] only in the fourth and fifth moments.
However, absorption (appanā) occurs. It is stated that from this point on, the process is called "impulsion" (javana), because it is close to the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
Since this was stated after having analyzed that very [process], it cannot be rejected.
For just as a man running toward the edge of a precipice, even if he wishes to stop, is unable to plant his foot at the boundary and falls right over the precipice, so too—

It is not possible to attain absorption (appanā) in the sixth or seventh [moment], because they are too close to the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). Therefore, it should be understood that absorption occurs only in the fourth or fifth moments.
Moreover, that absorption lasts for only a single thought-moment; for there is no such thing as a fixed duration (addhānapariccheda) across seven locations.

In the first absorption; in the mundane higher knowledges (*abhiññā*); in the four paths; in the fruition immediately following the path; in the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) jhānas of the fine-material and immaterial realms;
in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as a condition for cessation (*nirodha*); and in the attainment of fruition for one emerging from cessation.
Herein, the fruition immediately following the path does not occur beyond the third [path]. It is a condition for cessation.
The base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception does not exist beyond two [moments]. In the realms of form and formlessness, there is no limit to the life-continuum (bhavaṅga);

in all other instances, there is only a single moment of consciousness. Thus, absorption (appanā) consists of only a single moment of consciousness. Thereafter follows the lapse into the life-continuum.
Then, having interrupted the life-continuum, there is adverting (āvajjana) for the purpose of reviewing the jhāna, followed by the reviewing of the jhāna.

And at this point, having indeed secluded himself from sensual pleasures and secluded himself from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and possesses the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
In this way, he has attained the first jhāna, which is abandoned of five factors, endowed with five factors, excellent in three ways, and perfected in ten characteristics.
There is the earth-kasina.
70. In that context, “quite secluded from sensual pleasures” means having become secluded from, separated from, and departed from sensual pleasures.
Furthermore, this particle *eva* (quite) should be understood as having the sense of restriction (*niyama*). And because it has the sense of restriction, therefore, in that [state], the first jhāna—

This indicates that even though sensual desires are not actually present at the time of entering and abiding [in the first jhāna], they constitute an obstacle to that first jhāna, and that its attainment occurs precisely through the relinquishing of those desires. How so?
By making the restriction "quite secluded from sensual desires," it becomes evident that this [seclusion] must indeed belong to the jhāna.
Sensual desires (*kāmā*) are the adversaries [of this state]; when they are present, this [state] does not arise, just as the light of a lamp does not appear when there is darkness.

Its attainment occurs only through the relinquishing of them, just as the further shore is reached only by relinquishing the near shore. Therefore, he establishes a restriction. In this regard, it might be asked:
why was this stated only in the first member of the compound and not in the second; what [is the difference] regarding unwholesome states (*akusala-dhammā*)?
"Could one enter and dwell in jhāna without having discriminated [from sense-desires]? This, however, should not be viewed in that way.

For this [term "discrimination"] was stated in the preceding phrase by way of its transcendence. Indeed, because it transcends the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu) and because it is the direct antidote to sensual lust, this jhāna is the very transcendence of sense-desires.
As it has been said: "This is the transcendence of sense-desires, namely, renunciation."

Furthermore, even regarding the subsequent word (*uttarapada*), it should be stated that the particle *eva* is brought forward [from the previous phrase], just as in the passage: "Right here, monks, is the ascetic; right here is the second ascetic.

For it is not possible to enter and dwell in jhāna without being secluded from other unwholesome states known as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). Therefore, [the text says]: "secluded indeed from sensual pleasures, secluded indeed from unwholesome states..."
This should be understood in this way for both pairs of terms as well.

And although in both pairs all kinds of seclusion—including seclusion by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-viveka*) and so forth, as well as bodily seclusion (*kāya-viveka*) and so forth—are included under the general term "secluded" (*vivicca*), nevertheless, only three types should be understood here:
bodily seclusion, mental seclusion, and seclusion by suppression (*vikkhambhana-viveka*).
By the phrase "by sensual pleasures" (kāmehi), both the sensual objects (*vatthukāmā*)—which are described in the *Niddesa* by way of the method beginning with "What are sensual objects?

Agreeable forms," and so forth—and the sensual defilements (*kilesakāmā*)—which are described right there in the *Vibhaṅga* as "desire is sensual pleasure, lust is sensual pleasure, desire-and-lust is sensual pleasure, intention is sensual pleasure, passion is sensual pleasure, intention-and-passion is sensual pleasure; these are called sensual pleasures"—are included.

All those [terms] mentioned should be understood as being included herein. For this being so, the phrase "quite secluded from sensual pleasures" (*vivicceva kāmehi*) is appropriately understood to mean "secluded even from objective sensual pleasures" (*vatthukāmehi*);

by this, bodily seclusion (*kāyaviveka*) is expressed. The phrase "secluded from unwholesome states" (*vivicca akusalehi dhammehi*) is appropriately understood to mean "secluded from defilement-sensual pleasures" (*kilesakāmehi*) or "from all unwholesome states"; by this, mental seclusion (*cittaviveka*) is expressed.
And here, by the mention of seclusion from sense-objects (*vatthukāma*) in the first [verse], the relinquishing of sensual pleasure is manifested;
by the mention of seclusion from defilements (*kilesakāma*) in the second, the embracing of the happiness of renunciation (*nekkhammasukha*) is made clear.

Thus, precisely through these mentions of seclusion from sense-objects and defilements, by the first there is the abandoning of the basis for defilement, and by the second, the abandoning of the defilement itself. By the first...
It should be understood that by the first [verse], the relinquishing of the cause of greed is shown, and by the second, the relinquishing of the cause of folly.

Furthermore, by the first, purification of the means is manifested, and by the second, the nourishment of the underlying disposition (*āsaya*). This is the method, first of all, regarding the "sensual pleasures" mentioned here under the category of objective sensual pleasure (*vatthukāma*).
However, in the case of defilement as sensual pleasure (*kilesakāma*), it is simply sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) itself, which has many divisions such as "zeal" (*chanda*) and "lust" (*rāga*).

"Kāma" is intended here. Although it is included among the unwholesome (akusala), it is mentioned separately in the *Vibhaṅga* as the opposite of jhāna, according to the method beginning with: "Therein, what is kāma? It is desire (chanda) that is kāma.
Alternatively, it was mentioned in the first term because it is a defilement-kāma (kilesakāma), and in the second term because it is included among the unwholesome.
Furthermore, rather than saying "kāmato" (from kāma), it is said "kāmehi" (from kāmas) because of its manifold divisions.

Although other states also exist as unwholesome, only the hindrances are mentioned here because, in the Vibhaṅga, following the method beginning with "In this context, what are the unwholesome states?
Sensual desire," the hindrances are shown to be the opposites and adversaries of the jhāna factors that follow.
For the hindrances are the opposites of the jhāna factors, and it is the jhāna factors themselves that are their adversaries and destroyers.
It is said that these are "obstructive. For it is stated in the *Peṭaka*: "Concentration is the antidote to sensual desire; rapture is the antidote to ill will;
applied thought is the antidote to sloth and torpor; pleasure is the antidote to restlessness and remorse; and sustained thought is the antidote to doubt.
Thus, in this context, by the phrase "quite secluded from sensual desires," the seclusion consisting in the suppression of sensual desire is expressed.
By the phrase "secluded from unwholesome states" (*vivicca akusalehi dhammehi*), there is the inclusion by way of what is not explicitly mentioned:

first, by this [phrase], sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) among the five hindrances is included; second, by the remaining hindrances. Likewise, among the three unwholesome roots, by the first [phrase] greed (*lobha*)—which has as its object the fivefold division of the strands of sense pleasure—is included;
by the second, hatred (*dosa*) and delusion (*moha*), which have as their objects the bases for resentment and so forth, are included.

Or, regarding the states beginning with the floods (*ogha*): by the first [set], there is the abandoning of the flood of sensual desire, the yoke of sensual desire, the taint of sensual desire, the clinging to sensual desire, the bodily tie of covetousness, and the fetter of lust for sensual desire;

by the second, there is the abandoning of the remaining floods, yokes, taints, clingings, ties, and fetters. Furthermore, by the first, there is the abandoning of craving and those states associated with it;
by the second, there is the abandoning of ignorance and those states associated with it. Moreover, by the first, there is the abandoning of the eight [factors] associated with greed...
By the second [phrase], it should be understood that the seclusion by suppression of the remaining four unwholesome types of consciousness has been stated.
This, then, is the explanation of the meaning of the passage: "Quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unwholesome states.
71. Having thus far shown the factor of abandoning for the first jhāna, he now shows the factor of association.

"Accompanied by initial application (vitakka) and sustained application (vicāra)," and so forth, was stated. In this context, *vitakka* is the act of applying the mind; it is said to mean "investigating.
Its characteristic is the directing of the mind onto the object (*ārammaṇa*). Its function is striking and repeatedly striking [the object].
For it is said that through it, the practitioner makes the object struck by initial application, repeatedly struck by initial application. Upon the object...
It has the manifestation of leading the mind.

*Vicāra* is sustained application; what is meant is "moving along after. It has the characteristic of rubbing over the object; its function is to keep conascent states occupied with that object; it has the manifestation of binding the mind closely to the object.
And although these two are inseparable in some respects, by virtue of being gross and being the forerunner, *vitakka* is like the striking of a bell.
Vitakka is the mind’s initial application, like the first striking of a bell. Vicāra is the subsequent sustained following, characterized by subtle investigation;
it is like the resonance of the bell after the initial strike. Among these two, vitakka is expansive;
at the moment of its first arising, it acts as a stirring of the mind, like the flapping of wings by a bird wishing to fly into the air, or like the movement toward a lotus flower.

And for the bee whose mind is following after the scent: *santavutti* (tranquil movement) is the state of the mind being without excessive agitation, like the spreading of wings by a bird that has flown up into the sky, or like the hovering above the lotus of a bee that has fallen facing the lotus.
However, in the commentary on the *Dukanipāta*, it says: "Of a great bird traveling through the sky..."
"Vitakka is that which proceeds by way of the mental application toward the object, like the movement [of a bird] after taking hold of the wind with both wings and settling them;
vicāra is that which proceeds by way of sustained pressure, like the movement of one who is fluttering the wings for the sake of catching the wind"—
this statement is appropriate in the case of a continuous flow of occurrence.
However, their distinction becomes evident in the first and second jhānas.

Furthermore, when one holds a bronze vessel stained with dirt firmly with one hand and rubs it all over with the other hand using a paste of powder and oil, the hand that holds it firmly is like *vitakka* (initial application), and the hand that rubs it is like *vicāra* (sustained application). Likewise...
For a potter who, having set the wheel spinning with a blow from his staff, fashions a vessel, initial application (*vitakka*) is like the hand that exerts pressure,
while sustained application (*vicāra*) is like the hand that moves it here and there. Likewise, for one fashioning a circular rim,
initial application is like a thorn fixed in the center, while sustained application is like a thorn revolving around the outside.

Sustained application (vicāra) is like the subsequent rubbing [of the wood]. Thus, because it occurs together with this initial application (vitakka) and this sustained application, just as a tree is accompanied by its flowers and fruits, this jhāna is called "with initial application and sustained application" (savitakka-savicāra).
However, in the Vibhaṅga, it is stated in the manner of referring to a person: "He is endowed with this initial application and this sustained application; he is fully endowed," and so forth.
The exposition has been given. However, the meaning there should also be understood in exactly this way.

Regarding the term *vivekaja* (born of seclusion): here, *viveka* means "secludedness," which signifies the disappearance of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). Alternatively, *viveka* means "that which is secluded"; thus, it refers to the mass of states associated with jhāna that are secluded from the hindrances. Therefore, it is "born of seclusion" (*vivekaja*) because it arises from seclusion, or in that seclusion.
Regarding *pītisukha* (rapture and bliss): here, it is called *pīti* because it gladdens (*pīṇayati*). Its characteristic is endearingness; its function is to refresh the body and mind.

It has pervading as its essence and displays itself as rapture (*odagya*). Furthermore, this [rapture] is fivefold: minor rapture (*khuddikā-pīti*), momentary rapture (*khaṇikā-pīti*), showering rapture (*okkantikā-pīti*), uplifting rapture (*ubbegā-pīti*), and pervading rapture (*pharaṇā-pīti*).
Among these, minor rapture is only able to cause the hair on the body to stand on end.
Momentary rapture occurs like the flashing of lightning from moment to moment. Showering rapture is like the waves on the shore of the ocean...
It breaks again and again, entering the body like a wave. Rapture of uplift (*ubbegā-pīti*) becomes powerful, reaching the point of making the body leap upward into the air.
For instance, on the full moon day, the Elder Mahātissa, resident of Puṇṇavallika, went to the courtyard of the Cetiya in the evening;
seeing the light of the moon, he stood facing the Great Cetiya and thought: "At this very hour..."
Having seen the four assemblies paying homage to the Mahācetiya, she naturally gave rise to uplifting rapture (*ubbegā-pīti*) directed toward the Buddha by way of the object as it was perceived;
then, like a painted ball struck upon a floor of plaster, she leapt into the air and landed right there in the courtyard of the Mahācetiya.
Likewise, in the village of Vattakālaka, which was a dependency of the Girikaṇḍaka Monastery, there was a certain daughter of a family who...
With a rapture of transport born from a powerful object of the Buddha, she leaped into the air.
It is said that her parents, while going to the monastery in the evening to hear the Dhamma, said, "Dear child, you are heavily pregnant and cannot wander about at such an hour;
we shall go and listen to the Dhamma on your behalf," and so they departed.
Although she wished to go, being unable to resist their words, she remained behind at home; standing on the courtyard of the house,
she looked toward the courtyard of the Ākāsa Cetiya on Mount Girika by the light of the moon and saw the lamp-offering at the cetiya,
as well as the four assemblies performing circumambulations of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus after having made offerings of garlands, perfumes, and other items to the cetiya.
And she heard the sound of the community reciting the scriptures. Then, as she beheld the stupa resembling a heap of pearls, the thought occurred to her:
"Blessed indeed are those who, having gone to the monastery, are able to wander upon such a shrine-courtyard and hear such sweet discourse on the Dhamma!
As she looked at the stupa, which resembled a mass of pearls, an intense rapture (*ubbegā-pīti*) arose within her. She leaped into the air and, even before her parents, [she descended].
Descending from the sky onto the courtyard of the cetiya, she paid homage to the cetiya and stood listening to the Dhamma.
Then her parents approached and asked, "Daughter, by which path did you come? She replied, "I came through the air, not by a [terrestrial] path.
When they said, "Daughter, it is those whose taints are exhausted who travel through the air; how did you come?"
She said: "As I stood looking at the cetiya by the light of the moon, a powerful rapture (pīti) directed toward the Buddha arose within me.
Then, I was no longer aware of whether I was standing or sitting; rather, by means of the mental sign I had grasped, I leapt into the air and landed upon the courtyard of the cetiya."
Thus, uplifting joy (*ubbegā-pīti*) has the measure of causing one to leap into the air.
But when pervading joy (*pharaṇā-pīti*) arises, the entire body becomes suffused like a bladder filled by being blown up, and like the interior of a mountain submerged by a great flood of water.
This fivefold joy, as it takes conception and reaches maturity, gives rise to two kinds of tranquility (*passaddhi*).
It fulfills both bodily tranquility (*kāyapassaddhi*) and mental tranquility (*cittapassaddhi*).
Tranquility, taking conception and reaching maturity, fulfills both kinds of happiness: bodily and mental.
Happiness, taking conception and reaching maturity, fulfills three types of concentration: momentary concentration (*khaṇikasamādhi*), access concentration (*upacārasamādhi*), and...

"Absorption concentration" (appanā-samādhi). Among those [three kinds of joy], that which serves as the root for absorption concentration, increases along with it, and is associated with concentration—this is the "joy" intended in this context. As for the other:
"pleasure" (sukha) is so called because of its pleasantness, or because it thoroughly consumes and carves away afflictions of body and mind.
Pleasure (*sukha*) has the characteristic of being gratifying (*sātālakkhaṇa*); its function is to nourish associated states; its manifestation is assistance.

Although there is no dissociation between them in certain instances, joy (*pīti*) is the satisfaction derived from obtaining a desirable object, whereas pleasure is the experiencing of the flavor of what has been obtained.
Where there is joy, there is pleasure; but where there is pleasure, there is not necessarily joy. They are both included within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).
Rapture (*pīti*). Pleasure (*sukha*) is comprised within the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*).
Rapture is like seeing and hearing about water at the edge of a forest when one is exhausted by a desert; pleasure is like entering the shade of that forest and enjoying the water.

It should be understood that this was stated because these states become manifest at their respective times. Thus, this rapture and this pleasure belong to this jhāna, or [they arise] in this [jhāna].
"Jhāna has [it]" means that this jhāna is called "rapture and happiness" (*pītisukha*).
Alternatively, rapture and happiness together are "rapture-and-happiness," just like "Dharma and Vinaya" (*dhammavinaya*) and so forth. This jhāna has rapture-and-happiness born of seclusion;
or, since it exists in this jhāna, it is also "rapture-and-happiness born of seclusion. For just as with the jhāna itself, so too...
Here too, this joy and bliss is born of seclusion; since it possesses that quality, it is likewise appropriate to call it "joy and bliss born of seclusion" by means of a single compound.
However, in the *Vibhaṅga*, it is stated in the manner of: "This bliss is accompanied by this joy," and so forth.
But the meaning there should also be understood in exactly the same way.
"First jhāna": this will be explained further on. "Having attained" (*upasampajja*) means having approached;
it is said to mean "having reached. Or, it means "having fully acquired" (*upasampādayitvā*); it is said to mean "having accomplished. In the *Vibhaṅga*, however, it says:
"'Having attained' means the gaining, the obtaining, the reaching, the achievement, the touching, the realization, and the full acquisition of the first jhāna."
It has been stated. Its meaning should also be understood in this very way. "He dwells" (viharati):

having become possessed of the aforementioned type of jhāna, he accomplishes the movement, the conduct, the protection, the maintenance, the sustenance, the course, and the dwelling of his own being by means of a mode of conduct (iriyāpatha) corresponding to that [jhāna].
For this is said in the Vibhaṅga: "He dwells means he moves, he conducts himself, he protects..."
“He causes it to be done, he causes it to be maintained, he practices, he dwells; therefore it is said that ‘he dwells.
Regarding what was stated as “having abandoned five factors and being endowed with five factors,” therein [the first factor is] sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*).
The state of having abandoned five factors should be understood by way of the abandoning of these five hindrances: ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.
For as long as these are not abandoned, jhāna does not arise;
therefore, they are called the "factors of abandonment. Indeed, although other unwholesome states [are also present] at the moment of jhāna...
Although these [five hindrances] are abandoned, nevertheless, these very ones are specifically obstructive to the jhānas.

For a mind enticed by various objects through sensual desire (kāmacchanda) does not become concentrated on a single object. Or, being overcome by sensual desire, it does not enter upon the path for the abandoning of the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu).
And being struck against the object by ill-will (byāpāda), it does not proceed uninterruptedly.
Overcome by sloth and torpor, the mind becomes unwieldy. Possessed by restlessness and remorse, it remains unpeaceful and wanders about.
Stricken by doubt, one does not ascend the path that leads to the attainment of jhāna.
Thus, because these specifically act as obstacles to jhāna, they are called the factors to be abandoned.

Since, however, applied thought (vitakka) directs the mind onto the object and sustained thought (vicāra) binds it there, joy (pīti)—arising from the perfection of the mental application of a consciousness whose effort has been accomplished through those two for the sake of non-distraction—brings about exhilaration and pleasure (sukha) brings about intensification.
Then, this [consciousness], together with all its associated states, is characterized by these [qualities]: directing, binding, exhilarating, and intensifying.

Supported by these factors, one-pointedness is applied evenly and correctly to the single object; therefore, the state of being endowed with five factors should be understood by way of the arising of these five—namely, applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), rapture (*pīti*), happiness (*sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*).
For when these five have arisen, the meditative absorption (*jhāna*) is said to have arisen. Thus, these five are its constituent factors.
Therefore, one should not conclude that there is some other thing called "jhāna" distinct from these [factors].
Just as an army is called "fourfold" or music "five-instrumented," and the path is called "eightfold" by virtue of its constituent parts alone,
so too this [jhāna] is called "five-factored" or "endowed with five factors" by virtue of its constituent parts alone.
"It is said" (vuccati) should be understood as "it is to be known.
Although these five factors exist even at the moment of access concentration (upacāra), they are nevertheless stronger than the natural mind (pakaticitta) during access.
Here, however, they are even stronger than in access, having reached the characteristic of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara). In this regard—
For initial application (vitakka) arises placing the mind upon the object in a very clear mode; sustained application (vicāra) by way of repeatedly rubbing over the object;
and rapture and happiness (pītisukha) by way of pervading the entire body. Therefore it is said:
"There is nothing of his whole body that is not suffused with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion. One-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā) is also [present].
It arises touching upon its objects like the upper surface of a casket pressing against the lower surface;

this is the distinction between these [factors] and the others. In that regard, although one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*) is not explicitly mentioned in the text "with applied thought and sustained thought" (*savitakkam savicāram*), nevertheless, in the *Vibhaṅga* it is stated: "Jhāna is applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind."

Because it has been stated thus, it is indeed a factor (*aṅga*). For whatever intention the Blessed One had when making the summary (*uddesa*), that very same [intention] was revealed by him in the analysis (*vibhaṅga*).
Regarding "possessing the three kinds of excellence" (*tividhakalyāṇa*) and "endowed with the ten characteristics": here, however, it is by way of the beginning, middle, and end—
