The threefold goodness. Furthermore, by way of the characteristics of those very beginnings, middles, and ends, it should be understood as being endowed with ten characteristics.
Herein, this is the text:
"For the first jhāna, purification of the way is the beginning, the intensification of equanimity is the middle, and the encouragement is the end."
The conclusion [is the fourth jhāna]; the purification of the way (paṭipadāvisuddhi) is the beginning of the first jhāna. How many characteristics does the beginning have?
The beginning has three characteristics: the mind is purified from whatever obstructs it;
because of that purification, the mind enters upon the intermediate sign of serenity (samathanimitta); and because it has entered upon it, the mind leaps into that state. And that which...
The mind becomes purified through the removal of obstacles; and because of that purification, the mind enters upon the intermediate sign of serenity (samatha);
and because it has entered upon it, the mind leaps forward into that state. The purification of the way to the first jhāna is its beginning;
these three characteristics belong to the beginning. Therefore, it is said that the first jhāna is "good in the beginning."
And endowed with the three characteristics.
Regarding the cultivation of equanimity in the first jhāna: as for the middle [jhāna], how many characteristics does it have? The middle [jhāna] has three characteristics:
one looks on with equanimity at the purified mind; one looks on with equanimity at that which has entered into serenity.

He looks on with equanimity at the establishment of unity. That which he looks on with equanimity—the purified mind, that which has entered into serenity, and the establishment of unity—these are the three characteristics of the middle [state] of the first jhāna’s intensification of equanimity.
Therefore, it is said that the first jhāna is "beautiful in the middle."
It is also endowed with the three characteristics.
“The culmination of the first jhāna is its gratification; how many characteristics does that culmination have?
The culmination has four characteristics: therein, gratification is in the sense of non-transgression of the states arisen therein; [it is] of the faculties...”
Encouragement is in the sense of having a single flavor; encouragement is in the sense of driving forward the energy that has reached that state; encouragement is in the sense of repetition.
Encouragement is the conclusion of the first jhāna;
these are the four characteristics of the conclusion. Therefore it is said: "The first jhāna is beautiful in its conclusion and endowed with four characteristics."

In this context, some explain that "purity of the way" (*paṭipadāvisuddhi*) refers to access concentration together with its requisites; "intensification of equanimity" (*upekkhānubrūhanā*) refers to absorption;
and "gladdening" (*sampahaṃsanā*) refers to reviewing. However, since it is stated in the Canon:
"The mind that has attained unity both plunges into purity of the way, is intensified by equanimity, and is gladdened by knowledge," therefore [these stages] occur within absorption itself.
Purification of the way should be understood by way of arrival; the intensification of equanimity by way of the function of onlooking-equanimity toward the middle state;
and the encouragement by way of the accomplishment of the function of purifying knowledge through establishing the state of non-transgression regarding phenomena.

How so? For at the moment when absorption arises, the mind becomes purified from that mass of defilements known as the hindrances which are an obstruction to that jhāna. Because it is purified, being free from obstructions, it enters upon the intermediate sign of serenity (*samathanimitta*).
The "intermediate sign of serenity" is simply the absorption concentration (*appanāsamādhi*) occurring in a state of equilibrium.

Immediately after that, however, the preceding consciousness, by way of the transformation of a single continuity (*ekasantatipariṇāmanayena*), approaches suchness (*tathattam*) and is said to "enter" the medium sign of serenity (*majjhima-samathanimitta*).
Because it has entered in this way, through its approach to suchness, it is said to "launch into" (*pakkhandati*) it.
Thus, first of all, at the very moment of the arising of the first jhāna, there occurs the production of the mode existing in the preceding consciousness.
The purification of the path should be understood by way of its arrival.

Furthermore, because there is nothing further to be purified once it has been thus purified, one who does not exert effort toward further purification is said to "look on with equanimity" at the purified mind. This occurs for one who has entered into serenity (*samatha*) by way of attaining the state of serenity.
When one does not exert effort toward concentration, one is said to "look on with equanimity" at that which is proceeding toward serenity (*samatha*).
And because it is proceeding toward serenity, when the mind has abandoned contact with the defilements and is established in unity, one does not exert effort toward further establishing that unity;
thus, one is said to "look on with equanimity" at the establishment of unity. In this way, [equanimity] functions through the activity of "onlooking-equanimity" (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*).
The cultivation of equanimity is to be understood.
Furthermore, when equanimity has been thus cultivated, those twin dharmas known as concentration and wisdom—
which have arisen therein and proceed without one surpassing the other— and those faculties such as faith and the rest, from various defilements...
Because they are liberated, they proceed having become of a single flavor through the flavor of liberation;
and that energy which he exerts as appropriate for those states— which possess this state of being of a single flavor in not overstepping what leads thereto—

and that repetition which occurs at that moment— all these modes [of practice] are such because, by means of knowledge, one has seen the respective dangers and benefits in both defilement and purification, and has accordingly [applied them].

Because it has been gladdened, purified, and cleansed, it is indeed accomplished; therefore, it is said: "Gladdening should be understood as the accomplishment of the function of the purifying knowledge by means of establishing the state of non-transgression regarding phenomena.
In this context, knowledge becomes manifest through the influence of equanimity (upekkhā), as it is said: "The mind thus exerted..."
One regards them with thorough equanimity. Through the influence of equanimity and through the influence of wisdom, the faculty of wisdom becomes predominant.

Through the influence of equanimity, the mind is liberated from the various defilements; through the influence of liberation and through the influence of wisdom, the faculty of wisdom becomes predominant.
Because they are liberated, those states have a single flavor. In the sense of having a single flavor, this is "development. Therefore, it is the function of knowledge.
It is said that the conclusion consists of encouragement.

Now, regarding the phrase "the first jhāna has been attained with the earth-kasiṇa": here, it is called "first" because of its position in the numerical sequence, and it is also "first" because it arises first.

It is called "jhāna" (meditative absorption) either because of its intense contemplation of the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhānato*) or because of its burning away of opposing states (*paccanīkajhāpanato*).
The earth-disk (*pathavīmaṇḍala*), however, is called the "earth-kasiṇa" (*pathavīkasiṇa*) in the sense of being the whole;

likewise, the sign obtained by depending on that [disk], and the jhāna obtained with respect to the sign of the earth-kasiṇa. In this context, it should be understood that the jhāna is the "earth-kasiṇa.
With reference to this, it was said: "The first jhāna has been attained as the earth-kasiṇa."
76. Accomplishing Long Duration:
Once this has been attained in this way, that yogi must discern its modes, just as a hair-splitter or a cook does.
For instance, when a highly skilled archer is practicing for the sake of splitting a hair, on whichever occasion—
He pierces the hair; at that moment, he should grasp the configuration of his footstep, the bow-staff, the bowstring, and the arrow:
"Standing thus, having grasped the bow-staff in this way, the bowstring in this way, and the arrow in this way, the hair was pierced.
From then on, by accomplishing those very configurations in that same manner without fail, he would pierce the hair.
In the same way, the yogin must also discern these modes, such as suitability of food and so forth, thinking:
"Having eaten this particular food, while associating with such a person, staying in such a lodging, maintaining such a posture, at such a time, I attained this.
For in this way, even if those conditions are lost, he can reproduce them by fulfilling those modes once again.
Or, by making what is unskilled skillful, he will be able to enter [concentration] again and again.
And just as a skilled cook, while serving his master, observes whatever the master eats according to his preference and,
from then on, brings only such things as those, thereby becomes a sharer in profit— even so does this person.
When the moment of attainment has been reached, one who grasps the modes such as food and so forth, and accomplishes them, becomes a frequent attainer of absorption whenever it is lost.
Therefore, those modes must be discerned just like a hair-splitter or a skilled cook. And this was said by the Blessed One:
"Just as, bhikkhus, a wise, clever, and skillful cook serves a king or a royal minister with various delicacies..."
He would be served with soups—those that were sour, bitter, pungent, sweet, salty, unsalty, and those that were not salty.
That wise, clever, and skilled cook, monks, would grasp the sign from his master:
"This soup of mine was pleasing to my master today," or... [he would note whether it was not pleasing].
‘He brings this to him,’ or ‘He takes much of this,’ or ‘He speaks in praise of this’;
or ‘Today my husband’s curry was sour to my taste,’ or ‘He brings more of the sour variety,’ or ‘He takes much of the sour variety,’ or ‘He speaks in praise of the sour variety’...
[and so on] ...or ‘He speaks in praise of the unsalted variety. Thus, he—
Thus, monks, that wise, competent, and skilled cook gains clothing, gains wages, and gains gifts.
Why is that? Because, monks, that wise, competent, and skilled cook learns the preferences of his master. In the same way, monks, here some wise person...
A learned, skilled bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body... [and so on]...

he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, the mind in the mind, and phenomena in phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
As he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, his mind becomes concentrated and his defilements are abandoned.

He grasps that sign. Monks, that wise, competent, and skillful monk becomes an attainer of the pleasant dwellings in this very life and an attainer of mindfulness and clear comprehension. Why is that?
Because, monks, that wise, competent, and skillful monk has grasped the sign of his own mind.
Furthermore, for one who achieves those mental aspects through the grasping of signs, only access concentration (*appanā-matta*) is accomplished, not long-term stability.
Long-term stability, however, arises from the thorough purification of those states that are obstacles to concentration.
For a monk who has not sufficiently suppressed sensual desire by reflecting on the danger of sense-desires and so forth, but [has done so] by means of bodily tranquility...
If one enters into jhāna without having properly calmed bodily restlessness, without having thoroughly dispelled sloth and torpor by means of attention to the element of initiative and so forth,
without having completely eliminated restlessness and remorse by means of attention to the sign of serenity and so forth,
and without having sufficiently purified other factors that obstruct concentration, he—
Like a bee that has entered an unclean dwelling, or like a king who has entered an unpurified park, he quickly departs.

However, he who enters into jhāna after having thoroughly purified the states that obstruct concentration is like a bee that has entered a well-purified dwelling, or like a king who has entered a perfectly clean park.
And for the entire duration of the day, he remains within the attainment itself. Therefore, the ancients have said:
"One should dispel desire for sensual pleasures and ill will, With agitation, sloth, and doubt as the fifth."
"With a mind that brings joy through discernment, one should delight therein like a king who has reached the innermost chamber.
Therefore, one who desires long endurance [of attainment] should enter into jhāna after purifying the obstructive states. And for the sake of the full development of the cultivation of the mind...
The counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) as it has been acquired must be expanded. There are two stages for its expansion: access (upacāra) or absorption (appanā).
For it is permissible to expand it both after reaching access and after reaching absorption. However, it must certainly be expanded at one [of these] stage[s].
Thus it was said: "The counterpart sign as it has been acquired must be expanded."
77. The Method of Increasing the Sign:

Herein, this is the method of increasing. That yogi, having increased that sign by way of increasing the field, increasing the paddy, increasing the cooked rice, increasing the creeper, and increasing the cloth—just as a farmer, having delimited the area to be ploughed with a ploughshare, [proceeds] within that boundary...

He sharpens it; or rather, just as monks, when binding a boundary, first observe the signs and then bind it, even so he should gradually delimit with the mind—by one finger-breadth, two finger-breadths, three finger-breadths, or four finger-breadths—the sign as it has been acquired, and then expand it according to that delimitation.
However, it should not be expanded without having first delimited it.
Then, by way of delimiting the boundaries of the pariveṇa, vihāra, and sīmā— starting from a span and a cubit in size—
one should increase it by delimiting the extent of a village, town, district, kingdom, or the ocean, or even beyond that up to the limit of the world-system (cakkavāḷa).
For just as young swans, from the moment their wings grow, fly up into increasingly small areas, [so too should one expand].

Having practiced familiarity, they gradually approach the vicinity of the moon and sun; in the same way, the bhikkhu, having defined the sign according to the method described and increasing it, extends it as far as the limits of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) or even beyond that.
Then, in those places where he has increased the sign, upon the earth’s unevennesses—such as rises and falls, river ravines, mountains, and rugged terrain—
It is like a bull’s hide that has been struck by hundreds of spears.
Regarding that sign, the beginner who has attained the first jhāna should be one who frequently enters it, rather than one who frequently performs reflection;
for in one who frequently reflects, the factors of jhāna become coarse and weak.
Having offered them, they wait upon him. Because they have been presented to him in this way, they become conditions for his further striving.
Striving for a state of absorption that is not yet proficient, he falls away from the first absorption already attained and is unable to reach the second.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Bhikkhus, suppose there were a mountain cow, foolish, inexperienced, ignorant of the terrain, and unskilled at roaming over rugged mountains.
It might think to itself: ‘What if I were now to go to a region never before visited, eat grass never before tasted, and drink water never before drunk? But it does not place its front foot securely.
Having firmly planted her hind leg, she would lift her front foot;
she would go to a direction never before visited, eat grass never before tasted, and drink water never before drunk.
And in whatever place she stood, the thought would occur to her: "What if I were now to go to a direction never before visited... [and so on] ...drink water never before drunk? And to that place...
He would not return safely. Why is that? Because, monks, that mountain cow is foolish, incompetent, ignorant of the terrain, and unskilled in roaming over the rugged mountains;

even so, monks, here a certain monk who is foolish, incompetent, ignorant of the terrain, and unskilled, having withdrawn from sensual pleasures... [and so on] ... enters upon and dwells in the first *jhāna*.
To dwell [in that state]. He does not cultivate, develop, or frequently practice that sign, nor does he firmly resolve upon it;
thus it occurs to him: "What if, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought... I were to enter and dwell in the second jhāna?
Yet he is unable, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought... to enter the second jhāna.
To enter upon and dwell in it. It occurs to him: "What if I, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... were to enter upon and dwell in the first jhāna.
Yet he is unable to enter upon and dwell in the first jhāna, secluded from sensual pleasures...
This, monks, is called a monk who has fallen away from both sides, one who has been deprived of both, just as if...
"That cow from the mountains is foolish, incompetent, ignorant of the terrain, and unskilled in wandering over rugged mountains.
Therefore, he must first become one who has attained mastery in that very first jhāna by means of the five modes of mastery.
(The Discourse on the Five Masteries)
78. In this regard, there are these five masteries: mastery over adverting, mastery over attainment, mastery over resolution, mastery over emerging, and mastery over reviewing.
One adverts to the first jhāna wherever one wishes, whenever one wishes, and for as long as one wishes;
since there is no sluggishness in adverting, it is called mastery over adverting. One attains the first jhāna wherever one wishes... [and so on].
He enters [the attainment]; because there is no sluggishness in entering it, this is mastery in entering. The remaining [mastery-terms] should be detailed in the same way.

Here, however, is the explanation of the meaning: for one who has emerged from the first jhāna and first adverts to the applied thought (*vitakka*), after the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) has ceased, following the adverting consciousness that has arisen, four or five [moments of consciousness] arise having precisely that applied thought as their object.

The impulsions (javana) impel. Then follow two life-continuum moments (bhavaṅga), then again an adverting consciousness with the same object as the investigation, and then impulsions in the manner already described.
When one is thus able to direct the mind continuously through these five jhāna factors, then one’s mastery over adverting (āvajjanavasī) is accomplished.
This mastery, however, when it has reached its culmination, was displayed by the Blessed One at the Twin Miracle (yamakapāṭihāriya).
Or it may be obtained by others at such times. Beyond this, there is no mastery of adverting that is swifter.
However, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna’s capacity to enter attainment swiftly—like his taming of the Naga kings Nanda and Upananda—is called mastery of attainment (*samāpajjana-vasī*).
The capacity to remain for a moment the duration of a finger-snap, or ten finger-snaps, is called mastery of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna-vasī*).
Likewise, the capacity to emerge quickly is called "mastery over emergence" (*vuṭṭhāna-vasī*). To illustrate both of these, it is appropriate to relate the story of the Elder Buddhārakkhita.
That venerable one, having been eight years ordained, [stayed] at Therambatthala under the Elder Mahārohaṇagutta...

Seated in the midst of about thirty thousand powerful beings who had come to attend to the sick, he saw a king of the *supaṇṇas* leaping down from the sky with the thought, "I shall seize the attendant nāga king who is receiving the elder’s rice-gruel.
Immediately, [the elder] manifested a mountain, seized the nāga king by the arm, and entered therein. The king of the *supaṇṇas*—
Having struck him on the mountain, he fled. The Great Elder said: "Friend, had it not been for Buddharakkhita, we would all have been objects of reproach.
However, mastery in reviewing is said to be included within mastery in adverting; for in that context, the reviewing impulsions follow immediately after the adverting [consciousness].
The Discussion of the Second Jhāna (79).
Now, one who has mastered these five kinds of mastery emerges from the first jhāna with which he is proficient and perceives its fault thus:
"This attainment has the hindrances as its proximate enemy; it is weak in factors because of the grossness of applied and sustained thought. And therein [he sees] the fault.
Having seen this, he should attend to the second jhāna as peaceful, bring his attachment for the first jhāna to an end, and apply himself to the attainment of the second. Then,
when he has emerged from the first jhāna and is reviewing its factors with mindfulness and clear comprehension,
applied thought and sustained thought appear gross to him, while the rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind [appear peaceful].
When it appears as peaceful, then, for the sake of abandoning the gross factor and attaining the peaceful factor,

as he repeatedly brings that same sign to mind, thinking "earth, earth," there arises a mind-door adverting consciousness taking that very earth-kasiṇa as its object, having interrupted the life-continuum with the thought, "Now the second jhāna will arise."
Then, upon that very same object, four or five impulsion-moments (*javana*) arise;

at the conclusion of which one moment is fine-material-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) and belongs to the second jhāna, while the remaining moments are of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and of the aforementioned type.
At this point, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*), there is internal confidence and unification of mind.
He enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which is without applied thought and sustained thought, born of concentration, and possesses rapture and happiness. In this way,
he has attained the second jhāna based on the earth-kasiṇa, which is abandoned of two factors, endowed with three factors, beautiful in three ways, and perfected in ten characteristics.

80. Regarding the phrase "with the stilling of applied thought and sustained thought" (*vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā*): this means with the stilling and the transcending of these two, namely applied thought and sustained thought;
it is said that they are not manifest at the moment of the second jhāna.
Although it is true that none of the factors of the first jhāna exist in the second jhāna, for indeed, the contact and other factors in the first jhāna are quite different [from those in the second].

Others say it is here. However, it should be understood that the phrase "with the stilling of applied and sustained thought" is stated in this way for the purpose of illustrating that, through the surmounting of each successive gross factor, there is the attainment of the second jhāna and those following it beyond the first jhāna.

“Internal” (*ajjhatta*) here refers to what is internal by way of one's own [person] (*niyakajjhatta*). In the *Vibhaṅga*, however, it is stated merely as “internal, personal” (*ajjhattaṃ paccattaṃ*).
And because what is intended is that which is internal by way of one's own [person], the meaning here is: “born within oneself,” or “arisen in one’s own continuity” (*santāna*).
“Tranquillity” (*sampasādana*): tranquillity is said to be faith (*saddhā*). Because it is associated with tranquillity...
The jhāna is also "tranquillizing" (sampasādana), because it is associated with the color blue, like a blue cloth;

or else, because that jhāna tranquillizes the mind by being endowed with tranquillity and by the subsiding of the agitation caused by applied and sustained thought, it is therefore called "tranquillizing.
And in this interpretation of the meaning, the connection between the words should be understood as "tranquillizing of the mind."
In the previous interpretation of the meaning, however, the term *cetaso* (of the mind) should be construed with *ekodibhāvena* (by way of singleness).

Herein, this is the construction of the meaning: it rises alone (*eko udeti*), thus it is "singleness" (*ekodi*). The sense is that it rises as pre-eminent and supreme because it has not been overlaid by applied thought and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*).
For even what is supreme is called "one" (*eka*) in the world. Or else, it is "one" (*eka*) due to being devoid of applied thought and sustained thought.
It is also appropriate to say that it is "without companion. Alternatively, it is called *udi* because it causes the associated states to arise (*udāyati*), meaning it makes them emerge.
Being both "one" (*eko*) in the sense of being preeminent and "arising" (*udi*), it is *ekodi*; this is a designation for concentration.
Thus, because one develops and increases this *ekodi*, this second jhāna is "the state of *ekodi*" (*ekodibhāva*). Furthermore, as for this *ekodi*:
It belongs to the mind, not to a being, nor to a soul; therefore it is said, "the singleness of mind.
But surely this faith exists even in the first jhāna, and this concentration called "singleness" is present there too;
so why is this alone described as "tranquillity of mind and singleness of mind"? It is replied: because that first jhāna is agitated by applied and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra).
Like water agitated by ripples and waves, it is not perfectly serene; therefore, even though faith is present, it is not called "tranquillity" (*sampasādana*).
And because of this lack of perfect serenity, concentration (*samādhi*) is also not clearly manifest here, which is why it is not called "singleness" (*ekodibhāva*).
However, in this jhāna, faith is powerful, having found scope due to the absence of the hindrances of applied and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*).
And because concentration also becomes evident through the acquisition of a companion in strong faith, it should be understood that this [definition] alone was stated in this way.
In the *Vibhaṅga*, however, only this much is said: “‘Sampasādana’ is that which is faith, believing, conviction, and complete confidence.
‘One-pointedness of mind’ is that which is the steadiness of the mind... up to ... right concentration. Thus...
Furthermore, this commentary on the meaning should be understood in such a way that it does not contradict what has been stated above, but rather accords with and harmonizes with it. 81.
"Without applied thought and without sustained thought" means that because they have been abandoned through cultivation, there is no applied thought in this [state], or for this [state].
"Without applied thought. By this same method, it is "without sustained thought. It is also said in the *Vibhaṅga*:

"Thus, when this applied thought and this sustained thought have become stilled, calmed, subsided, passed away, utterly passed away, allayed, thoroughly allayed, dried up, completely dried up, and brought to an end, therefore it is called 'without applied thought and without sustained thought.'"
Here it is asked: "Is this meaning not already established by the phrase 'with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought'?

Then why is it stated again as 'without applied thought, without sustained thought'? It is replied: This is indeed so; the meaning is established, yet that [previous phrase] does not illuminate this specific meaning.
Did we not say: "But by the surmounting of each successive gross factor, from the first jhāna..."?
Furthermore, it is said, "With the stilling of applied and sustained thought (*vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā*)," in order to show that others attain the second jhāna and so forth.
Moreover, this serenity (*sampasādana*) arises from the stilling of applied and sustained thought, not from the turbidity of the defilements.

And through the stilling of applied and sustained thought, there is singleness (*ekodibhāva*), not as in access concentration (*upacārajjhāna*) due to the abandoning of the hindrances, nor as in the first jhāna.
"Through the non-manifestation of the [lower] factors"—this statement indicates the cause for the state of serene confidence and unification.
Likewise, "through the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, it is without applied thought and without sustained thought";

this indicates the cause for the state of being without applied and sustained thought, not because they are absent—as in the case of the third and fourth jhānas or as in the case of eye-consciousness and so forth. Thus, it indicates the cause for the state of being without applied and sustained thought.

It does not merely indicate the absence of applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*). Indeed, this expression “without applied thought, without sustained thought” (*avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ*) indicates precisely the mere absence of applied and sustained thought.
Therefore, even though it was mentioned previously, it must certainly be stated here as well.
The phrase “born of concentration” (*samādhija*) means born from the concentration of the first *jhāna*, or from the associated concentration. In that regard:

Although it was produced from the concentration associated with the first [jhāna] as well, nevertheless, this very concentration alone deserves to be called "concentration" because it is exceedingly immovable due to its freedom from the agitation of applied and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra), and because of its extreme clarity;
therefore, for the purpose of praising it, this alone is described as "born of concentration. "Rapture and happiness" is exactly as previously explained.
"Second": it is second by way of numerical sequence; it is also called "second" because one attains this as the second [meditative attainment].

As for what was stated, "abandoned of two factors and endowed with three factors," therein the state of being abandoned of two factors should be understood by way of the abandoning of applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
And just as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are abandoned at the moment of access (*upacāra*) to the first jhāna, [so too here...]

In this case, however, applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are not present in that way; moreover, at the very moment of absorption (*appanā*), this [first jhāna] arises even without them.

Therefore, they are called its "factors of abandoning" (*pahānaṅga*). As for rapture (*pīti*), pleasure (*sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*), it should be understood as being endowed with three factors by virtue of their arising.
Thus, what is stated in the *Vibhaṅga*: "Jhāna is confidence (*sampasāda*), rapture, pleasure... [and so forth].
When it is said, "one-pointedness of mind," that is stated figuratively in order to show jhāna together with its requisites.

However, excluding *sampasādana* (tranquillity), this jhāna consists of only three factors by way of those factors that have attained the characteristic of close contemplation (*upanijjhāna*) in the literal sense.
As it is said: "What, on that occasion, is the three-factored jhāna?"
“Rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind. The rest is exactly as described in the method for the first jhāna.
Regarding the discourse on the third jhāna:
having thus attained that [second jhāna] and become skilled in it through mastery in the five ways, from the familiar second jhāna...
Emerging from that state, he perceives its fault, thinking: "This attainment has applied and sustained thought as its proximate adversaries;
it is weak in its factors because of the grossness of the rapture described as 'whatever there is of rapture, which is an elation of the mind, by this it is declared to be gross.
Having thus seen the defect therein, he attends to the third jhāna as peaceful and brings his attachment to the second jhāna to an end.
Application should be made for the attainment of the third [jhāna].

Then, when he has emerged from the second jhāna and is reviewing the factors of that jhāna with mindfulness and clear comprehension, rapture appears gross to him, while pleasure and one-pointedness appear peaceful.
At that time, for the sake of abandoning the gross factor and for the sake of attaining the peaceful factors, he should direct that same sign as "earth..."
As he repeatedly brings "earth" to mind, thinking, "Now the third jhāna will arise," the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is interrupted;
taking that same earth-kasiṇa as its object, a mind-door adverting consciousness arises.
Then, four or five impulsion moments (javana) flash forth upon that very same object, at the conclusion of which one fine-material-sphere consciousness occurs.
The third jhāna is [of the formless sphere]; the remaining ones are sense-sphere jhānas according to the method already stated.
And at this point, through the fading away of rapture, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending; he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones declare:
"He who is equanimous and mindful dwells in happiness"; thus he enters and dwells in the third jhāna.

Thus, by this means, he has attained the third jhāna based on the earth-kasiṇa, which is abandoned of one factor, endowed with two factors, good in three ways, and possessed of ten characteristics. 83.
Therein, "with the fading away of rapture" (pītiyā ca virāgā): "fading away" (virāga) means either a sense of disgust toward, or the transcendence of, the aforementioned kind of rapture.

Or [it may be understood] as follows. Between the two, however, the word *ca* has the sense of conjunction; it conjoins either "tranquility" (*vūpasama*) or "the tranquility of applied and sustained thought" (*vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasama*).

In that context, when it conjoins only "tranquility," then the construction should be understood thus: "And with the fading away of rapture, and furthermore, because of tranquility. And according to this construction, "fading away" (*virāga*) has the meaning of disgust (*jigucchana*).

Therefore, this meaning should be understood as: "from the revulsion toward rapture and from its subsiding. But when one combines it with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, then the construction should be understood thus:
"and from the fading away of rapture, and furthermore, from the subsiding of applied and sustained thought.
In this construction, "fading away" (virāga) has the sense of "surmounting"; therefore, "from rapture... [the rest follows].
And by transcending [the first jhāna] and by the subsiding of applied and sustained thought—this is how the meaning is to be understood.

Granted that these applied and sustained thoughts have already subsided in the second jhāna itself, nevertheless, this was stated for the purpose of illustrating the path of this jhāna and for the purpose of praising it;
for when it is said, "by the subsiding of applied and sustained thought," this becomes evident.
"Surely the subsiding of applied and sustained thought is the path to this jhāna.

And just as in the case of the third noble path, although the five lower fetters such as personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) have not yet been abandoned, their abandonment is spoken of as "the abandoning of the five lower fetters" as a way of praising it;
this serves to generate enthusiasm in those striving for its attainment—exactly so it is here.
Even when the subsiding of applied and sustained thought (*vitakkavicāra*) has not yet occurred, the description of their subsiding constitutes a statement of praise.
Therefore, this meaning was stated as: "with the surmounting of rapture and with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought.
84. "And he dwells equanimous": here, it is called equanimity (*upekkhā*) because it views from a high standpoint (*upapatti*). It sees evenly; it does not fall into partiality.

The meaning is: "having sacrificed, he sees. Because one is endowed with that [equanimity] which is clear, vast, and firmly established, the possessor of the third jhāna is called "equanimous" (*upekkhaka*).

Furthermore, equanimity (*upekkhā*) is tenfold: equanimity as a factor of the sixfold contact, equanimity as a divine abiding (*brahmavihāra*), and equanimity as a factor of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*).
Equanimity of energy, equanimity of formations, equanimity of feeling, equanimity of insight, equanimity of neutrality, equanimity of jhāna, and equanimity of purification.
Therein, that which is described as: "Here, monks, having seen a form with the eye, a monk is neither glad nor sad... [is equanimity of neutrality].

“He dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending”—this is the equanimity that has come down [in the texts] as the state of not abandoning one’s naturally pure disposition when encountering the sixfold course of desirable and undesirable objects at the six sense-doors of one whose taints are destroyed;
this is called the six-factored equanimity (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*).

However, that equanimity which has come down [in the texts] as “he dwells having pervaded one direction with a mind accompanied by equanimity,” and which consists in an attitude of neutrality toward sentient beings, is called the equanimity of the divine abodes (*brahmavihārupekkhā*).

That equanimity which is described as "he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity dependent on seclusion," and which consists in the state of neutrality toward co-nascent phenomena, is called *bojjhaṅgupekkhā* (equanimity as an enlightenment factor).

However, that equanimity which is described as "from time to time he gives attention to the sign of equanimity," and which consists in energy that is neither too tense nor too lax, is called *vīriyupekkhā* (equanimity of energy).
As for the question, "How many kinds of equanimity regarding formations arise by way of serenity? How many kinds of equanimity regarding formations arise by way of insight?"...
Eight equanimities regarding formations arise by way of serenity; ten equanimities regarding formations arise by way of insight.

Thus, the equanimity that is a state of neutrality in the grasping of the reflective-stilling of the hindrances and so forth—as it has been handed down—is what is called "equanimity regarding formations" (*saṅkhārupekkhā*).

Furthermore, that equanimity designated as "neither-pain-nor-pleasure" which occurs in such passages as, "At whatever time a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen accompanied by equanimity," is called *vedanupekkhā* (equanimity as feeling).

That equanimity consisting in neutrality during investigation which occurs in such passages as, "He abandons what exists, what has come to be, and attains equanimity," is called *vipassanupekkhā* (equanimity of insight).

However, that equanimity which occurs among the factors beginning with desire (*chanda*) as "included" (*yevāpanaka*), being a state of evenness toward co-nascent states, is called *tatramajjhattupekkhā* (equanimity as specific neutrality).
That equanimity which has come down in such passages as “and he dwells in equanimity,” producing non-partisanship even toward that supreme bliss, is called *jhānupekkhā* (equanimity of absorption).

However, that equanimity which has come down in such passages as “the fourth jhāna, purified by mindfulness and equanimity,” being completely pure of all opposing factors and remaining inactive even while those opposing factors are being stilled, is called *pārisuddhupekkhā* (equanimity of purification).

Among these, there is the sixfold equanimity (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*), the equanimity of the divine abodes (*brahmavihārupekkhā*), the equanimity of the awakening factors (*bojjhaṅgupekkhā*), and the equanimity of specific neutrality (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*).

The equanimity of jhāna (*jhānupekkhā*), the equanimity of purification (*pārisuddhupekkhā*), and the equanimity of onlooking (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*) are identical in meaning; they are simply the equanimity of onlooking.
However, their distinction arises from the difference in their respective states, just as there is a distinction among a single being—such as a child, a youth, an elder, a general, or a king.
Therefore, where there is the six-factored equanimity (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*), there is no equanimity as a factor of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅgupekkhā*) and so forth. Where...
Or rather, it should be understood that when there is equanimity as a factor of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅgupekkhā*), the sixfold equanimity and so forth do not exist therein.
Just as these [types of equanimity] are identical in meaning, so too are equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) and equanimity regarding insight (*vipassanupekkhā*).
For it is wisdom alone that is divided into two according to its function. Just as, for example, when a man has entered his house at evening and [sees] a snake...
Just as one who, having taken up a staff with a goat-head, while searching, sees that [object] lying in a heap of husks;
and upon looking to see whether it is a snake or not, sees three *sovattika* grasses and becomes free from doubt;

and in the investigation of whether it is a snake or not, there is equanimity (*majjhattatā*)—even so, for one who has begun insight (*āraddhavipassaka*), regarding the three characteristics by means of insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*).
When, upon seeing the impermanent nature and so forth of formations, a state of equanimity arises, this is called "equanimity of insight" (*vipassanupekkhā*).
It is like that man who, having seized the snake firmly with the forked stick, considers the manner of releasing it, thinking:
"How might I release this snake without harming it, yet without allowing myself to be bitten by it?"

There is equanimity toward grasping when one is investigating. In the same way, the equanimity toward grasping at formations that belongs to one who sees the three realms as if they were ablaze because of having seen the three characteristics—this is called equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*).

Thus, when insight-equanimity (*vipassanupekkhā*) is established, equanimity regarding formations is also necessarily established. By this, however, [it is shown] in the context of discerning and grasping...

They are divided into two types by way of their function, which is termed "equanimity. However, energy-equanimity (*vīriyupekkhā*) and feeling-equanimity (*vedanupekkhā*), as well as one another and the remaining types, are indeed distinct in meaning.
Thus, among these various forms of equanimity, it is jhāna-equanimity that is intended here. Its characteristic is neutrality; its function is non-exertion.
"Its manifestation is non-affliction; its proximate cause is the fading away of rapture. Here it may be asked: "Is this not, in meaning, simply equanimity as specific neutrality?
And since that exists in the first and second jhānas as well, should it not be said there too that 'he dwells in equanimity'?
Why is it not mentioned there? Because its function is not manifest. For its function is not manifest [in those stages].

In that context, its function was overwhelmed by applied thought (*vitakka*) and the others. Here, however, because it is not overwhelmed by applied thought, sustained thought (*vicāra*), and rapture (*pīti*), it has become manifest in its function, as if with its head held high; therefore, it is said [to be present].
This concludes the explanation of the phrase "and he dwells in equanimity" (*upekkhako ca viharati*).
The complete commentary on the meaning. 85.
Now, regarding the phrase "mindful and clearly comprehending": here, one who remembers is "mindful" (*sato*); one who clearly understands is "clearly comprehending" (*sampajāno*).

Thus, mindfulness and clear comprehension are stated by way of the person. In this context, mindfulness has the characteristic of remembering, the function of not forgetting, and is manifested as protection.
Clear comprehension has non-delusion as its characteristic, investigating as its function, and scrutiny as its manifestation.
Although this mindfulness and clear comprehension exist even in the preceding jhānas— for one who is forgetful and lacking clear comprehension does not even achieve access concentration,
let alone absorption— nevertheless, because those jhānas are gross, on that plane...
Just as the movement of a man’s mind is easy [to control], the function of mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*) is not difficult there.

However, because this jhāna is subtle due to the abandoning of gross factors, the movement of the mind must be governed by the functions of mindfulness and clear comprehension—just as in the case of a man on the edge of a razor—as it is stated here alone. Furthermore, just as a calf that follows its mother...
Just as a calf that has been taken away from its mother cow, if left unguarded, returns once more to the cow, so too this bliss of the third jhāna,
having been removed from rapture (*pīti*), might— if not guarded by the protection of mindfulness and clear comprehension— return once more to rapture and become associated with it.
Furthermore, beings are attached even to pleasure, and this pleasure is exceedingly sweet.

Beyond that, there is an absence of pleasure. However, it should be understood that this [next passage] was stated right here in order to show this specific point: that in this state, there is no attachment to pleasure by the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension, and not otherwise.
Now, regarding the phrase "he experiences pleasure with the body," although for one possessing the third jhāna there is an application of mind toward the experience of pleasure...
It does not exist. Nevertheless, because there is pleasure associated with his mental body (*nāmakāya*),
or because his material body (*rūpakāya*) is suffused by an exceedingly refined matter produced by that pleasure associated with the mental body—
by virtue of which suffusion he would experience pleasure even after emerging from the jhāna— it is for the purpose of showing this meaning that [the text says] "and pleasure with the body."
"He experiences" is what was said.
Now, regarding the statement "the noble ones describe him as dwelling in happiness, mindful and equanimous":
here, for the sake of that jhāna, by reason of that jhāna, the noble ones—the Buddhas and others—describe and teach that person who possesses the third jhāna.
They describe it, establish it, reveal it, analyze it, make it plain, and clarify it; the intention is that they praise it.
How so? "Equanimous, mindful, abiding in happiness. Thus, the construction here should be understood as: "Having attained and abiding in that third jhāna."
But why do they praise it in this way? Because it is worthy of praise.
For he is equanimous even toward the third jhāna, which has reached the perfection of happiness through its exceedingly sweet bliss; he is not dragged away by attachment to that happiness.
And he is mindful because his mindfulness is established in such a way that rapture does not arise. Furthermore, because it is beloved by the noble ones and practiced only by the noble ones—
And because he experiences undefiled bliss with his mental body, he is worthy of praise.

Thus, it should be understood that because he is worthy of praise, the Noble Ones—proclaiming those very qualities that serve as the grounds for such praise—praise him in this way: "He dwells in happiness, mindful and equanimous."
"Third": it is the third in the numerical sequence; it is also called "third" because one enters this as the third attainment.
As for what was said—that it is "devoid of one factor and endowed with two factors"—here, the state of being devoid of one factor should be understood by way of the abandoning of *pīti* (rapture).
And this [rapture] is abandoned at the very moment of absorption (*appanā*), just like initial application (*vitakka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*) in the second jhāna.

Therefore, it is said that "it is abandoned by that. Furthermore, the possession of two factors should be understood by way of the arising of these two: bliss (*sukha*) and one-pointedness of mind (*citt’ekaggatā*).

Consequently, what is stated in the *Vibhaṅga*—"Jhāna is equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind"—is said figuratively in order to show jhāna together with its requisites.

However, setting aside equanimity and mindfulness-and-full-awareness, this jhāna consists of only two factors by way of those factors that have attained the characteristic of close contemplation in the direct sense. As it is said: "What at that time is the two-factored jhāna?
It is bliss and one-pointedness of mind. The rest is exactly as described for the first jhāna.
The Discussion of the Fourth Jhāna (87).

When that [third jhāna] has been attained in this way, having become one who has mastered it through the five modes in the manner already described, he emerges from the familiar third jhāna and reflects:
"This attainment has near-joy as its adversary; for whatever mental application there is therein toward 'this is happiness,' [that is an obstacle]."
"By this, that [third jhāna] is declared coarse"— having seen the fault therein, namely that the limbs [of concentration] are weak because of the coarseness of the pleasure thus described,

and having brought to mind the fourth jhāna as peaceful, one should exhaust attachment to the third jhāna and apply oneself to the attainment of the fourth. Then, when he has emerged from the third jhāna, mindful and clearly comprehending...
When, for one who is reviewing the factors of jhāna, pleasure— consisting of mental joy— appears gross,

while the feeling of equanimity and one-pointedness of mind appear peaceful, then, by repeatedly bringing that same sign to mind as "earth, earth" for the sake of abandoning the gross factor and attaining the peaceful factors, [the thought arises]: "Now, the fourth jhāna..."
“...will arise. Having thus interrupted the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), mind-door adverting consciousness arises, taking that same earth-kasiṇa as its object.
Then, four or five impulsion moments (*javana*) arise upon that very same object;

at the end of which one is fine-material-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) and associated with the fourth jhāna, while the remaining ones are of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and of the aforementioned type. This, however—

This is the distinction: because a pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) cannot serve as a condition for a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*adukkhamasukhā vedanā*) by way of the condition of repetition (*āsevana-paccaya*), and because a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling must arise in the fourth jhāna, therefore those [jhānas] are associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekkhā-vedanā*).
And precisely because they are associated with equanimity, even joy (*pīti*) is abandoned here. Up to this point, this [is the explanation] of pleasure...

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
Thus, by him, the fourth jhāna— devoid of one factor, endowed with two factors, excellent in three ways, and possessing ten characteristics— is attained.
There is the earth-kasiṇa.
88. Therein, "with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain" means with the abandoning of bodily pleasure and bodily pain.
"Previously" means that this occurs previously, not at the moment of the fourth jhāna. [The abandoning] of mental joy and mental grief...
"Disappearance" (*atthaṅgama*) means that both mental pleasure and mental pain have already disappeared;
what is meant is their abandonment. But when does their abandonment occur?
At the moment of the access concentration (*upacāra*) of the four jhānas. For joy (*somanassa*) [is abandoned] in the fourth jhāna.

It is abandoned at the very moment of access concentration (*upacāra*). Suffering, mental grief, and pleasure [are abandoned] at the moments of access to the first, second, and third jhānas respectively.

Thus, although their sequence of abandonment has not been explicitly stated here, the abandonment of pleasure, pain, joy, and mental grief—which were mentioned here according to the order of the enumeration of the faculties (*indriya*) in the *Indriyavibhaṅga*—should be understood accordingly.
If, however, these are abandoned at the very moment of access concentration (*upacārakkhaṇa*) for each respective jhāna, then why [is it said]:
"And where, monks, does the arisen faculty of pain cease without remainder? Here, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures...
attains and dwells in the first jhāna. It is here that the arisen faculty of pain..."?
“It ceases without remainder. And where does the arisen faculty of mental grief, the faculty of pleasure, and the faculty of joy cease without remainder?
Here, monks, with the abandoning of pleasure... [as before] ...a monk enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna; here the arisen faculty of joy ceases without remainder.”

Is it thus that cessation is said to occur only in the jhānas? Because of their superior cessation. For while there is a superior cessation of these [hindrances] in the first jhāna and so forth, it is not yet total cessation.
However, at the moment of access (upacāra), there is indeed cessation, though not a superior cessation.

For instance, even when the pain faculty has ceased in the access to the first jhāna due to the absence of various [sensory] invitations, it may still arise through contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like.
Or its arising may occur through an imbalance of the elements or through affliction by uneven postures, but never within access concentration (upacāra).
Even in access, this [pain] has ceased, yet it is not well-ceased because it has not been struck down by its opposite.
But within absorption (appanā), the entire body is suffused with happiness through the pervasion of joy; and for one whose body is suffused with happiness, the faculty of pain is thoroughly ceased.

Because it has been destroyed by its opposite. Furthermore, regarding the faculty of grief (*domanassindriya*) which was abandoned even in the access to the second jhāna—due to various acts of adverting—it arises when there is bodily fatigue and mental affliction, even though there are applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
Yet, it does not arise at all in the absence of applied and sustained thought. However, wherever it does arise, there applied and sustained thought have not yet been abandoned.

And because applied thought and sustained thought exist in the access to the second jhāna, they might arise there for him; but they certainly do not arise in the second jhāna itself, because their conditions have been abandoned.
Likewise, in the access to the third jhāna, although the faculty of pleasure has been abandoned, it might still arise when the body is touched by the sublime matter produced by joy;
but it certainly does not arise in the third jhāna itself. For in the third jhāna, joy—which is the condition for pleasure—has ceased entirely.

"Ceased": likewise, although the faculty of mental joy (*somanassindriya*) has been abandoned in the access concentration (*upacāra*) of the fourth jhāna, its arising might still occur because it has not been properly transcended due to the absence of equanimity (*upekkhā*) reached in absorption (*appanā*). However, this is not the case in the fourth jhāna itself.

For that very reason, the phrase "without remainder" (*aparisesa*) is employed in various places [in the Suttas] to indicate that the faculty of bodily pain (*dukkhindriya*) which arises here ceases without remainder.
Here it may be asked: "If these feelings have already been abandoned in the access (upacāra) stage of each respective jhāna, why are they brought together here?
It is for the purpose of grasping the bliss (sukha). For this feeling described here as "neither-painful-nor-pleasant" is subtle and difficult to discern;
it cannot be easily grasped. Therefore, just as, for example, [one treats] a person who is ill...
Or, just as a cowherd, for the sake of easily capturing a bull that cannot be caught by approaching it in such or such a manner, gathers all the cows into one pen;

then, while driving them out one by one, he causes even that [specific bull] to be caught when it comes along in the sequence, saying, "Catch this one!"—in the very same way, the Blessed One gathered all these together for the sake of easy comprehension. For thus...
Having shown these [feelings] together, it is possible to grasp that which is neither pleasure nor pain, neither mental joy nor mental grief,
as "this is the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Furthermore, it should be understood that these were spoken also for the purpose of showing the conditions for the neither-painful-nor-pleasant liberation of mind (*cetovimukti*).
For the abandoning of pain and so forth are its conditions. As it is said: “There are, friends, four conditions for the attainment of the mind-deliverance that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Here, friends, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure... [as above] ...enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
These, friends, are the four conditions for the attainment of the mind-deliverance that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant.”

Alternatively, just as the personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and other defilements, though already abandoned elsewhere, are said to be abandoned "there" for the sake of praising the third path, so too it should be understood that these [hindrances] are mentioned here for the sake of praising this jhāna.
Or else, it should be understood that these are mentioned here to show the extreme remoteness of lust and hatred through the destruction of their conditions.
For among these, pleasure is the condition for joy, and joy is the condition for lust; pain is the condition for grief, and...
Mental distress [is the nutriment] for hatred. Because lust and hatred, along with their conditions, have been destroyed by the destruction of pleasure and so forth, they become exceedingly remote.
"Neither-painful-nor-pleasant" means it is not painful due to the absence of pain, and not pleasant due to the absence of pleasure.

By this, he indicates here a third type of feeling that stands as the opposite of both pain and pleasure, rather than a mere absence of pain and pleasure. This third feeling is called neither-painful-nor-pleasant.

It is also called equanimity (*upekkhā*). It should be understood as having the characteristic of experiencing what is neither desirable nor undesirable; its function is neutrality; it is manifested as non-manifestation [of pleasure and pain];
and its proximate cause is the cessation of pleasure and pain. 89.
"Purity of mindfulness due to equanimity" means the purity of mindfulness produced by equanimity. For in this jhāna...
Mindfulness is perfectly pure, and that purity of mindfulness is produced by equanimity (*upekkhā*), not by anything else.
Therefore, this is called "purity of mindfulness through equanimity" (*upekkhā-satipārisuddhi*). It is also stated in the *Vibhaṅga*:
"This mindfulness becomes clear, purified, and bright by means of this equanimity; therefore it is called 'purity of mindfulness through equanimity. And by which...
Here, the complete purity of mindfulness occurs through equanimity; in its essential meaning, this should be understood as mental neutrality (*tatramajjhattatā*).
And here, it is not only mindfulness that is purified by it, but rather all associated states (*sampayutta-dhamma*) as well; however, the teaching is expressed under the heading of mindfulness.
In this regard, although this equanimity is also present in the three lower jhānas, just as during the day the radiance of the sun [overpowers other lights],...
Just as the crescent moon, even though it exists by day, is neither pure nor radiant because it lacks the night that is its own kindred and because it is not acting as a benefactor to itself,
so too this crescent-moon of equanimity-in-the-middle (tatramajjhattupekkhā) is neither pure nor radiant because it is overwhelmed by the heat of opposing states such as applied thought (vitakka),
and because it has not yet attained the night of its own kindred, which is the feeling of equanimity (upekkhā-vedanā).

Even though it exists within the various types of the first jhāna and so forth, it is not completely pure. Because it is impure, even the co-nascent factors such as mindfulness and the rest become impure, like the light of an impure crescent moon during the day.

Therefore, not even one among them is described as "purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. However, in this [fourth jhāna], because there is no longer the overpowering influence of the fire of opposing states such as applied thought (vitakka), [it is so described].
And because of the attainment of equanimity and feeling associated with that [state], this crescent moon of equanimity as the middle state is exceedingly pure.
Due to its purity, mindfulness and the other factors, though co-nascent, become pure and radiant like the light of a pure crescent moon.
Therefore, it should be understood that this alone is called "purity of mindfulness through equanimity."
"Fourth": it is the fourth in the numerical sequence; it is also called "the fourth" because one attains this as the fourth.

As for what was said, "abandoned of one factor and endowed with two factors," therein the state of being abandoned of one factor should be understood by way of the abandoning of mental joy (*somanassa*).
And that mental joy [is abandoned] precisely in the earlier impulsions within a single cognitive process (*ekavīthi*).
It is abandoned; therefore, that is called its "factor of abandoning.
However, the possession of two factors should be understood by way of the arising of equanimous feeling and one-pointedness of mind. The rest is exactly as described in the case of the first jhāna.
This, then, is the method regarding the fourfold jhāna.
90. Regarding the discourse on the five jhānas:
one who is producing the fifth jhāna, having emerged from the familiar first jhāna, perceives its defects by thinking, "This attainment has the hindrances as its proximate enemy;
it is weak in factors because of the grossness of applied thought (vitakka). Having thus seen its faults therein, he...
Having attended to the second jhāna as peaceful, one should bring to an end attachment to the first jhāna and apply oneself to the attainment of the second.

Then, when he has emerged from the first jhāna and is reviewing its factors with mindfulness and clear comprehension, mere applied thought (*vitakka*) appears gross to him, while sustained thought (*vicāra*) and the other factors appear peaceful. At that time, for the sake of abandoning the gross factor, [he should apply himself].

And for the sake of attaining tranquility, as one repeatedly brings that same sign to mind, thinking "earth, earth," the second jhāna arises in the manner already described. For this [jhāna], the abandoning factor is simply applied thought (vitakka) alone;
the four factors of possession are sustained thought (vicāra) and so forth. The rest is of the same kind as previously stated.
When that too has been attained, having become one who has mastery in the five ways according to the method already described, he emerges from the familiar second jhāna.

Seeing the defect therein—thinking, "This attainment has applied thought as its proximate enemy; it is weak in factors because of the grossness of sustained thought"—he attends to the third jhāna as peaceful and abandons attachment to the second jhāna.
Having mastered that, he should apply himself to the attainment of the third jhāna.

Then, when he has emerged from the second jhāna and is reviewing the factors of the jhāna with mindfulness and clear comprehension, sustained thought (*vicāra*) appears gross to him while the joy (*pīti*) and other factors appear peaceful.
At that time, for the sake of abandoning the gross factor and attaining the peaceful factor, he should take that same sign and [reflect]: "Earth..."
As he repeatedly brings "earth" to mind, the third jhāna arises in the same manner already described.

For this jhāna, sustained thought (*vicāra*) alone is the factor of abandoning; the three factors beginning with rapture (*pīti*), as in the second jhāna of the fourfold system, are the factors of possession.
The rest is of the same kind as previously stated.

Thus, that which is the second in the fourfold method becomes both the second and the third in the fivefold method by being divided into two. And those which are the third and fourth there become the fourth and fifth respectively. The first remains the first.
Thus ends the section on the Development of Concentration in the *Visuddhimagga*, composed for the delight of virtuous people.
The Fourth Chapter, titled "The Description of the Earth Kasiṇa. 5.
The Description of the Remaining Kasiṇas.
The Discourse on the Water Kasiṇa (Āpokasiṇakathā) 91. Now follows the detailed exposition on the water kasiṇa immediately after the earth kasiṇa.
Just as with the earth kasiṇa, so too one who wishes to develop the water kasiṇa should sit comfortably and seize the sign in water; once it has been prepared...

Or whether it was made or not made—all this should be expanded in detail. And as it is here, so it is everywhere. From now on, however, we shall say only what is distinctive without stating even this much.
Here too, for one who has merit through past deeds and has performed the preliminary service, even in water that has not been prepared, such as in a lotus pond or a lake, in a salt [water source]...
Or a sign arises in the ocean, as it did for the Elder Cūḷa-Siva. It is said that when that venerable one, having abandoned gain and honor,
boarded a ship at Mahātittha with the intention of living in seclusion and was traveling to Jambudīpa,
looking out over the great ocean, a counterpart sign (*kasiṇanimitta*) arose within him.
One who has not yet completed the preliminary work and who avoids the four defects of the *kasiṇa* should not take water of any of the colors— blue, yellow, red, or white—
but rather water that has not reached the ground and is caught in the air by a clean cloth,
or other such water that is clear, limpid, and undisturbed; with this, he should fill his bowl or water-pot to the brim.
Having filled it and placed it in a concealed spot at the edge of the monastery as previously described, one should not contemplate its color while sitting comfortably.

One should not attend to its characteristics. Rather, having made it conform to its support and having fixed the mind on the concept (paṇṇatti-dhamma) by way of its prominence, one should proceed by means of the well-known names for water—such as *ambu*, *udaka*, *vāri*, and *salila*—rather than by its specific designations.
“One should develop [the meditation] thinking, ‘Water, water.
As he develops it in this way, the two signs arise in due order according to the method already described. However, here the learning sign appears as if moving;
if the water contains bubbles of froth, it appears exactly like that.”
The defect of the kasiṇa appears. However, the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) appears motionless, like a jeweled fan placed in space, or like a circular mirror made of jewels.

With its mere appearance, that [sign] brings about access concentration (upacāra-jhāna), and by the method already described, one attains the fourfold and fivefold jhānas. This concludes the water kasiṇa.
92. The Discourse on the Fire Kasiṇa:
One who wishes to develop the fire kasiṇa must also apprehend the sign in fire.

In this regard, for one who has performed the preliminary service and possesses merit, when apprehending the sign in what is not artificially prepared, it may be done by means of a lamp flame, or on a hearth, or at the place where food is cooked.
Or, when looking at a mass of flames anywhere, such as in a forest fire, the sign arises—as it did for the Elder Cittagutta.
On the day of hearing the Dhamma, as that venerable one entered the Uposatha hall and was looking at the flame of a lamp, the sign arose for him.
But by another, it must be produced. Herein, this is the method of production: having split logs of soft heartwood and dried them, [one should proceed].
Having prepared it bit by bit, one should go to a suitable tree-root or a pavilion, heap it up in the manner of cooking grain, and kindle it.
Then, on a mat of straw, a hide, or a cloth, a hole measuring a span and four finger-breadths wide should be made.
Having placed that in front and sat down in the manner already described, [one should place] grass and sticks beneath...
Without attending to the smoke-crested top or the base, one should grasp the sign in the middle of the dense mass.
One should not review the color by way of "blue" or "yellow," and so forth; nor should one attend to its characteristic as heat.
Having made it merely the color of its support, one should fix the mind on the concept (paṇṇatti-dhamma) by way of its predominance.
Among the names for fire—such as *pāvaka*, *kaṇhavattanī*, *jātavedo*, and *hutāsana*—one should develop "fire, fire" by means of its well-known name alone.
As he develops it in this way, the two signs arise in due course according to the method already described. Therein, the learning sign (uggahanimitta) is...
It appears as if it were falling after repeatedly breaking through the net. However, for one who grasps it before it is perfected, the defect of the kasiṇa becomes apparent;
it appears as a fragment of a firebrand, or a lump of embers, or ash, or smoke.
The counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) is motionless, like a piece of red woolen cloth placed in the sky, or like a golden palm-leaf fan, or a pillar of gold.
It appears as if it were real. With its mere appearance, he attains access concentration (upacāra-jhāna), and by the same method already described, he reaches the fourfold and fivefold jhānas.
This concludes the fire kasiṇa. Now, the discourse on the air kasiṇa.
93. One who wishes to develop the air kasiṇa should also grasp the sign in the air.
And that should be done either by way of what is seen or by way of what is touched. For it is said in the commentaries: "One learning the air kasiṇa grasps the sign in the air;
he observes the top of a sugar-cane stalk being shaken or trembling, or the top of a bamboo stalk... or the top of a tree..."
“Or he discerns the hair-tip as it is moved and stirred, or he discerns what has touched the body.

Therefore, having seen a sugar-cane, a bamboo, or a tree standing with its top level, or the head of a man with thick hair being struck by the wind at a height of four finger-breadths, [one understands]: “The wind strikes this spot.”
Having established mindfulness, or else having established mindfulness on whatever part of the body the wind strikes as it enters through a window-opening or a crack in the wall,

one should develop the meditation on "wind, wind" by way of its obvious name among the synonyms for wind, such as *vāta*, *māluta*, and *anila*. Here, because of the expansion of the learning-sign (*uggahanimitta*), it is like milk-rice that has just been poured out.
The sign appears moving like a whirling firebrand; the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta), however, is well-settled and motionless.
The rest should be understood according to the method already described. This concludes the section on the air kasiṇa.
Now follows the discussion on the blue kasiṇa.
94. Next, one who is learning the blue kasiṇa takes the sign in something blue—whether in a flower, a cloth, or a color-element—as it is said.

First, for one who has performed meritorious deeds and possesses merit, [the sign arises] simply upon seeing such a thing as a grove of blue garlands, a floral arrangement at places of worship, or any one of the blue cloths or gems.
A sign arises. Alternatively, having taken blue lotuses, *girikaṇṇikā* flowers, or other such flowers, one should spread them so that neither the filaments nor the stalks are visible;
or, filling the bowl to the very brim with petals alone, they should be spread out. Or, having tied a bundle with a blue-colored cloth, it should be filled. At the rim—

Or it should be fastened like a drumhead. Or, having made a kasiṇa disk—either portable or fixed on a wall—using one of the elements such as bronze-blue, Palāsa-leaf-blue, or collyrium-blue, according to the method described for the earth kasiṇa, it should be demarcated by a dissimilar color.
Then, according to the method described for the earth kasiṇa, one should [contemplate] "blue, blue."
Mental attention should be applied. Here too, a defect in the kasiṇa appears in the learning sign; the hair-like filaments, the stalks, the gaps between the leaves, and so forth, manifest.
The counterpart sign, however, appears in space, released from the kasiṇa disk, like a crystal fan.
The rest should be understood in the manner already described. This is the blue kasiṇa.
The Discussion on the Yellow Kasiṇa (Pītakasiṇakathā) 95. This same method applies to the yellow kasiṇa as well. For it has been said:
"One learning the yellow kasiṇa takes the sign in something yellow—either in a flower, or in a cloth, or in a color-element. Therefore, here too, for one who has performed the preliminary work...
For one who possesses merit, such a sign arises simply upon seeing a garland-stand, a flower-strewn altar, or yellow cloth and relics,

just as it did for the Elder Cittagutta. It is said that when that venerable one saw the worship of a seat made with *pattaṅga* flowers at Cittalapabbata, the sign appeared in the very measure of the seat simultaneously with the sight itself.

It arose. By means of another object such as a *kaṇikāra* flower, or yellow cloth, or a yellow relic, one should form a kasiṇa according to the method described for the blue kasiṇa, and then direct the attention thus:
"yellow, yellow. The rest is exactly the same. This concludes the yellow kasiṇa.
Now follows the discussion of the red kasiṇa.
96. The same method applies to the red kasiṇa as well. For this has been said:
"One learning the red kasiṇa takes the sign in something red—either in a flower, or in a cloth, or in a colored mineral.

Therefore, here too, for one who has performed the preliminary work and possesses merit, there is such a thing as a grove of flowering trees like the *bandhujīvaka*, or a carpet of flowers, or a red cloth, or a red mineral.

Or, having seen some other [object], the sign arises. By means of the other [method], one should create a kasiṇa using flowers such as the *jayasumana*, *bandhujīvaka*, or red *koraṇḍaka*, or with red cloth, or with a relic, making it into a kasiṇa in the same manner as described for the blue kasiṇa;
then the attention should be directed thus: "Red, red. The rest is exactly the same. This concludes the red kasiṇa.
97. The Discussion on the White Kasiṇa:
Regarding the white kasiṇa as well, one who is learning the white kasiṇa grasps the sign in something white—whether in a flower, a cloth, or a color-element—according to the statement;
first, for one who has performed the preliminary work and possesses merit, it is of such a nature.
The sign arises as soon as one sees a garland of flowers, or a carpet of *vassika* and *sumana* blossoms, or a heap of white water-lilies and lotuses, or even a relic encased in white cloth;
it arises likewise upon a circle of tin, a circle of silver, or a circle of the moon.
Or else, by means of other such kinds of white flowers, or white cloth, or a relic.
Having prepared the kasiṇa in the same manner as described for the blue kasiṇa, one should direct the attention thus: "White, white.
The rest is exactly the same. This concludes the white kasiṇa.
Now follows the discussion on the light kasiṇa.
98. Furthermore, regarding the light-kasiṇa (ālokakasiṇa), one who is learning the light-kasiṇa grasps the sign in the light.

According to the statement, "In a hole in a wall, or in a lattice-window, or in the gap between door-panels," for a meritorious person who has performed the preliminary service, the sunlight or moonlight enters through any one of these—such as a hole in a wall—and falls upon the wall or the floor.
Or he produces a circle [of light] through the gaps between the branches of a dense-leaved tree, or through the openings in a bower of thick branches; having seen that, the sign arises.
By the other method as well, one contemplates that same aforementioned circle of radiance as "radiance, radiance" or "light, light."
Or it should be developed in this way: if one is unable to do so, one should light a lamp in a jar, close the mouth of the jar, make a hole in the jar, and place it against the surface of a wall.
Light from the lamp issues through that hole and forms a circle on the wall; that light should be developed as "light, light. This lasts longer than the other methods. Here—
The learning sign (uggahanimitta) is exactly like a circle drawn on a wall or on the ground. The counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) is like a dense, clear mass of light.
The rest is the same as before. This concludes the discussion on the light kasiṇa (ālokakasiṇa).
Now follows the discussion on the limited-space kasiṇa (paricchinnākāsakasiṇa).
99. Regarding the limited-space kasiṇa (*paricchinnākāsakasiṇa*), one who is learning the space kasiṇa takes the sign in space;

for it is said: "In a breach in a wall, or in a hole in a wooden panel, or in a gap between window-frames. Thus, for one who has previously performed meritorious deeds and possesses merit, the sign arises as soon as he sees any one of these, such as a breach in a wall.
For others, however, [it arises] in a well-covered pavilion or in a leather water-skin, a basket, or similar objects.
Or, having made a hole measuring one span and four fingers in some other place, or that very same hole such as a breach in a wall, one should develop it as "space, space.
Here, the learning sign (uggahanimitta) is exactly like the hole together with its boundaries such as the wall;
even when being expanded, it does not expand. The counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta), however, is simply a circle of space.
Having offered it, [the sign] appears; and as it is being increased, it increases. The remainder should be understood in the same manner as described for the earth-kasiṇa.
This concludes the limited-space kasiṇa.
Thus are the kasiṇas of the Ten-Powered One.
The All-Seeing One spoke these ten verses as the causes for the fourfold and fivefold jhānas within the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*).
Thus are they, and of them—
Having understood this method of meditation,
this further miscellaneous discussion concerning those very same subjects should also be understood.
Miscellaneous Discussion 100.
