For herein, by means of the earth-kasiṇa, there occurs the state of being one and then becoming many, and so forth;
or, having fashioned earth in space or on water, there is walking upon it with feet, or the performance of standing, sitting, and so on, according to the method of the limited and the measureless.
The attainment of the bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) and so forth are accomplished.

By means of the water-kasina (*āpokasiṇa*), such things as emerging from and submerging in the earth, the production of rain, the manifestation of rivers, oceans, and so forth, and the shaking of the earth, mountains, palaces, and so forth, are accomplished.
By means of the fire-kasina (*tejokasiṇa*), such things as smoking, blazing, the production of a shower of embers, and the exhaustion of fire by fire, are accomplished.
Whatever he desires— such as the power to burn things, the production of light for the purpose of seeing forms with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu),
and the incineration of the body by the fire element (tejodhātu) at the time of final Nibbāna—
all these succeed. Likewise, by means of the air kasiṇa (vāyokasiṇa), the ability to travel through the movement of the wind and the raising of wind and rain, and so forth, all succeed.

By means of the blue kasiṇa, there succeeds the manifestation of blue forms, the creation of darkness, the attainment of the bases of mastery according to the method of the beautiful and the ugly, the realization of the beautiful liberation, and so forth.

By means of the yellow kasiṇa, there succeeds the manifestation of yellow forms, the resolve that "it is gold," the attainment of the bases of mastery in the manner already stated, the realization of the beautiful liberation, and so forth.

By means of the red kasiṇa, the manifestation of a red form, the attainment of the bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana) in the manner already described, the achievement of the liberation of the beautiful (subhavimokkha), and so forth, are accomplished.

By means of the white kasiṇa, the manifestation of a white form, the removal of sloth and torpor, the dispelling of darkness, and the production of light for the purpose of seeing forms with the divine eye, and so forth, are accomplished.

By means of the light kasiṇa, there succeeds the manifestation of radiant forms, the removal of sloth and torpor, the dispelling of darkness, and the production of light for the purpose of seeing forms with the divine eye, and so forth.

By means of the space kasiṇa, there succeeds the uncovering of what is concealed, the assuming of postures by creating space even within solid earth or mountains, and traveling without obstruction through walls and other such barriers, and so forth.

All [these kasinas] receive this classification as "above, below, across, non-dual, and immeasurable. For it is said: "One person perceives the earth-kasina; above, below, across, non-dual, and immeasurable," and so forth.
In that context, "above" means facing the upper surface of the sky. "Below" means facing the lower surface of the earth. "Across" means delimited on all sides like a circular field.
Indeed, one person expands the kasina only upwards, while another...
Below, or in every direction; or for such-and-such a reason, he extends it in this way, just as one desiring to see forms with the divine eye extends his vision toward the light.
Therefore it is said: "above, below, and across. Furthermore, the term "non-dual" is stated for the purpose of showing that a single being does not undergo a change into another state.
For just as for one who has entered the water, there is only water in all directions and nothing else, even so...
The earth-kasiṇa is simply the earth-kasiṇa; there is no other division of that kasiṇa.
This same method applies everywhere. "Immeasurable" (appamāṇa) is said with reference to the immeasurability of its pervasion. For when one pervades it with the mind, one pervades it in its entirety.
One does not grasp a measure such as "this is its beginning" or "this is its middle."
101. Furthermore, those beings who are possessed of an obstruction of karma, or possessed of an obstruction of defilements, or possessed of an obstruction of ripening;

who lack faith, lack desire [for the good], and are dull-witted, being incapable of entering upon the certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states—as it has been said—among them, even for a single person, the development of even a single kasiṇa does not succeed. In that regard, by way of an obstruction of karma...

"Endowed with" means possessing actions of immediate retribution (*ānantariya-kamma*). "Endowed with the obscuration of defilements" refers to those with fixed wrong view, as well as hermaphrodites and eunuchs.
"Endowed with the obscuration of karmic result" refers to those with rebirth-linking consciousnesses that are rootless (*ahetuka*) or possess only two roots.
"Lacking faith" means being devoid of faith toward the Buddha and the other [Three Jewels]. "Lacking desire" means being devoid of the aspiration for the practice that is not contrary [to the goal].

"Lacking wisdom" means being devoid of both mundane and supramundane right view. "Unable to enter upon the certainty regarding wholesome states" means they are incapable of entering upon the Noble Path, which is designated as "certainty" and "rightness" with respect to wholesome states.
And this applies not only to the kasiṇas, but to none of these other meditation subjects either.
Meditative development does not succeed. Therefore, even for a clansman who is free from the obstruction of karmic result, he should avoid the obstructions of karma and defilements from afar;
and by increasing his faith, zeal, and wisdom through such means as hearing the true Dhamma and relying upon spiritual friends, he should apply himself to the practice of the meditation subject.
Thus ends the "Exposition of the Remaining Kasiṇas" in the Section on the Development of Concentration within the *Visuddhimagga*, composed for the delight of virtuous people.
The Fifth Chapter:
6. Exposition of the Meditation Subject on Foulness.
Explanation of the Terms Beginning with "Swollen."

102. Next, among the ten kinds of bloated corpses devoid of consciousness that were mentioned immediately after the kasiṇas—namely, the bloated, the livid, the festering, the fissured, the gnawed, the scattered, the hacked and scattered, the blood-stained, the worm-infested, and the skeleton—the corpse becomes inflated by the upward-moving wind at the conclusion of life, just like a bellows. In due order:
It is called *uddhumātaka* because it is bloated due to its state of being swollen; that which is bloated is itself *uddhumātaka*.

Alternatively, it is called *uddhumātaka* because it is bloated in a loathsome or contemptible manner. This is a designation for such a corpse. It is called *vinīla* when it has a discolored, bluish appearance;
that which is bluish is itself *vinīlaka*. Alternatively, it is called [loathsome] because it is contemptible.

*Vinīla* means bluish-black. This is a designation for a corpse whose flesh has swollen, which is red-colored in places where pus has accumulated, white-colored in other places, and predominantly blue-colored; it is like a body covered with a blue cloth.

*Vipubba* refers to the pus trickling out from fissures; "vipubba" is simply "vipubbaka. Alternatively, because it is loathsome, it is "corrupt" (*kucchita*) and "putrid" (*vipubba*), hence *vipubbaka*. This is a designation for such a corpse.

"Rent" (*vichidda*) is said to be that which has been split apart by being cut in two; "rent" itself is "the rent" (*vichiddaka*). Alternatively, it is called "the rent" because it is loathsome due to its being torn asunder. This is a designation for a corpse whose middle part has been severed.
"Torn apart" (*vikkhāyita*) is that which has been devoured here and there in various ways by dogs, jackals, and so forth;
"torn apart" itself is "the torn-apart" (*vikkhāyitaka*). Alternatively, it is called "the torn-apart" because it is loathsome due to its being devoured. Of such a [corpse]...
This is a designation for the physical body.
It is variously scattered and strewn; thus, being strewn, it is "the scattered" (*vikkhittaka*). Or, because it is loathsome and vile, it is "the scattered," hence "the scattered" (*vikkhittaka*).
[It is so called] because the hand is in one place, the foot in another, and the head in yet another—thus, from here and there.
This is a designation for a scattered corpse.

It is "mangled and scattered" (*hatavikkhittaka*) because it has been mangled in the manner previously described and is scattered; this is a designation for a corpse that has been mangled with a weapon upon its limbs and members in the shape of a crow’s foot and then scattered according to the method already stated.
It is "bloody" (*lohitaka*) because blood is sprinkled, scattered, and trickles here and there; this is a designation for a corpse smeared with trickling blood.
"Corpses" (*puḷava*) refers to worms; it is called "worm-infested" (*puḷavaka*) because it scatters worms. This is a designation for a corpse full of maggots. "Bones" (*aṭṭhika*) means simply bones.
Alternatively, it is called "bone" (*aṭṭhika*) because it is a loathsome bone due to its repulsiveness. This is a designation for both a skeleton and a single bone.
Furthermore, these [meditations], such as the bloated and so forth, also apply to the signs that have arisen based upon them.
These same names apply even to the jhānas attained upon these signs.
103. The bloated meditation subject (*uddhumātaka-kammaṭṭhāna*):
Having produced the sign of the bloated on a bloated corpse, [one contemplates] that which is called "the bloated."
A yogi who wishes to develop jhāna should approach a teacher of the type described above in the same manner as prescribed for the earth-kasiṇa and learn the meditation subject from him.
When the teacher explains the meditation subject to him, he should explain the procedure for going to see the sign of foulness,
the examination of the sign in its surroundings, the grasping of the sign in eleven ways, and the reviewing of the path traveled back and forth.
In this way, everything up to the conclusion of the method for absorption (*appanā*) should be explained.
Having thoroughly mastered all of that as well, one should go to a lodging of the kind previously described and dwell there seeking the sign of the bloated corpse (*uddhumātaka-nimitta*).
And while dwelling thus, [one should look for it] at the gate of such-and-such a village, or at the entrance to a forest, or on a path, or at the foot of a mountain.

Or, even upon hearing the words of those saying that a bloated corpse has been cast down at the foot of a tree or in a charnel ground, one should not proceed immediately, like someone leaping across a place where there is no ford.
Why? Because this foul object may be inhabited by wild beasts or by non-human beings;
in such cases, there might even be a danger to one's life. Furthermore, the path leading there...
It may be at a village gate, or at a bathing place, or at the edge of a field.

There, an object of a different class (*visabhāga-rūpa*) comes into range, or that very body itself becomes an object of a different class. For a man, a woman’s body is of a different class, and for a woman, a man’s body is of a different class;
and this, while still recently deceased, appears even as beautiful, whereby there is an obstacle to his holy life (*brahmacariya*).
It may be so. However, if one considers to oneself, "This is not a heavy burden for someone like me," then one may go while maintaining that reflection.
Furthermore, when going, one should inform the senior of the Saṅgha or some other well-known bhikkhu before departing. Why?

Because if, at the cemetery, he is overcome by undesirable objects such as the forms, sounds, and so forth of non-human beings, lions, tigers, and the like— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.*
Either his limbs will tremble, what he has eaten will not settle, or some other affliction will arise.
Then he will ensure that the bowl and robes are well-protected in the monastery; or else, having sent young novices, he will look after that monk.
Furthermore, thinking that a charnel ground is a place free from fear, they may even commit an act [of violence].
Thieves who had not yet committed their crime gathered together. Pursued by people, they abandoned their goods near a bhikkhu and fled.
Thinking, "We have seen the thief with his loot," the people seized the bhikkhu and mistreated him.
Then he [the bhikkhu] said to them, "Do not mistreat this man; he told me that he had gone away on such-and-such a mission."
Having informed the people, he will ensure their safety; this is the benefit of going after having explained [the matter].

Therefore, for a bhikkhu of the aforementioned type who has explained it and has developed a desire to see the sign of foulness, he should go—just as a noble king goes to his consecration site, a sacrificer to the sacrificial hall, or a poor man to the place where a treasure is hidden, filled with joy and gladness. Thus...
Having generated rapture and joy, one should proceed according to the method described in the commentaries. For this has been said:

"One who is learning the bloated sign of foulness goes alone, without a companion, with established mindfulness, without confusion, with sense faculties turned inward, with the mind not directed outward, reviewing the path traveled and yet to be traveled. In whatever..."
In a certain place, a bloated sign of foulness has been placed;
in that place, he notes the specific characteristics of a rock, or an anthill, or a tree, or a bush, or a creeper, and he makes them the object of his attention.
Having noted their specific characteristics and made them the object of his attention, he characterizes the bloated sign of foulness according to its essential nature, and also by way of its color.
[He examines it] by way of its characteristic, its shape, its direction, its location, its delimitation, its joints, its openings, its depressions, its elevations, and its surroundings.
He makes that sign well-grasped, retains it well-retained, and defines it well-defined.
Having made that sign well-grasped, having retained it well-retained, and having defined it well-defined...

Having thus determined [the path], he goes alone, without a companion, with mindfulness established and unconfused, with his sense faculties withdrawn within, and with his mind not directed outwardly, reviewing the path traversed and yet to be traversed.
Even while walking, he fixes his attention on a walkway oriented toward that same goal; even while sitting, he prepares a seat oriented toward that same goal.
“What is the purpose, what is the benefit of the thorough examination of signs? The thorough examination of signs has non-delusion as its purpose;
it has non-delusion as its benefit. What is the purpose, what is the benefit of the elevenfold apprehension of signs?
The elevenfold apprehension of signs has anchoring as its purpose; it has anchoring as its benefit. What is the purpose of the reviewing of the path gone over and the path not yet gone over?”
What is the benefit? The benefit of entering the path is the reviewing of the path already traversed and yet to be traversed; it is for the purpose of entering the path.
Seeing this benefit and perceiving it as a treasure, he establishes reverence and, with affection, binds his mind to that object, thinking:
"Surely by this way I shall be liberated from aging and death."
Thus, secluded from sensual pleasures... [as before] ...he enters and dwells in the first jhāna.
For him, there has been attained the first jhāna of the fine-material sphere, a divine abiding, and a basis for meritorious action consisting in development.
106. Therefore, one who goes to see a charnel ground for the purpose of disciplining the mind should strike the gong.
Even if he goes after having assembled a group, one who goes under the heading of a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) should go alone and without a companion,
not relinquishing his primary meditation subject but attending to it while taking a walking-stick or a staff for the purpose of warding off dangers such as dogs in the charnel ground;
and by means of establishing [the mind] well, he should maintain mindfulness that is not lost.
Having done this, one should go without the mind wandering outward, by ensuring that the mind remains within the six sense faculties, including the mind-faculty (*manas*).
As one is departing from the monastery, one should observe the door, noting: "I am departing via such-and-such a door in such-and-such a direction.
Then, the path by which one travels must be defined: "This path faces the eastern direction."
or it goes toward the west, north, or south, or toward the intermediate directions. Furthermore, by defining the path of travel as:
"In this place it goes to the left; in this place to the right;
and in this place there is a rock, in this a termite mound, in this a tree, in this a shrub, and in this a creeper"—thus one defines the path of movement.
One should go to the place where the sign is located; however, one must not go against the wind.

For if one goes against the wind, the stench of the corpse might strike the nose and disturb the brain, cause one to vomit food, or produce remorse with the thought, "I have come to such a place of corpses.
Therefore, avoiding the direction against the wind, one should go with the wind.

One must go. If it is not possible to go by way of the windward path—if there is a mountain, a precipice, a rock, a fence, a thicket of thorns, water, or a swamp along the way—one should go covering the nose with the corner of the robe.
This is his rule for going.
107. However, one who has gone in this manner should not yet look at the sign of foulness. The directions must be determined.
For to one standing in a particular direction, the object does not appear clearly, and the mind is not pliant.
Therefore, avoiding that spot, one should stand where the object appears clearly and the mind is [pliant].
It becomes workable; one should stand there. However, one must avoid standing both upwind and downwind.
For if one stands upwind, the mind of one who is oppressed by the stench of the corpse wanders.

If one stands downwind, if there are non-human beings (*amanussa*) dwelling there, they may become angry and cause harm. Therefore, one should step aside slightly and stand neither too far upwind nor too far downwind.
Standing thus, one should stand neither too far away nor too close, and neither with the feet nor with the head [too near].
For if one stands too far away, the object is not clear; if too close, fear arises; and if one stands with the feet or the head [too near], the entire loathsome aspect is not perceived evenly.
Therefore, one should look from a place that is convenient, neither too far nor too close.
It should be stationed at the middle part of the body.
Standing thus, one should observe the surrounding signs as described in the passage: "In that place, he notes a stone...
or a creeper, together with its characteristic marks. Herein, this is the method for observing them: if, for him—
In the vicinity of the sign, within the range of vision, there is a stone; that stone should be defined as:
"This stone is high or low, small or large, copper-colored, black, white, long, or round. Then, [one should define it thus]:
"In this particular place, this stone is the foul sign; this foul sign is this..."
It should be observed as "a stone. If there is an anthill, that too must be defined as "high or low, small or large, copper-colored, black, white, long, or circular. Then it should be observed:
"In this particular place, this is the anthill; this is the sign of foulness (asubhanimitta). If there is a tree, [it should be observed likewise].
That too must be defined as "an assattha tree, or a nigrodha, or a kacchaka, or a kapītana; tall or short, small or large, copper-colored, black, or white.
Then one should observe: "In this particular place, this is the tree; this is the sign of foulness (asubhanimitta). If it is a shrub, that too [must be defined] as "a sindi..."
It should be defined as either a *karamanda*, a *kaṇavīra*, or a *kuraṇḍaka* tree—whether tall or short, small or large.
Then one should observe: "In this particular place, this bush is the sign of foulness (*asubhanimitta*).
If it is a creeper, that too should be defined as either a *lābu*, a *kumbhaṇḍī*, a *sāmā*, a *kāḷavalli*, or a *pūtilatā*.
Then one should observe: "In this particular place, this is the creeper and this is the sign of foulness; this is the sign of foulness and this is the creeper.
As for what was said—that "one makes it with its sign" and "one makes it with its object"—that is included right here.
For one who defines [the object] again and again is said to "make it with its sign" (*sanimittaṃ karoti*).
By defining it by repeatedly pairing two things together—thinking, "This is a stone; this is the sign of foulness (*asubhanimitta*)," and "This is the sign of foulness;
this is a stone"—one is said to "make it with its object" (*sārammaṇaṃ karoti*).
Thus, having made it "with signs" and "with an object," it is said that one "defines it by way of its individual essence.
Therefore, it should be brought to mind by means of its individual essence—that state of being bloated which is unique to itself and not shared with anything else.
The meaning is that it should be defined by its individual essence and its own specific characteristic as "the bloated corpse."
110. Having thus defined it, the sign should be grasped in six ways: by color, by gender, by shape, by direction, by location, and by delimitation.
How so? The yogi should define this body by color as "black," "white," or "ruddy-skinned.
By gender, however, [he should define it] as "female gender" or "male gender."

Having determined [the color], one should determine it by way of its position, thinking: "This is the body of one who stands in the first stage of life, the middle stage of life, or the final stage of life.
By way of its shape, one should determine it according to the shape of the bloated corpse itself: "This is the shape of his head; this is the shape of his neck;
this is the shape of his hands; this is the shape of his belly; this is the shape of his navel."
One should define: "This is the shape of the waist; this is the shape of the thighs; this is the shape of the shanks; this is the shape of the feet.
As for direction, one should define: "In this body there are two directions: the lower direction below the navel, and the upper direction above it.
Or alternatively: "I am standing in this direction, while the sign of foulness is in this [other] direction."
It should be defined. By way of location, however, it should be defined thus: "In this place are the hands, in this the feet, in this the head, and in this the middle part of the body stands.
Alternatively, one should define it thus: "I am standing in this place; the sign of foulness is in this [place]. By way of delimitation:
"This body is bounded below by the soles of the feet and above by the hair of the head..."
One should define it as being bounded horizontally by the skin, and that within the space so defined, it is indeed filled with thirty-two kinds of corpses.
Alternatively, one should define it thus: "This is the limit of its hand; this is the limit of its foot; this is the limit of its head;
this is the limit of its middle body. Or, one should define it according to however much space it occupies.
One should delimit this very object as being "a bloated corpse of such-and-such a size.
However, it is not appropriate for a man to take a woman's body [as the object], nor for a woman to take a man's body. When the bodies are of a different gender, the object does not appear clearly;
rather, it becomes a condition for mental agitation. For it is said in the *Madhyama-aṭṭhakathā*: "Even a woman whose clothes have been removed remains obsessing the mind of a man."
Thus it has been said. Therefore, one should grasp the sign in this sixfold manner only from a body of the same class.

111. However, he who has cultivated the meditation subject in the presence of previous Buddhas, who has maintained the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), who has rubbed down the great primary elements, who has discerned formations, who has defined name-and-form, who has discarded the perception of a being, and who has performed the duties of a recluse and perfumed his mind with the scent of virtue— [End of excerpt]
A clansman who has cultivated meditation, possesses the seed, is supreme in knowledge, and has few defilements, finds that the counterpart sign appears to him at the very place where he looks.
If it does not appear in this way, then it appears for one who grasps the sign in these six ways.
But for one to whom it still does not appear even thus, [it appears] from the junction, from the opening, from the hollow, or from the dry land.
"Everywhere" means that the sign should again be apprehended in five ways. 112.
Therein, "by way of joints" means by way of the one hundred and eighty joints. But how will he discern the one hundred and eighty joints in a bloated corpse?
Therefore, he [should discern] the three joints of the right hand, the three of the left hand, the three...

It should be defined by way of its joints as follows: the joint of the right leg, the three joints of the left leg, one joint of the neck, and one joint of the waist—thus it is to be defined by way of the fourteen major joints.
As for "by way of openings" (*vivarato*): an opening (*vivara*) is the space between the hands, the space between the feet, the space of the abdomen, and the space of the ears;
thus it is to be defined by way of openings. Furthermore, the state of being closed or the state of being open regarding the eyes [should also be defined].
Or else, the state of being closed or the state of being open of the mouth must be defined. As for "the concave" (*ninnato*):
that part of the body which is concave—whether it be the eye sockets, the interior of the mouth, or the throat—must be defined. Alternatively, one may define it thus:
"I am standing on level ground, while the body is elevated. As for "the convex" (*thalato*): that part of the body which is elevated [must be defined].
One should define either the knee, the chest, or the forehead. Alternatively, one should define it by thinking, "I am standing on dry land and the body is sinking.
"From all sides" means the entire body should be defined from every side.
Having directed knowledge throughout the whole body, wherever it appears clearly, there one should [define] the bloated corpse.
“One bloated” is how the mind should be established. If it does not appear even in this way, there is a bloated corpse with the abdomen distended beyond its normal limits;
there, the mind should be established as “bloated, bloated.
113. Now, regarding the passage beginning with “he makes that sign well apprehended,” this is the analytical explanation:
That yogi should grasp the sign well in that body by means of apprehending the sign as it has been described.
Having established mindfulness well, he should advert to it. Performing this again and again, he should thoroughly examine and define it.
Standing or sitting at a place not too far from and not too close to the body, with his eyes...

Having opened the eyes and looked, the sign (nimitta) should be grasped. One should open the eyes and look a hundred times, a thousand times, thinking, "The repulsiveness of the bloated corpse, the repulsiveness of the bloated corpse," and then close the eyes and reflect upon it.
For one who practices in this way repeatedly, the learning-sign (uggahanimitta) becomes well-grasped. When is it well-grasped? When—
When the sign comes into range equally for one who looks with eyes open and for one who adverts with eyes closed,
then it is said to be well-grasped.
Having thus made that sign well-grasped, having reflected upon it so that it is well-reflected, and having defined it so that it is well-defined—
If he is unable to reach the culmination of development right there, then he should go to his own lodging alone and unaccompanied, just as described in the method for the journey,
attending to that same meditation subject, maintaining well-established mindfulness,
with the sense faculties withdrawn and the mind not directed outward.
As one is leaving the charnel ground, the path of arrival must be defined:

"The path by which I have departed goes toward the eastern direction, or it goes toward the western, northern, or southern direction, or it goes toward an intermediate direction; at this point it turns to the left, and at this..."

To the south; and having thus determined the path of approach—thinking, "In this place there is a rock, in this a termite mound, in this a tree, in this a shrub, and in this a creeper"—one who has arrived should resolve upon a walking path (caṅkama) that faces in that same direction.
The meaning is that one should walk on a patch of ground facing the direction of the sign of foulness (asubhanimitta).
When sitting down, even the seat should be prepared facing that same direction.

However, if in that direction there is a hollow, a precipice, a tree, a fence, or a quagmire, such that it is impossible to walk back and forth on that patch of ground facing that direction, and because of the lack of space, it is impossible to prepare a seat; then, even without looking toward that direction, [one should sit] according to the available space.
In that place, one should both walk up and down and sit; however, the mind must be directed toward that very same direction.
114. Now, regarding the questions beginning with “What is the purpose of observing the sign all around? and their answers beginning with “For the sake of non-delusion,” this is the intended meaning:
for one who, at an improper time, goes to the place where the bloated sign is located and observes the sign all around...
Having opened his eyes for the purpose of grasping the sign, as he gazes upon that dead body, it appears to him as if rising up,
as if overwhelming him, and as if pursuing him; seeing that loathsome and terrifying object, his mind becomes distracted and he becomes like one insane, filled with fear and trepidation.
One encounters hair-raising terror. Indeed, among the thirty-eight objects of meditation analyzed in the Pāḷi, there is no other object so terrifying as this one.
For in this meditation subject, one becomes what is called "one who has fallen away from jhāna. Why? Because of the extreme terror of the meditation subject.
Therefore, that yogin, steadying himself and establishing mindfulness well, [should contemplate] the dead body...
Once it has arisen, there is no such thing as "following after. For if a stone or a creeper standing near him were to move, his body would move as well;
but just as that stone or creeper does not move, so too his body does not move.
However, this manner of attending to you is born of perception and originates from perception.
"Your meditation subject has appeared today; do not fear, O bhikkhu.
Having dispelled their fear in this way and inspired laughter, he should cause the mind to move upon that sign. In this manner, one attains distinction.
It is with reference to this that it was said: "The observation of the surrounding signs is for the purpose of non-delusion."
Furthermore, by accomplishing the apprehension of the sign in eleven ways, one anchors the meditation subject.
For when he opens his eyes and looks, the learning sign (*uggahanimitta*) arises conditioned by that looking.
As he directs his mind toward it, the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*) arises. Directing his mind toward that, he attains absorption (*appanā*). Having stood in absorption—
Increasing insight, he realizes Arahantship. Therefore it is said: "The grasping of the sign in eleven ways is for the purpose of anchoring.
115. Regarding the phrase "reviewing the path gone over and the path not yet gone over is for the purpose of entering the right track": herein, that which pertains to the path already traversed...

And the reviewing of one who has arrived on the path has been mentioned; the meaning is that this is for the purpose of properly introducing him to the course of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
For if, while this bhikkhu is coming after having taken up the meditation subject, some people on the way ask him, "Venerable sir, what is today's date?
or ask questions, or offer him hospitality, [he must respond].
It is not proper for one who thinks, "I am a practitioner of meditation subjects," to depart in silence. One must explain the day's events and answer questions.
If one does not know, one should say, "I do not know. One should offer the appropriate hospitality.
For one who acts in this way, the newly acquired sign may be lost; yet even if it is lost, one must still explain the day's events when questioned.
One who does not know the question should say, "I do not know. One who does know may speak of it partially, and should also offer a greeting of welcome (*paṭisanthāra*).
Upon seeing an incoming monk, one must certainly perform the welcome for an incoming visitor.

Furthermore, there are the remaining duties: the duties regarding the shrine terrace (*cetiyāṅgaṇa-vatta*), the duties regarding the Bodhi-tree terrace (*bodhiyaṅgaṇa-vatta*), the duties regarding the Uposatha hall (*uposathāgāra-vatta*), the duties regarding the dining hall (*bhojanasālā-vatta*), the duties regarding the bathhouse (*jantāghara-vatta*), and the duties toward the teacher (*ācariya-vatta*), the preceptor (*upajjhāya-vatta*), the incoming visitor (*āgantuka-vatta*), the departing guest (*gamika-vatta*), and so forth.
All the duties prescribed in the Khandhaka must indeed be fulfilled. Even while he is fulfilling them, that fresh sign may vanish;

or, when he wishes to go back with the thought, "I will go and take up the sign again," he may be unable to reach even the charnel ground because it is infested by non-human beings or wild beasts, or the sign disappears. (The bloated corpse)
For indeed, after staying for only one or two days, it undergoes the state of lividity (*vinīlaka*) and so forth.
Among all meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*), there is none as difficult to obtain as this one.
Therefore, when the sign has thus vanished, that bhikkhu should sit down in his night-quarters or day-quarters and think: "I went out from the monastery by such-and-such a door..."
Having set out upon the path facing such-and-such a direction, I turned left at such-and-such a place and right at such-and-such a place.
At such-and-such a place there was a rock, and at such-and-such a place one of these: an anthill, a tree, a shrub, a creeper, or something else.
Having traveled by that path, I saw a foul object at such-and-such a place. There, facing such-and-such a direction...
Having stood there and observed the signs all around in such and such a manner, and having thus grasped the sign of foulness, one should review the path traveled back and forth,
from the point of leaving the charnel ground in a certain direction, along such-and-such a road, performing this and that action,
until arriving here and sitting down, right up to the place where one sits with the legs crossed in the full lotus posture.
As he reviews it in this way, that sign becomes manifest and stands before him as if placed right there.

The meditation subject enters the cognitive path in the same manner as previously described. Therefore it is said: "Reviewing the path traversed and not yet traversed is for the purpose of entering the cognitive path."
116. Now, seeing the benefits and perceiving [the object] as a jewel, having established reverence and feeling affection for it, one binds the mind to that object.

Herein, having directed the mind toward the repulsive aspect of the bloated corpse, having produced jhāna, and increasing insight (vipassanā) which has that jhāna as its proximate cause, one thinks: "Truly, by this practice..."
One must be one who sees the benefits, thinking: "I shall be completely liberated from old age and death.
Just as a man in distress, having obtained a precious jewel of great value, would perceive it as a treasure, thinking, "Ah, what a rare thing I have gained!
and, having conceived a sense of reverence for it, would protect it while cherishing it with abundant affection and joy; so too should one act.
In the same way: "I have obtained this meditation subject, which is difficult to find, like a precious gem for one who is in distress.
For one whose meditation subject is the four elements examines his own four great primaries; one whose meditation subject is mindfulness of breathing examines the breath at his own nostrils;
and one whose meditation subject is the kasiṇas, having prepared the kasiṇa, develops it as he pleases."

In this way, other meditation subjects are easily obtained. However, there is nothing more difficult to find than this, for [the subject of a corpse] remains for only one or two days, after which it reaches the state of a livid corpse and so forth.
Therefore, regarding that sign as a jewel, one should guard it with a sense of reverence and with joyful affection. At the night-quarters...
And whether standing by day or by night, one should repeatedly fix the mind upon that [object] as "the repulsiveness of the bloated, the repulsiveness of the bloated.
One should again and again advert to that sign and attend to it; it should be struck with thought and struck with applied thought.
117. As he practices in this way, the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) arises. Herein, this is the distinction between the two signs:
the learning sign (uggahanimitta) appears as unsightly, hideous, and terrifying to behold;
the counterpart sign, however, is like a person with stout limbs and members lying down after having eaten his fill. At the very moment he acquires that counterpart sign, [the hindrances subside].
By not attending to external sense-desires, sensual desire is abandoned through suppression.
Through the very abandonment of attachment, ill will is also abandoned, just as pus is removed when blood is let. Likewise, lethargy and drowsiness are abandoned by the arousal of energy;
restlessness and remorse by engaging in those things that are blameless and pleasing; and [doubt] by the direct realization of the specific distinction attained.
Doubt regarding the Teacher who teaches the practice, the practice itself, and the fruit of the practice is abandoned; thus, the five hindrances are abandoned.
And upon that very sign, there is *vitakka*, characterized by the directing of the mind toward it;
*vicāra*, which performs the function of scrutinizing the sign; *pīti*, which arises from the condition of having attained a distinguished realization; and for one whose mind is filled with joy...
Because of the arising of tranquility, there is tranquility; because of that, happiness arises;
and because concentration of mind arises for one who is happy, one-pointedness arises as a result of happiness—thus the factors of absorption (jhānaṅga) become manifest.

In this way, access concentration (upacārajjhāna), which is a reflection of the first absorption, is produced at that very moment. Hereafter, [the process continues] until the full absorption (appanā) of the first absorption.
And so too for the attainment of mastery; all this should be understood in the same manner as described for the earth-kasiṇa.
118. Regarding the meditation subjects beginning with the livid corpse (*vinīlaka*) that follow hereafter: when one is grasping the sign of foulness (*asubhanimitta*) as the bloated corpse...
The characteristic has been stated starting with the act of going, in the manner beginning: "He goes alone, without a companion, with mindfulness established.

All of that should be applied respectively by substituting, in each instance, the mere term *uddhumātaka* (the bloated) for [the other terms], such as: "while apprehending the foul sign of the livid," and "while apprehending the foul sign of the festering."
This should be understood according to the method already stated, including the analytical intention (*vinicchayādhippāya*).
However, this is the distinction: regarding a livid corpse (*vinīlaka*), attention should be directed thus: "The repulsiveness of the livid, the repulsiveness of the livid.
Here, the learning sign (*uggahanimitta*) appears with a variegated, blotchy color. As for the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*):
However, it appears by way of its prominence.
Regarding the "foulness of the festering," one should apply attention thus: "the foulness of the festering, the foulness of the festering.
Here, the learning sign (uggahanimitta) appears as if it were oozing. The counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta), however, appears motionless and perfectly still.
The "mangled" (vichiddaka) occurs on a battlefield, in a forest inhabited by thieves, or at a cemetery where kings have the thieves' limbs severed;
or it may be found in the wilderness at a place where men have been torn apart by lions or tigers.
Therefore, having gone to such a place, if even a body fallen in various directions comes into range through a single act of adverting, that is well.
If he does not come, one must not touch it with one's own hand; for by touching it, one falls into a state of misplaced confidence.
Therefore, it should be moved to a single spot by a monastery attendant, a novice, or someone else.
If no one is available, one should present it after creating a gap of one finger-breadth using a walking staff or a stick. Having presented it in this manner:
“Repulsiveness of the fissured, repulsiveness of the fissured”—thus the attention should be practiced.
Therein, the learning sign appears as if having a fissure in the middle; however, the counterpart sign appears as complete.
Regarding the gnawed corpse, the attention should be practiced thus: “repulsiveness of the gnawed, repulsiveness of the gnawed.”
In this case, the learning sign (uggahanimitta) appears exactly like what was seen here and there, as if gnawed. The counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta), however, appears complete.

As for the scattered corpse (vikkhittaka), one should either have it made with intervals of a finger’s breadth between each limb, or having done so oneself, one should contemplate it as the "repulsiveness of the scattered corpse" according to the method already described for the dismembered corpse (vicchiddaka).
The attention should be practiced thus: "the scattered, which is repulsive.
Here, the learning sign appears with gaps between its parts, but the counterpart sign appears as a complete whole.
The "mangled and scattered" is also found in the same locations mentioned for the "cut up"; therefore, regarding that:
Having gone there, one should cause the fingers to be placed finger-width apart according to the method already described, or having done so oneself, one should direct the attention, thinking:
"Repulsive as a mutilated and dismembered corpse, repulsive as a mutilated and dismembered corpse.
Herein, the learning sign appears like the opening of a wound, while the counterpart sign appears perfectly complete.

The "bloody" (lohitaka) [repulsiveness] is obtained at the time when blood flows from the hands, feet, and so forth of those who have received wounds in the circle of battle and the like, or from the mouths of those with burst boils, abscesses, and so forth.
Therefore, upon seeing that, one should direct the attention: "Repulsive as the bloody, repulsive as the bloody.
Herein, the learning-sign (uggahanimitta) has the appearance of a red banner fluttering as if struck by the wind.
It appears [as the learning sign]. However, the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) appears as perfectly still.
The "worm-infested" (puḷavaka) occurs after two or three days have passed, at the time when a worm-infested corpse is oozing from nine wound-openings.
Moreover, that [sign] appears having the exact size of the bodies of dogs, jackals, humans, cows, buffaloes, elephants, horses, pythons, and so forth.
It remains like a heap of rice. One should direct one's attention to it in any part as "repulsiveness of the worm-infested, repulsiveness of the worm-infested.
For the Elder Cūḷapiṇḍapātika Tissa, the sign appeared within an elephant carcass inside the Kāḷadīghavāpi lake.
However, in this case, the learning-sign (uggahanimitta) appears as if moving. The counterpart-sign (paṭibhāganimitta)—
It appears sitting there like a lump of rice-food.

As for the skeleton, it has been described in various ways according to the method beginning with: "As if he were to see a body cast away in a charnel ground—a skeleton with flesh and blood still remaining, bound together by sinews. In that context, wherever it is placed...

When it has appeared, one should go there in the same manner as before, and having made it an object with its signs and its features by means of the surrounding stones and so forth, one should characterize it in its essential nature as "this is a bone" and grasp the sign in eleven ways by way of color and the rest.
However, for one who looks at it as white in terms of color, it does not appear; rather, there occurs a confusion with the white kasiṇa.
Therefore, it should be observed as a "bone" solely by way of its repulsiveness. "Sex" (*liṅga*) here is a name for the hands and so forth;

therefore, it should be defined by way of sex according to the hands, feet, head, chest, arms, hips, thighs, and shanks. Furthermore, it should be defined by way of shape according to whether it is long, short, round, square, small, or large.
The directions and locations are exactly as previously described. By way of the boundaries of each respective bone...
Having defined it by way of delimitation, one should attain absorption (*appanā*) by taking whatever part appears clearly to the mind.

Furthermore, it should be defined by way of its depressions and elevations according to the low-lying and high-lying areas of each respective bone. By way of location as well, one should define it thus:
"I am standing on the depression; the bone is on the elevation," or "I am on the elevation; the bone is [on the depression]."
It should be defined by way of its length. Furthermore, it should be defined by way of the joints according to the places where two bones are joined together.
It should be defined by way of the gaps according to the intervals between the bones themselves.
However, having directed knowledge everywhere, it should be defined all around by way of location, thinking, "In this place is this bone. In this manner, regarding the sign...
If [the mind] does not settle there, it should be fixed on the frontal bone.
Just as it is here, so too this elevenfold method of grasping the sign should be observed as applicable to the preceding subjects such as the worm-infested corpse and the rest.
Furthermore, this meditation subject may be practiced with the entire skeleton.
It succeeds even with a single bone. Therefore, having grasped the sign in any one of those [bones] in eleven ways, the attention should be practiced thus:

"Repulsive as a skeleton, repulsive as a skeleton. It is said that here both the learning sign (*uggahanimitta*) and the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*) are exactly alike; this is appropriate for a single bone. [In the case] of a skeleton...
However, when the learning sign (uggahanimitta) is manifest, there is a state of gaping; in the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitte), a state of fullness is appropriate.

Even in the case of a single bone, it must be loathsome and terrifying by way of the learning sign, but by way of the counterpart sign, it must produce joy and gladness because it brings about access concentration (upacāra).
For in this context, that which is stated in the commentaries was said by way of providing an opening [for discussion]. For it is said there:
"In the four divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*) and the ten foulness meditations (*asubha*), there is no counterpart sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*).

In the divine abidings, the very breaking down of boundaries (*sīmasambheda*) is the sign; and in the ten foulness meditations, having set aside conceptualization, it is the state of repulsiveness itself."
Even after saying, "The sign (nimitta) indeed exists in what is seen," it was immediately stated again: "In this context, the sign is twofold:
the learning sign (uggahanimitta) and the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta). The learning sign appears deformed, hideous, and terrifying," and so forth.
Therefore, that which we have investigated and spoken of is precisely what is appropriate here.
Furthermore, the examples here include such things as the appearance of the entire female body as a mere collection of bones upon the Elder Mahātissa’s merely beholding a single tooth-bone.
Thus, these unattractive objects (asubha), whose fame was praised by the Thousand-Eyed One,
were spoken of by the Ten-Powered One as the causes for each respective jhāna.
Thus, having understood both those [factors] and their method of development,
this further miscellaneous discussion regarding them should also be understood.
Miscellaneous Discussion:
121. For among these, one who has attained jhāna in any one of them becomes free from greed, like one who is already devoid of lust, because greed has been thoroughly suppressed;

he thus conducts himself without longing. Even so, this classification of foulness that has been stated should be understood both in terms of the attainment of the body’s own nature and in terms of the different temperaments of those characterized by greed. For the physical carcass, when it reaches a state of repulsiveness—
It may have reached the state of a bloated corpse, or it may have reached the state of one of the others, such as the livid corpse and so forth.
Thus, whatever kind can be obtained, the sign must be grasped exactly as it is—whether as "the repulsiveness of the bloated" or "the repulsiveness of the livid.
In this way, it should be understood that the tenfold classification of the foul (asubha) is taught by way of the states reached by the body's nature.
And here, in particular, the bloated corpse is suitable for one who is lustful toward shape, because it demonstrates the ruin of the body’s configuration.
The livid corpse is suitable for one who is lustful toward the body’s color, because it demonstrates the ruin of the skin’s complexion.

The festering corpse is suitable for one who is lustful toward the body’s fragrance—such as that produced by garlands and perfumes—because it demonstrates the foul odor connected with the wounds of the body.
The *vichiddaka* (the fissured) is suitable for those who are attached to the solidity of the body, because it demonstrates the state of internal cavities.

The *vikkhāyitaka* (the gnawed) is suitable for those who are attached to the accumulation of flesh in certain parts of the body such as the breasts, because it demonstrates the destruction of that excellence of fleshly growth.
The *vikkhittaka* (the scattered) is [suitable] for those who are attached to the grace of the limbs and members, because it demonstrates the scattering of the limbs and members.

The "suitable" [meditation subject]: the "mangled and scattered" (hatavikkhittaka) is suitable for one who is attached to the perfection of the physical body, because it demonstrates the disintegration and transformation of the bodily aggregate.
The "bloody" (lohitaka) is suitable for one who is attached to the beauty produced by ornaments, because it demonstrates the repulsiveness of being smeared with blood.
The "worm-infested" (puḷavaka) is suitable for one who is attached to ownership of the body, because it demonstrates that the body is shared among many families of worms.
It is suitable. The skeleton is suitable for one who is attached to the perfection of teeth, because it demonstrates the repulsiveness of the bones of the body.
Thus, it should be understood that the classification of the foul (asubha) is stated as tenfold according to the different types of temperament characterized by lust.
Furthermore, since in all these ten kinds of the foul, just as in the case of a fast-flowing river with unsteady waters...

Just as a boat remains stationary in a river by the power of its rudder alone—it cannot be kept still without a rudder—so too, because the object is weak, the mind remains one-pointed by the power of applied thought (vitakka) alone; it cannot be established without applied thought.
Therefore, only the first jhāna occurs here, not the second and the others.
And even with respect to this repulsive object, joy and gladness arise through both the perception of its benefits— thinking, "Surely by this practice I shall be liberated from aging and death"—
and through the abandonment of the fever of the hindrances; just as joy arises in a refuse-remover who perceives the benefit, thinking,
"Now I shall receive a great wage," while standing over a heap of dung.
...as well as in the occurrence of emesis and purgation for a sick person suffering from the intense pain of disease. 122.

Furthermore, although this foulness (*asubha*) is tenfold, it is one in its characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*). The characteristic of all ten types is precisely their state of being impure, foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive.
By this characteristic, it is not only in a dead body that [foulness is found], but also in those who observe teeth and bones...

However, it may appear even in a living body, as in the case of the Elder Mahātissa who dwelt at Cetiyapabbata, or like the novice attendant of the Elder Saṅgharakkhita while he was looking down at the king seated upon the neck of an elephant.
For just as with a dead body, so too with a living one, it is indeed foul (asubha). In this context, however, the characteristic of foulness is [perceived] through the adventitious...
Because it is concealed by ornaments, it is not perceived. But in its natural state, this so-called body is a collection of more than three hundred bones,
joined together by eight hundred joints, bound by nine hundred sinews, smeared with nine hundred pieces of flesh, enveloped in moist skin,
covered by a thin film, full of holes and gaps, and constantly oozing and trickling like a pot of fat.
It is frequented by swarms of worms, a breeding ground for diseases, and a locus for states of suffering;
it constantly oozes from nine wound-like openings like a burst, ancient abscess. From both eyes, eye-secretions flow;
from the ear canals, ear-wax; from the nostrils, mucus; and from the mouth, food-remnants, bile, phlegm, and blood.
From the lower orifices flow excrement and urine; from the ninety-nine thousand pores of the body, the impure lymph drips.

Blue flies and other insects swarm around it. Even a king, if he were to wander from village to village with his hair as rough and disheveled as when he was born, without attending to it through the use of tooth-sticks, mouth-washing, head-anointing, bathing, or clothing—[would be treated with contempt].
Even one who is among the outcasts who throw away flowers or others of that sort is no different [from a king] in the repulsiveness of the physical body;
thus, there is no distinction whatsoever between the body of a king and that of an outcast in its impurity, foul odor, loathsomeness, and repulsiveness.
However, by cleaning away the dental plaque and other impurities with tooth-sticks, mouth-washing, and so forth, and by covering the private parts with various garments—
Having covered it with various colored fragrant ointments and having adorned it with flower ornaments and the like,
they bring it to a state where it can be grasped as "I" and "mine. Then, because it is concealed by this adventitious adornment,
men do not perceive the true nature of the female body— its characteristic of impurity— and women likewise [do not perceive the true nature] of the male body.
They take delight in it. Yet, in the ultimate sense, there is not even the slightest portion here that is fit to be clung to with passion.

For instance, when even a single part of the body—such as hair, body hair, nails, teeth, saliva, snot, feces, or urine—has fallen outside, beings do not wish to touch it with their hands; they recoil from it, feel ashamed, and loathe it.
Whatever remains here, though it is likewise repulsive, those who are shrouded by the darkness of ignorance and dyed with the passion of self-love grasp at it as "desirable,
lovely, permanent, pleasant, and a self. Grasping in this way, they are like one who, seeing a *kiṃsuka* tree in the forest,
is distressed upon seeing a flower that has not yet fallen from the tree and thinks, "This is a piece of meat."
They fall into agreement with Jarasiṅgāla. Therefore:
"Just as a jackal, having seen a flowering kiṃsuka tree in the forest, would go with great speed, thinking, 'I have found a tree of flesh!'"
The excessively greedy bee, having bitten each fallen flower,
seizes it thinking, "This is not meat, that is meat," even though both are on the tree.
So too, the wise person regards only that which has fallen away as foul.
Just as one might take up a corpse even when it is still on the body, so too do fools,
having grasped this body as pleasant and becoming infatuated with it,
commit evil deeds and are not released from suffering.
Therefore, a wise person should see the true nature of the putrid body— whether of one living or of one dead— as devoid of any state of beauty.
For this has been said:
Foul-smelling and impure is this body, a corpse comparable to a heap of filth;
reviled by those who have become eyes, this body is yet delighted in by fools.
Covered with raw skin, it is a great wound with nine openings.
Impurity flows out from every side, with a stench of rot.
If the interior of this body were like the exterior,
one would surely have to take up a staff to ward off the crows and jackals.
Therefore, a bhikkhu of a steady nature— whether it be a living body or a dead body—
should grasp the sign wherever the aspect of foulness is perceived and bring the meditation subject to absorption.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Visuddhimagga* composed for the delight of good people.
The Sixth Chapter, titled "The Description of the Meditation Subject of Foulness," in the Section on the Development of Concentration.
7. The Exposition of the Recollections (Cha-anussati-niddesa) 1. Discussion on the Recollection of the Buddha (Buddhānussati-kathā) 123.
Among the ten recollections enumerated immediately after the [meditations on] the foul (asubha), it is mindfulness itself that arises again and again.
*Anussati* is so called because it is mindfulness (*sati*) appropriate for a clansman who has gone forth out of faith, occurring precisely at the place where it ought to occur.
*Buddhānussati* is the mindfulness arisen with reference to the Buddha; this is a designation for mindfulness that has the qualities of the Buddha as its object.
*Dhammānussati* is the mindfulness arisen with reference to the Dhamma; [this refers to] mindfulness that has the qualities of the Dhamma—such as being well-expounded—as its object.

This is a designation for mindfulness. Mindfulness arisen with reference to the Sangha is "recollection of the Sangha" (saṅghānussati); this is a designation for mindfulness having as its object the qualities of the Sangha, such as being well-practiced.
Mindfulness arisen with reference to virtue is "recollection of virtue" (sīlānussati); this is a designation for mindfulness having as its object the qualities of virtue, such as being unbroken.

Mindfulness arisen with reference to generosity is "recollection of generosity" (cāgānussati); [this is a designation for mindfulness] having as its object the qualities of generosity, such as the state of being liberated and generous.
This is a designation for mindfulness (*sati*). Mindfulness arisen with reference to deities is "recollection of deities" (*devatānussati*);

this is a designation for mindfulness whose object is one's own qualities such as faith, having placed the deities in the position of witnesses. Mindfulness arisen with reference to death is "recollection of death" (*maraṇānussati*);
this is a designation for mindfulness whose object is the cutting off of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). [The body] consisting of the various parts beginning with hair...
"Body-referenced" (*kāyagatā*) means having gone to the form-body (*rūpakāya*) or having gone within the body;

thus, while it should be called "body-referenced mindfulness" (*kāyagatasati*), it is stated as "mindfulness directed to the body" (*kāyagatāsati*) without shortening the vowel, and this is a designation for mindfulness that has the sign of the bodily parts, such as hair and so forth, as its object.

Mindfulness arisen with reference to inhalation and exhalation is "mindfulness of breathing" (*ānāpānassati*); this is a designation for mindfulness that has the sign of inhalation and exhalation as its object.

This is a designation for mindfulness. Mindfulness directed toward peace is "recollection of peace" (*upasamānussati*); this is a designation for mindfulness that has the allaying of all suffering as its object. 124.
Thus, among these ten recollections, one who wishes first to develop the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*) must be endowed with verified confidence (*aveccappasāda*).
In a suitable lodging, having gone into seclusion and retired alone, the yogi should thus recollect the qualities of the Blessed Buddha: "Indeed, that Blessed One is an Arhat,
a Perfectly Enlightened One, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, a knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed,
a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One."

In this regard, the method of recollection is as follows: he recollects, "The Blessed One is indeed the Worthy One (Arahant), he is indeed the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha)... and so on, up to "...he is indeed the Blessed One. This means: "For these and those reasons. 125.

Therein, first of all, one recollects that the Blessed One is the Worthy One for these reasons: because he is far removed (*āraka*); because he has slain his enemies (*ari*) and the spokes (*ara*) [of the wheel of craving]; because he is worthy (*arahat*) of requisites and the like; and because there is no secrecy (*raha*) in his doing of evil. For he is far, very far indeed, from all defilements.
He is "Arahant" because he has destroyed the defilements along with their latent tendencies by means of the Path, owing to his being far removed (*āraka*) from them.
For one is called "far removed" when there is a lack of association between him and those [defilements];
and since the Lord is devoid of faults, he is therefore considered an Arahant.
126. Furthermore, he is an Arahant because the enemies that are the defilements have been slain by him through this Path.
Since all enemies—comprising lust and the rest—have been slain by the Protector with the sword of wisdom, for that reason also he is considered an Arahant.
127. Furthermore, this wheel of saṃsāra—which has ignorance, existence, and craving for its hub; volitional formations such as merit and so forth for its spokes;
and old age and death for its rim—is pierced by the axle consisting of the origin of the taints and yoked to the chariot of the three realms of existence.
Having stood upon the earth of virtue with the feet of energy at the seat of enlightenment, [the Blessed One] used the hand of faith to [grasp] that which brings about the destruction of karma...
Having taken up the axe of knowledge, he has "slain all spokes" (hatā arā); thus, because the spokes have been slain, he is an *arahaṃ*.
Alternatively, the "wheel of saṃsāra" refers to the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāravaṭṭa*). Of that wheel, ignorance is the hub because it is the root;
aging and death are the rim because they are the end. The remaining ten factors are the spokes, because they are rooted in ignorance and terminate in aging and death.
And therein, ignorance is the lack of knowledge regarding suffering and so forth. Ignorance in the sense-sphere existence is a condition for volitional formations in the sense-sphere existence;

ignorance in fine-material existence is a condition for volitional formations in fine-material existence; ignorance in immaterial existence is a condition for volitional formations in immaterial existence.
Volitional formations in the sense-sphere existence are conditions for rebirth-linking consciousness in the sense-sphere existence.
This is the method for the others as well. In the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava), rebirth-linking consciousness is a condition for name-and-form (nāmarūpa) in the sense-sphere existence;
likewise in fine-material existence (rūpabhava). In immaterial existence (arūpabhava), it is a condition for name alone.

In sense-sphere existence, name-and-form is a condition for the six sense bases (saḷāyatana) in sense-sphere existence; in fine-material existence, name-and-form is a condition for three sense bases in fine-material existence.
In the formless existence, name is a condition for one base in the formless existence.

In the sense-sphere existence, the six bases are a condition for the sixfold contact in the sense-sphere existence; in the fine-material existence, three bases are conditions for three types of contact in the fine-material existence;
and in the formless existence, one base is a condition for one type of contact in the formless existence.
It is a condition. In the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava), the six contacts are conditions for the six feelings in that same sense-sphere existence;

in the fine-material existence (rūpabhava), the three contacts are conditions for the three [feelings] in that very same existence; and in the immaterial existence (arūpabhava), the one [contact] is a condition for the one feeling in that very same existence.
In the sense-sphere existence, the six feelings are conditions for the six groups of craving (taṇhākāya) in that same sense-sphere existence; in the fine-material existence, the three...

In that very same way, three [factors] are conditions for one another; in the formless realm (*arūpabhava*), a single feeling is a condition for a single mass of craving (*taṇhākāya*) in the formless realm.
In each respective case, that specific craving is a condition for its corresponding clinging (*upādāna*); and clinging and the subsequent factors are conditions for becoming (*bhava*) and the rest.
How so? Here, a certain person, thinking "I shall enjoy sensual pleasures," engages in misconduct with the body conditioned by clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*).
One engages in misconduct by way of speech, one engages in misconduct by way of mind; through the fulfillment of such misconduct, one is reborn in the woeful states.
Therein, the karma that serves as the cause for that rebirth is *kammabhava* (kamma-existence); the aggregates produced by that karma are *upapattibhava* (rebirth-existence);
the arising of the aggregates is *jāti* (birth); their maturation is *jarā* (aging); and their dissolution is *maraṇa* (death).

Another person practices good conduct with the thought, "I shall experience the excellence of heaven," and through the fulfillment of that good conduct, he is reborn in heaven. In this case, the karma that serves as the cause for his rebirth there is called *kammabhava*; such is the method.

Furthermore, another person, thinking, "I shall experience the excellence of the Brahma-world," develops loving-kindness (*mettā*), compassion (*karuṇā*), appreciative joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekkhā*) precisely by way of the condition of clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*). Through the fulfillment of that development, he is reborn in the Brahma-world. In that case, his...
Kamma that serves as the cause for rebirth is "kamma-bhava"; the same principle applies here.
Furthermore, one who thinks, "I shall experience excellence in the formless realm," develops the attainments of the base of infinite space and so forth in that very manner;
through the fulfillment of that development, he is reborn in those respective states. That which serves as the cause for his rebirth therein—
Kamma is kamma-becoming; the aggregates produced by kamma are rebirth-becoming; the arising of the aggregates is birth;
their ripening is aging; and their dissolution is death. This same method applies to the other analyses rooted in clinging.
Thus, in the discernment of conditions, this ignorance is the cause, the formations are cause-originated, and both of these are cause-originated.
Wisdom regarding the knowledge of the stability of phenomena is as follows: "In the past period and in the future period, ignorance is the cause and formations are cause-born;
both of these are cause-born"—wisdom in the discernment of conditions is knowledge of the stability of phenomena.
In this same manner, all the phrases should be expanded in detail.

Therein, ignorance and volitional formations constitute one summary; consciousness, mentality-materiality, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling constitute another; craving, clinging, and becoming constitute another;
and birth, aging, and death constitute another. Here, the first summary refers to the past time-period, the two middle ones to the present, and birth, aging, and death to the future.
Furthermore, by the inclusion of ignorance and volitional formations, craving, clinging, and becoming are already included.
"These five factors are the kamma-process in the past; consciousness and the other four are the result-process now.
By the inclusion of craving, clinging, and becoming, ignorance and formations are already included; thus these five factors are the kamma-process now.
Since consciousness and the others are indicated by way of birth, aging, and death, these five factors [are the result-process] in the future."
The round of kamma-result (*vipākavaṭṭa*). These [factors] are twentyfold according to their modes.
Herein, there is one link between formations and consciousness, one between feeling and craving, and one between existence and birth;
thus the Blessed One knows, sees, and understands this dependent origination in its entirety—comprising four groups, three periods of time, twenty modes, and three links.
He penetrates it. In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge (*ñāṇa*); in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom (*paññā*). Therefore, it is said:
"Wisdom in the discernment of conditions is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*).

Having known those phenomena as they really are through this knowledge of the stability of phenomena, the Blessed One became disenchanted with them, detached from them, and was liberated from this wheel of saṃsāra described above.
Day and night he destroys them. Thus, because the spokes have been destroyed, he is an *arahaṃ*.
Since the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra have been destroyed by the sword of knowledge by the Lord of the World, for that reason he is called "Arahant."
129. Because he is the foremost among those worthy of offerings (*agga-dakkhiṇeyya*), he is worthy of the requisites such as robes and so forth, as well as special forms of worship.
For this very reason, whenever a Tathāgata has appeared, whichever gods or humans possess great influence do not perform their worship elsewhere.
Thus, for example, Brahmā Sahampati worshipped the Tathāgata with a jeweled garland as large as Mount Sineru; and other gods and humans likewise [worshipped him] according to their power.

And [there were] King Bimbisāra, the King of Kosala, and others. Even after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, the Great King Aśoka, having disbursed ninety-six koṭis of wealth for his sake, established eighty-four thousand monasteries throughout the entire Jambudīpa.
What need is there to mention the various other special offerings? He is also called "Arahant" because he is worthy of the requisites and so forth.
Since this Lord of the World deserves a distinguished offering together with its requisites,
people in the world deserve that which accords with their purpose.
Therefore, the Victor truly deserves this name.

And just as in the world some fools who consider themselves wise commit evil deeds in secret out of fear of ill repute, he never does so; thus, because there is no secrecy in his evil actions, he is *arahant* due to the absence of secrecy (*raha*).
For one such as he, there is no such thing as secrecy regarding unwholesome deeds.
Because he has abandoned [defilements] and because he is worthy of honor, he is renowned as an Arahant.
Thus, in every respect,
that Sage is so called because he is far removed from and has destroyed his enemies, the defilements.
"Having destroyed the wheel of saṃsāra, he is worthy of offerings and the like;
he does not perform secret evil deeds, and for that reason he is called 'Arahant' (Worthy).

(131) Furthermore, because he has awakened to all phenomena both correctly and by himself, he is the "Sammāsambuddha" (Perfectly Self-Awakened One). For it is thus that he [has realized] all phenomena...

The Buddha is truly enlightened; he is enlightened regarding things to be directly known as things to be directly known, regarding things to be fully understood as things to be fully understood, regarding things to be abandoned as things to be abandoned, regarding things to be realized as things to be realized, and regarding things to be developed as things to be developed.
And for this very reason it was said:
"What is to be directly known has been directly known, what is to be developed has been developed, and what is to be abandoned has been abandoned by me; therefore, O Brahmin, I am a Buddha.
Furthermore, the eye is the truth of suffering, and the prior craving that gives rise to it by being its root cause is [the truth of the origin].

The truth of origination, the non-occurrence of both [origination and suffering] is the truth of cessation, and the practice for the realization of cessation is the truth of the path—thus has he fully and personally awakened to all phenomena by extracting each term individually. This same method applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
By this very method, one should understand the six bases beginning with form, the six groups of consciousness beginning with eye-consciousness, and the contacts beginning with eye-contact.

The six contacts, beginning with eye-contact; the six feelings, beginning with those born of eye-contact; the six perceptions, beginning with the perception of form; the six volitions, beginning with the volition regarding form;

the six groups of craving, beginning with craving for form; the six applied thoughts, beginning with applied thought regarding form; the six sustained thoughts, beginning with sustained thought regarding form;
the five aggregates, beginning with the aggregate of form; the ten kasiṇas; the ten recollections; and [the meditation subjects] by way of the perception of the bloated, and so forth.
The ten perceptions, the thirty-two aspects beginning with head-hairs, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the nine existences beginning with sensual existence,
the four jhānas beginning with the first, the four immeasurables beginning with the development of loving-kindness,
the four formless attainments, and the factors of dependent origination— beginning with aging-and-death in reverse order and beginning with ignorance in forward order— should also be applied.
In this regard, here is the construction of the single phrase: aging-and-death is the truth of suffering; birth is the truth of origin;
the escape from both is the truth of cessation; and the practice for the realization of cessation is the truth of the path.
Thus, by extracting each individual term, he has perfectly, directly, awakened to, followed after, and fully realized all phenomena. Therefore it was said: "Perfectly, directly..."
"Furthermore, he is the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddho) because he has awakened to all phenomena (sabbadhammānaṃ buddhattā).

Moreover, he is one perfected in clear knowledge and conduct (vijjācaraṇasampanno) because he is endowed with clear knowledge (vijjā) and conduct (caraṇa). In this context, 'clear knowledge' refers to either the three clear knowledges or the eight clear knowledges.
The three clear knowledges should be understood according to the method stated in the Bhayabherava Sutta; [the eight clear knowledges are as follows:]..."

In the Ambaṭṭha Sutta, eight types of clear knowledge (*vijjā*) are mentioned, comprising the six higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) together with insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) and mind-made psychic power (*manomaya-iddhi*).

"Conduct" (*caraṇa*) refers to these fifteen factors: restraint through virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*), guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, the seven true qualities (*saddhamma*), and the four fine-material-sphere jhānas.
These very fifteen states should be understood as the "conduct" (*caraṇa*). For it is by means of these that the noble disciple conducts himself and proceeds toward the direction of the Deathless;

therefore, they are called "conduct. As it is said: "In this case, Mahānāma, the noble disciple is virtuous," and so forth—all of which should be understood according to the method explained in the *Majjhima Paṇṇāsa*.
By means of these true knowledges (*vijjā*) and this... [the Blessed One...]
He is endowed with conduct. Therefore, he is called "one perfected in knowledge and conduct" (*vijjācaraṇasampanna*).
In this context, the Blessed One’s perfection of knowledge stands having fulfilled omniscience; his perfection of conduct consists in his great compassion.
Having understood, through omniscience, what is beneficial and what is harmful for all beings, he avoids what is harmful through his great compassion.

He enjoins others to the goal, just as one who is perfected in true knowledge and conduct (vijjācaraṇasampanna) would. Therefore, his disciples are well-practiced, not ill-practiced like the disciples of those deficient in true knowledge and conduct, such as the "self-mortifiers" and others.
He is the Sugata because he has a beautiful gait, because he has gone to a beautiful place, because he has gone rightly, and because he has spoken rightly.
For even "going" is called "gone. And that going of the Blessed One was beautiful, pure, and blameless. But what was it?
It was the Noble Path. Because he has gone by means of that going to the secure direction without being attached, he is the "Well-Gone One" (Sugata) due to his beautiful going.
Furthermore, he has gone to that beautiful place—the deathless Nibbāna—and thus he is the "Well-Gone One" also because he has gone to a beautiful place.
And he has gone rightly by each respective path, not returning again to the defilements already abandoned. For this has been said:
"The defilements abandoned by the path of stream-entry—those defilements he does not repeat, does not return to, does not go back to; thus he is 'Well-Gone' (Sugata)...
up to... the defilements abandoned by the path of Arahatship—those defilements he does not repeat, does not return to, does not go back to."
