"Sugata" means: he has gone rightly (*sammā vā gato*) from the foot of Dīpaṅkara onwards up to the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), having practiced the right conduct that fulfills the thirty perfections (*pāramī*);

because he has gone rightly—acting solely for the welfare and happiness of the entire world while not falling into these extremes of eternalism, annihilationism, sensual pleasure, or self-mortification—he is thus "Sugata. Rightly...
He speaks appropriately in appropriate places; because he speaks rightly, he is also "Sugata" (Well-Gone).

Here is the supporting sutta: "Whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial, and which is unpleasant and disagreeable to others—that speech the Tathāgata does not utter. Whatever speech the Tathāgata knows..."
If a word is true, factual, and conducive to harm, even if it is unpleasant and disagreeable to others,
the Tathāgata does not speak that word. However, regarding a word that the Tathāgata knows to be true,
factual, and conducive to welfare, even if it is unpleasant and disagreeable to others, the Tathāgata is one who knows the proper time for its explanation.
Whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial, even if it is pleasing and agreeable to others—that speech the Tathāgata does not utter.

And whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be true and correct, yet unbeneficial, even if it is pleasing and agreeable to others—that speech too the Tathāgata does not utter. But as for that which the Tathāgata...

“He knows speech that is true, real, and connected with the goal, and which is pleasing and agreeable to others; in that regard, the Tathāgata is one who knows the proper time for the explanation of such speech.
Thus, he should be understood as “Well-Gone” (Sugata) because of his speaking rightly.

Furthermore, he is the “Knower of the World” (Lokavidū) because he has thoroughly understood the world in every respect. For the Blessed One [knows it] by way of its intrinsic nature, its origin, and its cessation.
"By means of the method for cessation" means that he experienced, knew, and penetrated the world in every respect. As it is said:

"Friend, regarding that where one is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and does not reappear—I say that the end of the world cannot be known, seen, or reached by traveling there; yet, friend, without reaching the end of the world..."

I declare the making of an end to suffering. Moreover, friends, it is in this very fathom-long carcass, endowed with perception and mind, that I proclaim the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the way leading to the cessation of the world.
The end of the world can never be reached by traveling.
And without reaching the end of the world, there is no liberation from suffering.
Therefore, the wise one who knows the world,
having reached the end of the world and lived the holy life, [is truly liberated].
"Having known the end of the world, the one who has attained peace does not long for this world or another.

(136) Furthermore, there are three worlds: the world of formations (*saṅkhāra-loka*), the world of beings (*satta-loka*), and the world of space (*okāsa-loka*). Among these, "one world" refers to all beings.

In the passages where "subsistence by nutriment" occurs, the world of formations (*saṅkhāraloka*) is to be understood. In the passages where "the world is eternal" or "the world is not eternal" occur, the world of beings (*sattaloka*) is meant.
As far as the moon and sun revolve, illuminating and shining forth in all directions...
“The world extends for a thousandfold; therein you exercise your power.
In the context where this occurs, it refers to the spatial world (*okāsaloka*). The Blessed One knew that as well in every respect. For instance, he said: “One world:
all beings subsist on nutriment. Two worlds: name and form. Three worlds: the three feelings. Four worlds...”
There are four nutriments. Five worlds: the five aggregates subject to clinging. Six worlds: the six internal sense bases.
Seven worlds: the seven stations of consciousness. Eight worlds: the eight worldly conditions. Nine worlds: the nine abodes of beings.
Ten worlds: the ten sense bases. Twelve worlds: the twelve sense bases. Eighteen worlds: the eighteen elements.”
This world of formations is also known by him in every respect.
For he knows the disposition of all beings, he knows their underlying tendencies, he knows their conduct, and he knows their inclinations;
he knows those with little dust in their eyes and those with much dust in their eyes, those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties, those of good character and those of bad character.
He knows beings who are easy to instruct and those who are difficult to instruct, those who are capable and those who are incapable;
therefore, the world of beings is known by him in every respect. And as is the world of beings, so too is the world of space.
For instance, one world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) is twelve hundred thousand, three hundred and fifty-four yojanas in length and breadth; but in circumference—
The entire circumference is three million six hundred and ten thousand four hundred and fifty [yojanas].
Therein—
Two hundred thousand and forty nahutas—
this much, by its thickness, is reckoned as this Earth.
Its support is as follows:
Four hundred thousand and eighty thousand [yojanas]— to this extent,
by its thickness, does the water rest upon the wind.
Its supporter as well—
Nine hundred thousand and sixty thousand leagues does the wind rise up into the sky;
such is the structure of the world.
And within this structure, the measurements in yojanas are as follows:
Sineru, the supreme mountain, plunges eighty-four thousand [yojanas] down into the great ocean and rises up from it by exactly that same measure.
Its dimensions decrease by half and half again, respectively, in due order.
Sublime peaks that plunge deep and rise high, variegated with diverse jewels:
Yugandhara, Īsadhara, Karavīka, Sudassana, Nemindhara,
Vinataka, Assakaṇṇa, and the vast mountain Brahā.
These seven great rocky mountains stand all around Sineru;
they are the abodes of the Great Kings, frequented by gods and yakkhas.
The Himavanta mountain is five hundred yojanas in height.
Three thousand yojanas in length and breadth,
adorned with eighty-four thousand peaks,
and with a circumference of three or five yojanas for its trunk, it is called a city.
With a trunk and branches fifty yojanas in girth on all sides,
extending a hundred yojanas in width and rising to that same height—
this is the Jambu tree by whose power Jambudīpa is made known.
Whatever is the size of the Jambu tree, that same is the size of the Citrapāṭaliya for the Asuras,
the Simbali tree for the Garuḷas, the Kadamba for Aparagoyāna, the Kappa tree for Uttarakuru, the Sirīsa for Pubbavideha,
and the Pāricchattaka for the Tāvatiṃsa devas. Thus said the ancients:
“The *pāṭalī*, the *simbalī*, the *jambū*, the *pāricchattaka* of the gods,
the *kadambo*, the *kapparukkha*, and the *sirīsa* is the seventh.
“It plunges eighty-two thousand [yojanas] deep into the great ocean.”
“Rising up to that very height, a mountain range of world-spheres stands encircling this entire world-system.
Therein, the moon’s disk is forty-nine yojanas; the sun’s disk is fifty yojanas; and so is the realm of the Thirty-three.
The realm of the asuras, the great Avīci hell, and Jambudīpa each measure ten thousand yojanas.
Aparagoyāna measures seven thousand yojanas, and likewise Pubbavideha. Uttarakuru measures eight thousand yojanas.
Furthermore, each of these great continents is surrounded by five hundred minor islands. All of this together constitutes a single world-system (cakkavāḷa).
There is one world-system; within the intervals between them are the world-antarika hells.

Thus, with infinite Buddha-knowledge, the Blessed One has known, understood, and penetrated infinite world-spheres and infinite world-systems. In this way, the world of space is known by him in every respect. Because he has thus known the world in every respect, he is the "Knower of the World" (lokavidū).
Furthermore, because there is no one superior to him in terms of his own qualities, he is "without a superior" (anuttara).

For in this way, he surpasses the entire world by means of the quality of virtue (*sīlaguṇa*), and also by means of the qualities of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
By the quality of virtue, he is unequaled, equal to the unequaled, peerless, matchless, and without rival... [and so on] ...by the quality of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
As it has been said: "Indeed, I do not see anyone in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās... [and so on] ...among the generation of beings consisting of devas and humans..."

"...more perfect in virtue than oneself for the sake of the multitude"—this is the detailed explanation. In this way, the *Aggapasāda-sutta* and others, as well as the verses beginning with "I have no teacher," should be explained in detail.
139. He trains those persons who are to be tamed; thus he is a "charioteer of persons to be tamed. It is said that he tames and disciplines them. In this regard:
"Purisadamma" refers to those fit to be tamed who are yet untamed— be they animals, human beings, or non-human beings. For instance, even among animal males,

the Blessed One tamed and rendered harmless such as the nāga kings Apalāla, Cūḷodara, Mahodara, Aggisikha, Dhūmasikha, and the nāga king Aravāḷa, as well as the elephant Dhanapālaka, and others like them.
I have established them in the refuges and in the precepts; and among human beings, Saccaka the son of the Nigaṇṭhas, the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha, Pokkharasāti, Soṇadaṇḍa, Kūṭadanta, and others;

and among non-human beings, Āḷavaka, Sūciloma, Kharaloma, the yakkhas, Sakka the king of the gods, and others—have been tamed and disciplined by various means of discipline. "Indeed, Kesi, I tame those to be tamed by men even with gentleness..."
“I discipline by means of harshness, and I also discipline by means of both gentleness and harshness. Herein, this sutta should be quoted in detail.

Furthermore, when the Blessed One teaches the first jhāna and so forth to those of purified virtue and so forth, or the higher path-practice to stream-enterers and others, he indeed disciplines even those already disciplined.
Alternatively, “the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed” is a single phrase; for the Blessed One [disciplines] men to be tamed in such a manner.
He guides [them] so that, sitting on a single seat, they run toward the eight directions without obstruction. Therefore, he is called "the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed.
In this regard, the following sutta should be cited in detail: "Monks, when an elephant to be tamed is guided by an elephant-tamer, it runs in only one direction."
140. He is called the Teacher (*satthā*) because he instructs [beings] appropriately according to the truths pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal (*paramattha*).
Furthermore, he is the Teacher because he is like a caravan leader (*satthavāha*); the Blessed One is a caravan leader.

Just as a caravan leader leads a caravan across a wilderness, leading it across a wilderness of thieves, a wilderness of wild beasts, a wilderness of famine, and a wilderness of waterlessness, and leads it safely across—so too is the Blessed One a teacher.
It leads them out, it brings them across, it causes them to reach the ground of safety; in the same way, the Blessed One—the Teacher, the Caravan-Leader—leads beings across the wilderness.
"He leads them across the wilderness of birth," and so forth; here the meaning should be understood according to this method of exposition (*niddesa*).
"Of gods and humans" means of both gods and humans. This is stated by way of defining the highest limit and by way of defining the class of persons capable [of liberation].
This has been said. However, the Blessed One is indeed the Teacher even for those who have gone into the animal realm by virtue of providing them with his instruction.
For even they, through hearing the Dhamma from the Blessed One, attain the excellence of the supporting condition (*upanissaya-sampatti*);

and by that very excellence of the supporting condition, they become partakers of the path and its fruit in their second or third existence. The divine sons such as Maṇḍūka and others serve as examples in this regard.
While the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma to the inhabitants of the city of Campā on the bank of the Gaggarā lotus pond, a certain frog caught the sign in the Blessed One’s voice.
A cowherd standing nearby, leaning on his staff, stepped on its head and crushed it. He died instantly and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven in a palace twelve yojanas in size.
He was reborn in a golden celestial mansion (*vimāna*). Like one awakened from sleep, he saw himself there surrounded by a host of nymphs and thought, "Aha!
I too have been reborn here; what deed must I have performed?

As he reflected, he saw nothing at all except for his having grasped the mental sign (*nimitta*) upon hearing the Blessed One’s voice. At that very moment, together with the celestial mansion, he arrived.
He bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One. The Blessed One, though already knowing, asked:
“Who is it that bows at my feet, shining with the glory of supernormal power, illuminating all directions with most excellent beauty?”
"In the past, I was a frog, moving through the water in the midst of the flood;
while I was listening to your Dhamma, a cowherd killed me.

The Blessed One taught him the Dhamma. There was a realization of the Dhamma for eighty-four thousand living beings. Having established himself in the fruit of stream-entry, the son of the gods smiled and departed.
141. Furthermore, whatever is known as an object of knowledge (*ñeyya*), he is "Awakened" (*buddha*) because he has awakened to all of it by means of the knowledge pertaining to liberation.
Or else, because he himself awakened to the Four Truths and awakened other beings as well, he is "Awakened" for these and other such reasons.
And in order to make this meaning understood, it is said: "He is *buddha* because he has awakened to the Truths."
The entire method of exposition, whether according to the *Niddesa* or the *Paṭisambhidā*, should be expanded upon as it occurs in the passage: “He who awakens the generation is a Buddha. 142.

As for the term *Bhagavā*, this is a designation expressing the highest esteem and reverence for him as the most distinguished of all beings in terms of his qualities. Regarding this, the ancients said:
“‘Bhagavā’ is the best of words; ‘Bhagavā’ is the supreme word.”
“Because he is possessed of great reverence (garu-gārava), the Blessed One (Bhagavā) is called by that name.
Alternatively, names are of four kinds: situational (āvatthika), indicative (liṅgika), causal (nemittika), and accidental (adhiccasamuppanna).
“Accidental” means, according to worldly usage, that which is arbitrary. In this regard, terms such as “calf,” “ox to be tamed,” or “bullock” are examples [of situational names].

That which is based on a particular occasion (*āvatthika*) [is a name]. That which is based on a characteristic mark (*liṅgika*), such as "the one with a staff," "the one with a parasol," "the one with a topknot," or "the elephant," and so forth; that which is based on a sign (*nemittika*), such as "one possessing the three knowledges" (*tevijja*) or "one possessing the six direct knowledges" (*chaḷabhiñña*), and so forth;
and that which arises adventitiously (*adhiccasamuppanna*), occurring without regard for the meaning of the words, such as "Sirivaḍḍhaka" or "Dhanavaḍḍhaka.
However, this name "Bhagavā" is *nemittika* (based on a sign); it was not given by Mahāmāyā, nor by King Suddhodana.
It was not made by eighty thousand kinsmen, nor by distinguished deities such as Sakka and Santusita.
And this has been said by the General of the Dhamma: "‘Bhagavā’—this name was not given by his mother...

[and so forth] ...this is a designation based on realization, pertaining to the end of liberation, which belongs to the Blessed Buddhas at the foot of the Bodhi tree, coinciding with the attainment of omniscience; that is to say, ‘the Blessed One’."
143. To explain those qualities on account of which this name [“Bhagavā”] was given, they recite this verse:
“He possesses (bhagī), he partakes (bhajī), he shares (bhāgī), he is the analyzer (vibhattavā);
he has broken (akāsi bhaggaṃ), he is venerable (garu), and he is fortunate (bhāgyavā).”
“He whose self is well-developed through many methods is called the Blessed One who has reached the end of existence.
The meaning of these various terms should be understood here according to the method stated in the *Niddesa*.
144. But there is this other method:
He is possessed of fortune, he has broken [defilements], he is endowed with [virtues], and he is distinguished by his excellences;
he is one who has enjoyed [the world] and has gone beyond existence—thus he is the Blessed One (Bhagavā) among all states of being.
In this regard, it should be understood that by taking the grammatical characteristics such as "the addition of a syllable" (vaṇṇāgama) and "the substitution of a syllable" (vaṇṇavipariyaya),

or by taking the characteristic of including [words] in the *pisodarādi* group according to the rules of phonology (*saddanaya*), he is called "Bhagavā" because he possesses the fortune (*bhāgya*) that has reached the further shore of generosity, virtue, and so forth, which produces mundane and supramundane happiness; thus,
where one would otherwise say "possessor of fortune" (*bhāgyavā*), he is called "Bhagavā."
But because [it is free] from shamelessness, lack of moral dread, anger, resentment, calumny, disparagement, envy, avarice, deceit, fraud, obstinacy, impetuosity, conceit, arrogance,
intoxication, negligence, craving, ignorance, the threefold roots of unwholesomeness, misconduct, defilements, stains, uneven perceptions, discursive thoughts, proliferations,
the fourfold perversions, the taints, fetters, floods, bonds, the states of being, the arising of craving, clinging, the five mental stumps, shackles, hindrances, and relishings—

He shattered all the hundreds of thousands of afflictions consisting of quarrels, disputes, and their roots; craving, the underlying tendencies of the body, the seven latent dispositions, the eight wrong views, the ten unwholesome courses of action rooted in craving, the sixty-two types of speculative views, and the hundred and eight modes of craving’s wandering.

Or, in brief, he destroyed the five Māras: the Māra of the aggregates of defilement, the Māra of volitional formations, the Māra of the deva-son, and the Māra of death. Therefore, because these have been broken...
He who has destroyed the perils (parissaya) should be called "Bhaggava," yet he is called "Bhagavā. And regarding this it is said:
"He whose lust is destroyed, whose hatred is destroyed, whose delusion is destroyed, and who is free from taints;
whose evil states are destroyed—he is therefore called Bhagavā."
The perfection of his physical body is illustrated by his being fortunate and possessing the marks of a hundred merits;

the perfection of his Dhamma-body by his having overcome all faults. Likewise, it is shown that he is highly esteemed by those in the world who are his peers, that he is approachable by both householders and those gone forth, and that he is capable of removing the suffering of body and mind from those who have approached him through both the giving of material gifts and the giving of the Dhamma.
Benefactorhood and the capacity to connect others with both mundane and supramundane happiness are thereby illuminated.

Furthermore, because the word *bhaga* occurs in the world in reference to six things—sovereignty, virtue, fame, glory, beauty, and effort—and because he possesses supreme sovereignty over his own mind, or else all aspects of that which is esteemed as mundane, such as the powers of *aṇimā*, *laghimā*, and so forth, in their full perfection; [the Blessed One is thus called Bhagavā].
There is. Likewise, there is the supramundane Dhamma; the exceedingly pure fame attained through qualities as they truly are, which pervades the three worlds;
and the splendor of all limbs and members, complete in every aspect, capable of producing delight in the eyes of people intent on beholding the physical body.
Because whatever benefit for oneself or others he has desired or prayed for is accomplished exactly in that way—

There is sensual pleasure (*kāma*), which is defined as the arising in a desired place; and there is effort (*payatta*), characterized as right exertion (*sammāvāyama*), which serves as the cause for attaining a state of being honored by the entire world.
Therefore, because he is endowed with these "fortunes" (*bhaga*), he is called the Blessed One (*Bhagavā*) in the sense that "he possesses fortunes.

Furthermore, because he has analyzed all phenomena (*dhamma*)—such as the aggregates (*khandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), truths (*sacca*), faculties (*indriya*), and dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*)—into their various categories beginning with the wholesome (*kusala*)...
Or, having analyzed and revealed [them], he has explained the noble truth of suffering in the sense of oppression, being conditioned, burning, and changeability;
the origin in the sense of accumulation, source, bondage, and obstruction; cessation in the sense of escape, seclusion, the unconditioned, and the deathless;
and the path in the sense of leading out, cause, vision, and predominance, [namely] wholesome states and so forth.
"Taught" (desita) is what is meant. Therefore, although "one who has analyzed" (vibhatta) should be said, he is called "Bhagavā.

And because he practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed the divine, brahma, and noble abidings; the seclusion of body, mind, and requisites; the void, the wishless, and the signless liberations;
and other mundane and supramundane superhuman states—therefore, he is "one who has enjoyed" (bhakta). Thus, he is "Bhagavā."
It should be said, "He is called Bhagavā.
However, because he has vomited out (*vanta*) the going (*gamana*)—that is, craving (*taṇhā*)—in the three realms of existence (*bhava*), he should be called *bhavesu vantagamana*.
From this compound, taking the letter *bha* from the word *bhava*, the letter *ga* from the word *gamana*, and the long vowel *ā* from the word *vanta*, [the name Bhagavā is formed].
Having performed [these deeds] and having taken them up, he is called "Bhagavā," just as in the world, although one should say *mekhalā* for a girdle of leather, it is called *mālā*. 145.
Thus, by these various reasons, that Blessed One is an Arahant...
[and so on] ...by these various reasons he is "Bhagavā. For one who recollects the Buddha’s qualities in this way, at that time the mind is not overwhelmed by lust.
The mind is not obsessed by lust, nor obsessed by hatred, nor obsessed by delusion. At that time, his mind is directed straight toward the Tathāgata.

Thus, for one whose hindrances have been suppressed by the absence of obsession with lust and the other defilements, and whose mind is directed straight toward the meditation subject, thoughts and explorations inclined toward the Buddha’s qualities proceed.

As one reflects upon and examines the qualities of the Buddha, rapture arises. For one whose mind is filled with rapture, through the tranquility that has rapture as its proximate cause, the disturbances of body and mind are stilled. For one whose disturbances have been stilled, both bodily and mental happiness arise.
For one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated by taking the qualities of the Buddha as its object; thus it proceeds in gradual succession.

The factors of absorption arise in a single moment. However, due to the profundity of the Buddha’s qualities, or because of being intent on recollecting his manifold attributes, the jhāna does not reach full absorption (appanā) but remains at the level of access concentration (upacāra).
Since it arises by way of recollecting the Buddha’s qualities, it is designated simply as "recollection of the Buddha" (buddhānussati).
Moreover, a bhikkhu devoted to this recollection of the Buddha becomes respectful and deferential toward the Teacher;
he attains an abundance of faith, an abundance of mindfulness, an abundance of wisdom, and an abundance of merit; he is filled with rapture and gladness;
he overcomes fear and terror and is capable of enduring suffering; and he acquires the perception of living in the company of the Teacher. Through the recollection of the Buddha’s qualities...
Even his body, having been inhabited by [the Buddha], becomes worthy of veneration like a shrine-house (cetiyaghara). His mind inclines toward the plane of a Buddha.
When he encounters a situation where a transgression might occur, shame and fear of wrongdoing (hirottappa) arise within him as if he were seeing the Teacher face-to-face.
Even if he does not penetrate further, he is destined for a happy destination.
Therefore, indeed, the wise person should practice heedfulness at all times toward this recollection of the Buddha,
which possesses such great power. This concludes,
for now, the introduction to the detailed exposition of the recollection of the Buddha.
2. Discourse on the Recollection of the Dhamma (Dhammānussati) 146.
One who wishes to develop the recollection of the Dhamma should, having gone to a secluded place and retired for meditation, reflect thus: "The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One;
it is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be personally realized by the wise. Thus...
The qualities of both the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*) and the ninefold supramundane Dhamma (*lokuttara-dhamma*) should be recollected.
Regarding the phrase "well-expounded" (*svākkhāto*): in this term, the Dhamma of the scriptures is included, whereas in the others, only the supramundane Dhamma is.

Therein, first, the Dhamma of the scriptures is well-expounded because it is excellent in its beginning, middle, and end, and because it proclaims the holy life (*brahmacariya*) that is meaningful, possessed of phrasing, complete in all its parts, and utterly pure.
For whatever single verse the Blessed One teaches, because of the all-beneficial nature of the Dhamma, it is excellent in the beginning through its first quarter,

excellent in the middle through its second and third quarters, and excellent in the end through its final quarter. A discourse with a single sequence of connection is excellent in the beginning by way of its introduction (*nidāna*),
excellent in the end by way of its conclusion (*nigamana*), and excellent in the middle by way of the remainder.
A discourse with multiple connections is "good in the beginning" by its first connection, "good in the end" by its final one, and "good in the middle" by the remaining ones.
Furthermore, it is good in the beginning because it possesses a source and an origin;

it is good in the middle because the meaning is presented without error in accordance with those to be trained, and because it is endowed with reasons and examples; and it is good in the end because it generates the acquisition of faith in the listeners.
And by means of the conclusion, it is "good in the end.

The entire Dhamma of the Dispensation is "good in the beginning" through virtue (*sīla*), which constitutes its own purpose; it is "good in the middle" through serenity (*samatha*), insight (*vipassanā*), the paths (*magga*), and the fruits (*phala*);
and it is "good in the end" through Nibbāna. Alternatively, it is "good in the beginning" through virtue and concentration (*samādhi*), and "good in the middle" through insight and the paths.

It is beautiful in the middle through its fruits and through Nibbāna; it is beautiful in the end through the attainment of Nibbāna. Alternatively, it is beautiful in the beginning because the Buddha has well-awakened to it;
it is beautiful in the middle because the Dhamma is well-proclaimed; it is beautiful in the end because the Saṅgha practices it correctly.

Or, for one who has heard it and is practicing for its sake, it is beautiful in the beginning with respect to the full enlightenment to be attained; [it is beautiful in the middle] with respect to the enlightenment of a Pacceka-Buddha...
It is beautiful in the middle and beautiful in its conclusion regarding the enlightenment of a disciple.
When it is being heard, because it suppresses the hindrances, it brings about goodness even through hearing; thus it is "beautiful in the beginning.
When it is being practiced, because it brings about the bliss of serenity and insight, it brings about goodness through practice; thus it is "beautiful in the middle."

Furthermore, when one has practiced accordingly and the fruit of that practice is accomplished, it brings about the state of *tādi* (the steadfast); thus, because it brings about the excellence of the fruit of practice as well, it is "good in the end.
In this way, because it is good in the beginning, middle, and end, it is "well-expounded.
Moreover, when the Blessed One teaches this Dhamma, he reveals both the holy life of the Dispensation (*sāsana-brahmacariya*) and the holy life of the Path (*magga-brahmacariya*).

He illuminates it through various methods; it is "possessed of meaning" (*sāttha*) because of its perfection of meaning according to what is appropriate, and "possessed of phrasing" (*sabyañjana*) because of its perfection of phrasing.
It is "possessed of meaning" due to its revealing, clarifying, explaining, analyzing, making plain, proclaiming, and connecting of the words of the meaning;

it is "possessed of phrasing" due to the perfection of its syllables, words, phrases, modes, etymologies, and definitions. It is [also] possessed of meaning through the profundity of its meaning and the profundity of its penetration.
It is "possessing meaning" (*sāttha*) due to the profundity of the Dhamma and the profundity of the teaching;

it is "possessing phrasing" (*sabyañjana*) due to being the domain of the analytical knowledges of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*) and of inspired eloquence (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*). It is "possessing meaning" because it is to be understood by the wise and inspires confidence in those who investigate;
it is "possessing phrasing" because it is credible and inspires confidence in worldly people. It is "possessing meaning" because its intention is profound.
It is "with phrasing" because its words are clearly articulated. It is "entirely complete" because it is whole and perfect, owing to the absence of anything that needs to be added.
It is "pure" because it is faultless, owing to the absence of anything that needs to be removed.
Furthermore, it is "meaningful" because of the excellence of the realization attained through practice, and it is "with phrasing" because of the excellence of the tradition through the scriptures.

It is "well-expounded" (*svākkhāta*) because it reveals the holy life (*brahmacariya*) that is complete, perfect, and pure—complete and perfect because it is endowed with the five aggregates of virtue and so forth, and pure because it is free from defilements, set forth for the sake of crossing over [saṃsāra], and indifferent to worldly gain.
Alternatively, it is well-expounded because it is properly expounded, as there is no perversion of meaning. For, in the case of the Dhamma of other sectarians...

The meaning undergoes perversion because of the absence of the obstructive nature in those things called "obstructive," and because of the absence of the leading-out nature in those things called "leading out. Therefore, they are indeed teachings poorly proclaimed;
the meaning of the Blessed One’s Dhamma does not undergo such perversion. [It remains clear that] "these things are obstructive" and "these things are leading out."
"Because the phenomena thus spoken do not transcend their true nature. In this way, first, the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*) is well-expounded.
Furthermore, the supramundane Dhamma (*lokuttara-dhamma*) is well-expounded because it has been taught as the practice corresponding to Nibbāna and as the Nibbāna corresponding to that practice.
As it is said: "The path leading to Nibbāna for his disciples has indeed been well-proclaimed by that Blessed One..."

“The practice and Nibbāna meet; the practice and Nibbāna coincide. Just as the waters of the Ganges meet and merge with the waters of the Yamunā, even so, the practice leading to Nibbāna well-expounded by that Blessed One for his disciples meets and merges with Nibbāna.
And herein, the Noble Path, not approaching either of the two extremes, is the Middle Way.

The practice itself is well-expounded because it is declared as the "Middle Way. The fruits of recluseship are well-expounded because they are declared as having "subsided defilements" precisely because the defilements have subsided.
Nibbāna is well-expounded because it is declared according to its actual nature as eternal, deathless, a refuge, a shelter, and so forth;
thus, the supramundane Dhamma is also well-expounded.

148. Regarding the term *sandiṭṭhika* (visible here and now): first, the noble path is "visible" because it must be seen by the noble person himself (*sāmaṃ*) as he brings about the absence of lust and other defilements within his own continuum. As it is said:
"O Brahmin, one who is lustful, overcome by lust, and whose mind is consumed by it, intends harm to himself, intends harm to others, and intends harm to both."

He intends. He experiences mental pain and dejection. When lust is abandoned, he does not intend for his own affliction, nor does he intend for the affliction of others, nor does he intend for the affliction of both;
he does not experience mental pain and dejection. In this way too, brahmin, the Dhamma is directly visible. Furthermore—

The supramundane Dhamma in its ninefold form is "visible here and now" (*sanditthika*) because whoever has attained it must see it for themselves through the knowledge of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*), setting aside the need to rely on the faith of others.
Alternatively, "praiseworthy view" is *sanditthi*;
that which triumphs by means of such a view is *sanditthika*. For in this context, the Noble Path triumphs by means of its associated [factors].
The noble fruit (ariyaphala) conquers the defilements by means of the vision that has become its cause, while Nibbāna does so by means of the vision that has become its object.

Therefore, just as one who wins with a chariot is called a "charioteer" (rathika), so too the ninefold supramundane dhamma is "visible here and now" (sanditthika) because it conquers by means of vision.
Alternatively, "seen" (diṭṭha) refers to seeing (dassana). That which is seen is "the visible" (sandittha); the meaning is "seeing. It is visible (sandittha).

It is "visible" (sanditthika) because it is worthy of being seen. For the supramundane state, when seen through the realization of cultivation and the realization of direct experience, turns back the fear of the round of existence.
Therefore, just as that which is worthy of being a cloth is called "clothing" (vatthika), so too that which is worthy of being seen is called "visible" (sanditthika).
149. "Akālika" means there is no improper time for it with respect to its giving of fruit; thus it is *akālika*.
It does not give fruit after wasting time such as five or seven days; rather, it is said to give fruit immediately upon its own occurrence.
Alternatively, it is *kālika* because an excellent time has arrived for its giving of fruit. What is that? It is mundane wholesome phenomena (*kusaladhamma*).
Furthermore, because it yields its fruit immediately, it is "timeless" (*akālika*). This is said with reference specifically to the Path itself.
It is called "inviting one to come and see" (*ehi-passika*) because it deserves the method of inviting one to come and see, expressed thus:
"Come, see this Dhamma. Why does it deserve that method? Because it exists and because it is utterly pure. It is not like an empty fist.
For even if one says, "There is gold or bullion," it is not possible to say, "Come, look at this. Why? Because it does not exist.

And even in the case of something that does exist, such as feces or urine, it is not possible to say, "Come, look at this," for the purpose of gladdening the mind by proclaiming its pleasant nature. On the contrary, it must simply be covered over with grass or leaves.

Why? Because it is impure. However, this supramundane dhamma, though ninefold, exists by its very intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) and is thus pure—like the full orb of the moon in a cloudless sky, or like a natural gem placed upon a pale cloth.
Therefore, because it both exists and is pure, it deserves the method of "come and see" (*ehi-passa*); hence, it is called *ehi-passiko*.
151. "To be led to" means "leading onward" (*opanayika*). Herein, this is the analysis: "Leading" (*upanaya*) is the act of leading.
It is "leading onward" (*opanayika*) because it deserves to be led into one's own mind by way of meditation, even while disregarding a burning garment or head.
That which is "leading onward" is "to be led onward" (*opanayika*). This applies to the conditioned supramundane dhamma. In the unconditioned...
But because it is worthy of being brought near by one’s own mind, it is *opanayyika*. The meaning is that it is worthy of being approached by way of realization.

Alternatively, the Noble Path is *upaneyya* because it leads toward Nibbāna; the states of fruition and Nibbāna are *upaneyya* because they are to be led toward the state of being realized. That which is *upaneyya* is precisely *opanayyika*.

“[It] is to be personally experienced by the wise” means [it is to be experienced] within each individual by all wise persons, such as those who understand through a condensed teaching (*ugghaṭitaññū*) and so forth.
It should be understood thus: "The path has been developed by me; the fruit has been attained; cessation has been realized.
For it is not by means of the path developed by the preceptor that the disciple's defilements are abandoned;
nor does he dwell at ease through the preceptor’s attainment of the fruit; nor does he realize the Nibbāna realized by him. Therefore, this [path] does not reside upon another's head.
It should be regarded as an ornament, yet it should be regarded within one’s own mind; what is meant is that it is to be experienced by the wise.
However, this is not the domain of fools. Moreover, this Dhamma is well-expounded. Why?

Because it is visible here and now (*sanditthika*). It is visible here and now because it is timeless (*akālika*). It is timeless because it invites one to come and see (*ehipassika*). And that which invites one to come and see is indeed worthy of being followed (*opanayika*).
153. As he thus recollects the qualities of the Dhamma, such as its being well-expounded, at that moment his mind is not obsessed by lust;
nor is it obsessed by hatred... [as before] ...nor is it obsessed by delusion. At that moment his mind is directed straight, having the Dhamma as its object.
Thus, in the same manner as previously described, for one whose hindrances have been suppressed, in a single moment—

The factors of absorption (jhānaṅga) arise. However, due to the profundity of the qualities of the Dhamma, or because of being intent on recollecting its manifold qualities, the jhāna reaches only access concentration (upacāra) without reaching full absorption (appanā).
Since this arises by way of recollecting the qualities of the Dhamma, it is designated simply as "recollection of the Dhamma" (dhammānussati).
Furthermore, a bhikkhu devoted to this recollection of the Dhamma regards the Teacher who teaches this Dhamma that leads to the goal as being endowed with these very qualities;
he does not see anyone in the past, nor even now, other than that Blessed One.
Thus, by seeing the qualities of the Dhamma, he becomes respectful and reverent toward the Teacher. Regarding the Dhamma:

One who treats the Dhamma with great respect attains the fullness of faith and other virtues; he becomes abundant in rapture and gladness, overcomes fear and terror, and is capable of enduring suffering.

He acquires the perception that he dwells in accordance with the Dhamma, and his very body—being permeated by the recollection of the qualities of the Dhamma—becomes worthy of veneration like a shrine-house for the sake of attaining the unsurpassed Dhamma.
The mind inclines [toward virtue], and when one encounters a situation that ought to be transgressed, shame and fear of wrongdoing arise in one who recollects the excellence of the Dhamma.
Yet, failing to penetrate further, one is nonetheless destined for a happy rebirth.
Therefore, the wise person should indeed practice heedfulness.
Thus, one should always [recollect] the recollection of the Dhamma, which possesses such great majesty.
This concludes the introductory exposition on the recollection of the Dhamma.
3. Discourse on the Recollection of the Saṅgha.
154. One who desires to develop the recollection of the Sangha should, having gone to a secluded place and being withdrawn in solitude, reflect thus:

"The Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing well; the Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing straightly; the Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing methodically;
the Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing appropriately—namely, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals."
“This Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
In this way, the qualities of the Noble Saṅgha are to be recollected. 155.
Therein, “well-practiced” means practiced well; it refers to the right practice, the non-retrogressive practice, and the conformable practice.
It means he has entered upon the practice that is not contrary [to the goal] and the practice in accordance with the Dhamma.
They are called *sāvakā* (disciples) because they listen attentively to the instruction and exhortation of the Blessed One. The *saṅgha* of disciples is the *sāvakasaṅgha*;

the meaning is a collection of disciples who have attained the state of being a community through the commonality of virtue and view. Furthermore, because that right practice is straight and free from crookedness...

It is called "straight" because it is not crooked, and it is also called "the noble method" (*ñāya*); furthermore, because it is appropriate, it has come to be designated as "proper conduct" (*sāmīcī*).
Therefore, the Noble Saṅgha who practices that [method] is said to be "practicing straightly," "practicing by way of the method," and "practicing with proper conduct.

In this context, those established on the path are "well-practiced" due to their possession of right practice. Those established in the fruit should be understood as "well-practiced" with reference to the past practice, because they have attained what was to be attained through right practice.
Furthermore, he is one who has practiced well because he has practiced according to the instructions in the well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya, and because he has entered upon the unerring practice.

He is one who has practiced straightly because he has practiced by means of the middle way, avoiding the two extremes, and because he has practiced for the sake of abandoning the faults of crookedness, curvature, and tortuousness of body, speech, and mind, as well as for the sake of practicing straightly.
"The Way" (ñāya) is said to be Nibbāna; he is one who has practiced the Way because he has practiced for its sake.
One who has practiced in such a way as to be worthy of practicing with propriety is called "one who practices with propriety" because of having practiced accordingly.
156. *Yadidaṃ* means "which are these. *Cattāri purisayugāni* (four pairs of persons): by way of pairs, the one established in the first path and the one established in the fruit constitute one pair;
thus there are four pairs of persons. *Aṭṭha purisapuggalā* (eight types of individuals) refers to them by way of individual persons.
According to this method—namely, one who stands on the first path and one who stands in the fruit—there are exactly eight types of persons (*puggala*).
In this context, the terms "person" (*purisa*) and "individual" (*puggala*) are synonymous; however, they are used here according to the capacity of those to be converted (*veneyya*).
This is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples, consisting of these four pairs of persons, or taken individually...
The eight types of persons constitute this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples. Regarding the term *āhuneyya* and so forth:

it is called *āhuna* because it is to be brought and offered (*ānetvā hunitabba*). The meaning is that even from afar, one should bring [offerings] and give them to those possessed of virtue. This is a designation for the four requisites.
Because he is worthy of receiving that *āhuna*, as it produces great fruit for him, he is *āhuneyya*. Alternatively, even from afar...
It is called the *āhavanīya* because everything that is brought (*āgantvā*) must be offered (*hunitabba*) therein;

or alternatively, it is called the *āhavanīya* because it is worthy of receiving offerings (*āhavana*) even from Sakka and others. Furthermore, there is the fire of the brahmins known as the *āhavanīya*, which they hold to be the one wherein what is offered bears great fruit.
If it is called *āhavanīya* on account of the great fruitfulness of what is offered, then the Saṅgha alone is the *āhavanīya*; for what is offered to the Saṅgha [bears great fruit].
It is of great fruit. As it is said:
"Though a person might tend a fire in the forest for a hundred years, if one were to honor for even a moment one whose self is cultivated..."
“That very same offering is better than a hundred years of sacrifice.

Thus, in another Nikāya, the term *āhavanīya* is identical in meaning here with the term *āhuneyya*; however, there is only a slight difference in their verbal form (*byañjana*). Such is the one worthy of offerings (*āhuneyya*).
Regarding the term *pāhuneyya*: here, *pāhuṇa* refers to dear and agreeable kinsmen and friends who have come from the cardinal and intermediate directions for one’s sake.
There is the gift for guests prepared with hospitality. Even that, setting aside such individual guests, is more fitting to give to the Saṅgha;
it is more fitting for the Saṅgha alone to receive it. For there is no guest equal to the Saṅgha.
Thus, he appears even during the interval between Buddhas, and he is endowed with those qualities that are continuously dear and agreeable.
Thus, because he is worthy of being given hospitality and worthy of receiving hospitality, he is "one worthy of hospitality" (*pāhuneyya*).
However, for those in whose text the reading is *pāhavanīya*, it means that since the Saṅgha deserves priority, it is "that which is to be offered here" by being brought there first;
thus it is *pāhavanīya*. Or alternatively, it is *pāhavanīya* because it is worthy of being offered in every way. And this [term] here—
For that very reason, he is called "worthy of hospitality" (*pāhuneyya*).

As for "offering" (*dakkhiṇā*), it refers to the gift that should be given out of faith in the next world. Because he is worthy of that offering, or because he is beneficial to the offering—since he purifies it by making it yield great fruit—he is "worthy of offerings" (*dakkhiṇeyya*).
Because he is worthy of the act of joining the palms in reverence performed by the entire world, placing both hands upon the head, he is "worthy of reverential salutation" (*añjalikaraṇīya*).
"An unsurpassed field of merit for the world" means a place for the growth of merit that is peerless for the entire world.

For just as the place where rice or barley grows for a king or a minister is called "the king’s rice-field" or "the king’s barley-field," so too the Saṅgha is the place for the growth of merits for the entire world.
For it is by depending on the Saṅgha that the merits leading to various kinds of welfare and happiness grow for the world.
Therefore, the Saṅgha is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
157. For one who thus recollects the qualities of the Saṅgha, such as its being well-practiced and so forth, at that time there is no obsession by lust.
The mind is not obsessed by hatred... [and so on] ... nor is the mind obsessed by delusion. At that time, his mind is directed straight toward the Saṅgha.
Thus, as in the previous method, for one whose hindrances have been suppressed, the factors of absorption arise in a single moment.
However, because of the profundity of the qualities of the Saṅgha and because of the inclination toward recollecting its manifold qualities, [the factors do not arise all at once].
Or, failing to reach absorption (*appanā*), it becomes a jhāna that has reached only access (*upacāra*).
Because it arises by way of recollecting the qualities of the Saṅgha, it is designated as "recollection of the Saṅgha" (*saṅghānussati*).
Furthermore, a bhikkhu devoted to this recollection of the Saṅgha possesses reverence for and deference toward the Saṅgha. There is an abundance of faith and the other [virtues].
He attains [these benefits]: he becomes abundant in rapture and gladness; he overcomes fear and dread; he is capable of enduring suffering;

he gains the perception of living in communion with the Saṅgha. His body, permeated by the recollection of the Saṅgha’s qualities, becomes worthy of veneration—like an Uposatha hall where the Saṅgha has assembled—and his mind inclines toward the realization of the Saṅgha’s qualities.
When he encounters a situation where an offense might be committed, a sense of shame and dread of blame arises before him as if the Saṅgha were actually present before his eyes;
and even if he does not penetrate further, he is destined for a happy rebirth.
Therefore, a person of wisdom should indeed practice heedfulness.
Thus, always [one should practice] this recollection of the Saṅgha, which possesses such great power.
This concludes the section on the detailed exposition of the recollection of the Saṅgha.
4. Discourse on the Recollection of Virtue (Sīlānussati).

158. Furthermore, one who wishes to develop the recollection of virtue (sīlānussati) should, having gone to a secluded place and retired in solitude, recollect his own virtues by way of their qualities such as being unbroken, thus:
"O, how my virtues are unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, unadhered-to, and conducive to concentration.
Thus should one recollect one's own virtues by way of the qualities of being unbroken and so forth.
And these are the virtues of the householder for the householder and the virtues of the one gone forth for the one gone forth.

Whether they be the virtues of the householder or the virtues of the one gone forth, those of which not even a single [precept] has been broken at the beginning or at the end are "unbroken" (*akhaṇḍāni*), like a garment whose hem is not torn; those of which not even a single [precept] has been broken in the middle...
"Broken" means they are not perforated like a garment pierced in the middle; thus they are "unperforated" (*acchidda*).

Those whose two or three [bones] are not broken in succession, and which do not possess a discordant color—such as black, red, or other hues—arising on the back or the belly in long, circular, or other shapes, like a cow with the body-color of its kind, are "not brindled" (*asabala*).
Those which are not broken in between are "without blemish" (*akammāsa*), because they are not like a speckled cow that is black due to being variegated with spots of a different color.

Alternatively, without distinction, all of them are "uncracked," "unbroken," "unspotted," and "without blemish" because they have not been impaired by the sevenfold union of sexual intercourse nor by evil states such as anger and malice. These very same [precepts]...

They are "free" because they have been liberated from the slavery of craving by establishing the state of freedom. They are "praised by the wise" because they are commended by the wise, such as the Buddhas and others.
They are "unadhered-to" because they cannot be adhered to by anyone—either through craving or views—in the manner of thinking, "There is this fault in your virtues.
They [lead] to access-concentration or absorption-concentration; or else...
Or rather, they are called "conducive to concentration" because they lead to path-concentration and even to fruition-concentration.
Thus, for one who recollects their own virtues of virtue such as being unbroken and so forth, at that time their mind is not obsessed by lust;
it is not obsessed by hatred... [and so on] ...it is not obsessed by delusion. At that time, their mind is indeed straight.
At that time, the mind is directed toward virtue; thus, as in the previous method, the factors of jhāna arise in a single moment for one whose hindrances have been suppressed.

However, due to the profundity of the qualities of virtue, or because of being intent on recollecting its various attributes, the jhāna reaches only access (upacāra) without reaching absorption (appanā). This [jhāna] occurs by way of the recollection of the qualities of virtue.
Because it has arisen, it is reckoned simply as "recollection of virtue. Furthermore,
a bhikkhu devoted to this recollection of virtue is respectful toward the training, conducts himself in a manner consistent with it, is diligent in hospitality,
is free from the fear of self-reproach and so forth, perceives danger even in the slightest faults, and possesses the fullness of faith and the other faculties.
He attains [this state] and becomes abundant in rapture and gladness. But failing to penetrate further, he has a happy destination as his ultimate end.
Therefore, a person of wisdom should indeed practice heedfulness constantly toward this recollection of virtue, which possesses such great power.
This concludes the section on the detailed exposition of the recollection of virtue (*sīlānussati*).
5. The Discourse on the Recollection of Generosity (*Cāgānussati*) 160.
One who wishes to develop the recollection of generosity, being naturally inclined toward generosity and constantly engaged in giving and sharing, [should do so as follows...]
It must be so. Alternatively, however, one who begins the development [of meditation] should make a formal undertaking, thinking:
"From this day forward, I shall not eat even a single mouthful of food without having first received an alms-offering.
Having made that resolution, on that very day, one should give an offering according to one's means and power to recipients distinguished by their virtues, and then take up the sign therein.
Secluded and withdrawn in private, one should recollect one’s own generosity by way of such qualities as being free from the stain of stinginess, thinking:

"It is a gain for me, it is a great blessing for me, that amidst a generation obsessed by the stain of stinginess, I dwell with a mind free from the stain of stinginess—generous, open-handed, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to charity, accessible to requests, and rejoicing in the distribution of gifts.
Thus should one recollect one's own generosity through the virtue of being free from the stain of stinginess.
In that regard, "What a gain for me indeed! means: "What a gain for me indeed," referring to those passages by the Blessed One concerning the donor, such as:
"Having given life, one becomes a partaker of life, whether divine or human"; "By giving, one becomes beloved and many resort to him";
and "One who gives is beloved, following the Dhamma of the virtuous," and so forth.
"The gains have been praised; they will certainly be my portion"—this is the intention. "It is well-gained by me indeed":
whatever this teaching or even human birth has been gained by me, that is truly well-gained by me. Why? Because while people are overwhelmed by the stain of stinginess...
[and so forth] ...I am one who delights in giving and sharing.
In that context, "overwhelmed by the stain of stinginess" means overcome by the stain of stinginess.

"Beings" (pajā) refers to sentient beings in the sense of their being born. Therefore, it refers to those beings who are overwhelmed by one or another of the dark qualities (kaṇhadhamma)—which corrupt the luminosity of the mind—characterized by an inability to endure sharing one's own prosperity with others, namely, the stain of stinginess.

This is the meaning here. "With a mind free from the stain of stinginess" means that one dwells with a mind free from the stains of greed, hatred, and so forth, as well as from stinginess. "I dwell with such a mind" means that I abide having attained a state of consciousness of the kind described above.
However, in the Suttas, when Mahānāma the Sakyan, who was a stream-enterer, asked about the dwelling supported by [the Buddha], it is said:
Because it was taught by way of living in dependence, it is said, "I dwell in a house. In this context, the meaning is "I dwell having overcome [the world].

"One who has abandoned renunciation" (*muttacāgo*) means one whose renunciation is cast off. "One with clean hands" (*payatapāṇī*) means one with pure hands; the sense is that his hands are always washed for the purpose of giving the gift to be given with his own hands and with due respect.
"Delighting in relinquishment" (*vossaggarato*): relinquishing is "relinquishment" (*vossaggo*), which is to say, total abandonment.
The meaning is as follows: one who delights (*rato*) in that relinquishment (*vossagga*) by way of constant application is called "one who delights in relinquishment" (*vossaggarata*).

"One devoted to begging" (*yācayoga*) means one who gives whatever others beg for; thus, the meaning is "devoted to begging" (*yācanayoga*). There is also a reading *yājayoga*, which means "joined with sacrifice" (*yāja*), that is to say, joined with what is termed sacrifice (*yajana*).
"Delighting in giving and sharing" (*dānasaṃvibhāgarata*) means one who delights both in giving (*dāna*) and in sharing (*saṃvibhāga*). For I [give] both... [giving].
The meaning is that he recollects thus: "I share even half of what is to be enjoyed by myself, and I find delight in both of these things. 161.
As he thus recollects his own generosity through such qualities as being free from the stain of stinginess, in that [act of recollection]...
At that time, the mind is not obsessed by lust, nor by hatred... [as before] ...nor by delusion.

At that time, his mind is directed straight toward generosity. Thus, for one whose hindrances have been suppressed in the manner described above, the factors of absorption (jhānaṅga) arise in a single moment.
However, because of the profundity of the qualities of generosity and because of his inclination toward recollecting the various kinds of qualities of generosity—
Or, without reaching absorption (*appanā*), it is simply a meditation (*jhāna*) that has reached access (*upacāra*).
Because it arises by way of recollecting the quality of generosity, it is known as the "recollection of generosity" (*cāgānussati*).
Furthermore, a bhikkhu devoted to this recollection of generosity becomes even more intent on generosity and possesses a disposition characterized by non-greed (*alobha*).
One who practices in conformity with loving-kindness becomes confident and full of rapture and gladness; yet, if one does not penetrate further, one is at least destined for a happy rebirth.
Therefore, the wise person should always practice heedfulness regarding this recollection of generosity, which possesses such great power.
This concludes the section on the detailed exposition of the recollection of generosity (cāgānussati).
6. Discourse on the Recollection of Deities (devatānussati) 162.
One who wishes to develop the recollection of deities should do so by means of the qualities beginning with faith that have been brought forth through the Noble Path.
One should be thus endowed. Then, having gone into seclusion and retired to a solitary place, one should reflect: "There are the gods of the Four Great Kings; there are the gods of the Thirty-three;
the Yāma gods; the Tusita gods; the gods who delight in creation; the gods who wield power over the creations of others; there are the gods of Brahmā’s retinue;
there are gods even higher than that—those deities who were endowed with such faith as this..."
"Having passed away from here and been reborn there, those deities possessed such faith; such faith exists in me as well. Possessed of such virtue...

such learning... such generosity... such wisdom as those deities possessed who, having passed away from here, were reborn there, such wisdom exists in me as well. In this way, the deities stand in the place of witnesses.
Setting aside one's own qualities such as faith, these [qualities] should be recollected.

Furthermore, in the Sutta it is said: "Mahānāma, on whatever occasion a noble disciple recollects his own faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom, as well as those of those deities, at that time his mind is not overwhelmed by lust."

It is said, "the mind becomes [calm]. Although this is what was said, it should nevertheless be understood that it was stated for the purpose of demonstrating that the deities, who are to be placed in the position of witnesses, possess qualities equal to one's own faith and so forth.
For in the Commentary, it is stated emphatically that one places the deities in the position of witnesses and then recollects one's own virtues.

163. Therefore, when he has first recollected the virtues of the deities and subsequently recollects the virtues of faith and so forth existing within himself, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust;
it is not obsessed by hatred... nor is it obsessed by delusion. At that time, his mind is directed straight toward the deities.
Just as in the previous method, the factors of jhāna arise in a single moment for one whose hindrances have been suppressed.

However, due to the profundity of the qualities such as faith, or because of being intent upon recollecting those various qualities, the jhāna reaches only access concentration (*upacāra*) without reaching absorption (*appanā*).
This is designated as "recollection of deities" (*devatānussati*) by way of recollecting the qualities of faith and so forth that correspond to the qualities of the deities.
Furthermore, a bhikkhu devoted to this recollection of deities becomes dear and pleasing to the deities;
he attains an even greater abundance of faith and other virtues, dwells filled with rapture and gladness, and, if he does not penetrate further,
has a happy destination as his ultimate end.
Therefore, indeed, the wise person should practice heedfulness at all times toward this recollection of deities, which possesses such great power.
This concludes the introductory section for the detailed exposition on the recollection of deities.
Miscellaneous Discussion 164.
Furthermore, in the detailed exposition of these [qualities], after stating such things as, "At that time, his mind is directed straight toward the Tathāgata," it continues:
"Mahānāma, a noble disciple whose mind is directed straight gains..."
It is said: “He gains knowledge of the meaning (atthaveda), he gains knowledge of the Dhamma (dhammaveda), he gains joy connected with the Dhamma; in one who is joyful, rapture arises.
In this context, the statement “he gains knowledge of the meaning” refers to the satisfaction that arises based on the meaning of such passages as “Thus indeed is the Blessed One,” and so forth.
The statement “he gains [knowledge of the Dhamma]” refers to the satisfaction that arises based on the actual text (pāḷi).
It should be understood that it is stated: "By means of both, one obtains joy associated with the Dhamma.

Furthermore, as for what was said in the *Devatānussati* (Recollection of Deities) regarding "having deities as the object," that should be understood as being stated either by way of the mind occurring in the prior stage having deities as its object, or by way of the mind occurring having as its object qualities similar to the qualities of deities, or qualities that produce the state of a deity.
165. Furthermore, these six recollections (anussati) are successful only for noble disciples (ariyasāvaka). For the qualities of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha are manifest to them.
They are endowed with virtues of morality such as being unbroken; with generosity free from the stain of stinginess;
and with qualities such as faith that resemble the qualities of deities of great power. And in the Mahānāma Sutta, regarding the stream-enterer—
These were spoken in detail by the Blessed One—who was asked about dwelling under dependence—for the very purpose of showing the dwelling under dependence for one who has attained the stream-entry.
Also in the *Gedha Sutta*: "Here, monks, a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata: 'Indeed, that Blessed One... [as before]...
At that time his mind is straight, having gone out, been released, and emerged from greed. Greed (gedha) means..."
“Monks, this is a designation for these five strands of sensual pleasure. And it is by making this very thing the object of their attention, monks, that some beings here are purified.

Thus, having purified the mind of the noble disciple through the power of recollection (*anussati*), [this teaching] was spoken for the sake of attaining further purification in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*).
Also, in the *Sambādhokāsasutta* taught by the Venerable Mahākaccāna: “It is wonderful, friend! It is marvelous, friend!

To what extent the opening has been discovered in the midst of confinement for the purification of beings... [and so on] ...for the realization of Nibbāna—namely, these six bases of recollection—by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One!”
“What six? Here, friends, a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata… [and so on] …in this way, some beings become pure in nature.
Thus it was spoken by way of the noble disciple’s attainment of the opportunity for the state of ultimate purity.
Also in the *Uposatha Sutta*: “And how, Visākhā, is there the noble *uposatha*? For one who is defiled, Visākhā…”
The purification of the mind comes about through effort. And how, Visākhā, does the purification of the defiled mind come about through effort?
Here, Visākhā, a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata.
Thus, for a noble disciple observing the Uposatha, the Uposatha is performed by way of the meditation subject for purifying the mind.
These were spoken for the purpose of showing that they yield great fruit. Also in the Ekādasanipāta it is said:
"Mahānāma, one who is endowed with faith is successful, not one who lacks faith.
One who is energetic, established in mindfulness, concentrated, and wise, Mahānāma, is successful, not one who is lacking in wisdom. In these..."
“Mahānāma, established in five qualities, you should further develop six qualities.
Here, Mahānāma, you should recollect the Tathāgata thus: ‘Indeed, that Blessed One...
Thus, this was spoken for the purpose of showing the dwelling to the noble disciple who asked: “Venerable sir, among us who dwell in various dwellings, by which dwelling should we dwell?”
Even so, this should be brought to mind even by an ordinary person (puthujjana) endowed with qualities such as perfectly pure virtue.
For even by way of hearsay, the mind of one who recollects the virtues of the Buddha and the others certainly becomes serene.
By the power of that serenity, having suppressed the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), one becomes filled with sublime joy, initiates insight (vipassanā), and may even realize Arahantship itself.
Like the Elder Phussadeva, who dwelt in Kaṭa-andhakāra.
It is said that when that venerable one saw a form of the Buddha created by Māra, he thought:

"If even this [image], still possessing lust, hatred, and delusion, shines so brightly, how much more must the Blessed One shine, for He is entirely free from lust, hatred, and delusion. Thus, with the Buddha as his object...
Having attained rapture and increased insight, he reached Arahantship.
Thus ends the section on the Development of Concentration in the *Visuddhimagga*, composed for the delight of virtuous people.
The Seventh Chapter: The Description of the Recollections.
8. The Description of the Meditation Subjects of Recollection.
The Discourse on Mindfulness of Death 167.
Now follows the exposition of the development of mindfulness of death, which comes immediately after this.

In this context, "death" is the cutting off of the life-faculty comprised within a single existence. As for that which is described as the total eradication of the suffering of the round of rebirth for Arahants—

There is death by total eradication, momentary death consisting of the destruction of formations at every instant, and conventional death—as in such expressions as "the tree is dead" or "the iron is dead. That [latter] is not what is intended here.
And that which is intended here is twofold: timely death and untimely death. Among these, timely death...
Death occurs through the exhaustion of merit, the exhaustion of the life-span, or the exhaustion of both.

Untimely death occurs by way of karma that interrupts the continuity of action. In this context, when death occurs despite the presence of a full complement of conditions for generating the continuity of the life-span, solely because the karma producing rebirth-linking has already reached its fruition, this is called death through the exhaustion of merit. [That which occurs] due to the excellence of the destination, time, nutriment, and so forth...
Death occurs by the exhaustion of a lifespan limited to only a hundred years, like that of people of the present day;
this is what is called death through the exhaustion of the life-span (*āyukkhaya*).

However, there is also death for those whose continuity (*santāna*) has been cut by karma capable of displacing them from their position at that very moment—such as Dūsī Māra, King Kalābu, and others—or by means of weapons and so forth due to past karma.
Death occurs when the continuity [of the life-faculty] is cut off by such means; this is what is called untimely death.

All of that is included within the cutting off of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) as previously described. Thus, mindfulness of death (*maraṇassati*) is the recollection of death, which is defined as the cutting off of the life-faculty.

168. One who desires to develop this, having gone to a secluded place and withdrawn in solitude, should apply systematic attention (yoniso manasikāra) either by reflecting, "Death will occur; the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) will be cut off," or simply, "Death, death.

For if one applies attention improperly (ayoniso), sorrow arises from recollecting the death of a beloved person, just as it arose for the mother of Vijāta upon recollecting the death of her dear son.
Delight arises when recollecting the death of an undesirable person, just as it does for enemies when they recall the death of their foes.
A sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) does not arise when recollecting the death of a neutral person, just as a corpse-burner feels no urgency upon seeing a dead body.
Terror arises when recollecting one's own death, just as a man of timid nature feels terror upon seeing an executioner with a raised sword.
It is like that. All of this occurs due to a lack of mindfulness, a sense of urgency (*saṃvega*), and knowledge.

Therefore, having observed dead and deceased beings here and there, and having reflected upon the death of those beings who previously possessed prosperity but have now died, one should apply mindfulness, a sense of urgency, and knowledge, and practice mental attention (*manasikāra*) in the manner of "Death will come," and so forth. Thus...
For when he develops it, he develops it properly; the meaning is that he develops it by means of the right method.

For it is precisely by developing it in this way that for some the hindrances are suppressed, mindfulness with death as its object becomes established, and the meditation subject reaches the stage of access concentration.
However, for one in whom this does not occur even at this point, [the meditation should be developed] by way of the presence of the executioner, and by way of success and failure.

Death should be recollected in these eight ways: by way of its drawing near, by way of the body’s being shared with many, by way of the weakness of life, by way of signlessness, by way of the limitation of the lifespan, and by way of the brevity of the moment.
In this context, "by way of the presence of an executioner" means because it stands as present like an executioner. For just as in the case of this [executioner]...
One should reflect that death is ever-present, just as an executioner stands ready with sword in hand, thinking "I shall cut off his head," as he draws it across the neck.
Why? Because it comes along with birth and because it takes away life.
For just as a mushroom emerges from the earth taking soil upon its very crown, so too do sentient beings.

They are reborn having already taken up aging and death. For indeed, immediately after the arising of their rebirth-linking consciousness, it reaches decay and breaks apart along with its associated aggregates, like a stone fallen from a mountain peak.
Thus, momentary death has arrived together with birth. Furthermore, since death is inevitable for one who is born, the death intended here is also [included].

It has come along with birth. Therefore, from the time of his birth, this being goes on toward his end just as the risen sun moves toward its setting and does not turn back even slightly from the place it has already reached;
or as a mountain river with a swift current, carrying away all that is in its path, flows and turns only forward and does not turn back even slightly—so too, he does not turn back even slightly.
He goes as if facing toward death. Therefore it is said:
"The young man who dwells in the womb for the very first night—he goes forth as if already set out; once he has gone, he does not turn back."
As he proceeds in this way, death itself draws near— like the drying up of small streams scorched by the summer heat,
like the falling of tree fruits whose stalks have been affected by the sap at dawn, like the breaking of clay vessels struck by a mallet,
and like the evaporation of dew-drops touched by the rays of the sun. Therefore he said:
“Days and nights pass by, life is cut short;
the lifespan of mortals is exhausted like the water of small streams.
There is fear for ripe fruits at any moment they might fall.”
Thus for mortals who are born, there is constant fear of death.
Just as the earthenware vessels made by a potter—
whether small or large, whether fired or unfired— [are all destined to break].
"Everything ends in dissolution; such is the life of mortals.
Like a drop of dew upon the tip of a blade of grass at the rising of the sun, such is the lifespan of human beings. Do not stop me, mother."
Thus, like an executioner with sword raised, this death that comes together with birth seizes life just as that executioner draws his sword across the neck;

having not seized it, he does not turn back. Therefore, because it comes together with birth and because it seizes life, death is indeed present right now, like an executioner with sword raised—thus it is "by way of the presence of the executioner."
Death should be recollected. 170.

As to "success and failure": here, what is called success shines only so long as it is not overcome by failure; nor is there any such thing as success that can remain after transcending failure. For instance:
"Having enjoyed the entire earth and having given away hundreds of millions, one may be happy [for a time];"
He attained lordship over a mere half-āmalaka fruit.
Yet, with that very same physical body, when his merit was exhausted, he faced death;
though previously free from sorrow, he fell into grief.
Moreover, all health ends in illness; all youth ends in old age; all life ends in death.
The entire world-dwelling is followed by birth, pursued by old age, overcome by illness, and struck down by death. Therefore it was said:
"Just as vast mountains, like great crags reaching to the sky,
might move all around, crushing [everything] in the four directions;
even so do old age and death overwhelm living beings."
Whether among khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, caṇḍālas, or pukkusas, he avoids nothing at all; he crushes them all.
There is no ground there for elephants, nor for chariots, nor for infantry.
“Nor can one be conquered by a battle of spells, nor by wealth.
Thus, by defining how the excellence of life ends in the calamity of death, one should recollect death in terms of prosperity and adversity. 171.
As for “by way of comparison”: it is by comparing oneself with others. In this regard, there are seven ways:

Death should be recollected by way of its withdrawal [of life], and by way of the greatness of fame, the greatness of merit, the greatness of strength, the greatness of psychic power, the greatness of wisdom, the case of the Paccekabuddhas, and the case of the Sammasambuddhas. How so?
This so-called death [spares] none—not even those of great fame, those with large retinues, those endowed with wealth and vehicles, nor even Mahasammata, Mandhata, or Mahasudassana.
It fell without hesitation even upon Daḷhanemi, Nimī, and others; how much more so, then, will it not fall upon me?
Even those great kings of high renown, such as Mahāsammata and the rest, have fallen under the power of death; what talk can there be of people like me?
Thus, first of all, it should be recollected by way of the greatness of his self-restraint.
How by way of the greatness of his merit?
Jotika, Jaṭila, Ugga, Meṇḍaka, and then Puṇṇaka.
These and others who are renowned in the world as "greatly meritorious"—all have met with death;
what talk can there be of those like me?
Thus, one should recollect [the Buddha] because of the greatness of his merit.
How is it by way of greatness of strength?
Vāsudeva, Baladeva, Bhīmasena, Yudhiṭṭhila,
and the great wrestler Cāṇura— all have fallen under the power of Death.
"Thus endowed with strength and power, so they are renowned in the world;
yet even these have gone to death—what then can be said of those like me?
Thus it should be recollected by way of the greatness of their strength.
How is it by way of the greatness of psychic power?
With only his big toe, he caused the Vejayanta Palace to tremble—
he who was not the foremost among those possessing psychic power, but the second chief disciple.
He too has entered the terrible jaws of death, like a deer into the mouth of a lion, along with all his psychic powers; what talk can there be of those like me?
Thus it should be recollected by way of the greatness of his psychic power.
How is it by greatness of wisdom?
