Apart from the Lord of the World, whatever other living beings there may be,
they do not equal even a sixteenth part of Sāriputta’s wisdom.
"Thus indeed, one of such great wisdom, the foremost chief disciple, has fallen under the power of death; what talk can there be regarding those like me?
In this way, he is to be recollected because of the greatness of his wisdom.

How is it compared to the Paccekabuddhas? Even those self-enlightened ones (*sayambhu*), who—like the horn of a rhinoceros—are peerless and have attained individual enlightenment (*paccekabodhi*) by crushing all the enemies that are the defilements through the power of their own knowledge and energy—even they were not released from death;
so how then shall I be released?
Relying on various signs, those great seers investigate with the power of their self-born knowledge and attain the destruction of the taints.
Dwelling in solitary practice, they are like the horn of a rhinoceros.
"Even those who have reached the shore do not escape death; what talk can there be of those like me?
Thus should one recollect from the perspective of the Paccekabuddhas.
How from the perspective of the Sammasambuddha? Even that Blessed One, whose physical body was adorned with the eighty minor marks and variegated with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man...

Even the Dhamma-body, which is enriched by the jewels of qualities such as the aggregate of virtue purified in every aspect, and which has reached the further shore of greatness in fame, greatness in merit, greatness in power, greatness in supernormal might, and greatness in wisdom—
the peerless one, equal to the unequaled, the matchless person, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—
even He was instantly extinguished by the onset of the rain of death, just as a great mass of fire is extinguished by the falling of a downpour of water.
Thus, for one of such great power, this Great Sage—
for whom death has come under its sway— there was neither fear nor shame.
He was devoid of shame and free from trepidation, the crusher of all beings.
"How will it not overcome a being such as myself?"—
thus should one recollect the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Having thus compared oneself with others who possess such greatness of glory and so forth, on account of the commonality of death;
For one who recollects, "Death will come to me just as it has for those distinguished beings," the meditation subject reaches the stage of access (upacāra).
Thus should death be recollected by way of comparison. 172.
By way of the body’s being shared with many: this body is shared with many. It is shared, for instance, with eighty species of worms.
Therein, creatures dependent on the skin eat the skin; those dependent on the hide eat the hide; those dependent on the flesh eat the flesh;
those dependent on the sinews eat the sinews; those dependent on the bones eat the bones; and those dependent on the marrow eat the marrow.
Right there they are born, grow old, and die; right there they pass excrement and urine. It is the body alone...
For them, there is the birth-chamber, the sickroom, the cemetery, the latrine, and the urinal.
Yet even they meet death through the provocation of swarms of worms.
And just as it is for these eighty families of worms, so too for the many hundreds of internal diseases and external threats such as snakes, scorpions, and the like, death occurs.
It is common to all conditions.
For just as when a target is set up at a crossroads, arrows, spears, javelins, stones, and so forth, coming from every direction, fall upon it, even so do all calamities fall upon the body.
And this [body] is subject to the falling of those calamities as well.
One surely meets with death. Therefore the Blessed One said: "In this case, bhikkhus, when the day has passed and night has begun, a bhikkhu reflects thus: 'There are many conditions for my death;
a snake might bite me, a scorpion might sting me, or a centipede might bite me, and by that I might come to my end.'"

"That would be an obstacle for me; I might stumble and fall into a chasm, or the food I have eaten might cause illness, or my bile might become disturbed, or my phlegm might become disturbed, or my wind-humors might become disturbed, and because of that I might die—that would be an obstacle for me.
Thus should death be recollected by way of the body's many shared vulnerabilities.
173. "Because life is weak" means that this so-called life is indeed powerless and fragile.

For the life of sentient beings is dependent upon inhalation and exhalation, dependent upon the postures, dependent upon cold and heat, dependent upon the primary elements, and dependent upon nutriment.
This [life] proceeds only as long as it obtains the regular functioning of inhalation and exhalation. When the breath has gone out through the nostrils...
However, when [the breath] enters within, or having entered does not exit, it is said that one is dead. Even among the four postures, they proceed only while maintaining their equilibrium;
yet, due to the excessive intensity of one or another, the life-formations (*āyusaṅkhāra*) are cut off.
Even between cold and heat, they proceed only while maintaining their equilibrium; however, by extreme cold—
Or it fails for one overcome by excessive heat. Even in the case of the great primary elements, they proceed only when maintaining their equilibrium.

However, through the provocation of one or another of the other elements—such as the water element and so forth—even a person endowed with strength may have a body that is rigid due to the earth element, or a body that is moist and putrid due to dysentery and the like, or one afflicted by a great fever, or one whose joints and ligaments are breaking apart.
Or, having offered [the sacrifice], he reaches the end of his life. Even in the case of physical food, life proceeds only for one who receives it at the proper time;
however, for one who does not obtain food, it comes to exhaustion. Thus, death should be recollected by way of the frailty of the life-span. 174.
By way of "signlessness" means by way of non-determination, that is to say, by way of the absence of a limit. For as regards sentient beings—
Life, disease, time, the laying down of the body, and destiny—
these five in the world of the living are signless and do not wait.
Therein, life first is signless because there is no fixed determination such as, "One must live only this long, and not beyond this."

For beings die even at the stage of the *kalala*; they die at the stages of the *abbuda*, *pesi*, *ghana*, and at one month, two months, three months, four months, five months, six months, seven months, eight months, nine months, and ten months [of gestation]. They also die at the very moment of emerging from the womb. Beyond that, they certainly die both within a hundred years and after a hundred years.

Disease (*byādhi*) is "signless" (*animitta*) because there is no fixed determination such as, "Beings die only from this particular disease and not from another. This is true even for diseases of the eye.

For beings die from any one of various causes, such as ear diseases and so forth. Time, too, is signless because there is no fixed determination such as, "One must die at this very time and not at another. For beings die even in the morning, or at any other time such as midday.
Even regarding the casting off of the body, there is no fixed rule such as, "The body of those dying here must fall right here and not elsewhere."

Thus, it is signless (*animitta*) because of the absence of such fixed determination. For the personal existence (*attabhāva*) of those born inside a village may fall outside the village, and that of those born outside may fall inside.
Likewise, it should be elaborated in many ways: those born on dry land may be in the water, or those born in the water may be on dry land.
As for the destination (*gati*), there is no fixed determination such as, "one who has passed away from here must be reborn here."

It is signless (*animitta*). For those who have passed away from the world of the devas are reborn even among humans; and those who have passed away from the human world are reborn anywhere at all, including the world of the devas and so forth.
Thus, like oxen yoked to a machine, the world revolves through the five destinies.
In this way, death should be recollected as being signless.
175. Regarding the limitation of time: the duration of human life is indeed limited nowadays.
One who lives long lives for a hundred years, or slightly more. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, this life of humans is short; the world beyond must be gone to;
what is wholesome must be done; the holy life must be lived; for there is no escaping death for one who has been born."
There is no immortality. Monks, whoever lives long lives for a hundred years, or a little more.
Human life is of short duration; a noble person should not despise it.
One should conduct oneself as if one’s head were on fire, for there is no escaping the arrival of death.
Furthermore, he said: “In the past, monks, there was a teacher named Araka. This entire sutta, adorned with seven similes, should be recited in detail.
Furthermore, he said: “And as for that monk, monks, who develops mindfulness of death thus:
‘O, may I live for a day and night! May I attend to the Blessed One’s teaching! Surely much would be accomplished by me!’”
“Monks, there is the monk who develops mindfulness of death thus:
‘Oh, may I live for a day so that I might attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; indeed, much would be accomplished by me!
And there is the monk, monks, who develops mindfulness of death thus: ‘Oh, may I live for even half a day... [or] ‘...for as long as it takes to eat a single meal...’”
"While I am eating almsfood, may I attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; indeed, much would have been accomplished by me.
And as for that monk, bhikkhus, who develops mindfulness of death thus:
"Oh, may I live just long enough to chew and swallow four or five mouthfuls, so that I might attend to the Blessed One’s teaching!"

"Alas, much indeed would have been accomplished by me!"—these, monks, are called bhikkhus who dwell negligently, developing mindfulness of death slowly for the sake of the destruction of the taints. But as for that bhikkhu, monks, who develops mindfulness of death thus:
"O, may I live just as long as it takes to chew and swallow a single mouthful of food," [he is one who dwells diligently].
“I would attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; indeed, much would have been accomplished by me.

And as for the monk, bhikkhus, who develops mindfulness of death thus: “O, may I live for just the interval between one inhalation and exhalation, or between one exhalation and inhalation, so that I might attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; indeed, much would have been accomplished by me.”
“‘May it be done by me. These, monks, are called bhikkhus who dwell heedfully, developing mindfulness of death for the destruction of the taints.

Thus, one should recollect death in terms of the limitation of the lifespan, reflecting: “The duration of life is limited and not to be trusted, being no more than the consumption of four or five mouthfuls of alms-food.”
176. *The brevity of the moment*: In the ultimate sense, the moment of life for sentient beings is exceedingly brief, lasting no more than the occurrence of a single state of consciousness (*citta*).

Just as a chariot wheel, while rolling, rolls upon only one portion of the rim, and while standing still, stands upon only one portion, even so is the life of sentient beings, lasting for only a single moment of consciousness. As soon as that consciousness has ceased—
A being is said to have ceased. As it has been said: "In the past moment of consciousness, one lived; one does not live; one will not live.
In the future moment of consciousness, one did not live; one does not live; one will live. In the present moment of consciousness, one did not live;
one lives; one will not live."
“Life and the physical self, and all pleasure and pain—these are joined with a single moment of consciousness; that moment passes swiftly.
Those [states] which have ceased for one who is dying, or for one remaining here,”
All aggregates alike have passed away without re-linking.
“He is not born by means of what has not arisen; he lives by means of the present;
with the breakup of the mind, the world is dead—this is the ultimate designation.”
Thus death should be recollected by way of its brevity in each moment. 177.
Thus, for one who recollects by means of any one of these eight aspects, the mind receives cultivation through the power of repeated attention;
mindfulness with death as its object becomes established, and the hindrances are suppressed.

The factors of absorption (jhānaṅga) become manifest. However, because the object is a phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature (sabhāvadhamma) and because it is capable of inducing a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvejanīya), the absorption does not reach full absorption (appanā), but remains at the level of access concentration (upacāra).

But supramundane absorption (lokuttarajjhāna), as well as the second and fourth formless absorptions (āruppajjhāna), reach full absorption even when the object is a phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature, due to the excellence of their cultivation (bhāvanāvisesa). This occurs by way of the progressive sequence of the development of purification (visuddhibhāvanānukkamavasena).
For it reaches only access concentration (upacāra), not the supramundane absorption (appanā). It is called "formless" (āruppa) by way of cultivation that transcends the object;
for in that case, there is merely the transcendence of the object of an absorption that has already reached absorption. But here, neither of those two exists.
Therefore, the jhāna is only one that has reached access. And because it arises through the power of mindfulness of death, it is designated simply as "mindfulness of death" (maraṇassati).
Furthermore, a bhikkhu devoted to this mindfulness of death is constantly diligent;

he acquires the perception of disenchantment with all states of existence, abandons attachment to life, becomes a censurer of evil, possesses no stores of requisites and is free from the stain of stinginess regarding them;
his perception of impermanence reaches maturity, and by following that very path, his perception of suffering does likewise.

And the perception of non-self becomes established. Just as beings who have not cultivated the mindfulness of death suddenly fall into fear, terror, and delusion at the time of death—as if overcome by wild beasts, spirits, snakes, robbers, or assassins—one does not fall into such states, but passes away fearless and undeluded.
If one does not attain the Deathless in this very life, then with the breakup of the body, one has a fortunate destination as one's lot.
"Therefore, indeed, the wise person should always practice heedfulness regarding mindfulness of death, which possesses such great power.
This concludes the introductory section for the detailed exposition on mindfulness of death.
The Discourse on Mindfulness Directed to the Body 178.
Now, that which has never before occurred except through the arising of a Buddha, and which was outside the scope of all other sectarians, is stated in various Suttantas:
"Bhikkhus, one thing, when developed and cultivated, leads to great spiritual urgency."
It leads to great benefit. It leads to great security from bondage. It leads to great mindfulness and clear comprehension.
It leads to the acquisition of knowledge and vision. It leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life.
It leads to the realization of the fruit of true knowledge and liberation. What is that one thing? Mindfulness directed toward the body… the Deathless.
“Monks, those who enjoy mindfulness directed to the body enjoy the deathless.
Monks, those who do not enjoy mindfulness directed to the body do not enjoy the deathless.
For those, monks, by whom mindfulness directed to the body has been undertaken, the deathless has been enjoyed… not enjoyed… lost… not lost… missed… not missed.”
Having thus praised [mindfulness directed to the body] in many ways, the Blessed One said:
"Bhikkhus, how is mindfulness directed to the body developed and cultivated so that it becomes of great fruit and great benefit? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest...

and so forth, by way of the section on breathing (*ānāpānapabba*), the section on postures (*iriyāpathapabba*), the section on the four kinds of clear comprehension (*catusampajaññapabba*), and the section on attention to repulsiveness (*paṭikkūlamanasikārapabba*).
The meditation subject of mindfulness directed to the body has been explained by way of these fourteen sections:
the section on the postures, the section on the four kinds of clear comprehension, and the section on attention to the elements. Now follows the exposition of its development.
Therein, since the section on the postures, the section on the four kinds of clear comprehension, and the section on attention to the elements—these...

Three [sections] are stated by way of insight (vipassanā). The nine sections on the charnel ground (sivathika) are stated specifically within the knowledges of insight (vipassanā-ñāṇa) by way of contemplation of danger (ādīnavānupassanā).

Furthermore, whatever development of concentration (samādhi-bhāvanā) might succeed here regarding the bloated corpse (uddhumātaka) and so forth, that has already been explained in the description of foulness (asubha-niddesa).
However, these two—the section on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna) and the section on attention to repulsiveness (paṭikkūla-manasikāra)—are stated here by way of concentration (samādhi).
Among these, the section on mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-pabba*) is a distinct meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) by way of mindfulness of breathing itself. As for that which is stated:

"Furthermore, monks, a monk contemplates this very body, from the soles of the feet upwards and from the hair of the head downwards, bounded by the skin, as full of various kinds of impurity: 'In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs... [and so on] ...urine.'"

Thus, having included the brain within the bone-marrow, the meditation subject of the thirty-two aspects taught by way of the contemplation of repulsiveness is what is intended here by "mindfulness directed to the body" (kāyagatāsati). 179.
Herein, this is the exposition of the development preceded by a commentary on the Pāḷi: "This very body... refers to this body composed of the four great elements.
The putrid body. "Above the soles of the feet" means from the soles of the feet upwards. "Below the hair of the head" means from the tips of the hair downwards.

"Enclosed by skin" means bounded on all sides by the skin. "He reviews it as full of various kinds of impurity" means he sees that this body is filled with various kinds of impurities such as hair and so forth.
How? "In this body there are head-hairs... down to... urine."

In this context, "there is" (*atthi*) means they exist. "In this" (*imasmiṃ*) refers to that which is said to be full of various kinds of impurities, from the soles of the feet upwards and from the hair of the head downwards, bounded by the skin.

"Body" (*kāye*) means in the physical frame. For the body is called "body" (*kāya*) because it is a collection of impurities and because it is the source (*āya*) of the hundred diseases, such as those of the eyes and so forth, as well as of the loathsome things like the hair and so on.

"Head-hairs, body-hairs": these are the thirty-two aspects beginning with head-hairs. In this context, the connection should be understood as follows: "In this body there are head-hairs; in this body there are body-hairs.
For [the body] extends from the soles of the feet upwards to the crown of the head, and from the skin downwards.
Searching in every way within this entire body, measuring only a fathom in height, one does not see even the slightest atom of purity—
whether it be gold, a gem, beryl, aloeswood, saffron, camphor,
or scented powders and the like; rather, one sees only various forms that are utterly foul-smelling, loathsome, and devoid of beauty.
One sees only the impurity, distinguished by the various parts such as head-hairs and body-hairs. Therefore it was said: "In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs... down to... urine.
This is the commentary here according to the connection of the words. 180.
Now, by a clansman who is a beginner and desires to develop this meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), [the following] of the kind described should be done...
Having approached a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitta), this meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) should be taken up.

When explaining this meditation subject to him, the teacher must explain sevenfold skill in learning and tenfold skill in attention. Therein, sevenfold skill in learning should be explained as follows:
by way of word, by way of mind, by way of color, by way of shape, by way of direction, by way of location, and by way of delimitation.

For in this meditation subject of attention to repulsiveness, even one who is a master of the Three Piṭakas must first perform a verbal recitation when attending to it. For to some, the meditation subject becomes clear precisely while they are reciting;
as was the case for two [monks] who had learned the meditation subject in the presence of the Elder Mahādeva, the dweller of Mount Malaya.

It was like the case of the elders. It is said that when they requested a meditation subject from the elder, he gave them the text of the thirty-two aspects (dvattiṃsākāra), saying, "Recite this very text for four months.

Although they were already proficient in two or three Nikāyas, because of their skill in grasping the sequence, while reciting the thirty-two aspects for four months, they became stream-enterers (sotāpanna). Therefore, [this is] the meditation subject.
The teacher, while speaking, should say to the pupil: "First, perform the recitation by way of speech.

And while performing it, he should divide [the body parts] into the five groups beginning with the skin and recite them in both direct and reverse order. For after saying, "Head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin," he must then say in reverse order: "Skin, teeth, nails, body-hairs, head-hairs."

Immediately after that, having stated: "In the pentad of the kidneys: kidney, flesh, sinew, bone, and marrow," one should again state them in reverse order: "kidney, marrow, bone, sinew, flesh; skin, teeth, nails, body hair, and head hair.
Then, having stated: "In the pentad of the lungs: heart, liver, midriff, spleen, and lungs," one should again state them in reverse order:
"lungs, spleen, midriff, liver, heart; kidney, marrow, bone, sinew, and flesh."
It should be said: "skin, teeth, nails, body hair, head hair.
Then, having mentioned the five beginning with brain—intestines, mesentery, stomach-contents, feces, and brain—one should again state them in reverse order:
brain, feces, stomach-contents, mesentery, intestines; lungs, spleen, and kidney.
The liver, the heart, the kidneys, the bone marrow, the bones, the sinews, the flesh, the skin, the teeth, the nails, the body hairs, and the head hairs—these are what should be stated.
Then, having mentioned the group of six beginning with fat as bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, and fat, one should again state them in reverse order:
fat, sweat, blood, pus, phlegm, and bile; followed by the brain, feces, the contents of the stomach, the small intestines, and the large intestine.
It should be stated as: lungs, spleen, midriff, liver, heart, kidneys, bone marrow, bones, sinews, flesh, skin, teeth, nails, body hair, and head hair.
Then, having mentioned the group of six secretions—tears, grease, spittle, snot, synovial fluid, and urine—one should again [recite them] in reverse order.
It should be said: urine, synovial fluid, snot, saliva, fat, tears, marrow, sweat, blood, pus, phlegm, bile, brain matter, feces, stomach contents,
intestines, mesentery, rectum, lungs, spleen, kidneys, liver, heart,
kidneys [repeated], bone marrow, bones, sinews, flesh, skin, teeth, nails, body hair, and head hair.
In this way, the recitation should be performed verbally for a hundred times, a thousand times, or even a hundred thousand times.
For by verbal recitation, the thread of the meditation subject becomes proficient; the mind does not wander here and there.
The divisions become clear and appear like a row of fingers or a series of fence posts.

Just as it is with verbal recitation, so too should recitation be performed mentally. For verbal recitation is a condition for mental recitation, and mental recitation is a condition for the penetration of characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*).
As for "color" (*vaṇṇato*), the color of the head-hairs and so forth must be defined.
As for "shape" (*saṇṭhānato*), the shape of those very same things must be defined.

Regarding "direction": in this body, from the navel upwards is the upper direction and downwards is the lower direction; therefore, this constituent part should be defined as a direction by determining that "this is the name of this direction.
Regarding "location": one should define the location of each part by determining that "this constituent part is established in such-and-such a location.
Regarding "delimitation": there are two kinds of delimitation, namely, delimitation by the similar and delimitation by the dissimilar. Therein, this...
The delimitation by way of homogeneity should be understood thus: "This portion is bounded below, above, and across by such-and-such.
The delimitation by way of heterogeneity should be understood thus: "Head-hairs are not body-hairs; body-hairs are not head-hairs.
Furthermore, while explaining this sevenfold skill in learning, [the teacher] says: "This meditation subject [is found] in such-and-such a Sutta..."
It has been explained by way of repulsiveness; having understood that it is [also] by way of elements in such-and-such a place, it should be described.

For this was explained solely by way of repulsiveness in the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta*. It was explained by way of elements in the *Mahāhatthipadopama*, the *Mahārāhulovāda*, and the *Dhātuvibhaṅga* suttas.
However, in the *Kāyagatāsati Sutta*, with reference to one for whom it appears by way of color, the four jhānas are taught.
[The parts] are analyzed. Therein, that which is explained by way of the elements (*dhātu*) is the meditation subject for insight (*vipassanā-kammaṭṭhāna*).

That which is explained by way of the repulsive (*paṭikkūla*) is the meditation subject for serenity (*samatha-kammaṭṭhāna*). This, however, is here [treated as] exclusively the meditation subject for serenity.
181. Having thus explained the sevenfold skill in learning, [one should proceed] neither too quickly nor too slowly, in due order...
Skill in attention should be explained in ten ways: by warding off distraction, by transcending conceptual designation, by gradual relinquishing, by absorption, and by the three types of discourses.
Therein, "gradually" means that this should be attended to in successive order starting from the recitation, not skipping over intervals. If one skips over intervals...
For just as an unskilled man, while climbing a thirty-two-rung ladder by skipping every other step,

falls with a weary body and fails to complete the ascent, even so, because he does not attain the gratification that is to be reached through the perfection of development, he falls with a weary mind and does not complete the development.
Furthermore, when attending to it in successive order, one should not attend to it too rapidly.
For if one attends to it too rapidly— just as a man who, having set out on a three-league journey,
fails to observe the turns and descents and travels back and forth a hundred times with great speed, even though he has exhausted the distance— [the path remains unmastered].

Just as one who goes must first ask for directions before proceeding, so too, if one reaches the conclusion of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) while it is still unclear, it will not bring about any distinction; therefore, it should not be attended to too quickly.
And just as it should not be too quick, so it should not be too slow either. For if one attends to it too slowly, just as if...
Just as for a man wishing to travel a three-league journey who lingers along the way among trees,
mountains, ponds, and so forth, the path is not exhausted; it must be completed over two or three days— so too,
the meditation subject does not reach its conclusion and does not become a condition for the attainment of distinction.
"By warding off distraction": having set aside the meditation subject, the mind's distraction toward external, manifold objects must be warded off.

For if it is not so warded off, just as when a man walking along a narrow, precipitous path fails to observe his footstep and looks here and there, his footing is lost; then, from a height of a hundred men...
Just as one must fall over a precipice, even so, when there is external distraction, the meditation subject declines and is ruined.
Therefore, it should be brought to mind by warding off distraction.
"By transcending the description" means that having transcended this description beginning with "head-hairs, body-hairs," one [contemplates] it as "repulsive."

The mind should be established. For just as when people see a well in the forest during a time of water scarcity, they tie some kind of marker there, such as a palm leaf, and later come by that marker to bathe and drink;
but when their path becomes familiar through frequent travel, then [they no longer need] the marker—
There is no need for such effort; they go and bathe and drink whenever they wish.

In the same way, when one attends to the head hairs and body hairs by way of their designation in the preliminary stage, the repulsiveness becomes manifest. Then, having transcended the designation "head hairs" and "body hairs," the mind should be fixed upon the repulsiveness itself.
"By successive relinquishing" means that one should attend to the parts by successively relinquishing whichever part does not appear clearly.
For when a beginner attends to "head-hairs," the attention proceeds until it comes to rest only upon this final part, "urine. And when attending to "urine," the attention proceeds...
The word "hair" (kesā) refers to this very first section.

As he attends to it again and again, some sections appear clearly while others do not. Therefore, he should perform his work on whichever parts do appear, until when two have appeared, one of them appears even more clearly. Thus...
Having established that very object, absorption should be produced by attending to it again and again.

Here is a simile for this: Suppose a hunter, wishing to catch a monkey living in a palm grove of thirty-two palms, were to pierce the leaf of the palm standing at the edge with an arrow and raise a shout; then that monkey—
Falling in succession from one palm tree to another, it would reach the very last palm;
having gone there, when the hunter acted in the same manner again, it would return by that same path to the first palm.
Being made to fall again and again in this way, it would rise up at each place where a shout was raised, and gradually, falling upon a single palm tree, it would land in its center.
Even when pierced while firmly grasping a pointed leaf from a budding palm tree, [the monkey] would not let go;
this should be understood as being exactly like that. Herein is the application of the simile: just as there are thirty-two palms in the palm grove, so too there are thirty-two parts in this body.
The mind is like the monkey. The hunter is like the practitioner (yogāvacara). The monkey’s dwelling in the palm grove of thirty-two palms is [like the mind’s dwelling in the body].
It is like the mind of a yogi wandering through the thirty-two parts of the body by way of the object;
it is like the monkey who, when a hunter pierced the leaf of the palm tree standing at the beginning with an arrow and raised a shout,
fell from one palm tree to another until it reached the last palm tree, once the yogi’s attention was directed toward "the head" in its proper sequence.
The settling of the mind occurs only at the very end of the sequence. The same method applies when returning again.
Just as a monkey repeatedly climbing up and down stands still only at the place where it was first called out, so too for one who attends repeatedly:
when certain objects appear and others do not, one should let go of those that do not appear and perform the preliminary work (*parikamma*) on those that do appear.
Gradually, having settled upon a single palm leaf, one should grasp firmly the tip of a young palm leaf in its center and pierce it;
even while being pierced, as if there were no rising from the posture, when two images eventually appear at the conclusion,
one should repeatedly bring to mind that which appears more clearly and thus generate absorption (*appanā*).

There is another simile: suppose a *piṇḍapātika* bhikkhu, living in dependence on a village of thirty-two families, were to receive two alms at the very first house on the first day and set aside one for later;
then on the following day, having received three, he were to set aside two for later; and on the third day, having received a bowlful right at the beginning, he were to go to the sitting hall.
One should enjoy it. This should be understood in the same way. For the thirty-two aspects (dvattiṃsākāra) are like the village of thirty-two families;

the practitioner (yogāvacara) is like the alms-collector (piṇḍapātiko); his dwelling in dependence on that village is like the meditator’s performance of the preliminary work (parikamma) on the thirty-two aspects;
and receiving two alms at the first house and declining the one beyond is like [the practice of moderation].
On the second day, having obtained three [instances], he discards them as if to hand them over to the next two;
and by attending to them again and again, he discards those that do not appear and attends to those that do, until he has performed the preliminary work on the two sections.
On the third day, just as one who receives a bowl full at the very beginning sits in the refectory and consumes it, so too [he attends] to whichever of the two is better established.
"Arises" means the production of absorption (*appanā*) by repeatedly attending to that very object.
Regarding "absorption": the intention here is that one should understand that absorption occurs in each individual part among the parts, such as the head-hairs and so forth.

And regarding "the three discourses": the intention here is that these three discourses—on higher consciousness, on coolness, and on skill in the factors of enlightenment—should be understood for the purpose of yoking energy with concentration. In this regard:
“Monks, a monk devoted to the higher mind should from time to time attend to three signs.
From time to time he should attend to the sign of concentration; from time to time he should attend to the sign of exertion;
from time to time he should attend to the sign of equanimity. If, monks, a monk devoted to the higher mind...”
If he were to attend exclusively to the sign of concentration, it is possible that his mind would lead to indolence.

If, monks, a bhikkhu devoted to higher consciousness were to attend exclusively to the sign of exertion, it is possible that his mind would lead to restlessness. If, monks, a bhikkhu devoted to higher consciousness...
If he were to attend exclusively to the sign of equanimity, it is possible that his mind would not become rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints.
But when, monks, a bhikkhu devoted to higher consciousness attends from time to time to the sign of concentration,
the sign of exertion, and the sign of equanimity, his mind becomes pliant.
It becomes workable and luminous, not brittle, and it is rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints.
"Just as, bhikkhus, a goldsmith or a goldsmith’s apprentice prepares a furnace; having prepared the furnace, he heats the mouth of the furnace;
having heated the mouth of the furnace, he takes up some gold with tongs and places it in the mouth of the furnace..."
Having placed it [in the furnace], he fans it from time to time, sprinkles it with water from time to time, and observes it with equanimity from time to time.
Monks, if that goldsmith or his apprentice were to fan that gold exclusively, there is the possibility that the gold would burn up. If, monks, the goldsmith...
Or if a goldsmith or a goldsmith’s apprentice were to sprinkle that gold entirely with water, it is possible that the gold would go out.
But if, monks, the goldsmith or the goldsmith’s apprentice were to entirely neglect that gold, it is possible that the gold would not reach full maturity. And when...
Monks, that goldsmith or goldsmith’s apprentice from time to time blows upon that gold, from time to time sprinkles it with water, and from time to time observes it closely;
that gold becomes soft, workable, radiant, and not brittle, and it properly adapts itself to the task at hand. Whatever kind of ornament—
If he desires it for a necklace, or for earrings, or for a neck-ornament, or for a golden garland, he attains that purpose.
"In the same way, monks, for one devoted to the higher mind... [the mind] becomes concentrated for the destruction of the taints.
And whatever state of direct knowledge is to be realized, toward which he inclines his mind, he realizes that direct knowledge."
“...in whatever sphere there may be, he attains the state of being capable of realizing it through action.
This sutta should be understood as pertaining to higher consciousness (*adhicitta*).
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with six qualities is capable of realizing the unsurpassed state of coolness.”
By what six? Here, monks, at whatever time the mind should be restrained, at that time he restrains the mind.
At whatever time the mind should be exerted, at that time he exerts the mind.
At whatever time the mind should be encouraged, at that time he encourages the mind.
At whatever time the mind should be looked upon with equanimity, at that time he looks upon the mind with equanimity.
And he is resolutely intent on the sublime and delights in Nibbāna. "Possessing these six qualities, monks, a bhikkhu is capable of realizing the unsurpassed state of coolness."
This sutta should be understood as the unsurpassed state of coolness.

Furthermore, skill in the factors of enlightenment has already been shown in the discussion on skill in absorption, where it says: "Bhikkhus, when the mind is sluggish, that is not the time for the development of the tranquility factor of enlightenment.
Thus, having properly grasped these seven kinds of skill in learning and this tenfold skill in attention, [one should proceed].
Having well defined it, that yogin should thoroughly master the meditation subject by means of proficiency in both respects.
However, if he finds it convenient to stay in the same monastery as his teacher, he need not have it explained in such detail;
rather, having well defined the meditation subject, he should apply himself to it, and after attaining distinction, [he should proceed] further and further.

It should be explained. One who wishes to dwell elsewhere, having had it explained in detail according to the method already stated, and having repeatedly recited it until all knotty points are severed, should abandon an unsuitable dwelling and live in a suitable monastery. Having cut off minor impediments, he should apply his attention to the repulsive in the manner described in the exposition of the earth-kasiṇa.
The preliminary work (parikamma) should be performed.
While doing so, one should first apprehend the sign (nimitta) in the hair. How?
Having plucked out one or two hairs and placed them on the palm of the hand, their color should first be defined. It is also permissible to look at the place where they were plucked out.
It is even permissible to look at water in a bowl or rice gruel in a bowl. When they appear black, one should attend to them as "black";
when they appear white, as "white. But when they appear mixed, they should be attended to according to whichever color predominates.
And just as with the head hairs, so too the sign should be grasped by observing the entire fivefold skin.
The Discourse on the Definition of the Parts (Koṭṭhāsa-vavatthāpana-kathā) 182.

Having thus apprehended the sign and defined all the parts by way of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation, they should be defined as repulsive in five ways: by way of color, shape, smell, habitat, and location.
Herein, this is the sequential explanation for all the parts. First, head-hairs are black by their natural color, the color of black ariṭṭhaka berries.
In terms of shape, it is long and cylindrical, having the shape of a balance-beam. In terms of direction, it is produced in the upper direction.
In terms of location, it is delimited on both sides by the ear-lobes, in front by the edge of the forehead, and behind by the nape of the neck.

It is the moist skin covering the skull that constitutes the location of the head-hairs. In terms of delimitation, the head-hairs enter into the skin covering the head to the extent of a grain of rice.
The delimitation by way of common characteristics (*sabhāga-pariccheda*) is as follows: [the hair] is delimited below by its own root-base, above by space, and across by one another;

thus, there are no two hairs together. The delimitation by way of uncommon characteristics (*visabhāga-pariccheda*) is as follows: "Hairs are not body-hairs, and body-hairs are not hairs"—in this way, the so-called "hairs" are a single, distinct component unmixed with the remaining thirty-one components.
This is the definition of head hairs by way of their color and so forth. 183.

This, however, is their fivefold definition by way of repulsiveness according to color and so on: These head hairs are repulsive by way of color; they are repulsive by way of shape, smell, habitat, and location.
For even if one sees something the color of head hair in a bowl of pleasant rice gruel or a bowl of rice, one thinks, "This is mixed with head hair."
They pull them out, they destroy them, and they feel disgust toward them. Thus, hair is repulsive by way of its color.
Even those who eat at night feel the same disgust upon touching a tuft of hair, whether it be from a grain husk or a piece of bark cloth; thus, it is repulsive by way of its shape.
Furthermore, the odor of hair that is devoid of any refinement—such as being anointed with oil or scented with flowers and incense—is utterly loathsome.
It is even more loathsome than that when cast into the fire. For although hair may not be repulsive in terms of its color or shape, it is indeed repulsive by its odor.
Just as the excrement of a young boy is yellow like turmeric in color and shaped like a lump of turmeric, so too is the bloated corpse of a black dog discarded in a rubbish heap.
In terms of color, it is the color of a ripe palmyra fruit. In terms of shape, it has the shape of a mudiṅga drum that has been rounded and set down.
Its fang is like a jasmine bud; thus, both in color and shape, it might not be repulsive, but in terms of odor, it is indeed repulsive.
In the same way, head hairs might also be non-repulsive in terms of color and shape, but they are certainly repulsive in terms of odor.
Just as vegetables grown in a place of filth through the seepage from a village are disgusting to city-dwellers and unfit for consumption,
so too, because hair is produced from the seepage of pus, blood, urine, feces, bile, phlegm,
and so forth, it is disgusting; this is their repulsiveness by way of their source.
These things called hairs grow upon a heap of thirty-one parts like a fungus arising on a mound of dung.
Because they grow in an impure location—like vegetables grown in a charnel ground or a rubbish heap, or like lotuses and water-lilies growing in mud—they are supremely disgusting;
this is their repulsiveness by way of location.
Just as with the head-hairs, so too the repulsiveness of all the body parts should be understood in five ways: by way of color, shape, smell, location, and habitat.
Furthermore, all of them should be defined individually by way of their color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation. 184.
Among these, first of all, the body-hairs (*loma*) do not, by their natural color, possess an unmixed blackness like that of the head-hairs; rather, they are blackish-brown.
They exist. By way of shape, they have downward-pointing tips and are shaped like the base of a palm tree. By way of direction, they are produced in two directions.

By way of location, setting aside the area where the head hairs are established and the palms and soles of the hands and feet, they are produced for the most part in the skin that envelops the rest of the body.
By way of delimitation, having entered to the depth of a fingernail's breadth into the skin that envelops the body, they are established below their own [surface].
They are delimited by their base below, by space above, and by one another horizontally; there are no two hairs together.
This is their delimitation by way of similarity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Their delimitation by way of dissimilarity (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
185. "Nails" is the name for the twenty nail-leaves. All of them are white in color. In shape, they have the form of fish scales.
In terms of direction, they are born in two directions: the toe-nails in the lower direction and the finger-nails in the upper direction.

In terms of location, they are established on the tips and backs of the fingers. In terms of delimitation, they are bounded on the two sides by the flesh at the tips of the fingers, internally by the flesh on the backs of the fingers, externally and at the tips by space, and crosswise by one another.

There are no two nails on the same finger; this is their delimitation by way of similarity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Their delimitation by way of dissimilarity (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
186. "Teeth": For one with a full set of teeth, there are thirty-two tooth-bones. These too, in terms of color, are white. In terms of shape, they are of various shapes.
Regarding them, first, in the middle of the lower row of teeth, there are four teeth [which are like] lumps of clay...
They are shaped like gourd seeds placed in succession. On both sides of these, there are two each—one-rooted and one-pointed, shaped like jasmine buds;
then two each—two-rooted and two-pointed, shaped like a cart-supporting block;
then two each—three-rooted and three-pointed; and then two each—four-rooted and four-pointed. This is also the case for the upper series.
The same method applies. By way of direction, they are born in the upper direction. By way of location, they are established upon the two jaw-bones. By way of delimitation:
they are delimited below by their own root-surface as it rests upon the jaw-bone, above by space, and across by one another;

there are no two teeth on the same side—this is their delimitation by way of similarity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Their delimitation by way of dissimilarity (*visabhāga-pariccheda*) is as follows: [and so forth].
But it is just like the hair. 187.
*Taca* (skin) refers to the skin that stands enveloping the entire body. Above that is the outer covering (*chavi*) of colors such as black, brown, yellow, and so forth;
even when gathered from the whole body, it is only the size of a jujube seed. As for the skin (*taca*), by way of color—
It is white. This whiteness becomes evident when the skin has been destroyed by the impact of flames, blows from weapons, and so forth.
As for its shape, it is the same as the shape of the body. This is the summary here.
In detail, however, the skin of the toes is the shape of a weaver’s shuttle-case; the skin of the back of the foot is the shape of a pair of sandals with straps.
The skin of the calves is shaped like a palm leaf used as a food container. The skin of the thighs is shaped like a long bag filled with rice.
The skin of the buttocks is shaped like a water-strainer made of cloth filled with water. The skin of the back is shaped like leather stretched over a wooden board.
The skin of the belly is shaped like leather stretched over the hollow body of a lute. The skin of the chest is for the most part square-shaped.
The skin of both arms is shaped like a quiver bound with leather. The skin of the back of the hands is shaped like a razor-case or like a case for a fan.
The skin of the fingers is shaped like a key-case. The skin of the neck is shaped like a collar.
The skin of the face is perforated here and there and is shaped like the nest of an insect. The skin of the head is shaped like a leaf-case.

And the practitioner who is investigating the parts [of the body] should, starting from the upper lip, direct his knowledge upwards and first define the skin that covers the mouth; then the skin of the frontal bone;
then the skin of the skull, which is like a hand placed between a bowl and its bag.
Having sent knowledge between the scalp and the skin, one should define the scalp by separating the skin from the bone as if they were joined together.
After that, the skin of the shoulder. Then the skin of the right hand in both forward and reverse order.
Then, by that same method, the skin of the left hand. After that, the skin of the back. That...
Having defined the skin of the right foot both in direct and reverse order, one should then define the skin of the left foot by that same method.
Thereafter, in successive order, the skin of the bladder, the belly, the heart, and the neck should be defined.
Then, immediately after the skin of the neck, having defined the skin of the lower jaw and brought it down to the edge of the lower lip, one should conclude. Thus...
For one who comprehends the gross within the gross, even the subtle becomes manifest. As to direction, it is born in two directions.
As to location, it stands enveloping the entire body. As to delimitation, it is delimited below by its base of support and above by space;
this is its delimitation by way of similar parts (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Its delimitation by way of dissimilar parts (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
188. There are nine hundred pieces of flesh. All of these, by way of color, are red, like the *kiṃsuka* flower. By way of shape:
the flesh of the calf is shaped like rice placed in a palm-leaf basket; the flesh of the thigh is shaped like a sitting mat (*nisadapota*);
the flesh of the buttocks is shaped like the edge of a hearth; the flesh of the back is shaped like a layer of palm sugar; and the flesh of the two sides...
The flesh of the belly has the shape of a coating of thin clay on a wicker basket. The flesh of the breasts has the shape of lumps of clay thrown down after being rounded off.
The flesh of the two arms has the shape of two large, skinless rats placed side by side.
As one thus discerns [the body] in its coarsest form, even the subtle becomes evident. By way of direction, it is born in two directions. By way of location, there are more than twenty...
It stands smeared with three hundred bones. As for its delimitation: it is delimited below by the surface resting on the skeletal mass, above by the skin, and all around by each other;

this is its delimitation by way of its own nature (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Its delimitation by way of what is not of its own nature (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
189. As for sinews, there are nine hundred sinews. By way of color, all the sinews are white. By way of shape, they are of various shapes.
For among them, starting from the upper part of the neck, five great sinews descend along the front side of the body, binding it;
five along the back side; five along the right side; and five along the left side. [The sinews] of the right hand...
Even when binding the right hand, there are five [tendons] on the front side of the hand and five on the back side. Likewise when binding the left hand.
Even when binding the right foot, there are five on the front side of the foot and five on the back side. Likewise when binding the left foot.
Thus, there are sixty great sinews called "body-supporters" that sustain the body.
Those that are called *kaṇḍarā* are also intertwined and have descended [into the body]; they all have the shape of a *kandaḷa* flower bud.
Others, however, stand covering various locations; they are finer than those and have the shape of cords or ropes.
Still others are finer than those and have the shape of withered creepers; others are even finer than those and have the shape of the strings of a great lute (*mahāvīṇā*).
Others are shaped like thick cords. The sinews on the backs of the hands and feet are shaped like the feet of birds.
The sinews in the head are shaped like a children’s net cap. The sinews in the back are shaped like a wet net spread out in the sun.
The remaining sinews following each respective limb and member are shaped like a suit of mail fastened to the body. As for direction, they are in two [directions].

They are born in all directions. In terms of location, they stand by binding together the bones throughout the entire body. In terms of delimitation: below, they are delimited by the surfaces resting upon the three hundred bones;
above, by the regions where they touch the flesh and skin; and across, they are delimited by one another.
This is their delimitation by way of similarity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Their delimitation by way of dissimilarity (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.

190. Regarding "bones": setting aside the thirty-two teeth-bones, there are the remaining sixty-four hand-bones, sixty-four foot-bones, sixty-four soft bones attached to the flesh, two heel-bones, two ankle-bones in each foot, two shin-bones, one knee-bone, one thigh-bone, and two hip-bones.
There are eighteen vertebrae, twenty-four ribs, fourteen breast-bones,
one heart-bone, two collarbones, two shoulder-blades, two upper-arm bones,
two pairs of forearm bones, seven neck bones, two jawbones, one nose-bone, two eye-bones, and two ear-bones.
There is one frontal bone; one skull bone; and nine cranial bones—thus there are exactly three hundred bones.
As for their color, they are all white. As for their shape, they are of various shapes.
Among them, the bones of the toes of the feet are shaped like *kataka* seeds; the bones of the middle joints immediately following those are...

The sixty bones [of the fingers and toes] are shaped like *panasa* fruits. The bones of the root-mountains (the metacarpals/metatarsals) are shaped like small drums (*paṇava*). The bones of the back of the foot are shaped like crushed *kandala* or *kandarāsi* roots.
The heel bone is shaped like the single stone of a palm fruit. The ankle bones are shaped like balls bound together for play.
The part of the shin bones where they rest upon the ankle bones is shaped like the peeled stalk of a *sindika* plant. The small shin bone—
It has the shape of a bow-staff. It is large and has the shape of the back of a withered snake. The knee-bone has the shape of a foam-bubble worn away on one side.
Therein, the part where the shin-bone is fixed has the shape of the sharp point of a cow’s horn. The thigh-bone has the shape of a badly whittled handle for an axe or a hatchet.
The part where it is fixed in the hip-bone has the shape of a play-ball. By that [thigh-bone], the part where the hip-bone is fixed...
It has the shape of a large *puṇṇāga* fruit with its tip cut off.
The two hip-bones (*kaṭiṭṭhi*) are joined together as one, having the shape of a potter’s kiln; individually, they have the shape of a blacksmith’s bellows-fastener.
The sacrum bone (*ānisadaṭṭhi*) situated at the corner has the shape of a cobra’s hood held with its mouth turned downward, [resting] upon seven or eight places.
"Full of apertures and interstices": the vertebrae of the spinal column are, internally, shaped like a series of head-caps placed one upon another;
externally, they are shaped like rounded beads. Between them, there are two or three thorns resembling the teeth of a saw.
Among the twenty-four ribs, those that are incomplete are shaped like the incomplete head of a sword, while those that are complete—
The bones of the head are shaped like a full-blown fan. All [the ribs] are shaped like the outspread wings of a white cock.
The fourteen breast-bones are shaped like the frame of an old chariot. The heart-bone is shaped like the blade of a spear.
The collarbones are shaped like small iron handles for axes. The shoulder-blades are shaped like Sinhalese hoes worn down on one side.
The bones of the upper arms are shaped like the handles of mirrors. The bones of the forearms are shaped like twin palm-bulbs.
The bones of the wrists are shaped like headbands and turbans placed together side by side. The bones of the back of the hands are shaped like crushed kanda-rasika roots.
Among the fingers of the hand, the bones of the proximal joints are shaped like small drums (paṇava). The bones of the middle joints are shaped like incomplete jackfruit seeds.
The vertebrae at the peak of the spine are shaped like *kataka* seeds.
The seven cervical vertebrae, when pierced with a rod and placed in succession, are shaped like a bamboo stalk, a wheel-rim, and a ring.
The lower jawbone is shaped like the iron hammer-and-rope of smiths; the upper jawbone is shaped like a scraping knife.

The bones of the eye-sockets and nose-sockets are shaped like young palm-stalks from which the pith has been removed. The frontal bone is shaped like the bowl of a conch-shell vessel placed face down.

The bones of the ear-lobes are shaped like the cases for a barber’s razor. Above the frontal bone and the ear-lobes, in the place where a headband would be fastened, it is shaped like a fragment of a broken bowl full of water with its rim folded inward.
The skull bone is shaped like a curved coconut with its top cut off.
The skull bones have the shape of a worn-out gourd pot set upon its rim.
As for their direction, they are located in two directions. As for their location, they reside without distinction throughout the entire body;
specifically, however, the skull bones rest upon the neck bones, the neck bones upon the vertebrae, and the vertebrae [upon the hips].
The hip bones rest upon the thigh bones; the thigh bones upon the knee bones; the knee bones upon the shin bones;
the shin bones upon the ankle bones; and the ankle bones are established upon the bones of the insteps. As for its delimitation:
it is delimited internally by the marrow, above by the flesh, and at its ends and base by each other. This is...
This is their delimitation by way of similarity. Their delimitation by way of dissimilarity, however, is the same as that of the head-hairs. 191.
"Bone marrow" (*aṭṭhimiñja*) refers to the marrow located inside those various bones. By way of color, it is white.
By way of shape, in the case of very large bones, it has the shape of the tip of a large bamboo shoot placed inside a bamboo tube and dried.
Regarding the minor and very minor bones: as for their shape, they are like the moistened, thin tips of bamboo shoots inserted into the joints of bamboo stalks.
As for their direction, they are located in two directions. As for their location, they are established within the bones.

As for their delimitation, they are delimited by the inner surfaces of the bones; this is their delimitation by way of similarity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Their delimitation by way of dissimilarity (*visabhāga-pariccheda*) is as follows: [text continues].
But it is exactly like hair. 192.
The kidneys are two pieces of flesh with a single attachment. As to color, they are pale red, the color of *pālibhaddaka* seeds.
As to shape, they are the shape of twin play-balls for children, or the shape of two mango fruits attached to a single stalk.

Or: by direction, it is born in the upper direction. By location, having emerged from the throat-pit, it proceeds a short distance with a single root and, being split into two, remains bound by thick sinews, surrounding the heart-flesh.
By delimitation, the kidney is delimited by its own kidney-parts; this is its delimitation by way of its own nature.
The delimitation by way of difference is exactly the same as that for the head-hairs.
193. "Heart" refers to the heart-flesh. By way of color, it is the color of the back of a red lotus petal.
By way of shape, it has the shape of a lotus bud placed face down with its outer petals removed. It is smooth on the outside, but inside...
It is like the interior of a *kosātakī* fruit. For those with wisdom it is slightly opened;

for those of dull wisdom it remains merely as a bud. Inside it there is a hollow about the size of a *punnāga* seed, wherein blood the measure of half a *pasata* collects, depending upon which the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) function. And this, moreover—
For one of lustful temperament, it is red; for one of hateful temperament, it is blackish; for one of deluded temperament, it is like water used for washing meat;
for one of discursive-thought temperament, it has the color of pea-soup; for one of faithful temperament, it has the color of a *kaṇikāra* flower;
and for one of wise temperament, it is clear, serene, undisturbed, bright, and utterly pure, radiant like a well-polished natural gem.
It appears. As to direction, it is born in the upper direction. As to location, it is situated within the body between the two breasts.
As to delimitation, the heart is delimited by its own cardiac portion; this is its delimitation by way of its own nature (*sabhāga-pariccheda*).
Its delimitation by way of what is dissimilar (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
194. *Yakana* means the twin layers of flesh. As to color, it is reddish-pale, the color of the back of a slightly red water-lily leaf.
As to shape, it is single at the base and twin at the tip, shaped like a *koviḷāra* leaf.
Furthermore, for those who are dull-witted, it is a single large one; for those with wisdom, there are two or three small ones. As to direction...
It is born in the upper direction; in terms of location, it stands on the right side within the space between the two breasts.
In terms of delimitation, the liver is delimited by its own liver-portion; this is its delimitation by way of its own nature (*sabhāga-pariccheda*).
Its delimitation by way of what is dissimilar (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
195. *Kilomaka* (membrane) is of two kinds, distinguished as concealed and unconcealed; it is the flesh that envelops [the internal organs].
Both these types are white in color, the hue of *dukūla* cloth or rags. As for their shape, they conform to the shape of their respective locations.
As for their direction, the concealed membrane is in the upper direction, while the other is produced in both directions. As for their location, the concealed membrane is found on the heart and...
Having covered the kidneys, the *kilomaka*—which remains un-covered—lies beneath the skin of the entire body, enveloping the flesh.
By way of delimitation, it is bounded below by the flesh, above by the skin, and on all sides by the portions of the *kilomaka* itself;

this is its delimitation by way of its own nature (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Its delimitation by way of what is not of its own nature (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
196. The tongue-muscle of the belly (pārśvaka). By way of color, it is blue, the color of a *nigguṇḍī* flower.
By way of shape, it measures seven finger-breadths, is unattached, and has the shape of the tongue of a black goat kid. By way of direction, it is born in the upper direction.
By way of location, it is situated on the left side of the heart, resting against the upper side of the abdominal membrane.
It is that in which the destruction of the life of beings occurs by the stroke of a weapon when it has been struck. By way of delimitation, it is delimited by its own parts;
this is its delimitation by way of similar parts (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Its delimitation by way of dissimilar parts (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
197. *Papphāsa* (lungs) refers to the lung-flesh, which is divided into thirty-two portions of flesh. By way of color, it is red.
In color, it is like the hue of an over-ripe udumbara fruit. In shape, it has the form of a thick piece of cake that has been unevenly cut.

Because it is struck by the heat of the fire born of karma (*kammaja-tejo*) arising from the absence of food and drink within, it is tasteless and devoid of nutritive essence (*rasa* and *oja*), like a lump of parched straw.
As for direction, it is located in the upper direction. As for location, it is inside the body between the two breasts.
It stands hanging down, covering the heart and the liver on top. By way of delimitation, it is delimited by the portion of the lungs;
this is its delimitation by way of similarity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Its delimitation by way of dissimilarity (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
198. *Anta* (the entrails): in a man it is thirty-two cubits long, in a woman twenty-eight cubits, [measured] across twenty-one places.
The inner intestinal coil is collapsed. By way of color, it is white, the color of lime plaster mixed with gravel.
By way of shape, it has the form of a snake whose head has been cut off and placed coiled within a red bowl. By way of direction, it is situated in two directions.
By way of location, because it is bound above at the gullet and below at the path of excrement, it is found within the interior of the body, bounded by the gullet and the path of excrement.

As for its location: it is situated within the interior. By way of delimitation, it is bounded by the inner part; this is its delimitation by way of its own nature (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Its delimitation by way of what is dissimilar (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
199. "The entrail" (*antaguṇa*) refers to the ligament binding the various parts of the intestines. As for its color, it is white, with the color of the root of the *dakasītalika* plant.
In terms of shape, it has the shape of the root of a water-cooling plant (*dakasītalika*). In terms of direction, it is produced in two directions.

In terms of location, for those performing work with a spade, axe, and so forth, at the time of drawing a machine, it remains like the cords of a machine, not slipping together at one end within the inner folds;
rather, it stands like a cord woven between the foot-wiping rope and the circular frame, [extending] across twenty-one [fingers].
It is situated between the internal organs. By way of delimitation, it is delimited by its own portion of the entrails; this is its delimitation by way of similarity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*).
Its delimitation by way of dissimilarity (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
200. *Udariya* (stomach contents) refers to what has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted within the belly. By way of color, it has the color of the food that has been swallowed.
By way of shape, it has the shape of rice grains loosely bound in a strainer. By way of direction, it is located in the upper direction.
By way of location, it resides in the stomach.
The stomach is the inner lining of the intestines, resembling a blister that has formed in the middle of a wet cloth when it is squeezed from both sides.
It is smooth on the outside, but inside it resembles a filthy silk garment wrapped around a mass of flesh and bones,
or it may be said to resemble the interior of a rotting jackfruit skin; therein, worms of thirty-two species,
such as *takkoṭakas*, *gaṇḍuppādakas*, *tālahīrakas*, *sūcimukhakas*, and *paṭatantasuttakas*, move about in dense clusters, crowding and swarming together.
They dwell there, and when food, drink, and so forth are unavailable, they leap up and cry out, striking at the heart-flesh;
and at the time of swallowing food, drink, and the like, they turn their faces upward and greedily scramble for two or three mouthfuls of what was first swallowed.
That place of these worms is a maternity chamber, a latrine, and a sickroom.

And there is a cemetery. Just as, for example, at the gate of a village of outcasts, during the summer season when the rain falls in heavy drops, various kinds of corpses—urine, feces, skin, bones, pieces of flesh, spittle, snot, blood, and so forth—are carried by the water and fall into a cesspool;
after two or three days have passed, they become churned into mud and water, swarming with families of worms, and heated by the force of the sun’s heat.
Just as a mass of froth and bubbles being emitted from above— deep blue in color, extremely foul-smelling and loathsome—
remains in a state unfit even to be approached or seen, let alone smelled or tasted;
even so is food and drink of various kinds, crushed by the pestle-like teeth and smeared with the spittle and saliva moved about by the tongue and hands.
Having fallen down, its excellence of color, fragrance, taste, and so forth having vanished at that very moment,
it becomes like the saliva or vomit of a weaver; enveloped by bile, phlegm, and wind, heated by the force of the digestive fire in the stomach,
teeming with swarms of worms, and emitting layers upon layers of froth and bubbles, it remains in a state of supreme putridity, foul stench, and loathsomeness.
Even upon merely hearing of it, a sense of repulsiveness regarding food, drink, and so forth arises, let alone after examining it with the eye of wisdom.
And wherever that fallen food, drink, and so forth undergoes fivefold separation—
one portion is consumed by living creatures, one portion is burnt up by the digestive fire, one portion becomes urine, one portion becomes feces, and one portion—
Having reached the state of chyle (*rasa*), it nourishes the blood, flesh, and so forth.

By way of delimitation, it is bounded by the lining of the stomach and by its own internal portion; this is its delimitation by way of similarity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Its delimitation by way of dissimilarity (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
201. *Karīsa* means feces. By way of color, it is for the most part the very color of the food swallowed. By way of shape...
Its shape is that of a space. By way of direction, it is located in the lower direction. By way of location, it resides in the receptacle for digested food (*pakvāśaya*).
The receptacle for digested food is situated between the base of the navel and the root of the spinal vertebrae at the end of the intestines;
it is about eight finger-breadths in height and resembles a bamboo tube. Just as rainwater falling on the upper surface of the ground flows down into it...
Just as it stands filling the lower part of the ground, even so whatever food, drink,
and so forth has fallen into the stomach is cooked by the digestive fire until it becomes frothy; then,

having been repeatedly pressed down like crushed sesamum and attained a smooth consistency, it trickles through the interior of the intestines and accumulates there, like yellow clay being poured into a bamboo tube.
It remains after being offered as an oblation. By way of delimitation, it is bounded by the membrane of the large intestine and by the portion of feces;
this is its delimitation by way of similarity. Its delimitation by way of dissimilarity, however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
202. "Brain" refers to the mass of marrow situated within the skull. By way of color, it is white, having the color of a cluster of *ahicchattaka* mushrooms.
It is also appropriate to call it "the color of spoiled milk" before it has reached the state of curd. By way of shape, it is the shape of its location.
By way of direction, it is born in the upper direction.
By way of location, it remains heaped together like four lumps of dough placed together, supported by the four seams within the skull. By way of delimitation, [it is delimited] by the skull...
It is delimited by the inner membranes and the portion of the brain; this is its delimitation by way of similarity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*).
Its delimitation by way of dissimilarity (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
203. *Pitta* (bile) refers to two types of bile: localized bile (*baddha-pitta*) and non-localized bile (*abaddha-pitta*). Among these, as for the color of localized bile:
Bound bile has the color of thick madhuka oil; unbound bile has the color of a withered *ākulī* flower. As for their shape, both are shaped according to their respective locations.
As for their direction, bound bile arises in the upper direction, while the other arises in two directions.

As for their location, excluding unbound bile, [the locations of bound bile] are the places where flesh is absent—namely, the hair of the head, body hair, teeth, and nails—as well as the firm, dry skin.
It remains pervading the remaining parts of the body like a drop of oil on water; when it is disturbed, the eyes become yellow and roll, the limbs tremble, and one scratches.

As for the "bound bile" (*baddhapitta*), it resides within a gall-bladder (*pittakosaka*) shaped like the pod of a large *kosātaki* gourd, situated between the heart and the lungs and supported by the liver tissue. When this [bile]...

When it is disturbed, beings become insane; with their minds deranged, they cast aside shame and fear of wrongdoing, and do what should not be done, speak what should not be spoken, and think what should not be thought.
As for its delimitation, it is delimited by the portion of bile; this is its delimitation by way of similarity.
Its delimitation by way of dissimilarity, however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
204. *Semha* (phlegm) is the phlegm within the interior of the body, measuring one *pattha* in quantity. By way of color, it is white, with the color of the juice of the *nāgabalā* leaf.
By way of shape, it has the shape of its location. By way of direction, it is produced in the upper direction. By way of location, it resides on the surface of the stomach.
At the time of swallowing food, drink, and so forth, it is just like duckweed or moss in water, or like wood or gravel [floating upon it].
Just as [water] falls, breaks into two, and then remains covering it over again, even so, when food, drink, and so forth fall [into the stomach],
they break into two and remain covering it over again; and when that [digestion] has become sluggish,
the belly becomes supremely loathsome, smelling of a corpse, like a ripe boil or like a rotten hen’s egg.
Then, due to that intense stench, both his breath and his mouth become foul-smelling, like a putrid corpse.
That man becomes subject to being told, "Go away, you stinking one! You are a crow!
And that [stomach], having increased and reached a state of thickness, like a covering board inside a latrine, suppresses the smell of the corpse within the belly-wall itself.

It remains. By way of delimitation, it is delimited by its own portion of phlegm; this is its delimitation by way of similarity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Its delimitation by way of dissimilarity (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
205. *Pubba* (pus) is that which occurs due to putrid blood. In terms of color, it has the color of a withered leaf. In a dead body...
Furthermore, it has the color of thick, putrid pus. In terms of shape, it is shaped according to its location. In terms of direction, it exists in two directions.
As for its location, there is no fixed place called the "site of pus" where it might remain accumulated;
rather, wherever a part of the body is struck by stumps, thorns, weapons, flames, and so forth, the blood coagulates there.
It cooks, or boils erupt such as carbuncles and pustules, and it remains in various places. By way of delimitation, it is delimited by what precedes it;
this is its delimitation by way of similarity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Its delimitation by way of dissimilarity (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
206. "Blood" refers to two kinds of blood: stored blood (*sannicita-lohita*) and circulating blood (*saṃsaraṇa-lohita*). Therein, stored blood...
By way of color, the stored blood (*saṇṇicitalohita*) has the color of thick, boiled lac juice; the circulating blood (*saṃsaraṇalohita*) has the color of thin lac juice.
By way of shape, both are shaped according to their respective locations. By way of direction, the stored blood is produced in the upper direction;
the other is produced in two directions. By way of location, setting aside the hair of the head, body hair, teeth, and nails, the circulating blood exists in the places where flesh is absent.
The stiff, dry skin remains covering the entire appropriated body, following the network of veins.
The accumulated blood fills the lower part of the region of the liver;
measuring about one *pattha* in quantity, it stands dripping little by little over the heart, kidneys, and lungs, moistening the kidneys, heart, liver, and lungs. In that...

For beings become thirsty when the blood, heart, and other internal parts are exhausted. By way of delimitation, it is delimited by its own portion of blood; this is its delimitation by way of similarity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*).
Its delimitation by way of dissimilarity (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
207. Sweat is the water element (*āpodhātu*) oozing from the pores of the body and other such openings. By way of color, it has the color of clear sesame oil or salt water.

By way of shape, it has the shape of a hollow space. By way of direction, it is produced in two directions. By way of location, there is no fixed place called the "location of sweat" where it might always remain like blood.

However, when the body is heated by the heat of a fire, the heat of the sun, changes in the seasons, and so forth, then [the sweat] is like a cluster of unevenly cut lotus stalks pulled up from water, or like a bundle of kumuda lily stems.
It trickles out as it were from all the openings of the pores of the body hairs; therefore, its shape should also be understood by way of those very openings of the body hairs.
Furthermore, the meditator who is discerning perspiration should attend to the sweat as existing by filling the openings of the body hairs.
As for its delimitation, it is delimited by the portion that is perspiration; this is its delimitation by way of its own nature (*sabhāga-pariccheda*).
The analysis of its specific characteristics (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that for hair.
Fat (*meda*) is a thick, oily substance. As for its color, it is the color of split turmeric. As for its shape:
