in one with a stout body, it has the shape of a piece of turmeric-colored fine cotton cloth placed between the skin and the flesh; in one with a lean body, it is like the flesh of the shanks.

The flesh of the thighs supported by the backbone, the flesh of the back, and the flesh of the belly—depending on these, it is arranged in double or triple layers, having the appearance of turmeric-dyed *dukūla* cloth or rags.
As for its direction, it is found in two directions.
As for its location, in a stout person it covers the entire body; in a lean person, it stands depending on the flesh of the shanks and so forth. It is reckoned as "moisture" (*sineha*).
Because it is supremely loathsome, even when it has gone [to the head], they do not take it for the purpose of oil for the head, nor for the purpose of oil for the nose and so forth.
As for its delimitation: it is delimited below by the flesh, above by the skin, and across by the portion of fat;
this is its delimitation by way of its own nature. Its delimitation by way of what is dissimilar, however, is exactly like that of the head-hairs.
208. Tears are the water element that trickles from the eyes. As to color, they are the color of clear sesame oil. As to shape, they have the shape of their location.
As to direction, they arise in the upper direction. As to location, they reside in the eye sockets.
However, this does not remain constantly accumulated in the eye sockets like bile in the gall-bladder; rather, it occurs when beings are born to a state of mental joy.
They laugh with loud laughter; they weep and lament, overcome by dejection;
or they consume such unwholesome food that their eyes are struck by smoke, dust, chaff, and the like.
Then, arising from these factors of joy, grief, unbalanced diet, and climate, [the humor] fills the eye sockets and remains there or flows out. And by means of the apprehension of tears...
The yogi should apprehend it by way of its remaining when the eye-sockets are filled. In terms of delimitation, it is delimited by the portion belonging to the eye;
this is its delimitation by way of similarity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Its delimitation by way of dissimilarity (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
209. *Vasa* is melted fat. By way of color, it is the color of coconut oil; it is also said to be the color of oil poured into gruel.
It is proper to speak [of it] as follows. By way of shape, it has the appearance of drops of oil spreading upon clear water when one is bathing.

By way of direction, it is produced in two directions. By way of location, it is mostly situated on the palms of the hands, the backs of the hands, the soles of the feet, the backs of the feet, the nostrils, the forehead, and the tops of the shoulders.

Furthermore, it does not remain permanently dissolved in these locations; rather, when [it is affected] by the heat of fire, the heat of the sun, unsuitable weather conditions, or an imbalance of the primary elements (*dhātu*), [it becomes visible].
Those parts become warm; then, at the time of bathing, they spread here and there like a drop of oil spreading over the surface of clear water.
In terms of delimitation, it is delimited by its own portion of fat; this is its delimitation by way of similarity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*).
Its delimitation by way of dissimilarity (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of head-hair.
210. *Kheḷa* (spittle) is the water element mixed with foam within the mouth. By way of color, it is white, the color of foam. By way of shape, it has the shape of its location;
it is also appropriate to say it has the shape of foam. By way of direction, it arises in the upper direction.
By way of location, it descends from both sides of the cheeks and rests upon the tongue. Furthermore, it does not remain constantly accumulated there.
But when beings see such food, or remember it, or place something hot, bitter, pungent, salty, sour, or acidic in their mouths;

or when their hearts feel weary, or when loathing arises toward anything at all—then saliva arises and, flowing down from both sides of the cheeks, settles upon the tongue. At the tip of the tongue...

It is thin at the tip and thick at the root-tongue; when raw grain, rice, or any other kind of solid food is placed in the mouth, it is capable of moistening it without being exhausted, just as water in a pit dug on a river sandbank moistens what is placed there.
As for its delimitation, it is bounded by the portion of saliva; this is its delimitation by way of homogeneity.
The analysis of its distinctness is the same as that for hair. 211.
*Siṅghāṇikā* (nasal mucus) is the impurity that trickles from the brain. By way of color, it is the color of the pith of a young palmyra stalk.
By way of shape, it has the shape of its location. By way of direction, it arises in the upper direction. By way of location, it fills the nostrils.
It remains there. It does not remain here always accumulated;

rather, it is just as if a man were to bind curd in a lotus leaf and prick it from below with a thorn, so that the curd, leaking out through that hole, would fall outside—in the same way, when beings weep, or when an imbalance of the elements arises due to incompatible food or temperature.
At that time, the brain matter, having become putrid phlegm within the head, flows down through the opening of the palate and nostrils;
it either remains filling the nostrils or trickles out. The meditator who discerns the *siṅghāṇikā* (nasal mucus) should discern it precisely by way of its remaining filling the nostrils.
As for its delimitation, it is delimited by the portion consisting of nasal mucus.
This is its delimitation by way of similarity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Its delimitation by way of dissimilarity (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of head-hairs.
212. *Lasikā* (synovial fluid) is the slimy, putrid substance within the joints of the body. By way of color, it is the color of *kaṇikāra* resin.
By way of shape, it has the shape of its location. By way of direction, it is found in two directions. By way of location, it performs the function of lubricating the bone joints.
It exists within the eighty joints while one is performing activities.
For one in whom this [wind] is sluggish, when they stand up, sit down, walk forward, walk backward, bend, or stretch, their bones creak;
it moves about as if making the sound of snapping fingers. [It extends] for a distance of only one or two yojanas.
In one who has walked, the air element becomes disturbed and the limbs ache. However, for one who possesses much [of this element], when rising, sitting, and so forth, the bones do not creak;
even after walking a long distance, the air element does not become disturbed, nor do the limbs ache.

In terms of delimitation, it is delimited by its portion of synovial fluid (*lasikā*); this is its delimitation by way of similarity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Its delimitation by way of dissimilarity (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.

213. "Urine" means the liquid of urine. By way of color, it is the color of bean-brine water. By way of shape, it has the shape of water placed inside a water-jar set with its opening facing downwards.
By way of direction, it is produced in the lower direction. By way of location, it is situated within the bladder (*vatthi*).
"Bladder" refers to the bladder-sack; just as when the juice of a *candana* plant is poured into an unglazed earthen jar, [the liquid remains] there.
It enters, yet no path of entry is discerned; even so, that which is emitted from the body enters, yet no path of entry is discerned, while the path of exit is manifest.
Furthermore, when the bladder is filled with urine, beings experience the urge, thinking, "I shall void. By way of delimitation, it is delimited by the interior of the bladder.
It is also delimited by its own liberated portion; this is its delimitation by the similar. Its delimitation by the dissimilar, however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.

Thus, having defined the parts beginning with the head-hairs by way of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation, one should contemplate them as repulsive in five ways—by way of color, shape, odor, habitat, and location—according to the method beginning with "not too quickly" and so forth.
For one who attends to [the body] as repulsive, at the conclusion of transcending conceptual designation (*paṇṇatti*),
just as when a man with sight looks at a garland of thirty-two kinds of flowers strung together on a single thread, all the flowers become manifest as if they were neither before nor after,
even so, for one looking at this body thinking "there are head-hairs in this body," all of those [parts] become manifest.
The parts become clear from beginning to end. Therefore it was said in the *Manasikārakosallakathā*:
“For when a beginner attends to ‘head-hairs,’ his attention proceeds until it reaches and rests upon this final section, ‘urine.
However, if he also applies his attention externally, then, when all the sections have thus become clear to him—
Humans, animals, and other beings, as they wander about, abandon their form as living creatures and appear merely as heaps and masses of constituent parts.
And the food, drink, and so forth being swallowed by them appear as if being thrown into those heaps and masses of parts.
Then, as he repeatedly brings to mind [the body] as "repulsive, repulsive" through the gradual process of dismemberment and so forth, it appears to him in due course...
Absorption (appanā) arises. Therein, the appearance of the head hairs and so forth by way of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation is the learning sign (uggahanimitta).
The appearance of them as repulsive in every aspect is the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta).
As one cultivates and develops that, absorption arises precisely through the first jhāna, according to the method already described for the meditation subjects on foulness (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna).
For one to whom only a single part [of the meditation object] is clear, or who, having attained absorption (*appanā*) in one part, does not apply further effort toward another,
only one [jhāna] arises. However, for one to whom many parts are clear,

or who, having attained jhāna in one, again applies effort toward another as well— for such a person, as in the case of the Elder Mallaka, there is a number of jhānas corresponding to the number of parts.
The first jhānas are produced.
It is said that the Venerable [Buddhaghosa], taking the Elder Abhaya, the Dīgha-bhāṇaka, by the hand, said, "Friend Abhaya, learn this question for now," and spoke thus:
"Regarding the thirty-two parts, there are thirty-two first jhānas for the Mallaka Elder..."
"One who attains it—if one enters it once by night and once by day—it is accomplished again within more than half a month;
but if one enters it every day, it is accomplished again within more than a month.

Thus, although this meditation subject succeeds by way of the first jhāna, it is called "mindfulness directed to the body" (kāyagatāsati) because it succeeds through the power of mindfulness regarding color, shape, and so forth.
And a bhikkhu devoted to this mindfulness directed to the body overcomes discontent and delights in it;
discontent does not overcome him, for he dwells having repeatedly overcome arisen discontent. He overcomes fear and dread and delights in it;
fear and dread do not overcome him, for he dwells having repeatedly overcome arisen fear and dread. He is patient...
He is one who endures cold and heat... [and] life-threatening conditions.
By means of the various colors of his hair and so forth, he becomes an attainer of the four jhānas. He penetrates the six direct knowledges (abhiññā).
Therefore, indeed, being heedful, let the wise man apply himself.
Thus, this mindfulness directed to the body has many benefits.
This concludes the section on the detailed exposition of mindfulness directed to the body. Now follows the discourse on mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*).
215. Now, after the Blessed One had thus praised it, saying:
"Monks, this concentration through mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, is peaceful and sublime, an unadulterated state of blissful dwelling;
and it causes those evil, unwholesome states that have arisen to vanish on the spot and to be stilled."—
“And how, bhikkhus, is concentration by mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so that it is peaceful and sublime,
an unadulterated state of happiness, a dwelling in bliss, and so that it causes evil, unwholesome states that have arisen to vanish on the spot and to subside?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut...”
Or he sits down, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him;
mindful, he breathes in, mindful he breathes out. Breathing in long, he understands: "I am breathing in long. Breathing out long...
[and so on] ...breathing in short... [and so on] ...or breathing out short, he understands: "I am breathing out short."
He understands. He trains thus: "I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body"; he trains thus: "I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body. He trains thus:
"I shall breathe in tranquilizing the bodily formation"; he trains thus: "I shall breathe out tranquilizing the bodily formation.
Experiencing rapture... experiencing pleasure... experiencing the mental formation...
“Calming the mental formations, I shall breathe in... experiencing the mind... gladdening the mind...
concentrating the mind... liberating the mind... contemplating impermanence... contemplating fading away... contemplating cessation.
‘Contemplating relinquishment, I shall breathe in,’ he trains himself; ‘contemplating relinquishment, I shall breathe out,’ he trains himself.”
Thus the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing with its sixteen bases has been explained. The method for its development now follows.
However, since it becomes complete in all its aspects only when explained in accordance with the commentary on the text, this exposition here is preceded by that commentary on the text.

216. “And how, bhikkhus, is mindfulness of breathing developed as concentration? Here, first, “how” is a question intended to set forth in detail the development of mindfulness of breathing as concentration in its various modes.
“And how, bhikkhus, is mindfulness of breathing developed as concentration” indicates the state that was asked about for the purpose of explaining it in its various modes.
“How, when practiced extensively... [etc. ...is it pacified? [The rest follows as in the text.]
The same method applies here as well. In this context, "developed" means either arisen or increased.

"Concentration through mindfulness of breathing" (*ānāpānassatisamādhi*) is concentration associated with the mindfulness that grasps the breath. Alternatively, it is the concentration within mindfulness of breathing;
thus, it is "concentration through mindfulness of breathing. "Cultivated" means performed repeatedly. "Tranquil and sublime" means both tranquil and sublime.
And it is sublime. In both cases, the word "only" (eva) should be understood as a restriction. What is meant?

Just as this meditation subject on foulness is both peaceful and sublime solely by way of penetration, yet—because its object is gross and its object is repulsive—is neither peaceful nor sublime by way of its object, so it is not [the case] for anyone else.
In one sense, it is neither peaceful nor sublime; however, it is peaceful and tranquil, being stilled both by the peace of its object and by the peace of the factors constituting penetration.
It is sublime both by the sublimity of its object and by the sublimity of its factors.
Therefore it is said: "It is both peaceful and sublime."
Regarding the phrase "an unadulterated and pleasant abiding" (*asecanako ca sukho ca vihāro*): here, "unadulterated" (*asecanaka*) means that there is no pouring (*secanam*) into it;
it is not mixed with anything else, but is distinct and unique. There is no state of being produced through preliminary work (*parikamma*) or access concentration (*upacāra*).

From the very moment of the initial application of attention, it is peaceful and sublime by its own intrinsic nature—this is the meaning. Some, however, explain "unadulterated" (*asecanaka*) as "not poured into" (*anāsittaka*).
They say it is "nutritious" because it is sweet by its very nature.
Thus, this dwelling should be understood as "delightful" and "pleasant," because it leads to the attainment of bodily and mental happiness at every moment of absorption.
"As they arise" means as they are not suppressed. "Evil" means base. "Unwholesome states" means states produced by lack of skill.
"It makes them vanish instantly" means it makes them vanish and suppresses them in a single moment. "It pacifies" means it thoroughly pacifies them.
Alternatively, because it pertains to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*), having gradually reached the growth of the Noble Path, it utterly cuts them off;
thus it is said that "it allays them."

This, however, is the summary of the meaning here: "In what manner, by what aspect, and by what method, monks, is mindfulness of breathing developed; in what manner is it practiced frequently so that it becomes peaceful...
[and] completely tranquil? 217. Now, expanding upon that meaning, he said: "Here, monks," and so forth.
In this context, "here, monks, a monk" means: monks, a monk in this dispensation. For the word "here" (*idha*) refers to one who produces mindfulness of breathing in all its modes.
This [passage] illustrates the teaching that serves as the support for the person and negates the existence of such a state in other teachings.
For it has been said: "Right here, monks, is the ascetic... [and so on] ...empty are the doctrines of others of ascetics other than these.
Therefore it was said: "In this teaching, the monks..."

“Having gone to the forest... or having gone to an empty hut”—this illustrates his selection of a dwelling suitable for the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassatisamādhi*).
For this bhikkhu’s mind, which for a long time has been diffused among objects such as forms and so forth, does not wish to mount the object of concentration on mindfulness of breathing;
like a chariot yoked to a wild bull, it runs only along the wrong path. Therefore, just as...
Suppose, for example, a cowherd named Gopa, wishing to tame a fraudulent calf that had grown fat by drinking all the milk from a fraudulent cow,
were to remove it from the cow, drive a large stake into the ground in a secluded spot, and bind it there with a rope. Then, that calf,
though struggling here and there, being unable to escape, would sit down right next to that very stake.

Or might fall upon it—just so, this bhikkhu, desiring to tame the corrupted mind that has long been nourished by drinking the essence of sense-objects such as forms, should withdraw it from those objects like forms and lead it into the forest... or into an empty hut;
there, he should bind it to the pillar of in-breathing and out-breathing with the rope of mindfulness. In this way, his mind [is tamed].

Even though it struggles here and there, being unable to find its former habitual object and thus unable to escape by breaking the tether of mindfulness, it settles down and lies down upon that very same object by way of access concentration (upacāra) and absorption (appanā). Therefore, the ancients said:
"Just as a man here might tie a calf to be tamed to a post, so too..."
“One should thus bind one’s own mind firmly to the object by means of mindfulness.

In this way, this lodging becomes suitable for his development. Therefore it was said: “This is an exposition of his selection of a lodging suitable for the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati).

Alternatively, because this is the preeminent [subject] among the various types of meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna), and because it was practiced by the Omniscient Buddhas, the Pacceka Buddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha—
The meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati-kammaṭṭhāna*), which is the basis for special attainments and for dwelling in happiness in this very life,

is not easy to develop without abandoning the vicinity of a village crowded with the sounds of men, women, elephants, horses, and so forth, because sound is a thorn to meditative absorption (*jhāna*). However, in a forest devoid of villages,
it is easy for the practitioner (*yogāvacara*) to master this meditation subject and attain the fourth *jhāna* of mindfulness of breathing.
Having brought that very [jhāna] to fruition as a basis, and having comprehended the conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), he was able to attain the supreme fruit of Arahantship.
Therefore, showing him a suitable dwelling place, the Blessed One said, "Whether gone to the forest," and so forth.
For the Blessed One is like a master of site-selection (*vatthuvijjācariya*); just as a master of site-selection, having surveyed the ground for a city, [proceeds to build it].
Having thoroughly examined it, he points out, "Build the city here," and when the city is completed in safety,
he receives great honor from the royal family; in the same way, the practitioner of yoga, having examined a suitable dwelling, points out,
"The meditation subject should be pursued here," and then, by one who is devoted to that meditation subject therein—
When a yogī attains *arahantship* by stages, he receives great honor, thinking, "Truly, that Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*).
This monk, however, is said to be like a leopard.

For just as a great king of leopards, having hidden himself in dependence upon a thicket of grass, a forest thicket, or a mountain thicket in the wilderness, [preys upon] wild buffalo, cattle-eared deer, wild boars, and so forth—

Just as a leopard seizes its prey, even so should this bhikkhu practicing the meditation subject in the forest and other such places be understood to seize, in due order, the paths of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship, as well as the noble fruits. Thus said the ancients:
"Just as the one called a leopard, Lying in wait, seizes its prey;..."
"In the same way, this son of the Buddha, devoted to practice and practicing insight,
having entered the forest, grasps the supreme fruit. Thus,
showing him the forest lodging as a ground suitable for the speed of his exertion, the Blessed One said, "Whether gone to the forest," and so forth.
218. Therein, "gone to the forest" (*araññagata*) means: having gone outside the threshold post (*indakhīla*), all this is called "forest," according to the definition stated as:
"A forest dwelling (*āraññaka*) is one that is at least five hundred bow-lengths distant.
Thus, he has gone to any forest that provides the bliss of seclusion. "Gone to the foot of a tree" (*rukkhamūlagata*) means: gone to the vicinity of a tree.

"Having gone to an empty place" means having gone to a secluded spot. And here, apart from the forest and the foot of a tree, it is also permissible to say that one has "gone to an empty place" even when staying in any of the remaining seven kinds of lodgings.
Thus, he has a lodging suitable for the three seasons, suitable for his temperament and physical constitution, and conducive to the development of mindfulness of breathing.
Having thus instructed [the meditator], he says that [the Teacher] sits down while demonstrating a peaceful posture that belongs neither to the side of depression nor to the side of agitation.

Then, showing the firmness of his sitting posture, the ease with which the inhalations and exhalations proceed, and the method for grasping the object, he says, "having folded his legs crosswise," and so forth.
In this context, "crosswise" (pallaṅka) refers to a seat bound around the thighs on all sides.
"Having folded" means having bound [the legs]. "Having set the body straight" means having placed the upper part of the body upright.
Having aligned the eighteen vertebrae edge-to-edge, for one sitting in this way, the skin, flesh, and sinews do not bend.
Thus, those pains that would arise moment by moment due to their bending do not arise. Among these...
When [the hindrances] do not arise, the mind becomes one-pointed; the meditation subject does not fall away, and it attains growth and expansion.
"Having established mindfulness facing the mouth" means having placed mindfulness facing toward the meditation subject. Alternatively, *pari* has the sense of embracing (*pariggaha*);
*mukha* has the sense of outlet (*niyyāna*); and *sati* has the sense of establishing (*upaṭṭhāna*). Therefore, it is called "facing the mouth."
"Being mindful"—the meaning here should be understood according to the method stated in the *Paṭisambhidā*. To summarize it:
"having established mindfulness that has discerned the way out. 219.
"Mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out": that bhikkhu, having sat down in this manner and having established mindfulness in this way, [proceeds].
Not abandoning that mindfulness, he breathes in mindful and breathes out mindful; what is meant is that he acts with mindfulness.
Now, in order to show the modes by which one acts with mindfulness, he said: "Breathing in long," and so forth.
For this has been stated in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, in the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of the very passage: "He breathes in mindful, he breathes out mindful."
“One practices with mindfulness in thirty-two ways. When one understands the unification of mind and non-distraction through long inhalation, mindfulness is established.
Through that mindfulness and that knowledge, one practices with mindfulness. [The same applies to] long exhalation… pe … inhalation while contemplating relinquishment.
[And] exhalation while contemplating relinquishment, when one understands the unification of mind…”
"For one who understands non-distraction, mindfulness is established. Through that mindfulness and that knowledge, he acts with mindfulness.
Regarding this, "breathing in long" means causing a long inhalation to proceed. "Inhalation" (assāsa) is the wind going out;
"exhalation" (passāsa) is the wind entering within—so it is stated in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*. However, in the commentaries on the Suttas...
This has been presented out of sequence. In that regard, for all those dwelling in the womb, at the time of emerging from the mother’s belly, first the internal wind goes out.
Afterwards, the external wind, taking up fine dust, enters within and is extinguished upon striking the palate.
In this way, inhalation and exhalation are to be understood.
However, their length or shortness should be understood by way of the distance [they traverse].
For just as water or sand that occupies a certain extent of space is called "long water" or "long sand," or "short water" or "short sand," so too,

even though the breaths are broken into fine particles, they are designated as "long" or "short" in relation to the elephant's body and the snake's body, which constitute their respective personal frames (*attabhāva*).
Having filled [the breath] slowly over a long duration, they emerge very slowly; therefore, they are called "long.
Having filled the short duration—consisting of the individual existence of dogs, hares, and so forth—quickly, they emerge very quickly; therefore, they are called "short.
Among humans, however, some breathe long in terms of time and duration, like elephants, snakes, and others.
And they breathe out. Some, like dogs, hares, and so forth, breathe with short breaths;

therefore, it should be understood that for them, those breaths which go out and come in over a long period of time are "long," while those which go out and come in over a brief period of time are "short."
In this regard, a bhikkhu, breathing in and breathing out long, understands in nine ways: "I am breathing in long; I am breathing out long.
It should be understood that for one who understands thus, the development of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body succeeds in one aspect.
As it is said in the *Paṭisambhidā*:
“How, breathing in long, does one know: ‘I am breathing in long’? Breathing out long, one knows: ‘I am breathing out long.
One breathes in a long inhalation reckoned as a duration; one breathes out a long exhalation reckoned as a duration;
one breathes in and breathes out long inhalations and exhalations reckoned as durations. Long inhalations and exhalations...”

As he breathes in and breathes out what is reckoned as a long duration, zeal arises. By means of that zeal, he breathes in a longer breath, more subtle than before, which is reckoned as a long duration. By means of that zeal, he breathes out a longer breath, more subtle than before...
[and so on] ...he breathes in and breathes out longer breaths, more subtle than before, which are reckoned as a long duration. By means of that zeal, even more subtle than before...
While breathing in and breathing out long breaths reckoned as a duration, joy arises.
Through that joy, he breathes in a long breath more subtle than before, reckoned as a duration.
Through that joy, he breathes out a long breath more subtle than before... [and so on] ...he breathes in and breathes out long breaths, both inhalation and exhalation, reckoned as a duration.
And he breathes out mindful. By way of gladness, he breathes in and breathes out long inhalations and exhalations—reckoned as a duration—that are even subtler than that;
as he breathes in and breathes out these long inhalations and exhalations, the mind turns away [from them] and equanimity becomes established.
In these nine aspects, the long inhalations and exhalations are the body. The establishment is mindfulness. The contemplation is knowledge. The body...
“Establishment is not mindfulness; mindfulness is both establishment and mindfulness. By means of that mindfulness and that knowledge, one contemplates that body.
Therefore, it is called ‘the development of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body as a body.

This same method applies to the short version as well. However, this is the distinction: just as here [in the long version] it says, “A long in-breath reckoned as a duration,” [so too in the short version].
It has been stated; likewise here, it is said: “Breathing in a short breath reckoned as short. Therefore, one should connect the text from the perspective of brevity up until:
“Thus, this is called the development of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body in the body.
In this way, by means of duration and by means of brevity, through these modes, one understands the in-breaths and out-breaths while [breathing] long...
Or, while breathing in long, he understands: "I am breathing in long"; ... pe ... or, while breathing out short, he understands: "I am breathing out short"—this is how it should be understood.
And for one who understands thus:
"The inhalation is long and short,"...
And the out-breath is also like that;
four colors proceed right at the tip of the nose, O Bhikkhu.
"220. ‘I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body... ... ‘I shall breathe out,’ thus he trains himself.
Making known and making clear the beginning, middle, and end of the entire body of in-breath, he trains himself: ‘I shall breathe in.
Making known and making clear the beginning, middle, and end of the entire body of out-breath, he trains himself: ‘I shall breathe out.’"
He trains thus. Making it known and making it evident in this way, he both breathes in and breathes out with a consciousness associated with knowledge.
Therefore, it is said: "He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in, I shall breathe out.
For to one bhikkhu, the beginning of the body of the in-breath or the body of the out-breath—which is scattered and dispersed—is evident, but not the middle or the end.
Thus, one is able to comprehend the beginning but becomes weary at the middle and the end.
For another, the middle is clear, but not the beginning or the end. For another, the end is clear, but not the beginning or the middle;
he is able to comprehend only the end, becoming weary at the beginning and the middle. For yet another, everything is clear, and he [comprehends] all of it.
He is able to grasp it and does not tire anywhere; showing that one should become like that, he said:
“‘I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body... pe ...I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body,’ thus he trains.
Therein, “he trains” means he strives or exerts himself in this way. Or else, the restraint of one who has become such is here the training in the higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*).
The concentration of one who has become thus is the training in higher mind; the wisdom of one who has become thus is the training in higher wisdom.

These three trainings he trains in, cultivates, develops, and makes much of with regard to that object, by means of that mindfulness and that attention—this is how the meaning should be understood here.

In that regard, because in the previous method there was only a matter of breathing in and breathing out, with nothing else to be done, from this point onward, however, one must apply oneself to the arising of knowledge and so forth.

Therefore, having stated the text in the present tense simply as "he understands: 'I am breathing in'" and "he understands: 'I am breathing out,'" [the following] concerns what is to be done from this point forward.

It should be understood that the text has been set down in the form of future tenses—such as "I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body"—in order to show the aspect of generating knowledge and so forth.
"He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in tranquilizing the bodily formation’ … [and] ‘I shall breathe out tranquilizing the bodily formation’" refers to the gross bodily formation.
He trains thus: "I shall breathe in and breathe out calming, tranquillizing, ceasing, and pacifying [the bodily formation].
In this regard, both the grossness and subtlety, as well as the tranquility, are to be understood as follows:
For previously, at the time when this bhikkhu had not yet gained mastery, both his body and mind were restless and gross. When the body and mind are gross...

When [the body and mind] are not calmed, the inhalations and exhalations are coarse; they proceed with greater force, the nostrils are no longer sufficient, and one remains breathing in and out through the mouth.
But when both the body and the mind have been grasped, then they become calm and tranquil. When these have subsided, the inhalations and exhalations become subtle.
They proceed such that they have reached a state where they must be discerned as to whether they exist or do not exist.
Just as when a man has run, or descended from a mountain, or lowered a heavy burden from his head and stands still, his inhalations and exhalations are coarse;
his nose is no longer sufficient, and he breathes in and breathes out through the mouth.

It persists. But when he has dispelled that fatigue, bathed, drunk, and lain down in the cool shade with a wet cloth over his heart, then those inhalations and exhalations of his become subtle, reaching a state where one must investigate whether they exist or not;
even so it was for this bhikkhu previously, at the time when [the breath] was not yet discerned.

The body... [and so on]... reaches the state of being investigated. Why is that? Because previously, during the time when it was not yet discerned, there was no application of mind, attention, mental engagement, or review with the thought, "I am calming the gross bodily formations";
but during the time when it is discerned, such exists. Therefore, compared to the time when it was not discerned, during the time when it is discerned, the bodily formation...
It becomes subtle. Regarding this, the ancients said:
"When both body and mind are agitated, [the breath] proceeds excessively;
when the body is no longer agitated, it proceeds subtly."
221. It is gross in the act of grasping, and subtle in the access to the first jhāna. In that [access] too it is gross, and subtle in the first jhāna.
It is gross in both the first jhāna and the access to the second jhāna, and subtle in the second jhāna.
It is gross in both the second jhāna and the access to the third jhāna, and subtle in the third jhāna. In both the third jhāna and the access to the fourth jhāna...

It is gross in the first jhāna, and in the fourth jhāna it becomes extremely subtle, reaching a state of non-occurrence. This, first of all, is the opinion of the Dīgha-bhāṇakas and the Saṃyutta-bhāṇakas.
The Majjhima-bhāṇakas, however, maintain that it is gross in the first jhāna and subtle in the access concentration (upacāra) of the second jhāna;

thus they hold that it becomes increasingly subtler in each successive access concentration compared to the jhānas immediately below them. According to the opinion of all of them, however, when [the breath] has not yet been fully grasped—
The bodily formation that is active [during the preliminary stage] subsides at the time of attainment.

At the time of attainment, the bodily formation active during the access to the first jhāna... [and so on] ...subsides in the fourth jhāna, while the bodily formation active during the access to the fourth jhāna subsides in the fourth jhāna itself.
This, then, is the method regarding serenity (samatha).

In insight meditation (*vipassanā*), however, the bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) occurring during the non-apprehension [of objects] is gross; it is subtle during the apprehension of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
That too is gross; it is subtle during the apprehension of derived matter (*upādārūpa*). That too is gross; it is subtle during the apprehension of all material phenomena.
That too is gross; it is subtle during the apprehension of the immaterial (*arūpa*). That too is gross; it is subtle during the apprehension of both the material and the immaterial. That too...
It is gross in relation to the discernment of conditions, but subtle in relation to the discernment of conditioned name-and-form.

That too is gross in relation to the discernment of conditioned name-and-form, but subtle in relation to insight that takes the characteristics as its object. That too is gross in relation to weak insight, but subtle in relation to powerful insight.
Therein, according to the method stated previously, each preceding stage is [surpassed] by the succeeding one.
The subsiding should be understood by way of the latter [stage]. Thus, both the gross and subtle states as well as the subsiding are to be understood here.
In the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, however, this meaning is stated together with the "Exhortation" and "Clarification":
"How does he train thus: 'I shall breathe in... shall breathe out, tranquilizing the bodily formation'? Which..."
What are bodily formations? Long in-breaths and out-breaths are bodily phenomena; being bound up with the body, they are bodily formations.
He trains in calming, stopping, and stilling these bodily formations...
such that by means of these bodily formations there is the bending, the inclining, the leaning, the bowing, the moving, the shaking, the trembling, and the quivering of the body.
He trains thus: "I shall breathe in tranquilizing the bodily formation"; he trains thus: "I shall breathe out tranquilizing the bodily formation.

By means of such bodily formations that there is no bending, no twisting, no stooping, no inclining of the body, but rather its being unshakable, unwavering, immovable, and unshaking—tranquil, subtle, and stilled.
“He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in, I shall breathe out, calming the bodily formation.
Indeed, he trains thus: ‘Calming the bodily formation, I shall breathe in’; he trains thus: ‘Calming the bodily formation, I shall breathe out.
If this were so, there would be neither the manifestation of the perception of wind, nor [the manifestation] of the in-breaths and out-breaths.”
There is no development [of concentration]. There is no development of mindfulness of breathing, nor is there development of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing;
and wise people neither enter into nor emerge from that attainment.
"Thus, indeed, he trains himself: 'I shall breathe in, I shall breathe out, tranquilizing the bodily formation. This being so..."

There is the development of the perception of air, there is the development of inhalation and exhalation, there is the development of mindfulness of breathing, and there is the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing;
and the wise both enter and emerge from that attainment. How so?
“Just as when a gong is struck, first coarse sounds arise;

because the sign of the coarse sounds has been well grasped, well attended to, and well retained, even when the coarse sounds have ceased, then afterwards subtle sounds arise. Because the sign of the subtle sounds has been well grasped, well attended to...”
Just as the mind continues to proceed even after a subtle sound has ceased by taking the sign of that subtle sound as its object—

because it was well apprehended, well attended to, and well retained— in the same way, first the coarse inhalations and exhalations proceed; and because the sign of those coarse inhalations and exhalations was well grasped, well attended to, and well retained, [the mind proceeds] even after the coarse inhalations and exhalations have ceased.
Then, afterwards, subtle inhalations and exhalations proceed. Because the sign of the subtle inhalations and exhalations has been well grasped,
well attended to, and well retained, even when the subtle inhalations and exhalations have ceased,
the mind does not go to distraction, as it takes that sign of the subtle inhalations and exhalations as its object.

“This being so, there is the development of the perception of wind, and there is the development of the in-breaths and out-breaths, and there is the development of mindfulness of breathing, and there is the development of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing;
and wise people both enter and emerge from that attainment. [The words: ‘Calming the bodily formation, he breathes in and breathes out’...”
“The body is the establishment; mindfulness is the awareness; discernment is the contemplation. The body is the establishment, but not the mindfulness;

mindfulness is both the establishment and the mindfulness. By means of that mindfulness and that discernment, one contemplates that body. Therefore, it is called ‘the development of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body as a body.’”
This, then, is the word-by-word commentary on the first tetrad taught here by way of contemplation of the body.
However, since this very tetrad is taught here as the meditation subject for a beginner,
while the other three tetrads are taught here by way of the contemplation of feelings, mind, and mental objects for one who has already attained jhāna.

Therefore, a clansman who is a beginner and desires to reach Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) by means of insight (*vipassanā*) which has the fourth *jhāna* on breathing as its proximate cause,

should perform all the duties such as the purification of virtue according to the method already explained, and then, in the presence of a teacher of the aforementioned type, [undertake] the fivefold [instruction].
The meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) should be learned.
In this regard, there are these five connections: learning, interrogation, establishment, absorption, and characteristics.
Therein, "learning" means the acquisition of the meditation subject; "interrogation" means the questioning regarding the meditation subject.
“Appearance” means the appearance of the meditation subject. “Absorption” means the absorption of the meditation subject.

“Characteristic” means the characteristic of the meditation subject; what is meant is the discerning of the specific nature of the meditation subject, thinking, “This meditation subject has such a characteristic.
One who learns the meditation subject with these five links does not weary himself, nor does he trouble his teacher.
Therefore, having had a small portion recited and having practiced it for a long time, one should thus master the meditation subject consisting of five sections. Then,
residing either in the presence of the teacher or elsewhere in a lodging of the kind previously described, with minor impediments severed,
having finished the meal and dispelled the drowsiness following eating, one should sit comfortably and recollect the virtues of the Triple Gem.
Having gladdened the mind and not becoming confused by even a single word from the teacher’s instruction, one should attend to this meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*).
Herein, this is the method of attention:
Counting, following, touching, fixing, and observing;
Turning away (*vivaṭṭanā*), purification (*pārisuddhi*), and the reviewing of those [factors].
Therein, counting (*gaṇanā*) is simply counting. Following (*anubandhanā*) is continuous flow (*anuvahanā*). Touching (*phusanā*) is the point of contact. Fixing (*ṭhapanā*) is absorption (*appanā*).
Observing (*sallakkhaṇā*) is insight (*vipassanā*). Turning away (*vivaṭṭanā*) is the path (*magga*). Purification (*pārisuddhi*) is the fruit (*phala*). And of those...
"Reviewing" means reflection.
In this regard, this beginner’s son of good family should first attend to this meditation subject by means of counting.
And when counting, he should not stop below five, nor should he go beyond ten.
One must not allow a break in between. For when one places the count below five, the arising of consciousness flutters in a cramped space, like a herd of cattle confined in a narrow pen.

When one leads it beyond ten, the arising of consciousness becomes dependent on mere counting. And for one who allows a break in between, [the thought arises]: "Has my meditation subject reached its peak?"
The mind does not waver [thinking], "No. Therefore, having avoided these faults, one should count.
And while counting, one should first count by slow counting, like the counting of a grain-measurer.
For a grain-measurer, having filled a *nāḷi* measure, says "One" and pours it out. Then, while filling it again, seeing some chaff and discarding it—
He says, “one, one. This same method applies to “two, two,” and so forth.

In exactly the same way, by taking whichever [breath] appears among the inhalations and exhalations, he should count—beginning with “one, one” and so on, up to “ten, ten”—only after having clearly observed each instance as it occurs.
As he counts in this manner, the incoming and outgoing inhalations and exhalations become manifest to him.
Then, having abandoned that slow counting—the counting by grain-measurers—he should count by means of swift counting, the counting of cowherds.
For a clever cowherd, taking pebbles and so forth in his lap, staff and rope in hand, goes to the cattle-pen early in the morning;
striking the cows on their backs and sitting atop a crossbar, he counts each one as it reaches the gate.
As soon as a cow reaches the door, he throws a pebble at it and counts, "One, two.
Having spent the three watches of the night in a cramped space, the herd of cattle, as they emerge one after another, rubbing against each other, comes out in dense clusters with great speed.
With that great speed, he counts, "Three, four, five, ten."
"Let him count," it is said; thus, for one counting in this manner according to the previous method, the inhalations and exhalations become manifest and move rapidly again and again.

Then, knowing that "they move repeatedly," he should not grasp them at the inside or the outside, but grasping each one as it reaches the door [of the nostrils], he counts: "one, two, three, four, five, six."
"One, two, three, four, five, six, seven... pe... eight, nine, ten"—in this way, one should count quickly and steadily.
For when the meditation subject is bound up with counting, the mind becomes one-pointed by the power of counting alone, just as a boat is steadied in a violent current by means of a rudder.
As he counts thus very rapidly, the meditation subject appears as if it were occurring without interruption.
Then, knowing that it occurs without interruption, he should count with great speed in the same manner as before, without discerning the air both inside and outside.
For when one makes the mind enter together with the air entering within, [the breath] inside...
It is as if filled with fat and struck by the wind. When one draws out the mind along with the outward-exiting breath, the mind becomes distracted by external, diverse objects.

However, for one who develops the practice by fixing mindfulness on every spot touched [by the breath], the meditation succeeds. Therefore it was said: "Without grasping the breath internally and externally..."
"One should count with increasing speed in the same manner as before.

For how long, then, should this be counted? It should be counted until mindfulness, independent of counting, becomes established upon the object of the in-breath and out-breath. For counting is solely for the purpose of establishing mindfulness on the object of the in-breath and out-breath by cutting off thoughts that have strayed outward.
224. Having thus attended to it by means of counting, one should attend to it by means of following. "Following" refers to the counting.
Having withdrawn [the mind], it is the continuous following of the inhalations and exhalations by means of mindfulness. And that is not by way of following their beginning, middle, and end.
For the navel is the beginning of the wind exiting outward, the heart is the middle, and the tip of the nose is the end.
The tip of the nose is the beginning of the wind entering inward, the heart is the middle, and the navel is the end. As he follows this [wind]:
A mind that has become distracted is both agitated and restless. As it is said:

"For one who follows with mindfulness the beginning, middle, and end of the in-breath, because the mind has become distracted internally, both body and mind become agitated, restless, and trembling. [The same applies to] the out-breath, following its beginning, middle, and end with mindfulness..."
"For one who pursues [the breath] with a mind distracted by the external, both body and mind become agitated, perturbed, and trembling.
Therefore, when attending to it for the sake of following, one should not attend to it by way of its beginning, middle, and end;
rather, one should attend to it by way of touching and by way of fixing. By way of counting and following...
For there is no separate attention by way of touching and placing;
rather, while counting, one attends by means of both counting and touching at each spot touched.
Then, withdrawing the counting right there and following those [spots] with mindfulness, and placing the mind through absorption, one attends by way of both following and touching.

And it is said that he "attends to it for the purpose of establishing. This meaning is to be understood through the similes of the cripple and the doorkeeper mentioned in the *Aṭṭhakathās*, as well as the simile of the saw mentioned in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.
225. Herein, this is the simile of the cripple: Just as a cripple [watches] the swing of a mother and son playing on a swing—
Having thrown it down, he sits right there at the foot of the swing’s pillar;
as the swing’s plank comes and goes, he sees both its ends and its middle, yet he does not exert himself for the purpose of seeing those two ends and the middle.
In the same way, this bhikkhu, standing at the foot of the pillar of anchoring through mindfulness, [observes] the swing of the inhalation and exhalation.
Having cast [the mind] right there upon the sign, he sits with mindfulness; as the breaths enter and exit,
he follows their beginning, middle, and end with mindfulness at the point where they touch,
fixing the mind there and seeing them, yet he does not exert himself for the sake of seeing them— this is the simile of the cripple.
226. This, moreover, is the simile of the gatekeeper: Just as a gatekeeper does not examine the men inside or outside the city, asking, "Who are you?
Where have you come from? Where are you going? Or what is in your hand?"—for these are not his burden—but examines each person only as they arrive at the gate; even so it is for this bhikkhu.
The winds that have entered within and the winds that have gone outside are not a burden; only those that reach the door are a burden—this is the simile of the gatekeeper.
As for the simile of the saw, it should be understood from the beginning as follows. For this has been said:
“The sign, the inhalation and exhalation, and the objectless single mind—
for one who does not know these three things, development is not attained. The sign,
the inhalation and exhalation, and the objectless single mind...”
“And for one who knows these three things, development is found.
“How is it that these three things do not become objects for a single consciousness, yet these three things are not unknown,
the mind does not fall into distraction, exertion is evident, and the application is accomplished?”
Does he attain distinction? Suppose, for example, a tree were set upon a level piece of ground, and a man were to cut it with a saw.
By way of the saw-teeth touching the tree, the man’s mindfulness becomes established;
he does not attend to the saw-teeth as they come or go, nor to the saw-teeth that have come or gone.
They become known; exertion is manifested, the application is accomplished, and distinction is attained.
"Just as a tree trunk is placed on level ground, so is the sign for anchoring.
Just as the teeth of a saw, so are the in-breaths and out-breaths. Just as a man's mindfulness is established by means of the teeth of the saw touching the tree..."
Just as a person with saw-teethed teeth does not attend to them when they come together or go apart, nor are those teeth unknown to him when they come or go;
yet his effort is evident, he accomplishes his task, and he attains distinction— in the same way,
a bhikkhu sits having established mindfulness at the tip of the nose or on the feature of the mouth, and [does not attend] to what comes or goes.
When he attends to the incoming and outgoing breaths, the incoming and outgoing breaths are not unknown whether they have come or gone;
his striving becomes manifest, he accomplishes the application, and he attains distinction.
"What is 'striving'? For one who has aroused energy, both body and mind become wieldy; this is..."
Exertion. What is the application? For one who has aroused energy, the defilements are abandoned and discursive thoughts are stilled;
this is the application. What is the distinction? For one who has aroused energy, the fetters are abandoned and the underlying tendencies are exhausted;
this is the distinction. Thus, these three states do not become objects for a single [moment of] consciousness, nor do these three...
The phenomena remain unknown, yet the mind does not fall into distraction; exertion is evident, the application is accomplished, and one attains distinction.
"For whom mindfulness of breathing is fulfilled and well-developed..."
“Gradually accumulated, just as taught by the Buddha, it illuminates this world like the moon released from clouds.
This is the Simile of the Saw. Here, however, it should be understood that the sole purpose [of this simile] is non-attention (*amanasikāra*) according to its successive application.
228. For some who attend to this meditation subject, the sign arises before long, and the fixing known as absorption—which is adorned with the remaining jhāna factors—is accomplished.
However, for others, from the very time they begin attending by means of counting, as the bodily agitation subsides through the gradual cessation of coarse inhalation and exhalation, the body also—
The mind also becomes light, and the body feels as if it has attained the state of leaping into the air.
Just as when one with a stiff body sits on a bed or a chair, the bed or chair sinks down, creaks, and the coverlet becomes wrinkled;
but when one with a supple body sits, neither the bed nor the chair sinks, nor does it creak, nor does the coverlet wrinkle.
It takes up the posture; the bed and chair become as if filled with cotton wool. Why? Because when the body is not agitated, it becomes light.

In the same way, from the time one begins to attend through counting, as the bodily agitation subsides by means of the gradual cessation of coarse inhalation and exhalation, both the body and the mind become light;
the body becomes as if it has attained the state of leaping into the air.
When his gross inhalation and exhalation have ceased, the mind proceeds with the sign of the subtle inhalation and exhalation as its object.
When that too has ceased, it continues to proceed with a successively subtler and subtler sign as its object. How so?
Just as if a man were to strike a bronze bowl with a large iron rod, there would be a great sound at once.
If it were to arise, his mind would proceed with gross sounds as its object. When the gross sound has ceased, thereafter his mind proceeds with subtle sounds as its object;
when that too has ceased, it continues to proceed one after another with ever more subtle sound-objects.
It should be understood in this way. And this has also been said:
“As when a bronze gong is struck,” and so on in detail.
For while other meditation subjects become clearer and clearer as one develops them further, this one does not do so.
On the contrary, for one who develops it further, it becomes more subtle and does not even come into focus; thus it is.
But when he does not attend to him, that bhikkhu should not rise from his seat, shake out his leather mat, and depart.
What should be done? He should not rise [thinking], “I will ask the teacher,” or “Now my meditation subject is lost.
For if he goes away after disturbing his posture, the meditation subject becomes ever new and fresh.
Therefore, one should bring it to mind while remaining exactly as one is sitting.
Herein, this is the method for bringing it to mind: having recognized that the meditation subject is not present, that monk should reflect thus:
"Where do these so-called in-breaths and out-breaths exist, and where do they not exist? Or in whom [do they exist]?"

"It exists," or "for whom does it not exist? When one reflects in this way, knowing that these [states] do not exist within the mother's womb, nor for those submerged in water, nor likewise for those who have become unconscious, nor for the dead, nor for those attained to the fourth jhāna, nor for those possessing existence in the fine-material or immaterial realms, nor for those who have attained the cessation of perception and feeling—one should thus reproach oneself by means of oneself: "Are you not, O wise one, [one of these]?"

“Neither while in the mother’s womb, nor submerged in water, nor unconscious, nor dead, nor attained to the fourth jhāna, nor possessed of existence in the fine-material or immaterial realms, nor attained to cessation—[in these states] do the in-breaths and out-breaths exist;
yet, because of dullness of wisdom, you are unable to discern them. Then, by means of the mind’s natural range of contact, he established his mind and applied attention.
It should be practiced. For these [breaths] proceed by striking the nostril-aperture of one with a long nose, and the upper lip of one with a short nose.
Therefore, he should establish a sign, thinking: "They strike this particular spot.
It was for this very purpose that the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, I do not say of one who is muddled in mindfulness and lacking clear comprehension..."
“I speak of the development of mindfulness of breathing.

For although any meditation subject whatsoever succeeds only for one who is mindful and clearly comprehending, this meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing is especially weighty and a weighty development; it becomes clear even to one who is attending to something other than it.
This is the sphere of attention belonging only to Great Beings—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the sons of the Buddhas;
it is neither limited nor cultivated by limited beings. To whatever extent it is attended to, it becomes increasingly peaceful and subtle.
Therefore, in this regard, powerful mindfulness and wisdom are required.
For just as when sewing a smooth cloth, the needle must be fine and the needle-eye even finer,
so too at the time of developing this meditation subject— which is like a smooth cloth— mindfulness,
which corresponds to the needle, and the wisdom associated with it, which corresponds to the needle-eye, must both be powerful.
Furthermore, a bhikkhu endowed with that mindfulness and wisdom need not search for those in-breaths and out-breaths anywhere other than the place where they naturally touch.
It is like a farmer who, having plowed his field and released his oxen to graze, sits down in the shade to rest;
then those oxen might rush off quickly into the forest. Now, there is a clever farmer...
Then, wishing to take them back and yoke them again, he did not wander through the forest following their tracks;
rather, taking his reins and goad, he went straight to the bathing-place where they were accustomed to descend, and there he either sat down or lay down.
Then those oxen, having grazed for part of the day, descended to the bathing-place, bathed, and drank.
Having seen them standing after they had backed out, he would bind them with a rein, prick them with a goad, lead them back, yoke them again, and then perform his work;
in the same way, that bhikkhu should not seek those in-breaths and out-breaths anywhere other than the place normally touched by them.
Rather, taking the rein of mindfulness and the goad of wisdom, he should fix the mind on the place normally touched.
Mindfulness should be applied. For one who applies the mind in this way, those [signs] will appear before long, like oxen at a watering place.
Then, having bound them with the rein of mindfulness and yoked them to that very spot, he should repeatedly devote himself to the meditation subject, piercing them with the goad of wisdom.
231. As he devotes himself to this in such a way, the sign (nimitta) appears before long. However, it does not appear in exactly the same way for everyone.
On the contrary, some say that for some person it appears producing a pleasant touch, like a tuft of cotton wool, like a tuft of kapok, or like a stream of air.
This, however, is the analysis found in the commentaries: for some, this [wind element] is like the form of a star, like a round gem, or like a round pearl;
for some, it has a rough touch, like a cotton seed or like a wooden core needle;
for some, it is like a long silk thread, like a garland of flowers, or like a column of smoke; and for some—
It appears like a spread-out spider’s web, like a mass of clouds, like a lotus flower, like a chariot wheel, like the lunar disc, and like the solar disc.
Furthermore, this [appearance] is just as when many bhikkhus are sitting after having recited a sutta together, and one bhikkhu asks: "In what manner did it appear to you?"
When it was said, "This sutta appears thus," one said, "To me it appears like a great mountain river.
Another said, "To me like a row of forest trees. Yet another said, "To me like a single tree with cool shade, full of branches and heavy with fruit.
For to them, that very same sutta appeared differently due to the diversity of their perceptions.
It appears. Thus, even a single meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) appears as diverse due to the diversity of perception.
For this is born of perception, has its source in perception, and originates from perception. Therefore, it should be understood that it appears as diverse due to the diversity of perception.
And herein, the consciousness having the in-breath as its object is one thing, that having the out-breath as its object is another, and that having the sign (nimitta) as its object is yet another.
For one who lacks these three qualities, the meditation subject reaches neither absorption (appanā) nor access (upacāra).
But for one who possesses these three qualities, that very meditation subject reaches both access and absorption. For this has been said:
“The sign, inhalation, and exhalation—these are not the object of a single consciousness;”
“For one who does not know three things, development is not found:
the sign, the inhalation and exhalation, and the single-pointedness of mind as their object.
For one who knows these three things, development is found.”
232. When the sign has appeared in this way, that bhikkhu should go to the teacher and announce:
"Venerable sir, such a sign appears to me. The teacher, however, should not say, "This is the sign," or "This is not the sign.
Instead, he should say, "It is so, friend," and tell him, "Continue to attend to it again and again."
He should be told [this]. For if one were told "the sign," he might fall into complacency; if told "not the sign," he might become despondent and lose heart.
Therefore, without saying either of those two, he should be directed toward mental attention (*manasikāra*) alone. Thus say the Dīgha reciters. But the Majjhima reciters say:
"Friend, this is the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*); attend to it again and again."
“...should be called a true person. Then he should fix his mind on that very sign.
Thus, from this point forward, his development proceeds by way of fixing. For this was said by the ancients:
“Fixing the mind on the sign, Discerning its various aspects;”
“The wise man binds his own mind to the inhalation and exhalation.

From the moment the sign (nimitta) thus appears to him, the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are indeed suppressed, the defilements (kilesa) are settled, mindfulness (sati) is established, and the mind is concentrated by access-concentration (upacāra-samādhi). Then, by means of that sign...
It should be attended to by way of its color, not examined by way of its characteristics.

Furthermore, just as the womb of a Cakkavatti queen or a farmer’s crop of rice and barley must be carefully guarded, so too should [the mind] be well protected by avoiding the seven unsuitable things, such as improper dwellings, and by cultivating those same seven suitable things. Having thus protected it, [one should proceed].
Having brought about growth and increase by means of repeated attention, one should accomplish the ten kinds of skill in absorption and apply evenness of energy.
As he strives in this way, the fourfold and fivefold jhānas arise in that sign according to the same sequence described for the earth kasiṇa.

233. Thus, when a bhikkhu has produced the fourfold and fivefold jhānas here, he—desiring to reach complete purification by expanding his meditation subject through the stages of observation and turning away—makes that same jhāna familiar and reaches mastery in five ways;
then, having defined name-and-form, he establishes insight. How so? For from that attainment...
Having emerged from that, he sees the origin of the in-breaths and out-breaths as both the body born of karma (*karajakāya*) and the mind.

For just as wind moves when a blacksmith’s bellows are blown, depending upon the bellows, the person, and the appropriate effort, even so the in-breaths and out-breaths depend upon the body and the mind.
Then, he regards both the in-breaths and out-breaths, as well as the body, as form (*rūpa*), and the mind as...
He defines those associated states as "formless. This is the summary here; however, the detailed analysis of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) will be revealed later.
Having thus defined name-and-form, he searches for its condition. And searching, he sees it.

He dispels doubt concerning the occurrence of name-and-form throughout the three periods of time. Having dispelled his doubt, he applies the three characteristics by means of the comprehension of aggregates.

Then, having abandoned the ten imperfections of insight—such as the "illumination" and so forth—which arise prior to the contemplation of rise and fall, and having defined the knowledge of the path that is free from imperfections as the "Path," he abandons the perception of arising and practices the contemplation of dissolution.

Having reached the limit of the nineteenfold knowledge of reviewing, one who— by contemplating dissolution through uninterrupted observation of the passing away of all conditioned phenomena that appear—
becomes disenchanted, dispassionate, and liberated, attains the four noble paths in due order, establishes himself in the fruit of arahantship,
and becomes the foremost recipient of offerings in the world with its devas.

To this extent, the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing—beginning with counting and ending with insight—is completed. This concludes the commentary on the first tetrad in its entirety.

As for the other three tetrads, since there is no separate method for developing the meditation subject in them, their meaning should be understood in this way according to the method of word-by-word commentary.

"Experiencing rapture": he trains himself, thinking, "I shall breathe in and I shall breathe out, making rapture known, making it manifest. In this context, rapture is experienced in two ways: by way of the object (*ārammaṇato*) and by way of non-confusion (*asammohato*).
How is rapture experienced by way of the object? He enters the two jhānas accompanied by rapture.
At the moment of attainment, through the acquisition of the jhāna, rapture is experienced by way of the object; [this refers to] the object...

Because of being clearly understood. How is it through non-delusion? Having entered and emerged from two jhānas accompanied by rapture (*pīti*), one contemplates the rapture associated with those jhānas in terms of its exhaustion and vanishing.
At the moment of insight (*vipassanā*), rapture is clearly understood through non-delusion by means of the penetration of characteristics (*lakkhaṇa-paṭivedha*).
For this has been said in the *Paṭisambhidā*:
“Through long in-breaths, for one who understands the unification of mind and non-distraction, mindfulness is established.
By means of that mindfulness and that knowledge, that rapture is clearly experienced. Through long out-breaths... through short in-breaths...
through short out-breaths... through in-and-out breaths while experiencing the whole body... while tranquilizing [the bodily formation]...”
For one who understands one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind by way of the bodily formation consisting of in-breathing and out-breathing, mindfulness is established.
By means of that mindfulness and that knowledge, that rapture is experienced. As one adverts to it, that rapture is experienced;
as one knows, sees, reviews, resolves the mind, and is resolved through faith, energy [is exerted].
"For one who exerts effort, establishes mindfulness, concentrates the mind, understands with wisdom, and realizes that which is to be directly known, that which is to be fully understood,
that which is to be abandoned, that which is to be developed, and that which is to be realized— that rapture is experienced. In this way, that rapture is experienced."
In this same manner, the remaining phrases should also be understood according to their meaning. However, there is this slight distinction here:

the experience of pleasure (*sukha-paṭisaṃveditā*) should be understood as occurring by way of three jhānas, while the experience of mental formations (*citta-saṅkhāra-paṭisaṃveditā*) should be understood as occurring by way of all four.

"Mental formations" refers to the two aggregates beginning with feeling (*vedanā*). Furthermore, in the phrase "experiencing pleasure," it is for the purpose of showing the plane of insight (*vipassanā-bhūmi*) that—
“‘Pleasure’: there are two kinds of pleasure, bodily pleasure and mental pleasure,” so it is said in the *Paṭisambhidā*.
“Calming the mental formations”: the meaning is that he calms, brings to cessation, each gross mental formation as it arises.
This should be understood in detail in the same manner as explained for the bodily formations.
Furthermore, here in the section on rapture (*pīti*), feeling (*vedanā*) is stated under the heading of rapture; in the section on pleasure (*sukha*), feeling is stated by its own specific name.

In the two sections on mental formations (*cittasaṅkhāra*), because of the statement, "Perception and feeling—these mental states are bound to the mind and are mental formations," it should be understood that this tetrad is taught according to the method of contemplation of feeling (*vedanānupassanā*), namely, as feeling associated with perception.
235. In the third tetrad as well, the experiencing of the mind by means of the four jhānas should be understood.
"Gladdening the mind" means he trains himself: "I shall breathe in and I shall breathe out gladdening, gladdening, cheering, and cheering the mind.
In this context, gladdening occurs in two ways: by way of concentration and by way of insight.
How by way of concentration? He enters the two jhānas accompanied by rapture (*pīti*). At the moment of attainment, he gladdens and delights the mind with the rapture associated with that attainment.

How by way of insight (*vipassanā*)? Having entered the two jhānas accompanied by rapture and emerged from them, he contemplates the rapture associated with those jhānas as subject to destruction and vanishing. Thus, at the moment of insight, the [rapture] associated with the jhāna...
Making rapture the object, one gladdens and rejoices the mind. One who practices in this way is said to "train thus: 'I shall breathe in and breathe out gladdening the mind.
"Concentrating the mind" means placing the mind evenly and establishing it evenly upon the object by means of the first jhāna and so forth.
Alternatively, having entered and emerged from those jhānas, when one contemplates the consciousness associated with the jhāna as subject to destruction and vanishing,
momentary one-pointedness of mind arises through the penetration of the characteristics at the moment of insight.
By means of this momentary one-pointedness of mind thus arisen, he places the mind evenly upon the object and establishes it evenly.
“It is said: ‘He trains thus: “I shall breathe in concentrating the mind; I shall breathe out concentrating the mind.

By ‘liberating the mind,’ he means liberating and releasing the mind from the hindrances by means of the first jhāna, from applied and sustained thought by means of the second, from rapture by means of the third, and from pleasure and pain by means of the fourth.”
Alternatively, having entered those jhānas and emerged from them, he contemplates the consciousness associated with the jhāna as subject to destruction and vanishing. At the moment of insight,
while liberating the mind from the perception of permanence through the contemplation of impermanence, from the perception of pleasure through the contemplation of suffering,
from the perception of self through the contemplation of non-self, from delight through the contemplation of disenchantment, and from passion through the contemplation of dispassion...
While liberating the mind from passion by means of the contemplation of cessation, and from grasping by means of the contemplation of relinquishment, he breathes in and breathes out.
Therefore it is said: "He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in and breathe out liberating the mind.
It should be understood that this tetrad was taught in this way by way of the contemplation of the mind.

236. Regarding the fourth tetrad, first, in the phrase "contemplating impermanence" (*aniccānupassī*), impermanence (*anicca*) is to be understood; impermanence-ness (*aniccatā*) is to be understood; the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) is to be understood; and the one contemplating impermanence (*aniccānupassī*) is to be understood.
In this context, "the impermanent" refers to the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandhā*). Why? Because they possess the nature of arising, passing away, and change.

"Impermanence-ness" is the very arising, passing away, and change of those same aggregates, or their non-existence after having existed; it is the momentary dissolution of produced things due to their inability to remain in that same state.
"Bheda" means breaking up. "Contemplation of impermanence" (aniccānupassanā) is the contemplation that form and so forth are impermanent by way of their impermanence.

"One who contemplates impermanence" (aniccānupassī) is one endowed with that contemplation. Therefore, one who breathes in and breathes out while being thus constituted should be understood here as training thus: "I shall breathe in and breathe out contemplating impermanence."

Regarding the phrase "contemplating fading away" (*virāgānupassī*): here, there are two kinds of fading away—the fading away through destruction (*khayavirāga*) and absolute fading away (*accantavirāga*).
Of these, fading away through destruction is the momentary dissolution of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*). Absolute fading away is Nibbāna.

Contemplation of fading away is both insight (*vipassanā*) and the Path (*magga*), which proceed by way of seeing both of those. Breathing in while being endowed with both of these types of contemplation...

And while breathing out, it should be understood that he trains thus: "I shall breathe in and I shall breathe out contemplating fading away. The same method applies to the phrase "contemplating cessation.
Regarding "contemplating relinquishment," there are two kinds of relinquishment here: relinquishment as giving up, and relinquishment as leaping forward.
Relinquishment itself is the contemplation; thus it is "contemplation of relinquishment. This is a designation for insight and the path.
For insight (vipassanā), by way of "overcoming through substitution" (tadaṅgavasena), abandons defilements along with the formative activities of the aggregates (khandhābhisaṅkhāra);

and by seeing the fault in the conditioned, it leaps into Nibbāna, which is the opposite of that [conditioned state], because of its inclination toward it. Thus, it is called both "renunciation as abandonment" (pariccāga-paṭinissagga) and "renunciation as leaping forward" (pakkhandana-paṭinissagga).
The Path (magga), by way of complete eradication (samucchedavasena), abandons defilements along with the formative activities of the aggregates.
Because one leaps into Nibbāna by making it the object, it is called both "renunciation-relinquishment" and "leaping-relinquishment.
Furthermore, because each preceding knowledge is observed by the subsequent one, it is called "contemplation.
Being endowed with this twofold contemplation of relinquishment, while breathing in and breathing out—
“It should be understood that one trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in and I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment.
This fourth tetrad is stated by way of pure insight (suddha-vipassanā) alone; the preceding three, however, are by way of both serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā).
