Thus, the development of mindfulness of breathing with its sixteen bases (vatthu) should be understood by way of these four tetrads.”
Thus, by way of these sixteen bases, this mindfulness of breathing is of great fruit and great benefit.

In this regard, its state of being of great benefit should be understood through such qualities as its peacefulness, based on the statement: "Monks, this concentration through mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, is peaceful and sublime," and so forth; and also by virtue of its capacity to cut off discursive thought.

For this [practice], by virtue of its peaceful, sublime, and refreshing state of blissful abiding, cuts off the mind’s wandering hither and thither due to thoughts that create obstacles to concentration, and makes the mind face exclusively toward the object of mindfulness of breathing.
Therefore it is said: "Mindfulness of breathing should be developed for the cutting off of thoughts."
Furthermore, its great benefit should be understood by way of its being the root for the fulfillment of true knowledge and liberation (vijjā-vimutti). For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness;
the four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment; the seven factors of enlightenment..."
“...when practiced extensively, it fulfills true knowledge and liberation.
Furthermore, its great benefit should be understood from the fact that it brings about the clear comprehension of the final in-breaths and out-breaths.
For this was said by the Blessed One: “Rāhula, when mindfulness of breathing has been thus developed and thus practiced extensively...”
“Even those final in-breaths and out-breaths, they too cease only when known, not when unknown.
In this context, with respect to cessation, there are three kinds of finality: finality of existence, finality of jhāna, and finality of death.

For among existences, in-breaths and out-breaths occur in the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), but they do not occur in the fine-material or immaterial existences (*rūpabhava* and *arūpabhava*); therefore—

These are the final [states] of existence (*bhavacarimaka*). They occur during the first three jhānas but do not occur in the fourth; therefore, they are called the final [states] of jhāna (*jhānacarimaka*).

However, those which arise together with the sixteenth consciousness preceding the death-consciousness and cease simultaneously with the death-consciousness are called the final [states] of death (*cuticarimaka*). These are what is intended here by the term "final" (*carimaka*).

It is said that for a bhikkhu devoted to this meditation subject, because the object of mindfulness of breathing has been thoroughly mastered, when he adverts to their arising at the moment of arising of the sixteenth consciousness immediately prior to the death-consciousness, their arising becomes manifest to him.
When he adverts to their presence, their presence also becomes manifest to him. When he adverts to their dissolution...
And their destruction becomes manifest.
For a bhikkhu who has attained Arahantship by developing some other meditation subject than this, the duration of his life may be either limited or unlimited;
but for one who has attained Arahantship by developing this mindfulness of breathing with its sixteen bases, [the duration is fixed].
The life-span of one who has attained [this state] is indeed limited. Knowing, "Only this much of my life-force will now proceed,
and no further," he performs all his duties— such as tending to his body, dressing, and putting on robes— solely through his own natural disposition, and then closes his eyes,
just like the Elder Tissa who dwelt at Koṭapabbata Monastery and the Elder Mahātissa who dwelt at Mahākarañjiya Monastery.
It was like the Elder Piṇḍapātika Tissa in the great kingdom of Devaputta, and like the two elder brothers who dwelt at the Cittalapabbata Monastery.
Herein is an illustration by way of a single instance:
it is said that on the day of the full-moon Uposatha, one of the two elder brothers recited the Pātimokkha.
Having been reinstated and surrounded by the community of monks, he went to his own dwelling place.
Standing on the walking-path, he looked at the moonlight, reflected upon his own life-force (*āyusaṅkhāra*), and said to the community of monks:
"How have you previously seen monks passing into final Nibbāna? Thereupon, some said: "We have seen them passing into final Nibbāna while still seated on their seats."
“Have you ever seen them before? Some replied, “We have seen them sitting cross-legged in the air.
The Elder said, “Now I shall show you one who attains final nibbāna even while walking.

Then, having drawn a line on the walkway, he said, “Starting from this end of the walkway, I will go to the opposite end and, upon returning, I shall attain final nibbāna only after reaching this line.”
Having spoken thus, he descended to the walking path, went to the far end, and while returning, at the very moment he stepped upon a line with one foot,
he attained final Nibbāna. Therefore, indeed, being heedful, a wise person should constantly devote themselves to mindfulness of breathing, which possesses such manifold benefits.
This concludes the section on the detailed exposition of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*). 239.

Regarding the recollection of peace (*upasamānussati*), which was taught immediately after mindfulness of breathing: one who wishes to develop this recollection of peace should go to a secluded place...

While in seclusion, one should recollect the qualities of Nibbāna, which is defined as the subsiding of all suffering, in this way: "Bhikkhus, among all phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion (*virāga*) is declared the foremost;

that is to say, the crushing of pride, the removal of thirst, the uprooting of attachment, the cutting off of the cycle of existence, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. Thus should the qualities of Nibbāna be recollected.

In this context, "as far as" (*yāvatā*) means "however many. "Phenomena" (*dhammā*) means intrinsic natures. "Conditioned or unconditioned" (*saṅkhatā vā asaṅkhatā vā*) means either produced by causes coming together and combining, or not so produced.
"Dispassion is declared the foremost of these phenomena" means that among those conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, dispassion is declared the foremost;
it is called the best, the supreme. In this regard, "dispassion" (*virāga*) does not mean merely the absence of lust.

Now, as for this "the crushing of intoxication" … [as it continues] … "Nirvana"—that unconditioned dhamma which receives such names as "the crushing of intoxication" and so forth, should be understood as dispassion (*virāga*).

For because all intoxications—such as the intoxication of conceit and the intoxication of manhood—become crushed, non-intoxicating, and destroyed upon reaching it, it is therefore called "the crushing of intoxication. And because, by reaching it, [all things are abandoned]...
All thirst for sense pleasures is brought to subdual and comes to an end; therefore it is called "the subduing of thirst.
Furthermore, because by means of that [path], the attachments to the five strands of sensual pleasure go to total eradication, it is called "the eradication of attachment.
And because by means of that, the round of existence in the three planes is cut off, it is called "the cutting off of the round."
But because, by resorting to it, craving is completely exhausted, fades away, and ceases, it is therefore called the "destruction of craving," "dispassion," and "cessation.
Furthermore, because this [Nibbāna] prevents, binds, and stitches together the four modes of birth, the five destinations, the seven stations of consciousness,
and the nine abodes of beings so that they do not continue from one state to another, it is so named.
It is called *nibbāna* because it has gone forth from, escaped from, and is dissociated from craving (*taṇhā*), which receives the designation "blowing out.
Thus, peace, known as *nibbāna*, should be recollected by way of these qualities such as the crushing of intoxication.
Or else, other [qualities] too were taught by the Blessed One: "Monks, I shall teach you the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*)... the truth (*sacca*)... the further shore (*pāra*)..."

In such suttas as, “I shall teach you, bhikkhus, that which is very hard to see... that which is ageless... that which is stable... that which is non-proliferated... that which is deathless... that which is auspicious...

that which is secure... that which is wonderful... that which is free from calamity... that which is free from affliction... that which is purification... that which is an island... that which is a refuge...
that which is a shelter,” the qualities of peace (*upasama*) are described; it should be recollected by means of these as well.

As he thus recollects peace by way of its qualities, such as the crushing of intoxication, his mind at that time is neither obsessed by lust, nor by hatred, nor by delusion. At that time, his mind is directed straight toward peace;
thus, for one whose hindrances have been suppressed in the manner described under the Recollection of the Buddha and other such practices—

The factors of absorption (jhānaṅga) arise in a single moment. However, due to the profundity of the qualities of tranquility, or because of an inclination toward recollecting various kinds of qualities, the jhāna reaches only access concentration (upacāra) without reaching full absorption (appanā).
This, by way of recollecting the qualities of tranquility, is reckoned simply as "recollection of peace" (upasamānussati).
Like the six recollections, this too succeeds only for a noble disciple;
nevertheless, it should be brought to mind even by an ordinary person who values tranquility. For even through the power of hearing about it, the mind gains confidence in tranquility.
Furthermore, a bhikkhu devoted to this recollection of tranquility sleeps happily, wakes happily, and has peaceful faculties.
For he becomes one whose mind is peaceful, endowed with shame and fear of wrongdoing, inspiring, resolute in the sublime, a teacher and an object of veneration for his fellow celibates.
Yet, failing to penetrate further, he is destined for a happy destination.
Therefore, indeed, being heedful and discerning, you should cultivate [this].
"Thus there are manifold benefits in serenity, which is noble and peaceful.
This is the section of the detailed exposition on the recollection of peace (*upasamānussati*).
Thus ends [the chapter] in the *Visuddhimagga* composed for the delight of the virtuous.
The Eighth Chapter, titled "The Description of the Meditation Subjects of Recollection," in the Section on the Development of Concentration.
9. The Exposition of the Divine Abidings:

A Discourse on the Development of Loving-kindness 240. Following the recollections as meditation subjects that were listed, there are loving-kindness (mettā), compassion (karuṇā), appreciative joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekkhā).
One who wishes to develop loving-kindness among these four divine abodes (brahmavihāras) should first, as a beginner practitioner,
having severed all impediments and taken up a meditation subject, perform his meal duties and dispel the drowsiness following the meal;
then, sitting comfortably on a well-prepared seat in a secluded place, he should first reflect upon the danger in ill-will and the benefit in patience.
Why? Because by means of this meditation, hatred is to be abandoned and patience is to be attained.

And it is not possible to abandon anything whose danger has not been seen, nor to attain anything whose benefit has not been understood. Therefore, the danger in hatred should be seen by way of such passages as: "Friend, one who is hating, overcome by hatred, with mind obsessed by it, even kills a living being," and so forth.
The benefit of patience should be understood by way of such passages as: “Patience is the supreme austerity; the Buddhas declare Nibbāna to be supreme”;
“One who possesses the power of patience is an army of strength—him I call a brahmin”;
and “There exists nothing superior to patience.”

Thus, for the purpose of withdrawing the mind from the fault of aversion which has been seen as a danger, and for the purpose of joining it with patience whose benefits have been understood, the development of loving-kindness (*mettā*) should be undertaken. And by one who undertakes it, the classification of persons must first be known:
"In regard to these persons, loving-kindness should not be developed at first; in regard to these, it should not be developed at all."
Indeed, this loving-kindness (*mettā*) should not first be developed toward these four types of persons: the disagreeable person, the very dear friend, the neutral person, and the hostile person.
It should not be developed specifically toward those of a different gender. It should certainly not be developed toward one who is dead.
For what reason should it not first be developed toward the disagreeable and the others? Because one who places the disagreeable in the position of the beloved undergoes exhaustion.
One who places a dearly beloved friend in the position of neutrality becomes weary; even at the arising of a slight suffering, he is as if overcome by weeping.
Likewise, one who places a neutral person in the position of the venerable or the beloved becomes weary.
When recollecting an enemy, anger arises; therefore, these [meditations] should not be developed first toward those who are unloved and so forth.
However, in one of a different gender, lust arises for that very person when they cultivate it with specific intent.
It is said that a certain son of a minister asked a forest-dwelling elder, "Venerable sir, toward whom should loving-kindness be cultivated?
The elder replied, "Toward a beloved person. That man’s own wife was dear to him; as he cultivated loving-kindness toward her, he engaged in a wall-battle all night long.
Therefore, it should not be developed specifically toward those of a different gender.
Furthermore, one who develops it toward a deceased person reaches neither access concentration nor absorption.
It is said that a certain young bhikkhu began to develop loving-kindness (mettā) directed toward his teacher, but his loving-kindness did not proceed. He went into the presence of the Great Elder...
Having gone there, he said, "Venerable sir, my attainment of the meditation on loving-kindness (*mettā-jhāna*) is indeed familiar to me, yet I am unable to enter it;
what could be the reason? The Elder replied, "Friend, you must search for the sign (*nimitta*).

While searching, he learned that his teacher had passed away; directing his mind toward another person and radiating loving-kindness, he attained the absorption. Therefore, [the meditation] should certainly not be developed when [the object] has died.

241. First of all, however, one should develop it repeatedly toward oneself alone, thinking either, “May I be happy and free from suffering,” or, “May I maintain myself as one who is without enmity, without ill will, without affliction, and happy.
This being so, as for what is stated in the Vibhaṅga:

“And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu dwell pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness? Just as, for example, having seen a person who is dear and pleasing, one would feel loving-kindness toward them; even so, he pervades all beings with loving-kindness.”
“And as for what is said in the *Paṭisambhidā*:
‘In five ways should the liberation of mind through loving-kindness, which has no specific object, be developed:
“May all beings be free from enmity, free from affliction, free from distress, and may they look after themselves happily. May all breathing things... may all creatures...’”’”

"May all persons... may all those included within the cycle of individual existence be free from enmity, free from affliction, free from distress, and may they maintain themselves in happiness"—so it was said.
And in the *Mettasutta*: "May they be happy and secure..."

“May all beings be happy-minded,” and so forth—this [that you have cited] is contradicted [by your position]. If it is argued that the development [of loving-kindness] toward oneself is not mentioned there, that is not a contradiction. Why? Because that was stated by way of absorption (*appanā*), whereas this is stated by way of being a witness (*sakkhibhāva*).
For even if one were to cultivate loving-kindness toward oneself for a hundred or a thousand years in such a manner as, “May I be happy,” and so on...
One develops [this], yet absorption does not arise for him.

However, for one who develops it with the thought, "May I be happy," taking oneself as a witness—thinking, "Just as I desire happiness, am averse to suffering, desire to live, and do not desire to die, so too are other beings"—there arises in other beings the desire for their welfare and happiness. This was also said by the Blessed One:
“Having wandered through all directions with my mind,
I found nothing anywhere dearer than myself.
Thus, each person holds themselves dear.”
"Therefore, one who desires their own welfare should not harm another."—By saying this, this method was demonstrated. 242.
Therefore, for the sake of establishing oneself as a witness, one should first pervade oneself with loving-kindness (mettā), and immediately thereafter, for the sake of setting happiness in motion...
Regarding this person who is dear and pleasing, respected and worthy of esteem— whether it be a teacher (*ācariya*), one equal to a teacher, a preceptor (*upajjhāya*), or one equal to a preceptor—

one should develop loving-kindness (*mettā*) by recollecting the reasons for their being dear and pleasing, such as their generosity and kind words, and the reasons for their being respected and worthy of esteem,
such as their virtue (*sīla*) and learning (*suta*), in this manner: "May this good person be happy and free from suffering," and so forth.
In such a person, absorption (appanā) may indeed be achieved;

however, this bhikkhu, not being satisfied with that much alone and desiring to break down the barriers, should next develop loving-kindness (mettā) toward a very dear friend, then from the very dear friend toward a neutral person, and from the neutral person toward a hostile individual. And while developing it, in each successive stage...
Having made the mind supple and wieldy, one should apply it to each successive person immediately following the previous one.
However, for one who has no hostile person, or for whom—due to being of the nature of a Great Being (mahāpurisa)—no perception of enmity arises even toward others who cause harm, he [should reflect]:
"My mind of loving-kindness toward neutral persons has become supple and wieldy; now, I shall [apply it] to him..."
One should not even entertain the thought, "I am directing [my mind] toward an enemy. However, with reference to those who do possess such a mind, it was said:
"Loving-kindness should be developed toward a hostile person by way of equanimity. 243.
But if, while he is directing his mind toward an enemy, resentment arises due to his recollecting the offense committed by that person, [he should apply the following remedy].
Then, by repeatedly entering into and emerging from the attainment of loving-kindness toward any of those aforementioned persons,
and repeatedly directing loving-kindness toward that person, he should dispel resentment. If, even while striving in this way, it does not subside,
then he should proceed according to the "Simile of the Saw" instruction and other such teachings.
One should strive again and again for the abandoning of aversion.
And this should be done by admonishing oneself in this way: "O you who are prone to anger! Has it not been said by the Blessed One:
'Bhikkhus, even if bandits with saws were to hack away your limbs one by one, whoever should give way to a mind of malice therein would not be following my instruction'?"
“Worse than that is he who, being angry, returns anger in kind;
by not returning anger for anger, one wins a battle difficult to win.
He acts for the benefit of both, himself and the other.”
“Furthermore, knowing that another is provoked to anger, he who remains composed and mindful.
And: “Monks, these seven things, which are pleasing to an enemy and serve to create enmity, come upon a woman or a man who is prone to anger.
What are the seven? Here, monks, an enemy desires for an enemy thus: ‘Oh, may this person be ugly!’”
"May this person be ugly. Why is that? Monks, an enemy does not rejoice in the beauty of his enemy.

Monks, when a person is angry, overcome by anger, and possessed by anger, even though he may be well-bathed, well-anointed, with hair and beard trimmed, and clothed in white garments, he is nevertheless ugly.
He becomes overcome by anger. This, monks, is the first thing that is pleasing to an enemy and conducive to an enemy’s purpose that comes upon an angry woman or man.
Furthermore, monks, an enemy wishes this for his enemy: “O, may this person sleep in discomfort!
… [and so on] … “May he not have abundant wealth! … [and so on] … “May he not possess riches! … [and so on].

"He would not be possessed of fame... [and so on] ...he would not be possessed of friends... [and so on] ...upon the dissolution of the body, after death, he would not reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
For what reason? "Monks, an enemy does not rejoice at the going of an enemy to a happy destination.
This person, monks, who is angry, overcome by anger, and possessed by anger, engages in misconduct with the body..."
“He engages in misconduct by body, speech, and mind.

Having engaged in misconduct by body, speech, and mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, even in hell, being overcome by anger.
And: “Bhikkhus, just as a torch made from a funeral pyre, burning at both ends and smeared with excrement in the middle, serves neither as firewood for a village nor...”
“It spreads, but it does not spread for the sake of firewood in the forest. Monks, I say that this person is just like that,” and:
“Now, by being angry in this way, you will not be a follower of the Blessed One’s teaching;
and by retaliating, you become worse than the person who was angry and will not win the battle that is so difficult to win. Furthermore, regarding those things that create enemies...”
“You will only be making yourself for yourself, and you will become like a torch carried by a corpse.
(244) While he is thus striving and exerting himself, if that resentment subsides, that is good.
If it does not subside, then whichever quality has become stilled and purified in that person—
When recollected, it brings about confidence; having recollected this or that, resentment should be dispelled.
For in some cases, only one's bodily conduct is tranquil. And the state of being tranquil is known by all people when one performs many duties and observances.
However, one’s verbal and mental conduct may still be untranquil. In such a person...
Without reflecting on that, one should instead recollect the very tranquility of his bodily conduct.
For some, it is only the verbal conduct that has become tranquil, and this state of tranquility is known by all people;
for he is naturally skillful in hospitality, gentle, pleasant to converse with, friendly, and open-faced.
He speaks first and concludes the teaching with a sweet voice; he delivers a discourse on the Dhamma with well-rounded words and phrases.
However, his bodily conduct and mental conduct are not yet tranquil. Without considering those, one should remember only his tranquility of verbal conduct.
In some cases, only the mental conduct is tranquil, and the state of that tranquility is evident to all people during such acts as paying homage at a cetiya.
It becomes manifest. For one whose mind is not calmed, when worshipping a shrine, the Bodhi tree, or the elders, does not worship with due respect;
he sits in the Dhamma-hall with a distracted mind or nodding off.
But one whose mind is calmed worships with full confidence, lending an ear and fixing his attention, manifesting clarity of mind through body or speech.
While practicing, one listens to the Dhamma. Thus, for some, mental conduct alone is peaceful while bodily and verbal conduct are not;
in such a case, without considering those latter two, one should recollect only the peace of their mental conduct.
However, for another, not even one of these three qualities is peaceful; regarding that person, [one should reflect: "Even though..."
"He is now wandering in the world of humans; however, after the passing of a few days, he will fill eight great hells and sixteen secondary hells.
Compassion should be established [toward him]. For it is by depending on compassion that resentment is pacified.

In some cases, these three qualities become pacified; for such a person, whatever one wishes, that should be recollected. Indeed, for such a person, the development of loving-kindness (*mettā*) is not difficult.

And to clarify this meaning, the *Āghātapaṭivinaya-sutta* from the Pañcaka-nipāta should be cited in detail: "Friends, there are these five ways of removing resentment, wherein the resentment that has arisen in a bhikkhu should be entirely dispelled.
But if, even while he is making such an effort, resentment still arises, then he should admonish himself in this way:
“If suffering has been inflicted upon you by an enemy within your own domain,
why do you wish to inflict suffering upon his mind, which is outside his domain?
Having abandoned your circle of kinsmen who are so helpful and whose faces are bathed in tears— ”
Why do you not abandon anger, which causes great harm, as if it were an enemy?
To uproot those very virtues you protect, you have instead nourished what is called anger;
who is more dull-witted than you?
“You are angry because another has done an ignoble deed;
why then do you yourself wish to do the very same thing?
If another has done something unpleasant to you simply because he wished to cause you harm,”
By giving rise to anger toward him, do you fulfill his wish?
Whether or not you, being angry, will actually cause him suffering,
you are certainly afflicting yourself right now with the pain of your own anger.
“If your enemies have ascended the path of harmful anger, why do you too,
by becoming angry, merely follow in their footsteps?
Whatever harm has been done to you by an enemy out of hatred, [that very thing you are now emulating].”
Cut off that very same hatred; why do you distress yourself for no reason?
Because of the momentariness of all phenomena, those aggregates by which you were wronged have ceased;
toward whom now, here, should you be angry?
“He who causes suffering to another—who is he to whom that person would cause it in his absence?
Since he too is a cause of suffering, why are you angry with him as a ‘friend’?
(246) If, however, resentment does not subside even when he admonishes himself in this way, then by him—his own...
And one should reflect upon the fact that both oneself and others are owners of their own actions. In this regard, first, one should reflect about oneself in this way:
"O friend, what will you do by being angry with him? Will not this very action, rooted in hatred, lead to your own harm?
For you are the owner of your action, the heir of your action, born of your action, bound to your action, and have your action as your refuge."
Whatever karma you shall perform, of that you will be the heir;

yet this karma of yours is neither capable of accomplishing perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*), nor solitary enlightenment (*paccekabodhi*), nor the plane of a disciple (*sāvakabhūmi*), nor any of the attainments such as the state of a Brahmā, a Sakka, a Cakkavatti, or a local king;
rather, it is capable only of leading you away from the Teaching and bringing about the state of a scavenger and so forth.
"Furthermore, this karma leads to various specific sufferings such as those of the hell-beings.
By doing this, you are like a man who, wishing to strike another with glowing embers or excrement held in both hands, first burns and defiles himself."
Having thus reflected upon one’s own ownership of kamma, one should likewise reflect regarding another:
“What will this person achieve by being angry with you? Will it not rather lead to his own harm?
For this venerable one is the owner of his kamma, the heir of his kamma... [as before] ...whatever kamma he shall perform, he will be the heir of that. And this...”

This karma is not capable of accomplishing either perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*), solitary enlightenment (*paccekabodhi*), the stage of a disciple (*sāvakabhūmi*), or any of the attainments such as the status of a Brahmā, a Sakka, a Cakkavatti, or a local king;

rather, this karma leads to being excluded from the Dispensation (*sāsana*) and results in the state of a scavenger (*vighāsāda*) and various specific sufferings of the hells (*nerayika*). While performing this, he—
Just as a man standing with the wind at his back, wishing to sprinkle dust upon another, only sprinkles himself, so it is said by the Blessed One:
“He who offends an unoffending man,
a pure person free from blemish;”
“Evil follows that fool,
just as fine dust thrown against the wind. If, however,
even while reflecting thus on his own ownership of kamma, his mind is not pacified, then he should recollect the virtues of the Teacher’s former conduct.

In this regard, the method of reflection is as follows: "O renunciant, did not your Teacher, even while he was still a Bodhisatta prior to his full enlightenment—while yet unenlightened—fulfill the perfections for four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons, during which time he never allowed his mind to become corrupted, even toward those who sought to kill him or were his enemies? For example, in the Sīlavant Jātaka."
Furthermore, when his ministers rose up to prevent a rival king— who had been brought by a wicked minister hostile to his own queen—
from seizing a kingdom three hundred yojanas in extent, he did not even allow them to touch their weapons. Again,
when he was being buried alive after digging a pit knee-deep in a raw cemetery together with a thousand ministers, he did not experience even the slightest corruption of mind.
Without resorting to the effort of sifting through the dust for the sake of devouring the corpses that had come there, he regained his life through the power of a *yakkha*.
Having entered his own chamber of glory and seen his enemy reclining upon the bed of splendor, he felt no anger;
instead, he made a mutual pact with him, established him in the position of a friend, and said:
“A wise man should indeed aspire; he should not lose heart.
For I see myself as I was when I wished.

In the *Khantivādī Jātaka*, when the foolish King of Kāsi asked, “What do you profess, ascetic? and the Bodhisatta replied, “I am known as a ‘Teacher of Forbearance’ (Khantivādī),” the king had him beaten with thorny whips and had his hands and feet cut off, yet he did not give way to even the slightest anger.
It is not surprising that one who has gone forth in old age would act in this way. However, in the *Cūḷadhammapāla Jātaka*, even while still a mere infant lying on his back, he said:
“The arms of Dhammapāla, anointed with sandalwood paste, are being cut off;
O King, my life-breaths are being choked, for I am the heir to the earth.”
While his mother was thus lamenting, her father, the king named Mahāpatāpa, had her four hands and feet cut off as if they were stalks of bamboo.
Not being satisfied even with that, he commanded, "Now cut off her head. Upon this command, [Dhammapāla thought]:
"This is now the time for you to restrain your mind; now, O Dhammapāla, toward your father who has ordered the cutting off of your head..."
"Be even-minded toward these four: the man who would cut off your head, your lamenting mother, and yourself.
Having thus firmly resolved upon this strong commitment, he did not manifest even the slightest trace of ill-will.
And this is not at all surprising that one who was a human being acted in such a way; for even when he was a tusker among animals, Chaddanta—
Even when he became an elephant and was pierced in the navel by a spreading arrow, he did not allow his mind to become corrupted toward the hunter who had done him harm. As it is said:
"Though struck by a broad arrow, the elephant..."
With a mind free from malice, he addressed the hunter:
"For what purpose, for what cause, my good man, have you killed me? Or by whom was this plot devised?"

Having spoken thus, when she said, "Venerable sir, I have been sent by the chief queen of the King of Kāsi for the sake of your teeth," he fulfilled her wish. He severed his own two teeth—which were radiant with the beautiful splendor of the emission of six-colored rays—and gave them to her.
Having become a great monkey, he spoke to the man whom he himself had rescued from the mountain precipice:
"This is food for humans, just like other wild animals in the forest."
“What if I were to kill this monkey and eat him when I am hungry?
I shall go forth as one who has provided himself with provisions, taking his flesh as my travel-rations;
thus I will cross the wilderness, and it will serve as my sustenance.”
Having thought thus, he lifted up a stone and crushed it upon his head; then, looking at that man with eyes filled with tears, he said:
"Do not do such a thing to me, O venerable sir!
You are indeed long-lived; you ought rather to restrain another."
Having spoken thus, without corrupting his mind toward that man and without considering his own suffering, he brought that very man to the land of safety.
Having become the Naga king named Bhūridatta, he resolved upon the Uposatha precepts and lay upon the summit of an anthill;
even while being drenched over his entire body with a medicinal oil resembling the fire at the end of an aeon, and being placed within a chest throughout all of Jambudīpa...
Even while being made to play [with him], he did not harbor even the slightest malice toward that brahmin. As it is said:
“Though they cast me into a basket, And though they trample me with their hands, I do not become angry at Alampāna, For fear of breaking my virtue.”
Even when he was the Naga king Campeyya and was being tormented by a snake-charmer, he did not give rise to even the slightest malice in his mind. As it is said:
“Then too, while I was living righteously and observing the Uposatha, The snake-charmer seized me and played with me at the king’s gate.”
“Whatever color he contemplates— blue, yellow, or red—
I become like that which he has thought, following his mind.
I can turn dry land into water, and I can turn water into dry land.”
“If I were to become angry with him here, I could reduce him to ashes in an instant.
Yet, if I fall under the power of my mind, I shall decline in virtue;
and for one who has declined in virtue, the supreme goal is not accomplished.”
Having become the Naga King Saṅkhapāla, he was pierced in eight places with sharp spears;
thorny creepers were inserted into the wounds, a strong rope was fastened around his nose, and he was carried away on a carrying-pole by sixteen Bhojaputta executioners.
As his body was dragged along the surface of the earth, he experienced great suffering.
Although he was capable of reducing all those Bhojaputta youths to ashes by the mere glance of his angry look,
he opened his eyes and did not display even the slightest sign of malice.
As it is said:
“On the fourteenth and the fifteenth,
I always observe the Uposatha;
then the sixteen Bhojaputta youths arrived.”
Having taken a strong rope and a snare,
the hunters seized me from all sides and led me away, having pierced my nose and passed the rope through it.
"I endured such suffering, not violating the Uposatha.
Not only these, but he performed many other wonders, such as those found in the Mātuposaka Jātaka and others. Of him—

Now, for one who points to that Blessed One—the Teacher who has attained omniscience and possesses the quality of forbearance unequaled by anyone in the world including the devas—it is exceedingly improper and unseemly to give rise to a mind of resentment. 248.
Even if, while thus reflecting on the qualities of the Teacher’s past conduct, his defilements [should persist] for a long time...
For one who has entered into servitude, that resentment does not subside; therefore, he should reflect upon the "beginningless cycle of rebirths" (*anamataggiya*). For it is said therein:

"Monks, such a being is not easily found who has not previously been one's mother, who has not previously been one's father, who has not previously been one's brother, who has not previously been one's sister, who has not previously been one's son, or who has not previously been one's daughter.
Therefore, one should arouse such a thought toward that person: "Indeed, this person was my mother in the past for ten months..."
Having carried her in his womb, he nurtured her by removing urine, feces, saliva, snot, and so forth without disgust— as if they were yellow sandalwood—
caressing her chest, tending to her with every limb, and supporting her; and having become her father,
he engaged in trade by traveling along goat paths, thorn paths, and the like, even sacrificing his own life for my sake in a battle with troops arrayed on both sides.

"Having entered [the ship] and cast myself into the great ocean, and having performed other difficult tasks, he gathered wealth by various means with the thought, 'I shall support my little son,' and thus supported me.
Even when he was my brother, sister, son, and daughter, he rendered this and that assistance;
therefore, it is not fitting for me to harbor ill-will toward him."

249. But if he is still unable to extinguish the mind even in this way, then he should reflect upon the benefits of loving-kindness (*mettā*) as follows: “O renunciant, has it not been said by the Blessed One:

‘Monks, when the liberation of mind through loving-kindness is practiced, developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and well undertaken, eleven benefits are to be expected. Which ones?’”
What eleven? One sleeps in comfort, wakes in comfort, does not see evil dreams,
is dear to human beings, is dear to non-human beings, is protected by deities, fire, poison, or weapons do not affect one,
the mind quickly becomes concentrated, the complexion of the face brightens, and one dies unconfused.
‘If you do not penetrate further, you will go to the Brahma-world.
‘If you do not extinguish this mind, you will be excluded from these benefits. 250.
Furthermore, for one who is unable to extinguish it even in this way, the analysis of the elements (*dhātuvinibbhoga*) should be performed. How? “O renunciant, [analyze thus:]”
When you are angry with this, with whom are you angry? Are you angry with the hair of the head, or with the body hair, or with the nails...
[and so on] ...are you angry with the urine? Or else, among the hair and so forth, are you angry with the earth element, the water element, the fire element, or the air element?
Or rather, are you angry with those five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements that have been taken up?
"This venerable one is called so-and-so. Among these, with whom are you angry:
with the aggregate of form, or rather with the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness? Or with what are you angry: with the eye-base, or with the form-base?
… [and so on] … or with what are you angry: with the mind-base, or with the mental-object-base? Or with what are you angry: with the eye-element?
“Are you angry? At what? At the element of form? At the eye-consciousness element?... [and so on] ...at the mind element? At the mental-object element?

At the mind-consciousness element? For one who performs such an analysis of the elements in this way, there is no place for anger to take root, just as there is none for a mustard seed on the point of an awl, or for a painting in the sky.
251. However, one who is unable to perform the analysis of the elements (dhātuvinibbhoga) should practice the sharing of gifts.
One’s own belongings should be given to another, and what belongs to another should be taken by oneself.

But if the other person leads a wrong livelihood and possesses requisites that are unfit for use, then only what belongs to oneself should be given. For one who acts in this way, there is certainly...
Hostility toward that person subsides. Furthermore, even the anger that has followed the other person since past lives subsides at that very moment.
This was illustrated by the alms-collecting Elder who had three times vacated his lodging at the Cittalapabbata Monastery, saying:
"Venerable sir, this bowl, worth eight kahāpaṇas, was given to me by my mother, a female lay devotee; it is a righteous gain."
"Bestow merit upon the Great Female Lay Disciple," he said, and gave her the bowl as if it were one received by a great elder who had attained high status.
Such is the great power of this thing called giving. And it is said:
"Giving is the taming of the untamed; giving accomplishes all aims."
"By means of giving and by pleasant speech, they rise up and bow down.

(252) Thus, for one whose hostility toward a hostile person has been pacified, the mind proceeds toward that person through loving-kindness (*mettā*) just as it does toward dear, very dear, friends, and neutral persons.
Then, as he repeatedly extends loving-kindness toward himself...
One who is accomplishing equanimity toward four types of persons—those dear to oneself, those neutral, and hostile persons—should effect the breaking down of boundaries.

This is its characteristic: if, while one is sitting in a single place with these three persons—the dear, the neutral, and the hostile—making oneself the fourth, thieves should arrive and say, "Venerable sir, give us one bhikkhu."
When asked, “For what reason? they might say, “To kill him, take his throat-blood, and perform a sacrifice.
If, in that situation, the bhikkhu should think, “Let them take such-and-such a person or such-and-such a person,” the breaking of the boundary has not occurred.
Even if he should think, “Let them take me, but not these three,” the breaking of the boundary has still not occurred. Why is that?
For whoever he desires to harm, toward that person he becomes a seeker of harm, while toward all others he becomes a seeker of welfare.

But when he does not see even one among the four persons as deserving to be given to the thieves, and his mind proceeds with complete equanimity toward himself and those other three persons, the breaking down of the boundary has been accomplished. Thus said the ancients:
“Toward oneself, toward the neutral, and toward the fourfold kind of enemy—”
When one perceives diversity among living beings, even while possessing a mind of goodwill,
one is not said to be "skilled" if one does not obtain loving-kindness at will.
But when the four boundaries of a monk have been merged together, he is then called skilled.
“He pervades with loving-kindness equally the entire world together with its devas;
this is a great distinction from the former, for whose boundary no limit is known.
(253) Thus, at the very moment the boundaries were broken down, this bhikkhu obtained both the sign and the access concentration.
When the delimitation of the boundary has been made, however, by cultivating, developing, and repeatedly practicing that very sign, he attains absorption with ease,
in the same manner as described for the earth-kasiṇa. At this point,
he has attained [the jhāna] which is abandoned of five factors, endowed with five factors, and excellent in three ways.
The first jhāna, endowed with ten characteristics, is accompanied by loving-kindness. Once that has been attained, by cultivating, developing,

and frequently practicing that very same sign, one gradually reaches the second and third jhānas according to the fourfold system, and the second, third, and fourth jhānas according to the fivefold system.
For by means of one of the first jhānas and so forth, he dwells having pervaded one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness;

likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus, above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, immeasurable.

He dwells pervading [the world] with a mind free from hatred and free from ill will. For this transformation occurs only for one whose mind has attained absorption (appanā) by means of the first jhāna and so forth. 254.
And here, "accompanied by loving-kindness" means endowed with loving-kindness. "With the mind" means with the consciousness. "One direction" means...
This is stated with reference to a being first encompassed in each individual direction, by way of pervading all beings included within that single direction.
"Having pervaded" means having touched and made the object of focus. "Dwells" means he maintains the dwelling in the postures established upon the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*).
"Likewise the second" means just as [he dwells] having pervaded any one direction among the eastern and other directions.
He dwells; the meaning is that immediately after that, he does so likewise for the second, third, and fourth [directions].
Thus, by this same method, it is said "above" regarding the upper direction. "Below and across"—the lower direction and the intermediate directions are exactly like this.
In this context, "below" means downward; "across" means in the intermediate directions. Thus, in all directions within the circle of the hermitage...

"He sends forth his mind imbued with loving-kindness toward himself and draws it back again"—to this extent, the directed pervasion of loving-kindness (*mettā*) by encompassing a single direction has been shown.

However, the passage beginning with "in all places" (*sabbadhi*) is stated for the purpose of showing the non-directed pervasion. Therein, "in all places" (*sabbadhi*) means everywhere. "In all ways" (*sabbattatāya*)...
“By selfhood in all”—that is, by treating as oneself those divided into categories such as inferior, middling, superior, friend, enemy, and neutral;
it is said, "without making the distinction that 'this is another being,' but through equality with oneself.
Alternatively, "by all-selfhood" means not wavering even slightly outwardly from any part of the mind. "Possessing all" (*sabbāvanta*) means possessing all beings, or associated with all beings.

The meaning is as follows. "The world" refers to the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*). However, because there is the presentation of synonyms such as "vast" (*vipula*) and so forth, the phrase "accompanied by loving-kindness" (*mettāsahagatena*) is stated here once again.

Alternatively, since the word "thus" (*tathā*) or the particle "iti" is not used here—as they were in the case of the directed pervasion—therefore the phrase "with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness" is stated once more. Or else, this was stated by way of a conclusion. "Vast" (*vipulena*)...
And here, "vastness" (vipulatā) should be understood in the sense of pervasion. However, it is "exalted" (mahaggata) by way of its plane;

it is "immeasurable" (appamāṇa) by way of its proficiency and by way of having immeasurable beings as its object; it is "free from enmity" (avera) through the abandoning of the adversary that is ill-will;

and it is "unafflicted" (abyāpajja) due to the abandoning of mental distress—meaning it is without suffering. This is the meaning of the transformation described in the sequence beginning with "with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness."
255. Just as this transformation occurs only for one whose mind has attained absorption (appanā), so too that which is stated in the *Paṭisambhidā*:

"The liberation of mind through loving-kindness with unspecified pervasion in five ways, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness with specified pervasion in seven ways, and the liberation of mind through loving-kindness with directional pervasion in ten ways"—that too [occurs] only for one whose mind has attained absorption.
It should be understood that this is accomplished.
And therein, by means of these [resolutions]: "May all beings be free from enmity, free from ill will, free from distress, and may they maintain themselves in happiness;
may all breathing things, all creatures, all persons, and all who have entered upon a selfhood be free from enmity... [and so on]... may they maintain themselves in happiness."
The liberation of mind through loving-kindness (mettā cetovimutti) that is non-specifically directed should be understood by way of five modes.

By way of these seven modes: "May all women be free from enmity... [and so on]... may they maintain themselves; may all men, all noble ones, all ignoble ones, all deities, all human beings, and all those in the lower realms be free from enmity... [and so on]... may they maintain themselves."
The liberation of mind through loving-kindness should be understood as all-pervasive:
"May all beings in the eastern direction be free from enmity... [and so on]... may they maintain themselves in well-being.
May all beings in the western direction, all in the northern direction, all in the southern direction, all in the eastern intermediate direction..."

May all beings in the western intermediate direction, all in the northern intermediate direction, all in the southern intermediate direction, all in the downward direction, and all in the upward direction be free from enmity... may they dwell in safety.
May all living beings, creatures, persons, and individualities included within the eastern direction be free from enmity... may they dwell in safety. All [those] in the eastern direction...
May all women in the eastern direction, all men, the noble ones, the ignoble ones, gods, humans, and those in the states of woe, be free from enmity...

[and so on] ...may they dwell in safety. May all women in the western direction, the northern, the southern, the eastern intermediate direction, the western, the northern, the southern intermediate direction, the downward direction, and the upward direction... [and so on] ...[be free from enmity... may they dwell in safety.

"May those in the states of deprivation be free from enmity, free from affliction, free from distress, and may they maintain themselves in happiness"—it is by these ten modes that the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (mettā cetovimutti) as a pervasion of the directions is to be understood.

In this context, "all" (*sabba*) is a term used to denote inclusion without remainder. "Beings" (*satta*) refers to those who are attached and clinging through desire and lust for the aggregates, such as form and the rest; for this has been said by the Blessed One: [as in the *Sattasutta*].
“Rādha, it is because one is attached, thoroughly attached, to whatever desire, lust, delight, and craving there is for form—therefore one is called a ‘being.

… [It is the same] for feeling … perception … volitional formations … and for consciousness: it is because one is attached, thoroughly attached, to whatever desire, lust, delight, and craving there is for it—therefore one is called a ‘being.’”

However, by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhīsadda*), this designation applies even to those free from lust, just as the term "palmyra fan" (*tālavaṇṭa*) is applied to a particular type of fan made of split bamboo.
Grammarians, for their part, do not investigate the meaning and maintain that it is a mere name.
Those who do investigate the meaning, however, maintain that because of its association with the quality of being (*satta*), it is called a "sentient being" (*satta*).
"Breathing beings" (*pāṇa*) means those whose existence depends upon inhalation and exhalation; this is the meaning. "Beings" (*bhūta*) means those that have come into being;
the meaning is those who have arisen or been produced. "Pun" refers to hell (*niraya*). "Those who go there" are persons (*puggala*);

the meaning is that they go [to it]. "Individual existence" (*attabhāva*) refers to the body, or rather, to the pentad of aggregates (*khandha-pañcaka*), because it exists merely as a designation based upon that.
“Included within that selfhood” means *attabhāvapariyāpannā*. “Included” (*pariyāpannā*) means delimited; the sense is that they are contained within it.
And just as with the term “sentient beings” (*satta*), so too the remaining terms should be understood—having applied them by way of conventional usage—as all being synonyms for “all sentient beings.
Certainly, other terms such as “all creatures” (*sabbe jantū*) and “all living beings” (*sabbe jīvā*) are also synonyms for “all sentient beings.”
However, taking these five specifically by way of their manifest form, it is said: "Loving-kindness as liberation of mind through unspecified pervasion has five modes.
As for those beings who possess diversity not merely in name—such as "living beings" and so forth—but also in actual substance:

If they were to wish [for all beings], their non-specific pervasion would be obstructed; therefore, without grasping the meaning in that way, one should pervade with non-specific loving-kindness by means of one or another of these five modes.
And here, "May all beings be free from enmity" is one absorption; "May they be free from affliction" is another.
Absorption (*appanā*). "Free from ill will" means devoid of malice. "May they be free from distress"—this is one absorption. "Free from distress" means without suffering.
"May they maintain themselves happily"—this is another absorption.
Therefore, among these phrases as well, loving-kindness (*mettā*) should be pervaded according to whichever one is most evident. Thus, regarding the five aspects, there are four absorptions.
By way of non-specific pervasion (*anodhisopharaṇa*), there are twenty attainments (*appanā*).
However, by way of specific pervasion (*odhisopharaṇa*) through seven modes, there are twenty-eight based on four [of those]. And here, "women" and "men" are stated by way of gender (*liṅga*);
"noble ones" and "non-noble ones" are stated by way of noble ones (*ariya*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*); "deities" and "human beings" [are stated]...
"Those in the states of woe" (vinipātika) refers to them by way of rebirth.

However, in the pervading of the directions, there are two hundred beings—twenty for each of the ten directions—according to the method beginning with "all beings in the eastern direction," and so forth; and [furthermore], according to the method beginning with "all women in the eastern direction," and so forth, for each individual direction...
By taking twenty-eight for each direction, there are two hundred and eighty, which makes four hundred and eighty attainments (*appanā*).
Thus, all those mentioned in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* amount to five hundred and twenty-eight attainments.

By developing loving-kindness as the liberation of mind (*cetovimutti*) through any of these attainments, this practitioner obtains the eleven benefits described in the manner beginning with, "He sleeps in comfort."

258. Regarding "he sleeps happily": unlike other people who sleep in pain, tossing and turning and scratching themselves, he does not sleep thus, but sleeps happily; even when falling asleep, he is as if one who has attained meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).

Regarding "he wakes up happily": unlike others who wake up in pain, yawning, stretching, and tossing about, he does not wake up thus, but wakes up happily and without agitation, like a lotus flower opening.
"He does not see an evil dream" means that even when dreaming, he sees only auspicious dreams;
he is as if paying homage to a cetiya, as if making an offering, or as if listening to the Dhamma.
For whereas others see themselves surrounded by thieves, oppressed by wild beasts, or falling down a precipice, [he does not].
Thus one does not see an evil dream.
"One becomes dear to human beings" means that, like a pearl necklace fastened upon the chest or a garland worn upon the head, one becomes dear and pleasing to human beings.
"One becomes dear to non-human beings" means that just as with human beings, so too one becomes dear to non-human beings, like the Elder Visākha.
It is said that he was a householder in Pāṭaliputta. While living right there, he heard:
"The island of Tambapaṇṇi is adorned with a garland of cetiyas and illuminated by the light of the saffron robes;
it is possible to sit or lie down in whatever place one desires, for it is conducive to the climate, conducive to lodgings, conducive to individuals, and conducive to hearing the Dhamma."
"Everything is easily obtained here.

Having entrusted his mass of wealth to his wife and children, he departed from his home with only a single kahāpaṇa tied to the hem of his garment and lived for one month on the seashore, watching for a ship. Due to his skill in commerce...
Having purchased goods at this place and selling them at that place, he accumulated a thousand [pieces of money] through righteous trade within that very month.
Gradually arriving at the Mahāvihāra, he requested the going forth.
When he was led to the boundary for the purpose of ordination, he let that purse containing the thousand pieces fall to the ground through the opening of his belt.
When asked, “What is it? he replied, “A thousand kahāpaṇas, Bhante. When told, “Lay follower, since the time of your going forth it is not possible to deliberate on this;

you must deliberate on it right now,” he thought, “Let those who have come to Visākha’s place for the going-forth ceremony not depart empty-handed,” and having released [the money] by scattering it in the boundary pavilion, he went forth and received full ordination.

Thus, having reached five years of seniority, having mastered the two Matikas, and having performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony, he took up a meditation subject suitable for himself. He traveled about, spending four months in each monastery and living a life of balanced engagement.

While traveling in this manner, the Elder Visākha, standing in the midst of a forest and roaring with confidence, spoke these words while seeking out his own virtues: "The Elder stands in the heart of the forest, Visākha, thundering with power;
Seeking his own excellence, He has uttered this very meaning."
“From the time you were ordained until the time you arrived here,
there has been no stumbling whatsoever in between— oh, what a gain for you, dear sir!
As he was going toward the Cittalapabbata Monastery, he came upon a forked path and thought, “Is this the way, or is that one?”
He stood there reflecting. Then a deity dwelling on that mountain extended her hand and, saying, "This is the way," she showed it to him.
He went to the Cittalapabbata Monastery and, having stayed there for four months, lay down after thinking, "I shall depart at dawn.
At the head of the walking path, a deity dwelling in a *maṇila* tree sat upon a step of the staircase and wept.
The Elder asked, "Who is this? "I am Maṇiliyā, venerable sir. "Why are you weeping? "Because of your departure.
"What benefit do you see in my staying here? "When you stay here, venerable sir, non-human beings attain mutual friendliness; now that you have gone, they will engage in quarreling."

“They will speak even what is indecorous. The Elder said, “If you have a comfortable stay while I am living here, that is well,” and after staying there for another four months, he again formed the intention to depart as before.
The deity wept once more in the same manner. By this very means, the Elder remained right there, and right there...
"One who attains final nibbāna": thus, a bhikkhu dwelling in loving-kindness becomes dear even to non-human beings.
"Deities protect him": just as parents protect a child, so do deities protect him.
"Neither fire, nor poison, nor weapon affects him": this refers to the body of one dwelling in loving-kindness, such as that of the female lay follower Uttarā.

Just as fire does not affect, nor does it enter, the body of the Elder Cūḷasiva, the reciter of the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, or as poison does not affect the novice Saṅkicca, or as a weapon does not affect him—it is said that it does not injure his body.
In this connection, they also relate the story of the cow. It is said that once a cow stood letting a stream of milk flow for her calf; one...
Thinking, "I shall pierce her," the hunter brandished with his hand and released a long-handled spear.

It struck her body and passed through like a palm leaf, neither by the power of access concentration (*upacāra-bala*) nor by the power of absorption (*appanā-bala*), but solely due to the strength of the mother cow's powerful mind of affection for her calf.
Such is the great majesty of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
"His mind quickly becomes concentrated": for one who dwells in loving-kindness, the mind becomes concentrated very swiftly;
there is no sluggishness in him. "The complexion of his face brightens": his face becomes clear in color, like a ripe palm fruit loosened from its stalk. "He dies unconfused":
for one who dwells in loving-kindness, there is no such thing as death in delusion; he passes away just as if falling asleep, entirely undeluded.

"Penetrating further" means that being unable to attain Arahatship beyond the attainment of loving-kindness (*mettā-samāpatti*), one passes away from here and is reborn in the Brahma-world like one waking from sleep.
This is the detailed exposition on the development of loving-kindness. Now follows the exposition on the development of compassion (*karuṇā*).
259. However, one who wishes to develop compassion (*karuṇā*) should begin the development of compassion after reflecting upon the disadvantage of lack of compassion and the benefit of compassion.
Furthermore, when beginning that, one should not start with a beloved person and so forth.

For a beloved person remains in the very position of being beloved; an extremely dear friend remains in the very position of being an extremely dear friend; and a neutral person [remains in the position of being neutral].

The neutral remains in the very place of neutrality; the unloved remains in the very place of being unloved; the enemy remains in the very place of being an enemy. Those who are of a different gender or are deceased are simply not the field [for this meditation].
“And how does a bhikkhu dwell pervading one direction with a mind imbued with compassion?
Just as one might feel compassion upon seeing a person who is miserable and poorly provided for, even so he dwells pervading all beings with compassion.”
However, because it is stated in the *Vibhaṅga* that "it pervades," one should first of all see some person worthy of compassion—
having fallen into extreme distress, impoverished, poorly endowed, a wretched man with his food cut off, sitting in an almshouse with an alms-bowl placed before him,
with swarms of worms oozing from his hands and feet, and uttering cries of lamentation. Having seen such a person, [one should cultivate compassion].
“Alas, this being has fallen into distress; may he indeed be released from this suffering!”—thus should compassion be aroused.
If one does not find such a person, then even a happy person who commits evil deeds should be treated with compassion by way of a simile involving an executioner.
How so? Just as when a king issues the command, “Kill him!”, and the king’s men seize a thief together with his stolen goods...
Having bound him in groups of four, they lead him to the execution ground while dealing him hundreds of blows.
People give him hard foods, soft foods, garlands, perfumes, ointments, and betel;
and although he goes along eating and enjoying them as if he were happy and endowed with wealth, nevertheless, no one thinks, "This man is happy and possesses great wealth."
People feel compassion for such a person, thinking: "This poor fellow is now about to die; for whatever step he takes, he draws closer to death.
In the same way, a monk who practices the meditation subject of compassion should feel compassion even for a happy person, thinking: "Although this poor fellow is happy for now..."

"He enjoys his wealth well-prepared; yet, because there is not even a single good deed performed through any of the three doors, he will now experience no small amount of suffering and mental distress in the states of deprivation.
Having thus felt compassion for that person, one should thereafter proceed by this same method toward a dear person, and then toward a neutral person.
Then, one should gradually develop compassion toward the enemy.
However, if resentment arises toward that enemy in the manner previously described, it should be pacified in the same way as was taught for loving-kindness (*mettā*).
Furthermore, even if someone has been kind to you, if you see them beset by some misfortune—such as the loss of relatives, illness, or the ruin of wealth—you should [apply the practice].

Or, even in their absence, having heard of them, one should regard them with compassion in every way, thinking, "This person is indeed suffering," because they have not transcended the suffering of the round of existence (vaṭṭadukkha).
Then, by breaking down the boundaries between the four types of persons— oneself, a dear person, a neutral person, and an enemy— in the manner already described, one should cultivate, develop,
and repeatedly practice absorption (appanā) through the threefold and fourfold jhānas in the same way as was explained for loving-kindness (mettā), using that [compassion] as the basis.
In the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā*, however, the sequence is stated as follows: first, the hostile person should be the object of compassion;
having made the mind soft toward him, then the miserable person, then the dear person, and finally oneself. This sequence does not accord with the text which says, "the miserable, the ill-fated.
Therefore, one should begin the meditation here according to the method already described, break down the boundaries, and attain absorption (*appanā*).
It should be increased. Beyond that, this versatility— consisting of "the unspecified pervasion in five ways, the specified pervasion in seven ways,
and the directional pervasion in ten ways"— as well as the benefits such as "one sleeps happily," etc., should be understood in the same manner as described for loving-kindness (*mettā*).
This is the detailed exposition on the development of compassion (*karuṇā*).
Regarding the exposition on the development of sympathetic joy (*muditā*):
one who begins the development of sympathetic joy should not, at first, begin it with respect to dear persons and so forth. For...

A dear person is the proximate cause for sympathetic joy (*muditā*) by the mere fact of their being dear, let alone one who is neutral or an enemy. Those who differ in gender or are deceased are certainly not suitable objects.
However, an extremely dear companion may indeed be the proximate cause; this is the one referred to in the Commentary as a "drinking companion.
For such a person rejoices along with another in their joy; having laughed first, they speak afterwards. Therefore, that person is the first instance of sympathetic joy.

It should be pervaded. Or, having seen or heard of a beloved person who is happy, adorned, and rejoicing, one should arouse sympathetic joy (*muditā*), thinking: "This being truly rejoices; oh, how good! Oh, how excellent!
It is for this very purpose that it was said in the *Vibhaṅga*: "And how, monks, does a monk, having pervaded one direction with a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy..."
...dwells? Just as one would be gladdened upon seeing a person who is dear and pleasing, even so does he pervade all beings with gladness.
Even if that companion in revelry or that dear person was happy in the past, but is now, however, in a state of misery—
Having taken on a difficult form, one should first recollect his state of happiness in the past, thinking, "In the past, he was thus possessed of great wealth, a large retinue,
and was constantly joyful," and by grasping that very aspect of his joy, one should generate sympathetic joy (*muditā*).
Or else, one should think, "In the future, having again obtained such success, he will travel about on the backs of elephants, on horseback, in golden palanquins, and so forth."
One should also generate sympathetic joy by taking up the aspect of sympathetic joy even in the future.
Having thus generated sympathetic joy toward a dear person, one should then gradually practice sympathetic joy toward a neutral person and thereafter toward an enemy.
Absorption should be developed. However, if there is resentment toward an enemy according to the method previously described, [one should proceed as follows].
Having pacified that [thought] in the same manner as described for loving-kindness (*mettā*),
one should break down the boundaries by means of equanimity toward these four persons— namely, "these three and oneself"— and by repeatedly practicing, developing, and cultivating that sign,
one should extend the absorption (*appanā*) through the triple and quadruple jhānas in the same manner as described for loving-kindness. Beyond that, "in five ways..."
“Non-pervasive [loving-kindness] is in seven ways, pervasive is in ten ways, and directional pervasion is in ten ways”—this is the transformation.
And the benefits, such as “one sleeps happily,” etc., should be understood in the same manner as stated for loving-kindness (*mettā*).
This is the detailed exposition on the development of sympathetic joy (*muditā*).
261. Discourse on the Development of Equanimity:

Now, one who wishes to develop the development of equanimity (*upekkhā-bhāvanā*)—having already attained the third jhāna in the fourfold sequence beginning with loving-kindness (*mettā*), and having emerged from that familiar third jhāna—should do so because [the previous stages] involve attention associated with affection for beings through such phrases as "may they be happy," and because they move in the vicinity of aversion (*paṭigha*) and attachment (*anunaya*).

Having seen the disadvantage in the preceding [stages] due to their grossness through association with joy, and the advantage in equanimity due to its peaceful nature, one should generate equanimity by looking on with indifference toward that person who is naturally neutral. After that, [one should do so] toward dear persons and the rest.
For this has been said: "And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu, with a mind accompanied by equanimity, [regard] one direction..."
“...and dwells pervading [them]. Just as one would be equanimous upon seeing a person who is neither pleasing nor unpleasing, even so does he pervade all beings with equanimity.
Therefore, having generated equanimity toward a neutral person according to the method described, one should then do so toward a dear person, and thereafter toward a friend who is like a companion.

"Then towards the enemy": thus, having established a breaking down of boundaries by means of equanimity in all cases—namely, "towards these three and towards oneself"—that sign should be practiced, developed, and cultivated.
As he does so, the fourth jhāna arises in the very same manner as described for the earth kasiṇa.
But does this [supernormal power] also arise for one who has attained the third jhāna in the earth-kasiṇa and so forth? It does not arise. Why?

Because of the dissimilarity of the object. However, it arises only for one who has attained the third jhāna in the meditation on loving-kindness (*mettā*) and so forth, because of the similarity of the object.
Beyond that, both the transformation and the acquisition of benefits should be understood in the same manner as described for loving-kindness.
This is the detailed exposition on the development of equanimity.
Having understood that these are the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) spoken by the Supreme Brahmā, [one should practice them].
Furthermore, this incidental discussion regarding these [four immeasurables] should be understood.

For, as to their meaning: first, among loving-kindness (*mettā*), compassion (*karuṇā*), appreciative joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekkhā*), *mettā* means "she loves" (*mejjatīti*); the sense is that she flows with affection.

Or, it is called *mettā* because it exists toward a friend (*mitte bhavā*), or because it is the activity of a friend (*mittassa esā pavatti*). When there is suffering in others, the hearts of the virtuous tremble.
It is called *karuṇā* because it acts (*karoti*). Or, it is called *karuṇā* because it "buys" (*kiṇāti*)—that is, it harms and destroys—the suffering of others.

Or, it is called *karuṇā* because it is extended (*kiriyati*) toward those who suffer by way of pervading them. It is called *muditā* because those who possess it rejoice through it, or it itself rejoices, or it is simply the act of rejoicing.
It is called *upekkhā* because one looks on with equanimity (*upekkhati*) by abandoning mental preoccupation such as "May they be free from enmity," and by attaining a state of neutrality.

263. Regarding the characteristics and so forth here: loving-kindness (*mettā*) has the characteristic of proceeding in a manner that promotes welfare; its function is to provide welfare; it is manifested as the subduing of ill-will; and its proximate cause is the perception of beings as endearing.
Its success is the pacification of ill-will (*byāpāda*); its failure is the arising of attachment.

Compassion (*karuṇā*) has the characteristic of proceeding in a manner that removes suffering; its function is the inability to bear the suffering of others; it is manifested as non-cruelty (*avihiṃsā*).
It has as its proximate cause the perception of the state of helplessness in those overcome by suffering. Its fulfillment is the pacification of cruelty; its failure is the arising of sorrow.
Sympathetic joy (muditā) has the characteristic of rejoicing; its function is non-envy; it is manifested as the removal of discontent;
it has as its proximate cause the perception of the prosperity of beings. Its fulfillment is the pacification of discontent; its failure is the arising of derision.
Equanimity has the characteristic of occurring in a state of neutrality toward beings; its function is to see beings with impartiality; it is manifested as the subsiding of aversion and attraction;

and its proximate cause is the vision of the ownership of kamma, which occurs in this way: “Beings are owners of their kamma; by whose wish will they become happy, or be freed from suffering, or not fall away from the attainment they have reached? Thus it is rooted in the vision of the ownership of kamma.
The subsiding of aversion and attraction is its success; the arising of ignorance-based equanimity rooted in the household life is its failure.
Furthermore, for all four of these divine abodes (brahmavihāras), the common purpose is both the bliss of insight (vipassanā-sukha) and excellence in existence (bhava-sampatti).

Their specific, individual purposes are as follows: here, loving-kindness (mettā) has the purpose of counteracting ill-will (byāpāda); [compassion] has the purpose of counteracting cruelty (vihiṃsā); [sympathetic joy] has the purpose of counteracting discontent (arati); and [equanimity] has the purpose of counteracting lust (rāga).
The other [is as follows]. And this has also been said:
"For this, friends, is the escape from ill will, namely, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (mettā).

For this, friends, is the escape from cruelty, namely, the liberation of mind through compassion (karuṇā). For this, friends, is the escape from aversion, namely, the liberation of mind through sympathetic joy (muditā)."
“Mental liberation. For this, friends, is the escape from lust, namely, equanimity as mental liberation.
And here, for each one, there are two adversaries according to their proximity or distance.
For lust is the proximate adversary of the divine abiding of loving-kindness, like an enemy walking close by a man, because of its similarity in nature through the perception of good qualities.
Therefore, one quickly finds an opportunity [to harm]; for that reason, loving-kindness must be well-guarded against it.
Just as a man’s enemy who dwells in a thicket such as a mountain is a distant adversary due to being of a different nature, so too is ill will;
therefore, one should practice loving-kindness toward it fearlessly. It is impossible that one would practice loving-kindness and yet also harbor anger.

In the case of the divine abode of compassion (*karuṇā-brahmavihāra*), sorrow arises when one regards the non-attainment of forms cognizable by the eye— which are desirable, lovely, pleasing, charming, and connected with worldly bait—
or when one recollects what was previously attained but is now past, ceased, and changed. Such sorrow as this [is included].

"Household-based dejection" is what is described by such passages as "this is called household-based dejection. Because it shares the same nature as the perception of misfortune, household-based dejection is an immediate adversary.
Cruelty, however, is a distant adversary because its nature is dissimilar. Therefore, one should practice compassion while remaining fearless toward it.
It is impossible that one would both exercise compassion and yet inflict harm with the hands or other means.
Regarding the divine abiding of sympathetic joy (*muditā-brahmavihāra*): when one regards the acquisition of forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable...

[and so on] ...connected with worldly gain, or when one recollects what was previously acquired, past, ceased, and changed, there arises mental gladness; such mental gladness as this is called [sympathetic joy].

Household-based joy (*gehāsita-somanassa*)—which has been described in the manner beginning with "household-based joy"—is an immediate adversary because it shares the same nature as the perception of success.
Discontent (*arati*), however, is a distant adversary because its nature is dissimilar to that [of household-based joy].

Therefore, one should develop sympathetic joy (*muditā*) free from fear of that [discontent]. And being joyful, one will dwell in remote lodgings and in superior wholesome states (*adhikusala-dhamma*).
That he would become weary is impossible.

However, regarding the divine abiding of equanimity: "Having seen a form with the eye, equanimity arises in the fool, the deluded worldling, who has not reached the goal, who has not conquered the result [of kamma], who does not see danger, and who is an unlearned worldling."
“Such equanimity as this does not transcend form; therefore, it is called ‘worldly’ (gehasita) equanimity.

According to this method of exposition, the worldly equanimity of ignorance is an immediate adversary because it shares a common nature with [the defilements] through its failure to investigate faults and virtues.
Lust and aversion are distant adversaries due to their dissimilar nature. Therefore, one should maintain equanimity, being free from fear of them.
"It will be equanimous, and yet it will be lustful and it will strike back"—this is impossible.
