For all these [meditations], the desire to act is the beginning; the suppression of the hindrances and so forth is the middle;
and absorption (*appanā*) is the conclusion. As for the object, by way of the phenomena of designation, it may be one being or many beings. In access concentration...
Or, once absorption (appanā) has been attained, there is the expansion of the object.

Herein, this is the method of expansion: just as a skilled ploughman, having delimited the area to be ploughed, then ploughs it, so too, first delimiting a single dwelling, one [contemplates] that "the beings in this dwelling are free from enmity."
Loving-kindness (*mettā*) should be developed according to the method beginning with "May they be happy. In this regard, having made the mind supple and wieldy, one should delimit two dwellings.
Then, by gradual stages, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, one street, half a village, a village, a district, a kingdom, and one direction—in this manner, as far as one [direction].
One should develop loving-kindness toward beings here and there within the world-system, or even beyond it; likewise for compassion and the others.
This is the sequence for the expansion of the object here.
Furthermore, just as the formless attainments are the outcome of the kasiṇas, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the outcome of concentration, [so too is the case here].
The fruition attainment is the outflow of insight; the attainment of cessation is the outflow of both serenity and insight.
Likewise, here the divine abiding of equanimity is the outflow of the preceding three divine abidings.

For just as it is impossible to place rafters and roof-ribs in the air without first erecting a pillar and installing a framework of beams, so too is the third jhāna [the basis for the subsequent stages].
"Without [these], it is not possible to develop the fourth.
268. Here it might be asked: Why are these—loving-kindness, compassion, gladness, and equanimity—called "divine abodes" (*brahmavihāra*)?
Why are there exactly four? What is their sequence, and why are they called "immeasurables" (*appamaññā*) in the Abhidhamma? It is said in reply:
In this context, the status of these as "divine abodes" (*brahmavihāra*) should be understood both in the sense of their excellence and in the sense of their faultlessness.

For these abodes are excellent because they constitute the right practice toward sentient beings. And just as the *brahmās* dwell with faultless minds, so too practitioners associated with these states dwell having become equal to the *brahmās*; thus they are called "divine abodes" by virtue of their excellence and their faultlessness.
269. And as for the question beginning "Why four?", this is the answer:
They are four by way of the Path of Purification (*Visuddhimagga*) and so forth, but they are five by way of the aspects such as benefit (*hita*) and so on.
They proceed without measure and have that as their object;
therefore they are called "immeasurables" (*appamaññā*).

For among these, loving-kindness (*mettā*) is [the antidote] for one who has much ill-will (*byāpāda*), compassion (*karuṇā*) for one who has much cruelty (*vihesā*), and sympathetic joy (*muditā*) for one who has much discontent (*arati*).
Equanimity is the path of purification for one who is full of lust. Furthermore, because attention toward beings is fourfold—
consisting of bestowing welfare, removing harm, rejoicing in success, and remaining effortless— and because, just as a mother has four sons—

one infant, one sick, one in the prime of youth, and one who has gone abroad to attend to his own affairs— and she desires the growth of the infant, the removal of the sickness from the sick one, [the maintenance of health] for the one in the prime of youth...
Those who desire the long endurance of their attainment of youthfulness do not occupy themselves with any other method while intent on their own duty;

likewise, one who dwells in the immeasurables must also act toward all beings by way of loving-kindness and the rest. Therefore, from this perspective of the Path of Purification and so forth, there are only four immeasurables.
Because one who wishes to develop these four [immeasurables] must first proceed toward sentient beings by way of the manifestation of the aspect of welfare—
since loving-kindness (*mettā*) has the manifestation of the aspect of welfare as its characteristic— and because, for those very beings for whom welfare has thus been wished,

one must proceed by way of the manifestation of the aspect of removing suffering upon seeing, hearing, or inferring their being overcome by suffering— since [compassion] has the manifestation of the aspect of removing suffering as its characteristic.

And there is compassion (*karuṇā*). Then, having seen the attainment of those for whom one has thus wished for welfare and the removal of suffering for which one has wished, one acts by way of rejoicing in that attainment;

thus, sympathetic joy (*muditā*) has the characteristic of rejoicing. Beyond that, however, because there is nothing further to be done, one should proceed in a manner of neutrality known as equanimity (*ajjhupekkhakatā*); thus, equanimity has the characteristic of the occurrence of a neutral state.

And equanimity (*upekkhā*). Therefore, among these, loving-kindness (*mettā*) is mentioned first by way of its aspect of wishing for welfare and so forth; then compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity—this sequence should be understood.
Furthermore, all of these operate within an immeasurable range (*appamāṇa-gocara*), for immeasurable beings constitute their objective field.

Furthermore, one should develop loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables] toward even a single being throughout such an extent; thus, without grasping a limited measure, they proceed by way of pervading everything.
Therefore it was said:
"By way of the *Visuddhimagga* and so forth, there are four..."
But because they proceed in sequence toward immeasurable objects by way of the aspects of "benefit" and so forth,
they are therefore called "immeasurables" (appamaññā).
270. Thus, although these [four immeasurables] share a single characteristic by virtue of having an immeasurable range, the first three consist only of the triad and tetrad of jhānas.

Why? Because they are not dissociated from joy (*somanassa*). But why are they not dissociated from joy? Because they are the escape from ill-will (*byāpāda*) and other states originating from displeasure (*domanassa*).
The last one, however, consists only of the remaining single jhāna. Why? Because it is associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekkhā-vedanā*).
For the divine abiding of equanimity, which proceeds with an attitude of neutrality toward beings, does not function without the feeling of equanimity (*upekkhā-vedanā*).
271. But one might say this: "Since it was stated by the Blessed One without distinction in the *Aṭṭhaka-nipāta* regarding all four immeasurables:
'Therefore, monk, you should develop this concentration both with applied thought and sustained thought, and also without applied thought...'"
"You should develop [the first jhāna] with directed thought and evaluation; you should develop it without directed thought but with evaluation;
you should develop it with rapture; you should develop it without rapture; you should develop it accompanied by pleasure; and you should develop it accompanied by equanimity.
Therefore, the four immeasurables consist of the fourfold and fivefold jhānas. Thus, Māhausa, should you be told. For in this way...
If that were so, the contemplations of the body and so forth would also possess fourfold and fivefold jhānas;

yet even the first jhāna is absent in the contemplations of feeling and the rest, let alone the second and subsequent ones. Therefore, do not misrepresent the Blessed One by grasping merely at the literal shadow of the words;
for the Buddha’s word is profound, and it must be understood according to its intended meaning by attending upon a teacher.

272. This is the intended meaning there: "It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.
It is said that when that bhikkhu had thus requested a teaching on the Dhamma, because he had previously heard the Dhamma right there [and yet failed to attain realization],...

He remained there and did not go to perform the duties of a recluse; therefore, the Blessed One rebuked him, saying, "In this very way, some empty persons here entreat me alone, and when the Dhamma has been spoken, they think that they must follow me alone.
Then, because he was endowed with the necessary conditions for attaining Arahatship, the Blessed One spoke to him while instructing him:
“Therefore, bhikkhu, you should train yourself thus: ‘My mind will be established within, well-composed;
and arisen evil unwholesome states will not remain obsessing the mind. In this way, bhikkhu, you should train yourself.
By means of this exhortation, basic concentration consisting of mere one-pointedness of mind with respect to one's own internal [states] is stated. From that...
In order to show that one should not be satisfied with just this much, but rather that this very concentration must be further developed, it is said:

“When, monk, your mind is established within, well-composed, and arisen evil unwholesome states do not remain obsessing the mind, then you, monk, should train yourself thus: ‘May my mind-liberation through loving-kindness...’”
“It will have been developed, made much of, made a vehicle, made a basis, established, consolidated, and well undertaken.
“In this way, monk, you should train yourself. Having thus explained the meditation by way of loving-kindness (*mettā*), he further said:
“Monk, when this concentration has been developed and made much of by you in this way, then, monk, you—this...”
"It was said: 'You should develop the basic concentration accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought... [and so on] ...you should also develop it accompanied by equanimity.

Its meaning is this: when, O monk, this basic concentration has been developed by you in this way through loving-kindness, then, without being satisfied with just that much, you should develop this basic concentration upon other objects as well, [attaining] the fourfold and fivefold jhānas."
"You should develop it in the manner beginning with 'making it accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought,' and so forth.

Having said this, he further shows that one should also perform the development of the remaining divine abidings, such as compassion, preceded by those [first two], upon other objects by way of the fourfold and fivefold jhānas: "From the time, O bhikkhu, when this..."
"Samādhi, thus developed and cultivated, becomes such that the bhikkhu should train himself:
'May compassion be my liberation of mind,'" and so forth.

Having thus shown the development preceded by loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the rest by way of the fourfold and fivefold jhānas, he further [shows] that preceded by the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*) and the rest.
In order to show this, after saying, "When, monk, this concentration has been thus developed and cultivated by you, then, monk, you should train yourself thus:
'I will dwell contemplating the body as a body,'" and so forth, [it continues]:
"When, monk, this concentration has been thus developed and well-developed by you, then, monk, wherever..."
“You will go only at ease; wherever you stand, you will stand at ease;
wherever you sit, you will sit at ease; wherever you lie down, you will lie down at ease.
Thus he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship. Therefore, they possess only the threefold and fourfold jhānas.

It should be understood that loving-kindness and the others [are associated with multiple jhānas], whereas equanimity is associated with the remaining single jhāna. And it is explained exactly thus in the Abhidhamma.

273. Thus, although these [meditations] exist in two ways—namely, by way of the threefold and fourfold jhānas, and by way of the remaining single jhāna—one should understand their distinct excellence of power, which differs from one another by way of the "supreme beauty" and so forth, as in the *Haliddavasana Sutta*.
For these have been described by distinguishing them through their respective states of supreme beauty and so forth. As it is said:

"Bhikkhus, I declare that the liberation of mind through loving-kindness has supreme beauty as its limit. Bhikkhus, I declare that the liberation of mind through compassion has the base of infinite space as its limit.

Bhikkhus, I declare that the liberation of mind through gladness has the base of infinite consciousness as its limit. Bhikkhus, I declare that [the liberation of mind through equanimity] has the base of nothingness as its limit."
“Monks, I call this the liberation of the mind through equanimity.
But why are these stated in this way? Because they serve as the respective supporting conditions (*upanissaya*). For to one who dwells in loving-kindness (*mettā*), sentient beings are not repulsive.
Then, through his familiarity with the non-repulsive, his mind [becomes established] upon non-repulsive, pure colors such as blue and so forth.
When one applies it, the mind enters into that state with ease. Thus, loving-kindness (mettā) is the proximate cause for the liberation of the beautiful (subhavimokkha), but nothing beyond that;
therefore, it is said to have "the beautiful as its limit" (subhaparama).
However, for one who dwells in compassion (karuṇā), as they contemplate the sign of forms—such as the blow of a staff—and the suffering experienced by others, through that compassion...
Through the occurrence of the process of existence, the danger in form becomes thoroughly understood.

Then, because the danger in form has been thoroughly understood, when he removes any one of the earth-kasina or other such objects and directs his mind toward space as the escape from form, his mind enters into it with ease.
Thus, compassion is the decisive support for the base of infinite space, but not beyond that.
Therefore, they are said to have the base of infinite space as their limit.

However, for one dwelling in sympathetic joy (*muditā-vihārin*), because the occurrence of sympathetic joy arises as he contemplates the consciousness of beings who have experienced joy through various causes of gladness, his mind becomes habituated to grasping at consciousness. Then, having attained [the next stage] in due order...
When one transcends the base of infinite space and directs the mind toward consciousness—the sphere where the sign of space was the object—the mind enters into that state with ease;
thus, sympathetic joy (*muditā*) is the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the base of infinite consciousness, but not for what follows it.
Therefore, it is said to have the base of infinite consciousness as its limit.

But for one who dwells in equanimity, because there is no mental preoccupation such as, “May beings be happy,” or “May they be freed from suffering,” or “May they not be deprived of the happiness they have attained,” and because the mind is turned away from grasping at ultimate objects such as pleasure and pain,

his mind is free from the suffering of grasping at what does not exist in reality. Then, for him whose mind is habituated to being turned away from grasping at ultimate objects and whose mind is free from the suffering of grasping at what does not exist in reality—

And when one transcends the base of infinite consciousness attained by successive stages and directs the mind toward the non-existence of consciousness—which does not exist by way of intrinsic nature and is the ultimate reality—the mind enters that state with ease.
Thus, equanimity is the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the base of nothingness, but not for what follows it; therefore, it is said to have the base of nothingness as its limit.

274. Thus, having understood the power of these [perfections] by way of their excellence in beauty and so forth, it should further be known that all of them bring to fulfillment all wholesome qualities such as giving and the rest.

For great beings possess minds that function with equanimity toward all beings due to their inclination toward their welfare, their inability to endure the suffering of beings, their desire for the distinguished attainments reached by beings to endure for long, and their absence of partiality toward any beings.
Without making a distinction such as, "this one should be given to, this one should not be given to," they give gifts that are the cause of happiness for all beings.
Avoiding harm to them, they undertake virtue. For the sake of fulfilling virtue, they resort to renunciation.
To achieve non-delusion regarding what is beneficial and harmful for beings, they purify their wisdom. [For the sake of] beings...

They constantly exert energy for the sake of the welfare and happiness [of others]. Having attained the state of a hero through supreme energy, they forgive the various offenses committed by sentient beings.
They do not deceive those to whom they have given a promise, saying, "We shall give this to you" or "We shall do this for you.
They possess unwavering resolve for their welfare and happiness. Toward them, with unwavering loving-kindness...

They are the first to act; they do not expect a return for their equanimity. Thus, having fulfilled the perfections (*pāramitā*), they bring to completion all wholesome qualities (*kalyāṇadhamma*)—including the ten powers (*dasabala*), the four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*), the six unique knowledges (*asādhāraṇañāṇa*), and the eighteen qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadhamma*).
In this way, these very perfections are the fulfillers of all wholesome qualities, beginning with generosity (*dāna*).
Thus ends the exposition on the Divine Abidings (Brahmavihāra) in the Section on the Development of Concentration within the *Visuddhimagga*, composed for the delight of virtuous people.
The Ninth Chapter.
10. Exposition of the Formless. Commentary on the First Formless State.

275. Next, regarding the four formless attainments (āruppa) mentioned immediately after the divine abodes (brahmavihāra): one who wishes first to develop the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana) reflects thus:
"Indeed, it is on account of forms that there arise the taking up of sticks, the taking up of weapons, quarrels, strife, and disputes;
but this [base of infinite space] is entirely free from form. Having reflected thus, for the sake of disenchantment with and dispassion toward forms alone—

According to the statement, “He practices for the sake of cessation,” one sees the danger in the material form consisting of the body by way of these thousands of afflictions— such as taking up sticks, as well as diseases of the eyes, ears, and so forth— and, in order to transcend that,
one arouses the fourth jhāna in any one of the nine kasiṇas beginning with the earth-kasiṇa, excluding the limited-space kasiṇa.

Although, by means of the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere, his gross material form has been transcended, nevertheless, since even the kasiṇa-form is merely a counterpart of that [gross form], he desires to transcend that as well. How so?
Just as a man afraid of snakes who, while being pursued by a snake in the forest, flees with speed and, having reached a place where he has fled, sees a painted snake—
Whether it be a palm leaf, a creeper, or a rope, upon seeing even a crack in the cracked earth, he is indeed afraid and terrified;

he has no desire at all to look at it. And just as a man living in the same village with a hostile person who seeks his harm, being oppressed by that person through execution, imprisonment, house-burning, and so forth, [flees] to another village—

Having gone there for the sake of staying, even if he sees a man there whose appearance, voice, and conduct are identical to those of his enemy, he still fears and trembles; he has no desire at all to look upon him.
Herein is the application of the simile: it is like the time when those men were afflicted by either a snake or an enemy.
The time when the bhikkhu possesses the material form of the body by way of its object is like those [enemies] being present.
The time when the bhikkhu transcends the material form of the body by means of the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere is like their fleeing with speed or going to another village.
And it is like seeing, in the place where they fled or in the other village, drawings on walls, palm leaves, and so forth, as well as a man resembling an enemy.
Just as one who desires not to see fear and terror [flees], so too the bhikkhu perceives even the kasiṇa-form as being of that same nature and desires to transcend it.
Herein, similes such as those of the dog struck by a boar or the man terrified of a pisāca should also be understood.
Thus, having become disenchanted with the kasiṇa-form which was the object of the fourth jhāna, he desires to depart from it.
Having attained mastery in five ways and emerged from the fourth fine-material-sphere jhāna with which he is proficient, he perceives the danger in that jhāna in these ways:

"This takes as its object the material form that I have grown weary of," and "It has near joy as its adversary," and "It is gross compared to the peaceful liberation," and so forth. However, there is no grossness of factors in this case.
Just as this form consists of two factors, so too do the formless attainments.
Having seen the danger there in this way and exhausted his attachment, he attends to the base of infinite space as peaceful and boundless;
then, having spread out the kasiṇa either as far as the limits of the world-system or as much as he desires, he enters it.
Directing his attention to the space touched by that [kasiṇa], thinking, "Space, space" or "Infinite space," he removes the kasiṇa.
In removing it, he neither rolls it up like a mat nor takes it out like a cake from a bowl;
rather, he simply does not advert to it, does not attend to it, and does not review it. By not adverting to it and not attending to it, [he removes it].
Not reviewing it, but attending instead to the space touched by it as "space, space," one is said to "remove the kasiṇa.
Even while being removed, the kasiṇa neither turns back nor recedes;
rather, it is said to be "removed" solely in dependence upon the non-attention to it and the attention to "space, space"—it is merely the space resulting from the removal of the kasiṇa.
It appears. Whether it is called "the space cleared by the removal of the kasiṇa," "the space touched by the kasiṇa," or "the space secluded from the kasiṇa," all this is one and the same.
He repeatedly adverts to that sign of the space cleared by the removal of the kasiṇa, thinking, "space, space," and subjects it to reasoning and reflection.
As he thus repeatedly adverts to it and subjects it to reasoning and reflection...
The hindrances are suppressed, mindfulness becomes established, and the mind enters into concentration through access.
He repeatedly practices, develops, and cultivates that sign.

As he thus repeatedly adverts to it and brings it to mind, just as the fine-material-sphere consciousness arises regarding the earth-kasiṇa and so forth, so too does the consciousness of the base of infinite space arise in space.

He applies [the mind]. Here too, in the earlier part, three or four impulsion moments (*javana*) belong to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and are associated with equanimous feeling (*upekkhā-vedanā*) alone.
The fourth or fifth is of the formless sphere (*arūpāvacara*). The rest is exactly according to the method explained for the earth-kasiṇa.
This, however, is the distinction: when the formless-sphere consciousness has thus arisen, that bhikkhu is like one who has boarded a ship.
Just as a man, having tied one of the [objects] such as a pot-mouth with a cloth— whether blue, yellow, red, white, or some other color— and while looking at it,
might stand watching only the sky once that cloth has been carried away by the force of the wind or by some other means;
even so, having previously dwelt looking at the kasiṇa-circle with the eye of jhāna...
By means of this preliminary mental attention, “Space, space,” when that sign has been suddenly removed,
he dwells beholding only space. To this extent, through the complete surmounting of perceptions of form,
the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [thinking] “space is infinite,” he enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
"...dwells," it is said.
277. In this context, "in every way" (*sabbaso*) means in all modes, or the sense is "of all [them] without exception.

"Of perceptions of form" (*rūpasaññānaṃ*) refers both to the fine-material-sphere jhānas expressed by way of their characteristic of perception and to their respective objects. For the fine-material-sphere jhāna itself...
"Form" (*rūpa*) is spoken of in such passages as "possessing form, he sees forms"; its object is also referred to as "he sees external forms, beautiful and ugly.
Therefore, here "perception of form" (*rūpasaññā*) is a designation for the fine-material-sphere absorption (*rūpāvacara-jhāna*) described by way of its perception.
It is called "having form as its perception" (*rūpasaññaṃ*) because its perception has form as its object. Form is its [object].
This is what is meant by "they surmount. It should be understood that this is a designation for the object of consciousness consisting of the earth-kasiṇa and so forth.
"Surmounting" means through fading away and cessation. What is meant?
Through the fifteen types of perception of form—comprising the wholesome, resultant, and functional states known as jhānas—and these nine [perceptions] based on the earth-kasiṇa and so forth...
Through the fading away and cessation of perceptions of form in their entirety and without exception— perceptions which are reckoned as objects—
one enters and dwells in the base of infinite space, both by reason of that fading away and by reason of that cessation.
For it is not possible for one who has not completely transcended perceptions of form to enter and dwell in this state.

In this context, because there is no transcendence of perception for one who is not dispassionate toward the object, and when perceptions have been transcended, the object itself has necessarily been transcended;
therefore, without explicitly stating the transcendence of the object, it says: "Therein, what is the perception of form?
It is the perception of one who has attained the meditative absorption of the fine-material sphere, or one who has been reborn therein, or one who dwells in happiness in this very life."
"Or perception (saññā), the act of perceiving, the state of having perceived—these are called perceptions of form.
One has transcended, passed beyond, and completely surmounted these perceptions of form. Therefore it is said: 'by the complete surmounting of perceptions of form.
Thus, in the Vibhaṅga, the surmounting of perceptions alone is stated. However, since [this state] is to be attained by means of surmounting the object (ārammaṇa)—

These attainments do not [occur] upon a single object in the manner of the first jhāna and so forth. Therefore, it should be understood that this commentary on the meaning has been composed by way of the surmounting of the object.
"The subsiding of perceptions of resistance" means by way of the resistance between the bases, such as the eye, and the objects, such as visible forms.

"Perception arisen" refers to perception of resistance (*paṭighasaññā*). This is a designation for perception of visible forms and so forth. As it is said: "In this context, what is perception of resistance?
Perception of visible forms, perception of sounds, perception of odors, perception of tastes, and perception of tangibles—these are called perceptions of resistance.
Of those five wholesome resultant [perceptions] and the unwholesome resultant [perceptions]...
"Of the five" means that they have been brought to non-arising, non-occurrence, by the total disappearance, abandonment, and non-emergence of even the ten perceptions of resistance (*paṭighasaññā*);
this is what is meant.
Granted, these do not exist for one who has attained the first jhāna and so forth; for at that time, [they do not arise] by way of the five sense doors.

The mind proceeds. Even though this is so, the mention of these [fetters] here should be understood as being for the purpose of praising this jhāna in order to generate enthusiasm for it— just as pleasure and pain, which have been abandoned elsewhere, are mentioned in the context of the fourth jhāna, or as personality-belief and the rest are mentioned in the context of the third path.
Alternatively, although those [fetters] do not exist even for one who has attained the fine-material-sphere absorption, they do not yet exist because they have not been abandoned.
For the development of the fine-material sphere does not lead to dispassion for the fine-material realm, and their occurrence is dependent upon that realm.
This development, however, leads to dispassion for the fine-material realm; therefore, it is appropriate to say that they are abandoned here.
Not only is it permissible to speak thus, but it is also entirely appropriate to maintain this position.
For it was precisely because those [hindrances] had not been abandoned prior to that point that the Blessed One described sound as a "thorn" for one who has attained the first jhāna.

And here, it is precisely because they have been abandoned that the immovability (*āneñjatā*) and the peaceful liberation (*santavimokkhatā*) of the formless attainments are stated. Furthermore, Āḷāra Kālāma was himself absorbed in a formless attainment.
He neither saw nor heard the sound of about five hundred carts passing by one after another. 279.
"Non-attention to perceptions of diversity" (*nānatta-saññānam amanasikārā*) means either: (1) perceptions occurring with respect to a diverse object, or (2) diverse perceptions themselves.
For it is said: "In this context, what are perceptions of diversity? They are the perceptions of one who has not attained meditative absorption and possesses the mind-element (*manodhātu*)."
"Or, for one possessing the mind-consciousness element, perception, perceiving, and the state of having perceived—these are called 'perceptions of diversity.

Having thus analyzed them in the *Vibhaṅga*, those perceptions intended here are those comprised within the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element of one who has not attained meditative absorption;

they occur with respect to a diverse range of objects consisting of various forms, sounds, and so forth, which possess diverse characteristics. And because these eight are wholesome perceptions of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
There are twelve unwholesome perceptions, eleven wholesome-resultant perceptions of the sense sphere, two unwholesome-resultant perceptions, and eleven functional perceptions of the sense sphere.
Thus, these forty-four perceptions are diverse, of different natures, and unlike one another;
therefore, they are called "diverse perceptions. By not attending to and not directing the mind toward all those diverse perceptions—
It is due to non-attention and non-reviewing; that is to say, because one does not direct the mind toward them, does not attend to them, and does not review them.
Furthermore, it is because in the existence produced by this jhāna, the aforementioned perceptions of form and perceptions of resistance do not exist.
Just as at the time of entering and dwelling in this jhāna in that very existence, the non-existence of those [perceptions] is stated in two ways—
as their surmounting and their disappearance. As for the perceptions of diversity, however, because these twenty-seven perceptions— namely, the eight wholesome perceptions of the sense sphere,
the nine functional perceptions, and the ten unwholesome perceptions— exist in the existence produced by this jhāna...

Therefore, it should be understood that it is said that there is "non-attention" to them. For even here, one who enters and dwells in this jhāna does so precisely by means of non-attention to them; however, one who attends to them has not attained [the jhāna].
And in brief, by the phrase "surmounting perceptions of form," the abandoning of all phenomena pertaining to the fine-material sphere is indicated.

It has been said. By the phrase "with the subsiding of perceptions of resistance and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity," it should be understood that the abandoning and non-attention toward all sense-sphere consciousnesses and mental factors are thereby expressed. 280.
Regarding the phrase "boundless space": here, it is called "boundless" (*ananta*) because neither its limit of arising nor its limit of passing away is discerned. "Space" (*ākāsa*)...
The space cleared by removing the kasiṇa is what is meant. Furthermore, its infinity should be understood here by way of mental attention (manasikāra).
For this very reason it is said in the Vibhaṅga: "One places the mind on that space, steadies it, and pervades it as infinite; therefore it is called 'infinite space.
Regarding the phrase "having attained and dwelling in the base of infinite space" (ākāsānañcāyatana): here, "infinite" (ananta) means that which has no end (n'assa anto). Space...

Infinite space is "ākāsānantaṃ"; that very infinite space is "ākāsānañcaṃ. That "ākāsānañcaṃ" is the "base" (āyatana) in the sense of a foundation for the associated states of jhāna, just as the gods have their own divine abode; thus it is the "base of infinite space" (ākāsānañcāyatana).
"Having attained, he dwells" means that having reached and accomplished that base of infinite space, he dwells in a mode of conduct corresponding to it.
This is the detailed explanation of the meditation subject of the base of infinite space.

Regarding the base of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana): one who wishes to develop the base of infinite consciousness should, by means of five ways, [reflect] upon the attainment of the base of infinite space.
Having mastered his mastery, and having seen the danger in the base of infinite space— thinking, "This attainment is an adversary to the fine-material-sphere jhānas that are near to it,
yet it is not as peaceful as the base of infinite consciousness"— he brings his attachment to that [base] to an end. Then, attending to the base of infinite consciousness as peaceful,
he repeatedly contemplates the consciousness that has arisen pervading that space, thinking, "consciousness, consciousness."
It should be adverted to, attended to, reviewed, and struck by thought and reflection;
however, one should not attend to it as "infinite, infinite.
As he thus repeatedly directs his mind toward that sign, the hindrances are suppressed, and mindfulness [arises].
He remains [therein], and by means of access concentration, his mind becomes concentrated. He repeatedly cultivates, develops, and makes much of that sign.
As he does so, just as the base of infinite space arises in relation to space, his consciousness—pervading space—attains the consciousness-infinity-sphere mind.
The method for absorption here should be understood in the same manner as already described. At this point, he has completely transcended the base of infinite space.
"Having completely transcended [the perception of] 'infinite consciousness,' one enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness"—thus it is said.

282. In this context, "all" is exactly as previously explained. Regarding the phrase "having completely transcended the base of infinite space," according to the method stated before, both the meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and the object (*ārammaṇa*) are the base of infinite space. For the object, too, is [defined] by the same method as before.
Because it is the object of the first immaterial jhāna, and because it is a "base" (āyatana) in the sense of being a foundation—
just as the deities are the base for the gods— it is called the base of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatana*). Likewise, because it is the source from which that jhāna arises,
it is also a "base" in the sense of being the region of origin— just as Kamboja is the base for horses— and thus it is also called the base of infinite space.

The base of infinite space. Thus, because this base of infinite consciousness is to be entered upon and dwelt in only after one has transcended both this jhāna and its object by means of non-occurrence and non-attention, it should be understood that these two are taken together and expressed as: "having completely transcended the base of infinite space."
"‘Infinite consciousness’: this means that one attends to the consciousness occurring after having pervaded [space] with the thought, ‘That very space is infinite,’ as ‘infinite consciousness.
Or, it is ‘infinite’ by virtue of the act of attention; for when one attends to that consciousness which has space as its object in its entirety, one attends to it as ‘infinite. What...
However, it is said in the Vibhaṅga: “‘Infinite consciousness’: he attends to that very space as pervaded by consciousness;
he pervades it infinitely; therefore it is called ‘infinite consciousness.
In this context, the instrumental case in the word *viññāṇena* should be understood in the sense of the accusative. For thus [it is explained] by the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā.
They describe its meaning as follows: it pervades the infinite; what is meant is that one attends to that very consciousness which has filled space.

Regarding the phrase "having attained and dwelling in the base of infinite consciousness" (*viññāṇañcāyatana*): here, "infinite" (*ananta*) means that it has no end (*anta*). "Infinite" itself is "infinitude" (*ānañca*).
Instead of saying "consciousness-infinitude" (*viññāṇānañca*), it is stated as "consciousness-infinity" (*viññāṇañca*). This is the meaning here.

This is a conventional term (*rūḷhīsaddo*). That consciousness is the "base" (*āyatana*) in the sense of being its foundation for the jhāna together with its associated states, just as the gods have the "abode of the gods" (*devāyatanam*);
thus it is the "base of infinite consciousness" (*viññāṇañcāyatana*). The rest is exactly as before.
This is the detailed exposition on the meditation subject of the base of infinite consciousness.
283. Discourse on the Base of Nothingness:
One who desires to develop the base of nothingness, having already attained mastery over the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness through five modes, [should reflect]:
"This attainment has the base of infinite space as its proximate adversary, and not the base of nothingness."

"Peaceful": having seen the danger in the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*) and having exhausted attachment to it, one should attend to the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*) as peaceful.

One should then attend to the absence, emptiness, and secluded nature of that very consciousness of the base of infinite space which served as the object for the base of infinite consciousness. How? Without attending to that consciousness, [one reflects]: "It does not exist..."
Or "it is void, it is void," or "it is secluded, it is secluded"—this should be brought to mind again and again, attended to, and reviewed; it should be struck by reasoning and struck by reflection.
As he thus directs his mind toward that sign, the hindrances are suppressed and mindfulness becomes established.
By means of this preliminary practice, the mind becomes concentrated. He repeatedly pursues, develops, and cultivates that sign.

As he does so, just as the base of infinite consciousness arises when vast consciousness pervades empty space, so too the mind of the base of nothingness arises regarding the state of emptiness, seclusion, and non-existence of that very same vast consciousness which had been proceeding by pervading space.
He applied himself. Here too, the method for absorption (appanā) should be understood according to the method already explained.

However, this is the distinction: when that absorption-consciousness has arisen, that bhikkhu—just as if a man, having seen a community of bhikkhus assembled in a circular hall or similar place for some business, were to go elsewhere and [return] only at the conclusion of their business after the assembly—[attains it].
When the monks have risen and departed, he comes back, stands at the door, and looking again toward that place, he sees it as empty indeed;
he sees it as secluded indeed. It does not occur to him, "So many monks have died or have gone away to other regions";
rather, he perceives only the state of non-existence, thinking, "This is empty, this is secluded. In the same way, previously in the sky...
Having dwelt perceiving with the eye of the consciousness-sphere jhāna the consciousness that has arisen,

when that consciousness has vanished through the preliminary mental attention of "there is nothing, there is nothing," he dwells perceiving its very non-existence, which is termed its disappearance. At this point,
having completely surmounted the base of infinite consciousness, [he enters the base of nothingness] thinking, "there is nothing."
“Having attained the base of nothingness, he dwells therein,” it is said.

284. Here too, “all” is exactly as previously explained. Regarding the “base of infinite consciousness,” here also, according to the method stated before, both the meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and the object are the base of infinite consciousness. For the object, too, is infinite consciousness according to the previous method.

Because it is the object of the second immaterial jhāna, it is the "base of infinite consciousness" (*viññāṇañcāyatana*), being a "base" (*āyatana*) in the sense of a foundation, like a divine abode for the gods. Likewise,

it is also the "base of infinite consciousness" because it is the "consciousness-infinity" (*viññāṇañca*) and it is a "base" in the sense of a place of origin, since it is the cause of the arising of that very jhāna— just as "Kamboja is the base of horses," and so forth.
Since this base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) is to be entered upon and dwelt in only after having transcended both this jhāna and its object by means of non-occurrence and non-attention,
it should be understood that these two are treated together when it is said: "having transcended the base of infinite consciousness."

"It is said that one attends to it thus: 'There is nothing' means 'there is not, there is not'; 'empty' means 'empty'; 'secluded' means 'secluded. As for what is stated in the Vibhaṅga: 'There is nothing—this very consciousness he causes to cease, he causes it to disappear, he makes it vanish;
he sees "there is nothing," therefore it is called "nothing. Although this refers to [the cessation] through destruction..."
It is stated as being like "comprehension" (*sammasana*); however, its meaning should be understood exactly as follows:

for when one does not advert to that consciousness, does not attend to it, and does not review it, but attends solely to its non-existence, its emptiness, and its secluded nature, one is said to "develop" (*abhāveti*), "dispel" (*vibhāveti*), and "make it vanish" (*antaradhāpeti*)—and not otherwise.
Regarding the phrase "having attained and dwelt in the base of nothingness" (*ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati*):
here, "nothing" (*akiñcana*) means that there is nothing whatsoever belonging to him; it is said that not even a mere fragment remains.

The state of being nothing is "nothingness" (*ākiñcañña*), which is a designation for the departure from the consciousness of the base of infinite space. That nothingness, in the sense of a basis (*adhiṭṭhāna*), [is the base of nothingness].
The base of this jhāna is called the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*) because it is like the abode of the gods (*devāyatana*) for the gods. The rest is exactly as before.
This is the detailed explanation of the meditation subject of the base of nothingness.
Now follows the discussion of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*).
285. However, one who wishes to develop the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception must have mastery over the attainment of the base of nothingness in five ways.
Then, [he should reflect]: "This attainment has the base of infinite consciousness as its proximate enemy, yet it is not as peaceful as the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception," or:
"Perception is a disease, perception is a tumor, perception is a dart; this is peaceful, this is sublime."
Having thus seen the danger in the base of nothingness and the benefit in what is higher— namely, "this is the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception"—
and having exhausted attachment to the base of nothingness, one attends to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as peaceful.
Thinking again and again, "This attainment of the base of nothingness, which occurred taking non-existence as its object, is indeed peaceful," [one enters it].
It should be adverted to, brought to mind, reviewed, and subjected to reasoning and reflection.

As he thus repeatedly directs his mind toward that sign, the hindrances are suppressed, mindfulness becomes established, and the mind enters into concentration by way of access. He cultivates and develops that sign again and again.

He cultivates it. As he does so, with the departure of consciousness, the mind of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana-citta) settles upon the four aggregates comprised within the attainment of the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana-samāpatti), just as in the case of the base of nothingness itself. The method for absorption (appanā-naya) here should be understood according to the method already described.
At this point, having completely transcended the base of nothingness, [he attains] the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
“Having attained, he dwells”—thus it is said.

Here too, “all” is exactly as previously explained. Regarding the phrase “having completely transcended the base of nothingness,” here too, according to the method stated before, both the jhāna and the object are the base of nothingness; for the object is indeed [defined] by the same method as before.
It is the "base of nothingness" (ākiñcaññāyatana) because it is both nothingness and a base (āyatana) in the sense of being a foundation, since it is the object of the third formless absorption,

just as the deities' abode is a base for the gods. Likewise, it is the "base of nothingness" because it is both nothingness and a base in the sense of being the region of origin, since it is the cause of the birth of that very absorption, just as Kamboja is the base for horses and so forth.
Since this base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is to be entered upon and dwelt in only after one has transcended both this jhāna and its object by means of non-occurrence and non-attention,
it should be understood that both of these taken together are expressed by the phrase "having completely surmounted the base of nothingness."
Regarding "the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception": it is called the "base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" because of the presence of that particular perception.
To show what kind of perception arises for one who has practiced accordingly, the *Vibhaṅga* first cites the phrase "neither percipient nor non-percipient," and then explains:
"He attends to that very base of nothingness as peaceful; [he attains] the attainment with a residue of formations..."
"He develops it; therefore it is called 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Regarding that, "he attends to it as peaceful" means:
"Truly peaceful is this attainment, in that it will remain even by taking the state of non-existence as its object"—thus he attends to it as "peaceful" because its object is peaceful.
If one attends to it as peaceful, how does the transcendence occur? It occurs through the absence of desire to attain [the higher jhāna].

For although he attends to it as peaceful, he still possesses this mental application, attention, and reflection: "I shall advert to this, I shall attain it, I shall resolve upon it, I shall emerge from it, and I shall review it."
It does not exist. Why? Because the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is more peaceful and more sublime than the base of nothingness.
For example, it is as when a king, accompanied by great royal majesty and mounted on the back of a noble elephant, wanders through the streets of the city;
meanwhile, ivory workers and other craftsmen, having firmly donned a single garment and wrapped their heads with a single cloth, [work] with ivory powder and such.
Seeing them with their bodies covered in soot, performing various crafts such as ivory-carving and the like, he thinks, "Oh, how clever these masters are! They can indeed perform such crafts!
Thus he is satisfied by their skill, yet it does not occur to him, "Oh, would that I might renounce my kingdom and become such a craftsman! For what reason?
Because of the great benefit of royal glory, he proceeds having completely transcended the craftsmen.
In the same way, although he attends to that attainment as peaceful, nevertheless, there is no such mental application in him as:
"I shall advert to this attainment, I shall enter it, I shall resolve upon it, I shall emerge from it, I shall review it."
There is application and attention.

As he attends to that as peaceful, he reaches—by the method previously described—that extremely subtle perception which has attained absorption, by means of which one is called "neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient"; it is said that he develops the attainment with residual formations.
"The attainment with a residue of formations" refers to the fourth formless attainment, wherein formations have reached an ultimate state of subtlety.
Now, in order to show the meaning of that which is called "the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" by way of the perception thus attained, [it is said]:
"The base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" refers to one who has entered the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

It is said: “the states of consciousness and mental factors of one who has attained [jhāna], or of one who has been reborn [in a fine-material or immaterial realm], or of one dwelling in happiness in this very life.
Among these, it is the states of consciousness and mental factors of one who has attained [jhāna] that are intended here. As for the meaning of the words:
because of the absence of gross perception and the presence of subtle perception, this jhāna—along with its associated states—is neither with-perception nor without-perception.

It is "neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Because it is included within the base of mind and the base of mental phenomena, it is both "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" and a "base," hence it is the "base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*).
Alternatively, the perception that exists here is called "neither-perception" because it is incapable of performing the function of clear perception;
it is called "nor-non-perception" because it still exists in a subtle state as a residue of formations. Thus it is "neither-perception-nor-non-perception."

It is called the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception because it is both "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" and, in the sense of being a foundation for the remaining mental factors, an "āyatana" (base).

Here, it is not only perception that is of such a nature; rather, feeling is also neither-feeling-nor-non-feeling, consciousness is neither-consciousness-nor-non-consciousness, and contact is also neither-contact-nor-non-contact.
This same method applies to the remaining associated mental states. However, this [attainment] is designated by way of its primary factor, perception.
It should be understood that the teaching has been given. This meaning is to be clarified by means of similes such as the oil for greasing the bowl.
It is said that a novice, having smeared his bowl with oil, set it aside; then, at the time of drinking rice-gruel, the Elder said to him, "Bring me the bowl.
He replied, "There is oil in the bowl, venerable sir. Thereupon [the Elder said], "Bring the oil, novice; we shall fill the tube."

When it was said, "Venerable sir, there is no oil," he replied. In that case, because it has been cooked inside [the vessel], in the sense of being unwholesome (akappiya) along with the rice gruel, one says "there is oil";
yet, in view of its inability to fill a tube or for other such purposes, one says "there is none.

Likewise, that perception is called "neither-perception" because it is incapable of performing the function of sharp perception; it is not "non-perception" because it still exists in a subtle state as a residue of formations.

What, then, is the function of perception (*saññā*) here? It is both the perceiving of the object and the generation of disenchantment (*nibbidā*) after having become the objective field for insight (*vipassanā*).
For this [perception] is unable to perform its function of perceiving as effectively as the fire element does its function of burning in warm water.
Just like the perception in the other meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), it also generates disenchantment after having become the objective field for insight.

He was unable to do so. For among other aggregates, there is no one—save for the Venerable Sāriputta—who is capable of attaining disenchantment after having comprehended the aggregates of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana) without having previously formed a fixed conviction regarding them.

However, one who possesses natural insight and great wisdom like that of Sāriputta would indeed be able to do it. He too [reflected]: "In this way, indeed, these phenomena arise without having previously existed..."

"Having offered it, they eat the remainder"— thus, this attainment has reached such subtlety by way of the comprehension of aggregates alone, and not by way of insight into phenomena one by one (anupadadhammavipassanā).
And just as this meaning is to be illustrated by the simile of the oil for greasing a bowl, so too it is to be explained by the simile of the water on the road.
It is said that as the Elder was proceeding on the path, a novice monk walking ahead of him saw a small amount of water and said, "Venerable sir, there is water;
take off your sandals. Then, when the Elder said, "If there is water, bring me my bathing cloth;
we shall bathe," the novice replied, "There is none, Venerable sir. In this matter, it is just as in the case of the mere wetting of the sandals.
"There is water" is how it appears; "there is none" is how it appears in the sense of being used for bathing.

Likewise, because it is incapable of performing the function of clear perception, it is "neither-perception"; because it exists by way of the subtle state of the remaining formations, it is "not non-perception.
And this meaning should be clarified not only by these similes, but also by other appropriate similes. "Having attained, he dwells"—this is exactly as previously explained.
This is the detailed exposition on the meditation subject of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Miscellaneous Discussion:
The peerless Lord has spoken of the fourfold formless attainment.
Having understood this, the miscellaneous discussion regarding it should also be understood.
For these four formless attainments exist by way of transcending the object: [289] Ārammaṇātikkamato, catassopi bhavantimā; (These four indeed come about through the transcendence of the object.)
The wise do not desire the transcendence of these [lower stages] as a mere factor.

For among them, the first is so called because of the transcendence of the sign of form; the second, because of the transcendence of space; the third, because of the transcendence of the consciousness that occurs in space;
and the fourth, because of the transcendence through the disappearance of the consciousness occurring in space. Thus, they are all defined by the transcendence of their respective objects.
It should be understood that these four are the formless attainments (*ārūppasamāpatti*). However, the wise do not accept the transcendence of factors (*aṅgātikkama*) in their case.
For there is no transcendence of factors in these as there is in the fine-material-sphere attainments (*rūpāvacarasamāpatti*);
for in all of them, there are only two jhāna-factors: equanimity (*upekkhā*) and one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*).
Even so, it should be understood that in this context, each subsequent simile is more refined than the preceding one,
like the successive stories of a palace and a garment.

For example, suppose on the lowest floor of a four-storied palace there were present the five refined sense-pleasures by way of divine dancing, singing, music, fragrant scents, garlands, food, bedding, coverings, and so forth;
on the second [floor], they would be more refined than those; on the third, even more refined than those;
and on the fourth, the most refined of all. In this case, although all four of those are indeed palace floors, there is no difference between them—

The distinction lies in the nature of the palace floor. Furthermore, by virtue of the excellence of the abundance of the five strands of sensual pleasure, each successive upper level is more refined than the one below it.

This is just as, for example, there might be cloths weighing four *palas*, three *palas*, two *palas*, and one *pala* made from the yarn spun by a single woman—coarse, thick, fine, and very fine respectively.

They were equal in length and breadth. In that regard, although those four robes were equal in both length and breadth—and there was no difference between them in terms of measurement—the latter ones were more excellent than each preceding one by virtue of their pleasant touch, their fineness, and their high value; even so, in the case of the four...
In these [jhānas], there are only these two factors: equanimity and one-pointedness of mind;

nevertheless, it should be understood that due to the distinction in their cultivation, each subsequent one here becomes more and more excellent through the increasingly refined state of those factors.
Thus, these become progressively more and more refined.
One is clinging to a foul pavilion; another depends upon that one;
another stands outside without depending on anyone; and yet another depends on each of those in turn.
Thus he stands with these four men in their respective order.
All four should be understood by the discerning person through their commonality.
Herein, this is the application of the meaning: it is said that in a certain impure place there was a pavilion.
Then a certain man, having arrived and feeling disgust for that impurity, took hold of that pavilion with his hands and stood there as if clinging to it. Then another...
Having arrived, he leaned against the man who was leaning against the pavilion. Then another person came and thought:

"Both this man leaning against the pavilion and the one leaning against him are in a precarious position. It is certain that they will perish when the pavilion collapses; well then, I shall stand outside.
Thus, without relying on the one leaning against the other, he stood outside. Then yet another arrived...
Having considered that the pavilion and those depending upon it were unsafe, and thinking that one standing outside was well-situated,
he stood leaning against it. In this context, the space cleared of the kasiṇa should be seen as the pavilion,
and the object of space as the man leaning against the pavilion due to his loathing for impurity, while the practitioner [leans] against it due to his loathing for the sign of form.

The base of infinite space; and the base of infinite consciousness, which proceeds by taking as its object the base of infinite space—just as a person leaning against a tent—is like a man supported by a tent.

Having considered that both of these are insecure, and not relying on that tent-like state, one stands outside, as it were, and does not take the base of infinite space as an object, but rather takes the non-existence of that [space] as its object.
Having considered the insecurity of the pavilion and what is supported by it, and regarding that which stands outside as being well-established,

one should see the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana) as occurring with reference to the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana), which is situated in the external region characterized by the absence of consciousness, as if standing supported by that [base of nothingness].
And while it is thus occurring:
"This [consciousness] takes that as its object precisely because of the absence of any other;
just as people, for the sake of their livelihood, attend upon even a king whose faults are well known."

For this base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception takes as its object even that base of nothingness—which, though seen to have faults in the sense that "this attainment has the neighboring base of infinite consciousness as its adversary"—because there is no other object available. How so?

Like people [relying on] a king, even though he is seen to have faults, for the sake of their livelihood. For just as one might rely on a person who is unrestrained and whose conduct of body, speech, and mind is harsh...
Just as people, though they perceive a fault in a king who is the lord of all directions—
thinking, "This man is of harsh conduct"— yet continue to live under him for the sake of their livelihood because they find no other means of subsistence; so too,
this base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception takes that base of nothingness as its object, even though it perceives a fault in it, because it finds no other object.
And while acting thus:
"As one who has ascended a long ladder, holding onto its rungs,
or as one who has ascended to the peak of a mountain, having reached its summit."
Or just as one who has climbed a mountain clings to his own knee,
so too does this [jhāna] proceed by clinging to jhāna.
Thus ends the Path of Purification (Visuddhimagga) composed for the delight of virtuous people.
The Tenth Chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Formless," in the Section on the Development of Concentration.
11. The Exposition of Concentration:

The Development of the Perception of Repulsiveness in Nutriment 294. Now follows the exposition of the development of the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment, which was listed immediately after the immaterial states as "one perception."

It has arrived there; thus it is called nutriment (*āhāra*). It is fourfold: edible food (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*), contact as nutriment (*phassāhāra*), mental volition as nutriment (*manosañcetanāhāra*), and consciousness as nutriment (*viññāṇāhāra*).
Now, what does each of these nourish here? Edible food nourishes matter consisting of the eightfold nutritive essence (*ojā-aṭṭhamaka-rūpa*).

Contact as nutriment nourishes the three types of feeling. Mental volition as nutriment nourishes rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) within the three realms of existence. Consciousness as nutriment nourishes name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) at the moment of rebirth-linking.
Among these, there is the fear of craving regarding edible food; the fear of approaching regarding contact as nutriment; the fear of rebirth regarding mental volition as nutriment;
and the fear of rebirth-linking regarding consciousness as nutriment. Thus, among those things that are fearful, edible food should be illustrated by the simile of the son’s flesh;
contact as nutriment by the simile of the flayed cow; and mental volition as nutriment by the simile of the pit of glowing embers.

"Consciousness as nutriment is like a hundred spears. Among these four nutriments, it is specifically the physical nutriment (kabaḷīkāra-āhāra)—divided into what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted—that is intended by the term "nutriment" in this context.
The perception that arises by way of grasping the repulsive aspect of that nutriment is called "perception of the repulsiveness of nutriment."

One who wishes to develop that perception of repulsiveness in nutriment should learn the meditation subject and, without missing even a single word of what was learned, go into seclusion and dwell alone.
Then, regarding the physical nutriment consisting of what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, the repulsiveness should be reviewed in ten aspects.
They are as follows: by way of going, by way of seeking, and by way of consumption.
By way of inclination, by way of repository, by way of being unripened, by way of being ripened, by way of fruit, by way of outflow, and by way of smearing.

295. Therein, "by way of going" means: having gone forth in such a teaching of great majesty, one should spend the entire night reciting the Buddha’s word or practicing the ascetic’s duty (samaṇadhamma), and rising early, perform the duties regarding the shrine-yard and the Bodhi-tree yard.
Having set out drinking water and water for washing, having swept the courtyard, and having attended to his body,
he ascended his seat and brought the meditation subject to mind twenty or thirty times. Rising and taking his bowl and robe, he went to the penance groves—
places that were free from the crowding of people, blissful in their solitude, endowed with shade and water, pure, cool, and delightful in their terrain.
Having abandoned the noble delight in seclusion and disregarding it, one must go toward the village for the sake of food,
like a jackal facing a charnel ground. And while going thus,
starting from the moment of descending from the bed or the chair, [one encounters] that which is strewn with foot-dust, house-lizards, excrement, and so forth.

The floor-covering must be stepped over. Then, because it is sometimes defiled by mouse droppings, lac-residue, and the like, the entrance hall (*pamukha*) must be seen as more repulsive than the inner chamber.

Because it is smeared with the droppings of owls, pigeons, and other birds, the lower floor is more repulsive than the upper floor. Then, at times, by means of old grass and leaves blown about by the wind...
Because it is defiled by the urine, feces, spittle, and snot of sick novices, as well as by water and mud during the rainy season, the pariveṇa is more repulsive than the lower floor.
The path leading to the vihāra should be seen as even more repulsive than the pariveṇa.
Then, having gradually paid homage to the Bodhi tree and the cetiya, while standing in the thought-hall (vitakkamāḷaka), [one perceives] what resembles a heap of urine...
Having failed to take leave of the shrine, so enchanting with its clusters of peacock feathers; the Bodhi tree, resplendent with the glory of celestial palaces;

and the monastery itself—thinking, "I must go for the sake of food, turning my back on such a delightful place"—he sets out and enters upon the path to the village, where he must encounter roads of stumps and thorns, as well as uneven paths torn apart by the force of water.
Then, as if covering a boil, he put on his lower robe; as if binding a cloth for a wound, he fastened his waistband; as if concealing a mass of bones, he donned his upper robe;

and as if taking out medicine from a bowl, he took out his alms-bowl. Upon reaching the vicinity of the village gate, he saw even elephant carcasses, horse carcasses, cow carcasses, buffalo carcasses, human carcasses, snake carcasses, and dog carcasses.
They must be looked at. And not only must they be looked at; even their scent, when it strikes the nose, must be endured.
Then, standing at the village gate, the village lanes must be surveyed for the purpose of avoiding dangers such as fierce elephants, horses, and the like.
This repulsiveness, beginning with the spread and ending with various corpses, must be stepped upon, seen, and smelled for the sake of food.
"Alas, what a repulsive food!"—thus should the repulsiveness of the act of going [for alms] be reflected upon. 296.
How [is it repulsive] in terms of seeking? Even having endured such repulsiveness in going, one who has entered the village clad in the outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*)...
One must wander through the village streets from house to house like a wretched man with a bowl in hand.
During the rainy season, at every step one takes, even the soles of the feet sink into the muddy water as far as the ankle-flesh;
one must hold the bowl with one hand and lift up the robe with the other. During the hot season, by the force of the wind...
One must wander with one’s body covered by dust, grass, and dirt that have arisen [from the ground].

Upon reaching the door of this or that house, one must behold cesspools and places for refuse that are mixed with fish-washings, meat-washings, rice-washings, spittle, snot, dog-dung, pig-dung, and so forth;
that swarm with worms and are surrounded by blue flies.
They even become places that must be stepped over, for those flies rise up and settle upon the outer robe, the bowl, and even the head.

When one has entered a house, some give and some do not give. Even among those who give, some offer yesterday’s cooked rice, old snacks, or even rotten fermented rice and cakes. And some who do not give say, “Please pass on.”
Some say, "Venerable sir," while others remain silent as if they did not see him; some turn their faces away;
and some address him with harsh words such as, "Go away, you shaveling!
Thus, one should depart after wandering for alms in the village like a wretched man.
From the moment of entering the village until the moment of leaving it, this [food]— repulsive with its water, mud, and so forth—
is something that must be stepped upon, looked at, and endured for the sake of food. "Alas, how repulsive is this food!"— in this way,
the repulsiveness of the search for food should be reflected upon.

297. How is it by way of enjoyment? When one has thus sought out food and is sitting comfortably in a pleasant place outside the village, as long as one has not yet dipped one’s hand into it, one is still able to invite a venerable bhikkhu or a modest person whom one sees there.
But as soon as one has dipped the hand into it out of a desire to eat, [one must say] "Take it!"—thus it is.
One should feel ashamed while speaking. But when one lowers the hand and kneads the food, the sweat that trickles down along the five fingers moistens even dry and hard rice, making it soft.
Then, having formed a mouthful from that food which has become lustrous through mere kneading, when it is placed in the mouth, the lower teeth—
The upper teeth perform the function of a mortar, the lower teeth perform the function of a pestle, and the tongue performs the function of a hand.
Having ground it there with the teeth-pestles like a dog’s morsel in a dog’s trough, it is rolled about by the tongue;
at the tip of the tongue it is smeared with thin saliva, but from the middle onwards it is smeared with thick saliva, in places not reached by the tooth-stick.

It smears with tooth-dirt. Thus smeared and crushed, that very substance—its specific color, fragrance, and consistency having vanished in that very instant—reaches a state of supreme loathsomeness, like the vomit of a dog sitting in a dog-tub.

Even though it is of such a nature, because it has passed beyond the range of sight, it becomes something to be swallowed; in this way, one should reflect upon its repulsiveness in terms of consumption.

298. How is it by way of the receptacle (*āsaya*)? Even when it has thus come to be used and enters within, because for Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and even for a Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavatti*), there is indeed one of four receptacles—namely, bile, phlegm, pus, or blood—whereas for those of little merit there are four receptacles;
therefore, for whichever [of these] the receptacle of bile (*pittāsaya*) is predominant, for that person...
One whose seat of phlegm is predominant becomes extremely repulsive, as if smeared with thick madhuka oil;
one whose seat of pus is predominant becomes like one smeared with the juice of *nāgabalā* leaves;
one whose seat of blood is predominant becomes extremely repulsive, as if smeared with dye.
In this way, repulsiveness should be reflected upon by way of its receptacle (āsaya).

299. How by way of its storage (nidhāna)? Having entered the interior of the belly, defiled by one or another of these four receptacles, it does not go to be stored in a golden vessel, nor in vessels made of gems, silver, and so forth. But if...
If it is swallowed by one who is ten years old, it remains for ten years in a place resembling an unwashed cesspool.
If it is swallowed by one who is twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, ninety,
or a hundred years old, it remains for a hundred years in a place resembling an unwashed cesspool.
In this way, repulsiveness should be contemplated by way of its storage.

How [is it contemplated] by way of being uncooked? Furthermore, while this food has reached such a place of storage, as long as it remains uncooked, it stays right there in that aforementioned manner—in a state of supreme darkness and gloom, where winds wafting the stench of various kinds of corpses circulate.
In that exceedingly foul-smelling and loathsome place— just as, for instance, during the heat of summer, when an unseasonal rain has fallen upon a cesspool at the gate of a village of Caṇḍālas,
the grass, leaves, mats, fragments of cloth, and the corpses of snakes, dogs, and humans lie there, heated by the sun’s rays and covered with froth and bubbles—
even so it was on that day, on the day before, and on the days prior to that.
Once swallowed, it all becomes one mass, covered by a film of phlegm, and as it is heated and steamed by the fire of the body, it becomes covered with froth and bubbles;
having thus reached a state of supreme loathsomeness, it remains. In this way, repulsiveness should be contemplated from the perspective of its being uncooked.
301. How [is it contemplated] from the perspective of its being cooked? When it has been cooked by that same bodily fire, it does not become gold, silver, or other such minerals.

Just as [gold ore] attains the state of gold, silver, and so forth, the food, while releasing froth and bubbles, becomes like the yellow clay placed in a tube after being ground with a fine grinding stone;
it attains the state of excrement and fills the receptacle for digested food (pakvāśaya), and attaining the state of urine, it fills the bladder.
In this way, the repulsiveness of what has been fully digested should be reflected upon.
302. How by way of its fruit? When it ripens properly, this [body] produces various kinds of filth such as head-hair, body-hair, nails, and teeth;
when it ripens improperly, it produces hundreds of diseases such as ringworm, itch, scabies, leprosy, consumption, cough, and dysentery.
This is its fruit. In this way, repulsiveness should be contemplated by way of its fruit.

303. How is it by way of outflow? Having entered through one door while being swallowed, it flows out through many doors in such ways as eye-secretion from the eye, ear-secretion from the ear, and so forth.
Furthermore, at the time of swallowing, it is swallowed with a great retinue; but at the time of flowing out, it becomes feces, urine, and the like.
Having approached, he is carried out all alone. On the first day, while consuming it, he is thrilled, overjoyed, elated, and filled with rapture and gladness.
On the second day, as he ejects it, his nose is pinched, his face is contorted, and he is loathsome and dejected.
And on the first day, having swallowed it, he was impassioned, greedy, clinging, and infatuated.
On the second day, having become disenchanted by staying for only one night, feeling distressed, ashamed, and loathing it, he casts it out. Regarding this, the ancients said:
"Food, drink, hard food, and costly delicacies, Having entered through a single door, flow out through nine doors."
“Food, drink, hard food, and costly delicacies—
he eats these together with his retinue, yet when he departs, he hides away.
Food, drink, hard food, and costly delicacies…”
He enjoys it with delight, yet he feels disgust when discarding it:
"Food, drink, hard food, and costly delicacies—
all become putrid after staying for but a single night."
In this way, repulsiveness should be contemplated by way of its natural outflow.
304. How by way of being smeared? Even at the time of consumption, it smears the hands, lips, tongue, and palate.
Because they are smeared by it, they become repulsive; and even when washed, they must be washed again and again for the purpose of removing the odor.

They must be washed. When it has been consumed, just as when rice is being cooked, the husks, chaff, and so forth float up and smear the surface of the cauldron, its rim, and its lid, even so, being cooked and floating up by the bodily fire that pervades the entire body, it smears the teeth in the form of dental tartar. [It likewise smears] the tongue, palate, and so forth.
By way of being spittle, mucus, and so forth, it smears the eyes, ears, nose, lower orifices, and other parts with eye-secretions, ear-wax, snot, urine, feces, and the like.
Because these gateways are thus smeared, they do not become clean or pleasant even when washed day after day;
having washed one part of them, the hand must be washed again with water.
It becomes so. When one has washed it once, and then washes it two or three times with cow dung, clay, or scented powder, the state of repulsiveness disappears;
thus should repulsiveness be contemplated by way of smearing. 305.
As he contemplates repulsiveness in these ten ways, striking it with reasoning and striking it with thought, [the following occurs].
Through the aspect of repulsiveness, edible food becomes evident. He repeatedly practices, develops, and cultivates that sign. As he does so, the hindrances are suppressed.
Because the specific nature of edible food is profound, his mind becomes concentrated through access concentration, though it does not reach absorption.
Here, however, perception is made manifest by way of grasping the repulsive aspect; therefore, this meditation subject goes by the name "perception of the repulsiveness of food.
Furthermore, the mind of a bhikkhu devoted to this perception of the repulsiveness of food recoils from craving for flavors.
He recoils and turns away. Like one seeking to cross a wilderness, he consumes the flesh of his own son as food, free from pride, solely for the purpose of crossing over suffering.

Then, with little difficulty, through the means of fully understanding physical nutriment (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*), his lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) comes to full understanding.
Through the means of fully understanding those five strands of sensual pleasure, he [fully understands] the aggregate of form (*rūpa-khandha*).
