He fully understands it. Furthermore, through the contemplation of the body’s repulsiveness—beginning with its state of being unripe and so forth—his development of mindfulness directed to the body reaches fulfillment;
he has entered upon the practice that is in conformity with the perception of foulness.
By relying on this practice, even if he does not attain the state culminating in the Deathless in this very life, he is destined for a happy destination.
This is the detailed exposition on the development of the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment.
306. Now, regarding the analysis of the four elements (*catudhātuvavatthāna*), which was thus listed immediately after the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment as "one analysis":
The exposition of development has been reached. In this context, "definition" (vavatthāna) means a definitive conclusion by way of discerning individual essences;

thus, the definition of the four elements is "the definition of the four elements. Mindfulness of elements, the meditation subject of the elements, and the definition of the four elements are one in meaning.
This [subject] has come down in two ways: in brief and in detail.
In brief, it is found in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta; in detail, in the Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta, the Rāhulovāda Sutta, and the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta.
For it says: "Just as if, monks, a skilled butcher or a butcher’s apprentice, having slaughtered a cow at a crossroads..."
“Just as if he were sitting after having divided it up limb by limb, even so, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu reviews this very body, however it is placed, however disposed, as consisting of elements:
‘In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.
Thus it is briefly presented in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta by way of the one of keen wisdom who takes the meditation subject of the elements.

The meaning of this is as follows: Just as a skilled butcher, or his apprentice who is supported by him with food and wages, having slaughtered a cow and carved it up, might be sitting at the crossroads—which is to say, the central point where four great highways meeting from the four directions intersect—having divided it into portions;
even so, a bhikkhu, by means of whichever among the four postures...
Because it remains in its own mode, it is "as it stands. Precisely because it stands as it is, one contemplates the body according to its elements thus:
"In this body there is the earth element... [and so on] ...the air element," seeing it exactly as it has been placed.
What is meant by this? It is like a butcher who, even while feeding a cow and even while bringing it to the slaughterhouse, [sees it as it truly is].

In that regard, even for one who has bound it and set it aside, or who is killing it, or who is watching it being killed and dead, the perception of it as a "cow" does not disappear so long as one has not split it open and divided it into pieces.
However, for one who has divided it and is sitting [there], the perception of it as a cow disappears and the perception of "flesh" arises. It does not occur to him: "I..."
"I am selling the cow; these people are taking the cow. Then it occurs to him, "I am selling meat;

these people are also taking meat. In the same way, for this bhikkhu, even when he was formerly a foolish worldling—both as a householder and as one who has gone forth—the perception of a "being," a "person," or a "pudgala" does not disappear at all.
...until he does not yet review this very body, as it is positioned and as it is disposed, by way of its resolution into its various components, according to the elements.
But for one who reviews it by way of the elements, the perception of a living being disappears, and the mind becomes settled precisely through the mode of the elements.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, just as if a skilled butcher or a butcher’s apprentice... were sitting [with a cow], even so..."
“Monks, a monk... [as before] ... [perceives] the air element. 307.
Furthermore, in the *Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta*: “And what, friends, is the internal earth element?
Whatever is internal, belonging to oneself, hard, solid, and clung-to (*upādinna*). That is to say: head-hairs, body-hairs... [as before] ... stomach, feces.”
"Or whatever else internally, within oneself, is hard, solid, and clung-to—this, friends, is called the internal earth element. And:
"And what, friends, is the internal water element? That which is internally, within oneself, liquid, fluid, and clung-to."
"Namely: bile... [and so on] ...urine, or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is water or watery, and is clung-to (*upādinna*).
This, friends, is called the internal water element. And:
"And what, friends, is the internal fire element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is fire or fiery, and is clung-to."
That is to say: that by which one is warmed, that by which one ages, that by which one is consumed, that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is properly digested;
or whatever else internally, within oneself, is fire or fiery, and is clung-to—this, friends, is called the internal fire element.
“And what, friends, is the internal air element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is air or airy, and is clung-to.

That is to say: winds that move upward, winds that move downward, winds in the belly, winds in the bowels, winds that course through the limbs, in-breath and out-breath, or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is air or airy.
“...that which is clung-to, this, friends, is called the internal air element.

Thus it is given in detail according to the meditation subject on the elements for one whose wisdom is not overly sharp. And as it is here, so it is in the *Rāhulovāda* and the *Dhātuvibhaṅga* suttas.
Herein, this is the commentary on the words not [yet] explained: first, regarding both “internally” and “individually,” these refer to what is one’s own.
It is a designation. "One's own" (*niyaka*) means born within oneself, included within one’s own continuum; this is the meaning.
Just as in the world a discussion concerning women is called "about women" (*adhitthī*), so too, because it occurs within oneself, it is called "internal" (*ajjhatta*);
and because it occurs repeatedly in dependence upon the self, it is also called "individual" (*paccatta*). "Hard" (*kakkhala*) means rigid. "Solidified" (*kharigata*)...
Harsh. Therein, the first is a statement of its characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), the second is a statement of its mode (*ākāra*).
For the earth element has the characteristic of hardness; it possesses a harsh mode, and therefore it is called "that which has gone to roughness" (*kharigata*).
"Appropriated" (*upātta*) means firmly grasped; the meaning is that it is firmly grasped, taken up, and clung to as "I" and "mine. "That is to say" (*seyyathidaṃ*)...
It is a particle (*nipāta*). Its meaning is "and what has been made by him. Showing that, he said, "Head-hairs, body-hairs," and so forth.
Herein, it should be understood that the earth element is demonstrated in twenty ways by including the brain.
Alternatively, the phrase "or whatever else" includes the earth element within the remaining three portions.

It is called *āpo* because it reaches (*appoti*) various locations by way of its nature of trickling. It is called *āpogata* because it has gone (*gata*) among the various kinds of water, such as that produced by kamma and so forth. What is that? It is the characteristic of cohesion belonging to the water element. It is called *tejo* by way of its heating;
it is called *tejogata* because it has gone among the various kinds of fire in the manner already described. What is that? It is the characteristic of heat.
And "by which" means by which [element] belonging to the fire element that has become disturbed, this body is heated, through the state of one-day-old decay and so forth.

He is born with a body. "By which he ages" means by which this body grows old, reaching a state of deficiency in the faculties, loss of strength, and the presence of wrinkles, grey hair, and so forth.
"By which it is consumed" means by which, when provoked, this body is consumed.
And that person, crying out, "I am burning! I am burning! [seeks] anointing with well-washed sappi (clarified butter), ghee, gośīrṣa sandalwood, and so forth.
And he desires the breeze from a fan. And "by which that which is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted goes to proper digestion" means:

by which this—whether it be the rice and so forth that is eaten, the drinks and so forth that are drunk, the flour-based snacks and so forth that are chewed, or the mangoes, honey, molasses, and so forth that are tasted—properly reaches maturation;
that is to say, it undergoes differentiation into the state of nutritive essence (*rasa*) and the other [tissues].
This is the meaning. Herein, the first three [elements] are originated by heat; the last one is originated solely by kamma. It is called "air" (*vāyo*) because of its blowing (*vāyanava*).
Or, it is "air-ness" (*vāyogataṃ*) because it has gone among the airs in the manner already described. What is that? Its characteristic is distension.
"Upward-moving winds" are the winds that ascend, causing the occurrence of eructations, belching, and so forth. "Downward-moving winds" are those that expel feces, urine, and the like.
The downward-moving winds are those that descend. The abdominal winds are the winds outside the intestines. The intestinal winds are the winds inside the intestines.
The limb-pervading winds are the winds that follow the network of vessels, spreading through every limb and member throughout the entire body, and which produce the actions of flexing and extending.
Inhalation (*assāsa*) is the wind entering the nostrils from within. Exhalation (*passāsa*) is the wind exiting the nostrils to the outside. Herein:
Furthermore, the first five [elements] have fourfold origination (*catusamuṭṭhāna*). In-and-out breaths (*assāsapassāsā*) have mind-origination (*cittasamuṭṭhāna*) alone.
In all cases, by the phrase "or whatever else," the water element (*āpodhātu*) and the others are included within the remaining categories.

Thus, the earth element is analyzed in twenty aspects, the water element in twelve, the fire element in four, and the air element in six; in this way, the four elements are detailed in forty-two aspects. This, then, is the commentary on the text (*pāḷivaṇṇanā*) here.

308. Furthermore, in this method of meditation (*bhāvanānaya*), for a bhikkhu of sharp wisdom, the detailed discernment of the elements (*dhātupariggaha*)—such as "head-hairs are the earth element, body-hairs are the earth element"—appears as a conceptual proliferation (*papañca*). [He reflects: "That which has the characteristic of hardness is the earth element;
that which has the characteristic of cohesion is the water element; that which has the characteristic of maturation is the fire element; that which..."
When he brings it to mind thus, "The characteristic of distending is the air element," the meditation subject becomes clear to him.
However, for one whose wisdom is not very sharp, when bringing it to mind in this way, it remains dark and indistinct;
it becomes clear only to one who brings it to mind in detail according to the previous method.

How so? Just as when two bhikkhus are reciting a text with many repetitions (*peyyāla*), the bhikkhu of sharp wisdom—having expanded the opening of the repetition once or twice—proceeds thereafter by way of both ends alone while reciting.
Therein, the one whose wisdom is not very sharp speaks thus: "What is this recitation? It is merely the flapping of lips."
“It does not allow one to finish; when recitation is done in this way, when will the tradition ever become proficient?
He, for his part, performs the recitation only by expanding upon every single phrase as it arrives. Then the other says to him:
“What kind of recitation is this that does not allow one to reach the end? When recitation is done in this way, when will the tradition ever reach its conclusion?”
"will go. In the same way, for one of sharp wisdom, the detailed discernment of the elements by way of the head-hairs and so forth appears as a mere proliferation (*papañca*).
However, for one who attends to them in brief by way of the method beginning with "that which has the characteristic of hardness is the earth element," the meditation subject becomes clear.
For the other who attends to it in that manner, it remains dark and unmanifest.
It becomes clear to one who attends to it in detail by way of the head-hairs and so forth.

Therefore, one of sharp wisdom who wishes to develop this meditation subject should first go into seclusion, retire alone, and after reviewing his entire material body, [reflect]: "Whatever rigidity or hardness there is in this body..."
"This is the earth element. That which has the nature of cohesion or fluidity is the water element.
That which has the nature of maturation or heat is the fire element. That which has the nature of distension or motion is the air element.
Having thus discerned the elements in brief, [he contemplates them] again and again as "earth element, water element," and so forth.
It should be adverted to, brought to mind, and reviewed as consisting merely of elements, devoid of a sentient being, and devoid of a soul. As he exerts himself in this way,

before long there arises in him a concentration that is merely access (upacāra) and does not reach absorption (appanā), because its object is a phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature, and it is embraced by the wisdom that illuminates the classification of the elements.
Alternatively, there are these four components taught by the General of the Dhamma for the purpose of showing that the four great elements lack any sentient being:
"Space enclosed by bone, sinew, flesh, and skin is reckoned simply as form.
Among these, by following each respective [component]...
Having repeatedly analyzed them with the hand of knowledge, one should discern the elements in the same manner as before: "Whatever among these is stiffness or hardness, this is the earth element.
Then, one should again and again advert to, attend to, and review them merely as elements—merely as earth element and water element—as being devoid of a sentient being and devoid of a living soul.

As he exerts himself in this way, before long there arises in him a concentration that, though not yet reaching absorption (*appanā*) because its object is a state of specific individual essence (*sabhāvadhamma*), is nevertheless sustained by the wisdom that illuminates the differentiation of the elements;
it is merely access (*upacāra*). This is the method of development for the analysis of the four elements as presented in brief.
However, it should be understood in detail as follows. One who desires to develop this meditation subject (*kammatthāna*) but does not possess exceptionally sharp wisdom...
Having thoroughly mastered the elements in forty-two aspects in the presence of a teacher,
the yogi— dwelling in a lodging of the kind described, having performed all his duties, and being gone into seclusion in solitude—

should contemplate them in these four ways: by way of a concise summary together with their constituent parts, by way of an analysis together with their constituent parts, by way of a concise summary of their specific characteristics, and by way of an analysis of their specific characteristics.
The meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) should be developed.
In this regard, how does one develop it by way of the concise method with its constituent parts? Here, a bhikkhu defines the stiffened state among the twenty components as the earth element.
Among the twelve components, he defines that which is in the form of fluid and characterized by cohesion as the water element.
He defines: "This is the water element. He defines the heat that cooks the four portions as "the fire element.
He defines the mode of distension in the six portions as "the air element.
As he defines them in this way, the elements become manifest to him. By repeatedly bringing them to mind and attending to them in the manner described, access concentration arises.
310. However, for one whose meditation subject does not succeed while developing it in this way, it should be developed by means of the analysis of its constituent parts.

How so? That monk should apply all that sevenfold skill in learning and tenfold skill in attention which was described in the exposition of the meditation subject of mindfulness occupied with the body under the thirty-two aspects. First, regarding those thirty-two aspects: [he should apply them] all.
Without omitting anything, beginning with the verbal recitation of the "five-bark" section and so forth in both direct and reverse order, one should perform all the procedures explained therein.

This indeed is the only difference: there, after attending to the head-hairs and so forth by way of their color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation, the mind is to be established by way of repulsiveness; here, however, it is by way of the elements. Therefore:
Having reflected upon the hair and the other [parts] fivefold each by way of color and so forth, at the conclusion the reflection should be carried out in this manner:
"These things called 'hair' are born on the skin that envelops the skull.
In this regard, just as when kuṇṭha-grass grows on the top of an anthill, the top of the anthill does not know, 'Kuṇṭha-grass is grown upon me,' nor do the kuṇṭha-grasses [know it]."

Just as they do not know, "We are born on the top of an anthill," even so the skin that envelops the skull does not know, "Hair is born upon me," nor do the hairs know, "We are born upon the skin that envelops the skull.
These phenomena are devoid of mutual intentionality or reflection. Thus, what is called "hair" is a distinct constituent part of this body.
The earth element is insentient, indeterminate, empty, devoid of a being, and rigid.

(312) Hairs grow on the skin that envelops the body. In this regard, just as when grasses and weeds grow in the site of an empty village, the site of the empty village does not know, "Grasses and weeds have grown upon me," nor do the grasses and weeds know [that they have grown there].
Just as one born in an empty village does not know, "I am born in an empty village," so too the skin that envelops the body does not know, "Hairs have grown upon me.
Nor do the hairs know, "We have grown upon the skin that envelops the body. These phenomena are devoid of mutual intentionality or reflection.
Thus, what is called "hair" is a distinct component of this body—insentient, indeterminate, and empty.
"Insentient and rigid, it is the earth element.
313. Nails are those grown on the tips of the fingers.

In this regard, just as when children play by piercing madhuka-wood sticks with splinters, the splinters do not know, "Madhuka-wood sticks have been placed upon us," nor do the madhuka-wood sticks [know the same].
Just as they do not know, "We have been placed upon the fingers," even so the fingers do not know, "Nails have grown upon our tips.
Nor do the nails know, "We have grown upon the tips of the fingers. These phenomena are devoid of mutual intentionality or reflection.
Thus, what is called "nails" is a distinct component within this body—insentient, indeterminate, and empty.
"Insentient and rigid is the earth element.

(314) Teeth grow on the jawbones. In this regard, it is just as when pillars have been set up by carpenters in stone mortars after being bound together with some kind of cement; the mortars do not know, "Pillars are standing upon us."
Nor do the pillars know, "We stand upon mortars"; even so, the jawbones do not know, "Teeth have grown upon us.
Nor do the teeth know, "We have grown upon jawbones. These phenomena are devoid of mutual concern or reflection.
Thus, what are called "teeth" are a distinct component within this body—insentient, indeterminate, and empty.
"Insentient and rigid is the earth element.
315. The skin stands enveloping the entire body.
In this regard, just as a great lute covered with moist ox-hide does not know, "I am covered by moist ox-hide," nor does the moist ox-hide [know the same].
Just as one knows, "The great lute is covered by me," even so the body does not know, "I am covered by skin.
Nor does the skin know, "The body is covered by me. These phenomena are devoid of mutual concern or reflection.
Thus, what is called "skin" is a distinct component in this body—insentient, indeterminate, and empty.
The earth element is insentient and rigid. 316.

It remains anointing the mass of flesh and bones. In this regard, just as a wall plastered with thick clay does not know, "I am plastered with thick clay," nor does the thick clay know, "By me the wall..."

In the same way, the skeletal frame does not know, "I am plastered over with flesh consisting of nine hundred distinct pieces," nor does the flesh know, "The skeletal frame is plastered over by me. These phenomena are devoid of mutual intentionality or reflection.
Thus, that which is called "flesh" is a distinct component within this body, insentient, indeterminate, and empty.
"Insentient and rigid is the earth element.
317. Sinew exists within the body, binding the bones together.
In this regard, just as when walls and rafters are bound together by creepers, the walls and rafters do not know, "We are bound by creepers," nor do the creepers know [the same].
"Just as we do not know, 'The wooden rafters have been bound together by us,' even so the bones do not know, 'We are bound together by the sinews.
Nor do the sinews know, 'The bones are bound together by us. These phenomena are devoid of mutual intentionality and reflection.
Thus, what is called 'sinew' is a distinct component in this body, insentient, indeterminate, and empty."
"Insentient and rigid, it is the earth element. 318.
Among the bones, the heel bone stands supporting the ankle bone; the ankle bone stands supporting the shin bone;
the shin bone stands supporting the thigh bone; the thigh bone stands supporting the hip bone.
It stands. The hip bone stands supporting the backbone; the backbone stands supporting the neck-bone;
the neck-bone stands supporting the head-bone. The head-bone is supported by the neck-bone;
the neck-bone is supported by the backbone; the backbone is supported by the hip bone; and the hip bone [is supported] by the thigh bones.
The thigh bone is established upon the shin bone; the shin bone is established upon the ankle bone;
the ankle bone is established upon the heel bone.
In this regard, just as among piles of bricks, wood, cow dung, and so forth, the lower ones do not know, "We support those above us,"...
"Standing having lifted up the one above. Nor do those above know, "We are supported by those below, each in turn.
In the same way, the heel-bone does not know, "I am standing having lifted up the ankle-bone.
The ankle-bone does not know, "I am standing having lifted up the shin-bone. The shin-bone does not know...
"I am standing having raised up the thigh-bone. The thigh-bone does not know, "I am standing having raised up the hip-bone.
The hip-bone does not know, "I am standing having raised up the backbone. The backbone does not know, "I am standing having raised up the neck-bone.
The neck-bone does not know, "I am standing having raised up the head-bone. The head-bone...
"As for 'established': the skull-bone does not know, 'I am established upon the neck-bone';
the neck-bone does not know, 'I am established upon the backbone'; the backbone does not know, 'I am established upon the hip-bone';
the hip-bone does not know, 'I am established upon the thigh-bone'; the thigh-bone does not know, 'I am established upon the shin-bone'..."
"Established. The shin bone does not know, "I am established upon the ankle bone.
The ankle bone does not know, "I am established upon the heel bone. These phenomena are devoid of mutual intentionality and reflection.
Thus, what is called "bone" is a distinct component in this body, insentient, indeterminate, empty, and devoid of a self.
"Stiffness is the earth element. 319.
Bone-marrow is that which resides inside various bones.
In this regard, just as when the tips of reeds or other such things are inserted inside bamboo joints and so forth, the bamboo joints do not know, "The tips of reeds have been inserted within us."
Nor do the bamboo tips and so forth know, "We are situated within the bamboo joints and so forth.
In the same way, the bones do not know, "Pith is situated within us," nor does the pith know, "I am situated within the bones.
These phenomena are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called "bone-pith" is a distinct component in this body.
The constituent part is insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, rigid, and is called the earth element.
320. The kidney is situated surrounding the heart-flesh, bound by a stout sinew that emerges from the throat, travels a short distance with a single root, and then splits into two.
Therein, just as [a fruit] is attached to its stalk...
Just as two mango fruits do not know, "We have been fastened together by a stalk," nor does the stalk know, "I have fastened these two mango fruits together"— even so, the thick sinew does not know,
"I have fastened the kidney to it," nor does the kidney know, "I have been fastened by the thick sinew. They are devoid of mutual intention or reflection.
These are the phenomena. Thus, what is called the "lung" is a distinct component within this body; it is insentient, indeterminate, empty, devoid of a living being, rigid, and the earth element. 321.
The heart is situated inside the body, supported by the middle of the cage of the breast-bones. In that regard, it is like the frame of an old chariot.

Just as a piece of meat placed upon a dilapidated chariot frame does not know, "I am standing supported by this chariot frame," nor does the piece of meat know, "I am standing supported by this worn-out chariot frame," even so,
the chest-bone cage does not know, "The heart is situated supported by me," nor does the heart [know the same].
It knows, "I am standing supported by the cage of the breast-bones. These phenomena are devoid of mutual intentionality or reflection.
Thus, that which is called the heart is a distinct component within this body:
insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, rigid, and the earth element.
322. The liver (*yakana*) is situated within the body on the right side, between the two breasts.

In this regard, just as the two twin lumps of flesh attached to the side of a mortar do not know, "The twin lumps of flesh are attached to me," nor does the twin lump of flesh know, "I am on the side of the mortar."
It adheres; even so, the right side within the breasts does not know, "The liver is situated depending on me," nor does the liver know, "I am situated within the breasts depending on the right side.
These phenomena are devoid of mutual intentionality or reflection. Thus, that which is called the liver in this body—
The separate portion is insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, rigid, and is called the earth element.
323. Among the membranes, the concealed membrane lies surrounding the heart and the kidneys.
The unconcealed membrane lies enveloping the flesh beneath the skin throughout the entire body. In this regard, it is like [flesh] wrapped in a rag.
The flesh does not know, "I am wrapped in a membrane," nor does the membrane know,
"I have wrapped the flesh. In the same way, the kidneys, the heart, and the flesh throughout the entire body do not know,
"I am covered by the *kilomaka* (spleen)," nor does the *kilomaka* know, "By me are the kidneys, the heart, and [the flesh] throughout the entire body..."
And flesh is concealed. These phenomena are devoid of mutual concern or reflection.
Thus, what is called the *kilomaka* (spleen) is a distinct component in this body, insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, rigid, and of the earth element. 324.
The *pihaka* (liver) is situated on the left side of the heart, resting against the upper side of the abdominal membrane. Therein—

Just as a lump of cow dung standing against the upper wall of a storehouse does not know, "I am standing supported by the upper wall of the storehouse," nor does the lump of cow dung know, "I am standing supported by the upper wall of the storehouse"— even so,
the upper wall of the abdominal membrane does not know, "The spleen is supported by me."
"Situated": the spleen does not know, "I am situated leaning against the upper side of the belly-wall.

These phenomena are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called the spleen is a distinct component in this body—insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, rigid, and the earth element.
325. The lungs are situated inside the body, hanging down and covering the heart and liver above, between the two breasts.
In this regard, just as when a bird’s nest is hanging inside an old barn, the interior of the old barn does not know, "A bird’s nest is hanging from me," nor does the bird’s nest know [the same].
Just as one does not know, "I am standing hanging inside an old well," so too that interior of the body does not know, "Lungs are hanging within me.
Nor do the lungs know, "I am hanging within such an interior of the body.
These phenomena are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, the lungs...
This is called the earth element in this body: a distinct component that is insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, rigid, and solid.
(326) "Excrement" refers to what is situated within the interior of the body, from the throat-passage down to the opening of the rectum.
In this regard, it is just as when a severed head, a corpse, or a heap of bones is placed in a blood-basin and set aside; the blood-basin does not know, "In me there is a corpse."
"Situated": The receptacle for the internal organs does not know, "I am situated in the blood-basin";
likewise, the interior of the body does not know, "The entrails are situated within me. Nor do the entrails know, "I am situated within the body.
These phenomena are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called "entrails" is a distinct component within this body.
The earth element is insentient, indeterminate, empty, devoid of a living being, and rigid.
(327) The intestinal tract is situated having bound twenty-one internal coils within the belly.

In this regard, just as when a circular foot-wiping rope is sewn together, the circular foot-wiping rope does not know, "The ropes have sewn me together," nor do the ropes know, "We have sewn the circular foot-wiping rope."
"Standing": even the strings do not know, "We are standing having sewn together this circle of foot-wiping strings.
In the same way, the anus does not know, "The rectum is standing having bound me," nor does the rectum know, "I am standing having bound the anus.
These phenomena are devoid of mutual intentionality or reflection.
Thus, that which is called "intestines" is a distinct component within this body; it is insentient, indeterminate, empty, devoid of a living being, rigid, and the earth element. 328.
"Stomach contents" refers to what has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, remaining in the stomach. In this regard, it is like [food] placed in a dog's trough.
In a dog’s trough, the dog’s trough does not know, “The dog’s vomit is situated in me,” nor does the dog’s vomit know, “I am situated in the dog’s trough.

In the same way, the stomach does not know, “Undigested food (udariya) is situated in me,” nor does the undigested food know, “I am situated in the stomach. These are devoid of mutual awareness and reflection.

These are the phenomena (*dhammā*). Thus, what is called "stomach contents" (*udariya*) is a distinct component in this body, insentient, indeterminate, empty, devoid of a living being, rigid, and the earth element.

329. Feces (*karīsa*) is situated at the end of the intestines, which resemble the joints of an eight-finger-breadth-long bamboo cane, within that which is known as the receptacle for digested food (*pakkāsaya*). Therein—
Just as, when fine yellow clay is pressed and placed inside a bamboo tube, the bamboo tube does not know,
"Yellow clay is situated within me," nor does the yellow clay know, "I am situated within the bamboo tube"— even so, the receptacle for digested food does not know,
"Feces are situated within me," nor does the feces know, "I am situated in the receptacle for digested food."
These phenomena are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, that which is called dung is a distinct component within this body;
it is insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, solid, and the earth element. 330.
Brain matter is situated inside the skull. In that regard, just as when [something] is placed inside an old gourd shell...
A lump of dough does not know, "A gourd vessel is situated within me," nor does the gourd vessel know, "A lump of dough is situated within me.

In the same way, the interior of the skull does not know, "Brain matter is situated within me," nor does the brain matter know, "I am situated within the interior of the skull. They do not know one another.
These states are devoid of mental application and reflection. Thus, what is called brain matter is a distinct component in this body;
it is insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, rigid, and the earth element.
331. Among the bile, the free bile is bound up with the life-faculty and remains pervading the entire body.
*Baddhapitta* (bound bile) is located in the gallbladder. In this regard, just as when oil has permeated a cake and remains therein,
the cake does not know, "Oil has permeated me and remains here," nor does the oil know,
"I have permeated the cake and remain here"— even so, the body does not know, "Unbound bile has permeated me and remains here," nor does the unbound bile [know the same].
It does not know, "I am situated pervading the body. Just as when a *kosātakī* gourd is filled with rainwater,
the gourd does not know, "Rainwater is situated within me," nor does the rainwater know, "I am situated in the *kosātakī* gourd"— even so, the gall-bladder does not know,
"Bound bile is situated within me," nor does the bound bile [know].
It knows, "I am situated in the gall-bladder. These phenomena are devoid of mutual intentionality or reflection.
Thus, that which is called bile is a distinct constituent in this body; it is insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, liquid, adhesive in nature, and the water element.
332. Phlegm, measuring the capacity of a single bowl, is situated on the surface of the stomach.

In this regard, just as a cesspool covered by a layer of froth does not know, "A layer of froth is situated upon me," nor does the layer of froth know, "I am situated upon the cesspool," even so the surface of the stomach does not know, "Phlegm is situated upon me. Nor...
It knows phlegm: "I am situated on the surface of the stomach. These phenomena are devoid of mutual concern or reflection.
Thus, that which is called phlegm is a distinct component within this body;
it is insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, liquid in nature, cohesive in form, and belongs to the water element.
333. First, the "unfixed location" (*anibaddhokāsa*): wherever a part of the body is struck by stumps, thorns, weapons, flames of fire, and so forth, the blood coagulates and festers there;
or else boils, pustules, and the like arise, and it remains right there.
In this regard, it is just as when sap oozes from a tree due to a blow from an axe or similar cause.

The parts of a tree that have been struck by blows and so forth do not know, "The sap is present in us," nor does the sap know, "I am present in the parts of the tree that have been struck by blows and so forth.

In the same way, the parts of the body that have been struck by stumps, thorns, and the like do not know, "Pus is present in us," nor does the pus know, "I am present in those parts. [They are] mutually...

These phenomena are devoid of mental application and reflection. Thus, what is called "purulent matter" (pubba) is a distinct constituent of this body, insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, liquid, and adhesive in nature; it is the water element. 334.
Regarding blood, there is circulating blood, which remains pervading the entire body like bile, and stored blood.
It stands filling the lower part of the region of the liver, moistening the kidneys, heart, liver, and lungs to the extent of a single *pattha* measure.
Regarding that, the analysis of the circulating blood is similar to that of free bile.
As for the other [blood], it is like water poured into a worn-out pot: while it moistens clods of earth and such things at the bottom, the clods and such things do not [absorb it].
They know, "We are being moistened by water. Nor does the water know, "I am moistening clods of earth, fragments, and so forth.
In the same way, the area below the liver, or the kidneys and other organs, do not know, "Blood is situated here, moistening us.
Nor does the blood know, "I am filling the area below the liver..."
It remains moistening the kidneys and so forth. These phenomena are devoid of mutual concern or reflection.
Thus, that which is called "blood" is a distinct component in this body; it is insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, liquid, adhesive in nature, and is the water element.
335. Sweat remains filling the openings of the pores of the head-hair and body-hair during times such as when heated by fire, and it also trickles out.

In this regard, just as when bundles of lotus roots, lily-stalks, or lotus stalks are pulled up from the water, the openings of those bundles do not know, "Water is trickling out from us," nor does the water trickling out from the openings of the bundles know, "I am trickling out."

Just as one knows, "I am trickling out through the openings of the sheaths of the lotus roots and so forth," even so the pores of the body hairs and head hairs do not know, "Sweat is trickling out from us.
Nor does the sweat know, "I am trickling out through the openings of the pores of the body hairs and head hairs.
These phenomena are devoid of mutual intentionality or reflection. Thus, that which is called "sweat" is a distinct entity within this body.
The portion that is insentient, indeterminate, empty, devoid of a living being, liquid in nature, and cohesive in form is called the water element (āpodhātu).
336. Fat (medo) is a solid unctuousness that, in a stout person, pervades the entire body, while in a lean person, it remains supported by the flesh of the calves and other such parts.
In this regard, just as when a heap of meat is covered with a turmeric-stained cloth, the heap of meat does not know, "I am supported by this..."
"A turmeric cloth remains [there]. Nor does the turmeric cloth know, "I am standing supported by a mass of flesh.
In the same way, the flesh throughout the entire body, or in the shanks and so forth, does not know, "Fat is standing supported by me.

Nor does the fat know, "I am standing supported by the flesh throughout the entire body, or in the shanks and so forth. They are devoid of mutual mental application (*ābhoga*) or reflection (*paccavekkhaṇa*).
These are the phenomena (*dhammā*). Thus, what is called "fat" is a distinct component within this body;
it is insentient, indeterminate, empty, devoid of a living being, a solid essence, and in its mode of cohesion, it is the water element (*āpodhātu*).
337. As for tears: when they arise, they either remain filling the eye sockets or flow out. In that regard—
Just as when young palm-tree hollows are filled with water, the young palm-tree hollows do not know,
"Water is staying within us," nor does the water in the young palm-tree hollows know, "I am staying within the young palm-tree hollows";
even so, the eye-hollows do not know, "Tears are staying within us," nor do the tears know, "I..."
"Situated in the eye sockets. These phenomena are devoid of mutual concern or reflection.
Thus, that which is called "tears" is a distinct component within this body; it is insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, liquid, adhesive in nature, and belongs to the water element.

338. Fat (*vasā*) is the melted grease found on the palms of the hands, the backs of the hands, the soles of the feet, the backs of the feet, the nostrils, the forehead, and the tops of the shoulders at times such as when heated by a fire.

In this regard, just as when oil is poured onto boiled rice, the rice does not know, "The oil is standing covering me," nor does the oil know, "I am standing covering the rice"—even so, the parts of the body such as the palms of the hands do not [know].
The fat does not know, "I am standing covering the hand-palms and other areas.
These phenomena are devoid of mutual intentionality or reflection.
Thus, what is called "fat" is a distinct constituent within this body—insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, and liquid in nature.
The water element has the characteristic of cohesion.
When there is a cause for the production of spittle, the spittle descends from both sides of the cheeks and rests upon the surface of the tongue.
Therein, just as the bottom of a well at the edge of a river where water flows without interruption does not know [the water], so too [the water element does not know itself].
"Water remains within me. Yet the water does not know, "I am remaining at the bottom of the well.
In the same way, the surface of the tongue does not know, "Saliva has descended from both sides of the cheeks and is staying upon me.
Nor does the saliva know, "I have descended from both sides of the cheeks and am staying on the surface of the tongue. They are devoid of mutual intentionality or reflection.
These are the phenomena. Thus, what is called "saliva" is a distinct component within this body;
it is insentient, indeterminate, empty, devoid of a living being, liquid in nature, and adhesive in form—it is the water element. 340.
As for snot: when it arises, it either remains filling the nostrils or it flows out.
In this regard, just as a bag filled with putrid curd does not know, "Putrid curd is contained within me," nor does the putrid curd know,
"I am contained within the bag," even so, the nostrils do not know,
"Snot is contained within us," nor does the snot know, "I am contained within the nostrils. They are devoid of mutual intentionality or reflection.

These are the phenomena. Thus, what is called "snot" is a distinct component in this body, insentient, indeterminate, empty, devoid of a being, liquid in nature, and adhesive in form; it is the water element.
341. Synovial fluid, performing the function of lubricating the joints, resides in the one hundred and eighty joints.
In this regard, just as when a die is lubricated with oil, the die does not know,
"Oil has been applied to me," nor does the oil know, "I have been applied to the die," even so the eight hundred joints do not know,
"Synovial fluid has been applied to us," nor does the synovial fluid know, "I have been applied to the eight hundred joints."
"Having been anointed, they remain. These phenomena are devoid of mutual concern or reflection.
Thus, what is called "synovial fluid" is a distinct constituent in this body; it is insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, liquid, cohesive in nature, and belongs to the water element.

342. Urine is situated inside the bladder. In this regard, just as when a porous jar with its mouth closed is placed in a cesspool, the porous jar does not know, "The cesspool liquid is situated in me," nor does the cesspool liquid know, "I am situated in the porous jar";
even so, the bladder does not know, "Urine is situated in me. Nor...
One knows the urine, thinking, "It is situated in the bladder. These phenomena are devoid of mutual concern or reflection.
Thus, what is called urine is a distinct component within this body; it is insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, liquid, adhesive in nature, and is the water element (*āpodhātu*).
343. Having thus applied attention to the head-hairs and so forth, one should consider: "That by which this body is warmed is a distinct component within this body;
it is insentient, indeterminate, empty, devoid of a sentient being, and its mode is that of maturation—it is the fire element (tejodhātu).
That by which it ages, by which it burns, and by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted undergoes proper digestion—this [is the fire element] within this..."

"One should direct one's attention to the fire-element portions as follows: 'The fire-element is a distinct component within the body, insentient, indeterminate, empty, devoid of a living being, and characterized by the mode of ripening.
344. Then, having discerned the upward-moving winds by way of their upward movement, and the downward-moving winds by way of their downward movement,"

Having discerned [the breath] in the abdomen by way of the abdomen, in the hollows by way of the hollows, in that which follows the various limbs by way of following the various limbs, and in the inhalation and exhalation by way of inhalation and exhalation, one understands: "The winds called 'upward-moving' are a distinct constituent in this body;
they are insentient, indeterminate, empty, devoid of a sentient being, and are the air element in the mode of distending."
"Downward-moving winds," "winds residing in the belly," "winds residing in the bowels," "winds following through the limbs and members," and "in-and-out breaths"—
these are a distinct component in this body, insentient, indeterminate, empty,
devoid of a living being, and having the mode of distending; thus should attention be applied to the wind-components.
As his attention proceeds in this way, the elements become clear to him. As he adverts to them and attends to them again and again, access concentration arises in the manner already described.
However, for one who develops it in this way and yet the meditation subject does not succeed, it should be developed by means of a brief summary of their specific characteristics.
It should be developed. How? In twenty parts, the characteristic of hardness should be defined as the earth element;
right there, the characteristic of cohesion as the water element; the characteristic of maturation as the fire element; and the characteristic of distension as the air element.

In twelve parts, the characteristic of cohesion should be defined as the water element; right there, the characteristic of maturation as the fire element; the characteristic of distension as the air element; and the characteristic of hardness as the earth element.
In the four portions, the fire element should be defined as having the characteristic of ripening.
The air element, inseparable from that, has the characteristic of distending. The earth element has the characteristic of hardness. The water element has the characteristic of cohesion.
In the six portions, the air element should be defined as having the characteristic of distending; therein, the characteristic of hardness [is the earth element].

"The earth element" is so called because its characteristic is supporting. "The water element" is so called because its characteristic is cohesion. "The fire element" is so called because its characteristic is maturation.
As he defines them in this way, the elements become manifest to him. By repeatedly adverting to them and attending to them, access concentration arises in the manner already described.
346. However, for one whose meditation subject does not succeed even while developing it in this way, it should be developed by analyzing its specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇavibhatti*).

How? Having discerned the head-hairs and so forth in the manner previously described, one should define the characteristic of hardness in the head-hairs as the earth element (*pathavīdhātu*), and the characteristic of cohesion right there as the water element (*āpodhātu*). The characteristic of ripening...
"The fire element" means that which has the characteristic of heating. "The air element" means that which has the characteristic of distending.
In this way, within each and every component, four elements must be defined. As he defines them in this manner, the elements become manifest.
By repeatedly bringing them to mind and attending to them, access concentration arises in the very way already described.

Furthermore, the elements should be brought to mind by way of these aspects: by way of the meaning of the word, by way of groups, by way of particles, by way of characteristics, etc., by way of origination,
by way of diversity and unity, by way of separability and inseparability, by way of similarity and dissimilarity, by way of the distinction between internal and external,
by way of inclusion, by way of conditions, by way of non-attention, and by way of the analysis of conditions.

347. Therein, for one reflecting on the meaning of the terms: it is "earth" (*pathavī*) because it is spread out (*patthaṭa*). It is "water" (*āpo*) because it flows (*appoti*), is moistened (*āpiyati*), or causes growth (*appāyati*).

It is "fire" (*tejo*) because it heats (*tejatīti*). It is "air" (*vāyo*) because it blows (*vāyatīti*). Furthermore, in general, they are called "elements" (*dhātu*) because they maintain their own specific characteristics, because they take up suffering, and because they are the basis for suffering.
Thus they should be reflected upon according to the meaning of the terms, both in their specific and general senses.

348. Regarding the term "Kalāpa": herein, the earth element has been demonstrated by way of twenty aspects, beginning with "head-hair, body-hair," and so forth; and the water element has been demonstrated by way of twelve aspects, beginning with "bile, phlegm," and so forth. In this context, because of the following:
"Color, odor, flavor, nutritive essence, And the four elements— From the combination of these eight things Arises the conventional designation 'head-hair.'"
Through the analysis of those very [parts], there is no conventional designation such as "head-hairs.
Therefore, head-hairs too are merely a cluster of eight dhammas. The same applies to body-hairs and the rest.
However, whichever portion therein is produced by kamma, that becomes a cluster of ten dhammas, including the life-faculty and the sex faculty. This is according to their predominance.
Furthermore, it is designated as the earth element and the water element. Thus they should be brought to mind by way of groups (kalāpa).

349. By way of powder: for in this body, when measured by a medium standard, the earth element—broken down into atoms and reduced to fine dust—might amount to a doṇa measure. That [earth element] is [surpassed] by the water element, which is half that measure.
Coordinated, sustained by the fire element, and expanded by the air element, it is not scattered nor destroyed; being neither scattered nor destroyed,
it assumes various conceptual distinctions of state such as female or male characteristics,
and manifests qualities such as smallness, largeness, long, short, firm, and hard.

Furthermore, the water element here, which exists in the form of cohesion, is supported by earth, sustained by fire, and distended by air; it does not leak out nor does it flow away. Not leaking and not flowing away, it demonstrates a state of being well-nourished.
And here, the fire element, which exists in the form of heat and has the characteristic of warmth, cooks what is eaten, drunk, and so forth;
supported by earth, embraced by water, and distended by air, it matures this body and brings about its excellence of complexion.
And because this body has been matured by that [wind element], it does not exhibit a state of putrefaction.

Furthermore, the wind element—characterized by motion and distension, supported by earth, held together by water, and sustained by fire—which permeates every limb and member, distends this body. And because it is distended by that [wind element], this [body...]
The body does not fall over; it remains upright. Struck by another air element, it displays intimation in the postures of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down;

it bends and extends, and it moves the hands and feet. Thus, this machine of elements, resembling an illusory form, proceeds as a deception for foolish people in the form of "woman," "man," and so forth.
In this way, it should be brought to mind as a mere collection of particles.

350. "By way of characteristics, etc. means: having adverted to the four elements thus, "What is the characteristic of the earth element? What is its function? What is its manifestation?", one understands:
the earth element has the characteristic of hardness, the function of acting as a foundation, and the manifestation of receiving.
The water element has the characteristic of trickling, the function of cohesion, and the manifestation of binding. The fire element has the characteristic of heat...

The water element has the characteristic of cohesion; its function is to intensify; it is manifested as support. The fire element has the characteristic of maturing; its function is to provide softness; it is manifested as maintenance. The air element has the characteristic of distension; its function is to cause motion; it is manifested as exertion.
Thus they should be brought to mind by way of their characteristics and so forth. 351. As to their origination:
these forty-two parts, beginning with head-hairs, which have been shown in detail under the earth element and the others—
The components have been shown. Among them, these four components—undigested food, excrement, pus, and urine—are produced solely by temperature (*utu-samuṭṭhāna*).

These four—tears, sweat, spittle, and snot—are produced by both temperature and consciousness (*utu-citta-samuṭṭhāna*). The heat that digests what is eaten and so forth is produced solely by karma (*kamma-samuṭṭhāna*).
In-and-out breaths are produced solely by consciousness (*citta-samuṭṭhāna*). All the remaining ones are produced by all four [factors].
Thus they should be brought to mind according to their origination.
352. As to diversity and unity: there is diversity among all the elements by way of their specific characteristics and so forth;

for the characteristic, function, and manifestation of the earth element are one thing, while those of the water element and the others are another. Thus, by way of their characteristics and so forth, as well as by way of their origination from kamma and so forth...
And although these elements are diverse, they possess unity by way of their materiality, great primary nature, element-nature, dhamma-nature, impermanence, and so forth.

For all these elements are "material" (*rūpa*) because they have not transcended the characteristic of being affected (*ruppana*). They are "great primaries" (*mahābhūta*) due to reasons such as their great manifestation and so on.

Regarding the phrase "due to great manifestation and so on": these elements are called "great primaries" for these reasons: because of their great manifestation, because of their commonality with the great primaries, because of their great maintenance, because of their great transformation, and because of their greatness and their being primary (*bhūta*).

Regarding the phrase "due to their great manifestation": for these [elements] manifest as great both in the unclung-to continuum (*anupādinnasantāna*) and in the clung-to continuum (*upādinnasantāna*). Among those in the unclung-to continuum, it is said:
"Two hundred thousand and forty nahutas— So much, by its thickness, Is reckoned this earth. (*Vasundharā*)
The greatness of their manifestation has already been explained in the description of the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*) by way of the aforementioned method.

Even within the continuum of what is clung-to (*upādinnasantāna*), they manifest as truly great through the bodies of fish, turtles, devas, *dānavas*, and so forth. For this has been said: "There are, monks, in the great ocean selfhoods (*attabhāva*) even a hundred leagues in size," and so on.

Regarding "due to the commonality with the great primary elements" (*mahābhūtasāmaññato*): for these [manifestations] are like a magician who, using nothing but water, displays it as a gem, or using nothing but a clod of earth that is not gold, displays it as gold.
And just as one who is neither a male spirit (*yakkha*) nor a female spirit (*yakkhinī*), while remaining so, displays the state of being a male spirit or a female spirit;
even so, while not being blue themselves, they display the derivative form (*upādārūpa*) that is blue, and while not being yellow, red, or white, they display the derivative form that is white— thus,
the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are so called because of their commonality with the great elements of a magician.
And just as when spirits and other such beings seize the great elements, no location for them is found either inside or outside those elements, yet they do not fail to exist in dependence upon them;

even so, these [great elements] are not found existing either inside or outside one another, yet they do not fail to exist in mutual dependence. Thus, because this is a matter beyond the reach of thought—*acinteyyatthānata*—[it is not to be conceptualized].
The great elements are so called because they share the same nature as the great elements of yakkhas and other beings.
Just as the great elements reckoned as a female yakkha deceive sentient beings by concealing her own terrifying nature with pleasing color, shape, and movement,

even so these [great elements] likewise [conceal their true nature] within the bodies of women, men, and so forth, by means of a pleasing skin-color and a pleasing configuration of their own limbs and members.
By means of pleasing gestures— such as the movement of hands, feet, fingers, and face— they conceal their own essential characteristic,
which consists of hardness and so forth, and thus deceive foolish people; because they do not allow one to see their true nature,
they are called "great elements" (*mahābhūta*) due to their deceptive character, sharing the common quality of being like female *yakkhas*.

"Because they are maintained by great requisites": because they must be maintained with great conditions. For these elements (bhūta) are called "great elements" (*mahābhūtāni*) because they proceed day after day with great sustenance such as food, clothing, and so forth, since they must be brought forward daily; or alternatively, they are "great elements" because they are elements that require great maintenance. "Because they undergo great change":

for these are subject to great changes whether they are non-clung-to (*anupādinnāni*) or clung-to (*upādinnāni*). Among these, the magnitude of change in the non-clung-to becomes manifest at the end of an eon (*kappa-vaṭṭhāne*); in the case of the clung-to, it is manifest at times when the elements are disturbed. Thus it is said:
Rising from the earth, it spreads as far as the Brahma-world;
when the world is consumed by fire, the flame of the radiant one leaps up.
A single world-system of a hundred thousand koṭis dissolves away.
When the world is destroyed by water through the wrath of the [deity],
a hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems are scattered;
when the world is destroyed by the agitation of the wind element.
The body becomes rigid, as if bitten by a woodpecker, due to the provocation of the earth element; it becomes like that very woodpecker.
The body becomes putrid, as if bitten by a rotten-mouthed creature.
Through the provocation of the water element, he becomes like one with a putrid mouth;
his body becomes scorched, as if bitten by the mouth of fire.
Through the provocation of the fire element, he becomes like one with a fiery mouth.
The body is cut, or it is pierced by the edge of a weapon;
through the provocation of the air element, it becomes as if by the edge of a weapon.
Thus, because they undergo great transformations, the primary elements are called "great elements" (mahābhūta).

Because they are great and because they are existent—these are "great" (*mahanta*) because they must be grasped with great effort, and "existent" (*bhūta*) because they are present; thus, by virtue of being great and existent, they are the "great elements" (*mahābhūtāni*).
In this way, all these elements are "great elements" due to reasons such as their great manifestation.

Furthermore, because they maintain their own specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇa*), and because they are the taking up of suffering and the basis for suffering, all of them possess the characteristic of an element (*dhātulakkhaṇa*).
They are *dhātus* because they have not passed away. They are *dhammas* because they bear their own characteristics and because they endure according to their own moments.
They are impermanent in the sense of destruction; they are suffering in the sense of terror; they are non-self in the sense of being coreless.
Thus, all of them are one in terms of form, the great elements, *dhātus*, *dhammas*, impermanence, and so forth; in this way, they should be brought to mind through their diversity and unity.

353. Regarding "separable and inseparable": these [characteristics] arise together; even in each individual group, such as the pure octad and so forth, they are inseparable in terms of location (*padesa*).
However, they are separable by way of their defining marks (*lakkhaṇa*). Thus, they should be brought to mind as being both separable and inseparable.
354. Regarding "homogeneous and heterogeneous": although these are inseparable in this manner, among them, the first two are homogeneous because of their heaviness.
Likewise, the latter [elements] are so because of their lightness. However, the former are dissimilar to the latter, and the latter are dissimilar to the former;
thus they should be brought to mind by way of similarity and dissimilarity.
355. By way of the distinction between internal and external: the internal elements are the basis for consciousness, the intimation, and the faculties.

They have supports, they have postures, and they originate from four ways. External [elements] are of the opposite kinds to those described; thus they should be brought to mind according to the distinction between internal and external. 356. As to inclusion:
the earth element originating from kamma is included in the same category as the other elements originating from kamma, because there is no difference in their mode of origination.
Likewise, those originating from consciousness and so forth are included in those originating from consciousness and so forth; thus...
They should be brought to mind by way of inclusion.

357. By way of condition: the earth element, being included within the water element, maintained by the fire element, and supported by the air element, serves as a condition by acting as the foundation for the other three great elements. The water element, being established upon the earth element and maintained by the fire element...
The air element, being supported by earth, held together by water, and expanded by air, acts as the condition for the cohesion of the other three great elements.
The fire element, supported by earth, held together by water, and expanded by air, acts as the condition for the maturation of the other three great elements.
The air element, supported by earth, held together by water, and matured by fire, acts as the condition for the expansion of the other three great elements.
"Having become [the earth element], it is a condition"—thus it should be brought to mind by way of its conditionality.

358. By way of non-attention: herein, the earth element does not know "I am the earth element," nor does it know "I am a condition by acting as the foundation for the other three great elements. Nor do the other three know "The earth element is our..."

They do not know that "having become a foundation, it becomes a condition. This same method applies everywhere; thus they should be brought to mind by way of non-attention. 359. By way of the analysis of conditions:
for the elements (dhātu), there are four conditions—kamma, consciousness (citta), nutriment (āhāra), and temperature (utu).
Among these, for those things originated by kamma, kamma alone is the condition, not consciousness and the others. For those originated by consciousness and the rest as well...
Only consciousness and the other [nutriments] serve as conditions, not the others. For those things originated by kamma, kamma is the productive condition (*janaka-paccaya*);
for the rest, it is a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) in a figurative sense. For those things originated by consciousness, consciousness is the productive condition;

for the rest, it is the postnascent condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*), the presence condition (*atthi-paccaya*), and the non-disappearance condition (*avigata-paccaya*). For those things originated by nutriment...
Nutriment is a productive condition for itself; for the others, it is a presence condition and a non-disappearance condition.
For temperature-originated phenomena, temperature is a productive condition; for the others, it is a presence condition and a non-disappearance condition.
A great primary element originated by kamma is a condition for other great primary elements originated by kamma, as well as for those originated by consciousness and so forth.

Likewise, there are those produced by mind, those produced by nutriment, and those produced by temperature. A great primary element produced by temperature is a condition for other great primary elements produced by temperature, as well as for those produced by karma and so forth.
In that regard, the earth element produced by karma is a condition for the others produced by karma by way of co-nascence, mutuality, support, presence, and non-disappearance.
And it is a condition by way of being a foundation, not by way of generating.
For the other three great elements within the continuity, it is a condition by way of support, presence, and non-disappearance, but not by way of being a foundation nor by way of generating.
Furthermore, among these, the water element is a condition for the other three by way of co-nascence and so forth, as well as by way of binding, but not...

By way of producing. For the other three continua, it is only by way of the conditions of support (nissaya), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata), not by way of binding (ābandhana) nor by way of producing (janaka).
Herein, the fire element is a condition for the other three elements both by way of co-nascence (sahajāta) and so forth, and by way of maturing (paripācana), but not by way of producing.
For the other three continua, it is only by way of the conditions of support, presence, and non-disappearance.

It is not by way of maturation, nor by way of generation. Herein, the air element is a condition for the other three elements by way of co-nascence and so forth, and also by way of distension, but not by way of generation.

For the other three continua, it is only by way of the conditions of support, presence, and non-disappearance, and not by way of distension, nor by way of generation. The same method applies to the earth element and others that are originated by mind, nutriment, and temperature.
And while these elements proceed by way of such conditions as co-nascence and the rest:
Dependent on one, three [proceed]; dependent on three, one proceeds in four ways;
dependent on two elements, two proceed in six ways.
For among earth and the other elements, each one depends on the other three; thus, depending on one, the three occur in four ways.
Likewise, among the earth element and the others, each one depends on the other three; thus, depending on three, the one occurs in four ways.
Furthermore, the latter two depend on the former two, and the former two depend on the latter two.
Dependent on the first two, the second and fourth arise; dependent on the second and fourth, the first and third arise;
dependent on the first and fourth, the second and third arise; and dependent on the second and third, the first and fourth arise.
Thus, dependent on two elements, two sets of six proceed.
Among these, the earth element is the condition for compression at the time of advancing, retreating, and so forth;
that same element, when accompanied by the water element, is the condition for establishing [the body]. The water element, when accompanied by the earth element, is the condition for lowering.
The fire element, when accompanied by the air element, is the condition for lifting up. The air element, when accompanied by the fire element, is the condition for drawing back and thrusting forward.
"It is a condition" means they should be brought to mind by way of this analysis of conditions.
For even when one brings them to mind by way of the meaning of the words and so forth, the elements become clear through each individual approach.
As one adverts to and brings them to mind again and again, access concentration arises in the very manner already described. This, moreover—
Because it arises through the power of the knowledge that defines the four elements, it receives the designation "definition of the four elements" (*catudhātuvavatthāna*).
Furthermore, a bhikkhu devoted to this definition of the four elements plunges into emptiness and eradicates the perception of a being.
Because the perception of a being has been uprooted, he does not give rise to conceptualizations such as wild beasts, spirits, or ogres.
He becomes a conqueror of fear and terror, a conqueror of discontent and delight; he does not undergo agitation or depression regarding the pleasant and the unpleasant.
Furthermore, he possesses great wisdom, culminating in the Deathless or having a happy destination as his final goal.
Such is the play of this supreme yogi of great power.
"The wise man should constantly practice the analysis of the four elements.
This is the exposition of the development of the analysis of the four elements.
At this point, in order to show the detailed explanation of concentration and the method of its development, [it was asked]: "What is concentration? In what sense..."
By way of the method beginning with the words "concentration," the inquiry has been conducted;
therein, the commentary on the meaning of the phrase "how it is to be developed" is completed in all its aspects.
For here, only two kinds are intended: access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*) and absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*). Among these, in the ten [meditation subjects]...
In the case of certain meditation subjects and in the states of consciousness preceding absorption (appanā), one-pointedness is access concentration (upacāra-samādhi).

In the remaining meditation subjects, the one-pointedness of mind is absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi). Both these types of concentration become developed through the cultivation of those respective meditation subjects.
Therefore, it is said: "The commentary on the meaning of the phrase 'How should it be developed? in all its aspects is completed."
The Discourse on the Benefits of Concentration (Samādhi-ānisamsa-kathā) 362.

As for what was asked—"What is the benefit of the development of concentration?"—in this regard, there are five kinds of benefits from the development of concentration, beginning with a pleasant abiding in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*).
For instance, those Arahants whose taints are destroyed, having entered [into jhāna], possess one-pointed minds.

They develop concentration with the thought, "We shall dwell happily during the day," and for them, the development of absorption concentration has the benefit of dwelling in happiness in this very life.

Therefore the Blessed One said: "But these, Cunda, are not called 'effacement' in the Noble One's discipline; in the Noble One's discipline, these are called 'dwelling in happiness in this very life.'"

For those in training and worldlings who, having emerged from attainment, cultivate [concentration] with the thought, "I shall practice insight with a concentrated mind," both the cultivation of absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*)—because it serves as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for insight—and the cultivation of access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*)—by way of finding space within a confinement—possess the benefit of insight.
Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, develop concentration. Bhikkhus, one who is concentrated..."
“A bhikkhu understands it as it really is.
But as for those who, having produced the eight attainments, enter the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā), and then, emerging from the attainment,
produce the direct knowledges according to the method described— such as being one and becoming many— they [do so] while aspiring for them.
When there is a basis, because it is the proximate cause for direct knowledge, the development of absorption concentration has direct knowledge as its benefit.

Therefore the Blessed One said: “Whatever state realizable by direct knowledge his mind inclines toward for the sake of realizing through direct knowledge, he attains the capacity to be a witness therein, in each and every case where there is a basis.”

When ordinary persons (*puthujjana*), whether aspiring for rebirth in the Brahma-world by thinking, "May we be reborn in the Brahma-world with our jhāna unimpaired," or not so aspiring, do not fall away from concentration, their development of absorption concentration (*appanāsamādhi*) has the benefit of bringing about a distinction in existence.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "Having developed the first jhāna to a limited degree, where..."
“They are reborn; they are reborn into the company of the gods who are Retainers of Brahmā,” and so forth.
Furthermore, the cultivation of access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*) also brings about a specific excellence within the happy destinies of the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*).
As for those noble ones (*ariya*) who, having produced the eight attainments (*samāpatti*), enter the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) for seven...
Thinking, "Having become mindless for days, we shall dwell in happiness, having attained cessation, Nibbāna, even in this very life," they develop concentration;
for them, the development of absorption concentration has cessation as its benefit. Therefore he said:
"Wisdom that masters the sixteen modes of conduct of knowledge and the nine modes of conduct of concentration is the knowledge of the attainment of cessation."
Thus, these are the five kinds of benefits from the development of concentration, beginning with dwelling in happiness in this very life:
“Therefore, regarding the practice of developing concentration, Which has manifold benefits and cleanses the stains of the defilements,
The wise person should not be negligent.”

And at this point, within the Path of Purification (Visuddhimagga) taught by way of virtue, concentration, and wisdom under the verse beginning, “A wise man, established in virtue,” concentration has also been fully elucidated.
Thus ends the Exposition of Concentration in the Path of Purification composed for the delight of the virtuous.
